SECTION 00.7

Self-assessment and team diagnostics

PERSONAL AWARENESS CHANNELS4
KIM DRILL OBJECTS10
ENGAGEMENT RINGS2
MALA'AB BLUE-ON-BLUE150+ .50-cal rounds
KIM REDUCED EXPOSURE5 seconds

You cannot read environment reliably if you have not read yourself. Extreme Ownership Ch 1 installs the self-diagnostic as a structural discipline — the leader owns every outcome in their sphere, and the first diagnostic move after failure is what in my planning, training, communication, supervision, or follow-up allowed this, rather than who let me down. Escape the Wolf's Personal Awareness layer supplies the first-person sensor data. Combat Tracking Guide's KIM drills and Appear to Vanish's photographic self-evaluation close the loop on measurable baseline performance. The self-assessment subsystem is the calibration layer for every other subsystem installed so far.

This section installs the self-and-team diagnostic subsystem. You load the Personal Awareness stack and its four internal channels, the extreme-ownership debrief protocol that converts failure into corrective SOP, the Mala'ab District friendly-fire case as the reference for what disciplined ownership looks like, the Excuse Cascade as the failure-mode inverse, the KIM drills that build observer-memory under pressure, the photographic self-evaluation that trains concealment baseline, the engagement-ring self-test that partitions close and long detection, the no-bad-teams-only-bad-leaders principle, the discipline-equals-freedom operating philosophy, and the install protocol, function indicators, failure indicators, and feed-forward handoffs. Sources: Extreme Ownership Ch 1 (Extreme Ownership discipline, Mala'ab case, Excuse Cascade, pharmaceutical VP case, no-bad-teams principle); Escape the Wolf (Personal Awareness, engagement-ring self-test); Combat Tracking Guide (KIM drill methodology); Appear to Vanish (photographic self-evaluation protocol).

00.7.1Personal Awareness — four internal channels

Escape the Wolf specifies four internal channels the operator audits continuously. The stack supplies first-person sensor data that calibrates every other awareness layer in the Total Awareness System.

Personal Awareness — four channels
01EMOTIONALAnger, fear, arrogance, fatigue, grief, sexual arousal, euphoria.
02PHYSICALInjury, illness, hunger, thirst, dehydration, sleep deficit, hypothermia, hyperthermia.
03COGNITIVEDecision fatigue, multitasking load, alcohol, drugs, medication, time pressure.
04EMITTED SIGNALSClothing, demeanor, equipment, visible attention, posture.

The stack is the filter on every other awareness layer. A fatigued operator reads baseline as suspicious. A suspicious operator reads fatigue as calm. An angry operator over-interprets adversary posture as provocation. An arrogant operator under-interprets adversary capability. Personal Awareness audits self before the operator audits environment; the order is non-reversible.

00.7.2Extreme Ownership — the structural discipline

Extreme Ownership Ch 1 installs the discipline that drives the subsystem. The leader owns every outcome in their sphere. On failure, the first diagnostic move is to identify the leader's own contribution — in planning, training, communication, supervision, or follow-up — before any external factor is examined. The principle extends downward: every team member owns their sector within the same discipline.

Extreme Ownership

The leader owns every outcome in their sphere. The first move after failure is to identify the leader's own planning, training, communication, supervision, or follow-up contribution. External factors are examined only after the internal contribution is fully accounted for. The principle applies at every level of the chain.

The mechanism is epistemic. An operator who defaults to external attribution never observes their own failure modes and therefore never corrects them. An operator who defaults to internal attribution observes the full corrective space and generates SOP revisions the external-attribution operator cannot. The discipline is not about accepting fault — it is about accessing the corrective surface that only internal attribution exposes.

00.7.3The after-action debrief protocol

Extreme Ownership's feedback loop runs the diagnostic at the team level. Extreme Ownership Ch 1 specifies the protocol step-by-step.

1. Failure occurs. 2. The senior leader publicly takes the blame in debrief. 3. Subordinates observe the top accept the reputational cost and offer their own honest self-assessments. 4. The team identifies true root cause rather than scapegoat. 5. Corrective change is implemented at the SOP and training level, not at the personnel level alone. 6. The training scenario for the next iteration is designed around the failure type. 7. The identical failure does not recur.

The protocol is sequenced. Out-of-order execution collapses it: if step 5 (SOP change) fires without step 2 (leader ownership), the team reads the change as blame-shift; if step 2 fires without step 4 (root-cause identification), the team reads the ownership as theater. The integrity of the protocol is the sequence, not the individual steps; every step enables the next.

00.7.4Mala'ab District — the reference case for ownership

Extreme Ownership Ch 1 documents the Task Unit Bruiser blue-on-blue in Mala'ab District, Ramadi, as the reference case for what disciplined ownership looks like under maximum pressure. The case ties directly into the Positive Identification failure covered in 00.4.14.

The scenario: an Iraqi soldier was killed, others were wounded, a SEAL was fragged in the face, 150+ .50-caliber rounds had gone into the building before the deconfliction error was caught. The SEAL element inside had been misidentified as an insurgent position. The investigation at Task Group Ramadi level demanded accountability.

Willink's handling. He walked the team through every failure point, accepted personal ownership for the overall outcome, identified his own planning and communication gaps that had placed the SEAL element in the building without deconfliction flowing down, and offered the chain of command a full accounting. The subordinate leaders, watching him take the blame, offered their own honest self-assessments. The root cause was identified as a deconfliction-communication failure structurally embedded in the current SOP. Revised SOPs were implemented. Training scenarios were designed around the failure type. Through the rest of the deployment, several subsequent mistaken-engagement incidents were prevented by the revised SOPs firing before escalation.

If I had tried to pass the blame on to others, I suspect I would have been fired, deservedly so. The SEALs in the troop, who did not expect me to take the blame, respected the fact that I had taken full responsibility for everything.

The lesson runs in two directions. Internal: ownership preserved the chain-of-command's trust in Willink. External: the SEALs under him committed harder to the mission because the top had demonstrated structural integrity at the hardest possible test.

00.7.5The Excuse Cascade — the inverse case

The failure mode inverts the protocol. Extreme Ownership documents the Excuse Cascade as the default team behavior when ownership is absent.

The Excuse Cascade

Leader blames external factors. Team perceives that blame is acceptable. Team blames each other. No diagnostic happens. The failure recurs compounded. Team morale collapses on the second iteration. Trust in leadership collapses on the third.

The reference case in the chapter is non-combat — a pharmaceutical VP whose distribution numbers were off. The VP blamed distribution managers, plant managers, sales managers, market conditions, and technology. Each level blamed the next. No correction occurred. The VP engaged Willink as a consultant, absorbed the Extreme Ownership principle, began taking structural ownership in every meeting, and the distribution problem resolved inside two quarters through SOP changes the prior blame environment had suppressed. The mechanism is identical in combat and in commerce; the discipline is universal because the epistemic structure is universal.

00.7.6KIM drills — observer memory under pressure

Combat Tracking Guide specifies the KIM drill methodology for building and measuring observer memory under stress. The drill runs in progressive-load form.

KIM drill progression
01BASELINEDisplay 10 everyday objects for one minute. Cover. List from memory.
02REDUCED EXPOSUREDisplay for 5 seconds. Same task.
03DISTRACTEDExposure plus concurrent task (conversation, reading, physical activity).
04DELAYED RECALLExposure, ten-minute delay, then recall.
05DUAL-TASKExposure under simultaneous cognitive load (mental math, navigation task).

The drill produces a trendline of observer accuracy under stress. An operator who scores 9/10 at baseline and 3/10 under distracted dual-task conditions knows their observer performance collapses under exactly the conditions operational life presents most often. Training addresses the drop — repeated exposure to the distracted and dual-task variants pulls the stressed score toward the baseline score over weeks. The operator who does not run KIM drills does not know their own observer accuracy under load, and plans the operation around an assumption their perception cannot meet.

00.7.7Photographic self-evaluation

Appear to Vanish specifies a loop for measuring concealment performance against the Seven Target Indicators from 00.1 and 00.2. The loop runs in the field with a partner.

1. Select a concealment position in the operational terrain. 2. Take the position. Hold stillness per the concealment protocol. 3. Partner photographs the operator from off-center angles at 5 m, 15 m, 30 m, and 50 m. 4. Operator emerges. Review the photos against the Seven Target Indicators — Shine, Shape, Silhouette, Shadow, Spacing, Movement, Surface-pattern. 5. Log each violation on a concealment worksheet. 6. Modify kit, position, or stillness protocol. 7. Repeat the cycle.

The companion drill: partners actively search for the operator while the operator holds stillness. The drill trains the physiological response to being hunted — sustained breath control, sub-minimum-movement discipline, and resistance to the urge to shift or check. An operator who has run the drill fifty times carries a calibrated sense of what their concealment actually looks like at each range, and the subsequent field deployment runs on the calibration instead of on the assumption.

00.7.8The engagement-ring self-test

Escape the Wolf specifies a two-ring partition of the operator's close environment. The operator audits each ring on a standing cadence.

Engagement rings — two-ring partition
01CLOSE RING0 to 25 m · Threats at contact or near-contact distance.
02LONG RING> 25 m · Threats at engagement or surveillance distance.

For each ring, the operator answers three questions. How do I detect threats at this range? Where is cover at this range? What is my immediate response at this range? The answers differ. Close-ring detection runs on peripheral vision, auditory, olfactory, and direct engagement. Long-ring detection runs on sustained visual scan, optics, and geometric pattern recognition. Close-ring cover is at arm's reach or one bound away. Long-ring cover is movement-plus-position — cover that requires reaching it before it becomes effective. Close-ring response is immediate action — block, evade, engage. Long-ring response is assessment plus positioning. The operator who audits both rings on a standing cadence runs the full response space; the operator who audits only one ring is surprised by threats in the other.

00.7.9No bad teams — only bad leaders

Extreme Ownership Ch 2's principle applies directly to the diagnostic. The same group of people produces different outcomes under different leadership. If the team fails, the first diagnostic is the leader's own behavior — their standards, their communication, their ownership, their follow-up.

The reference case in the chapter: a SEAL boat crew rotating under different leaders over successive training evolutions. The underperforming crew's leader was swapped with the top-performing crew's leader. Within one evolution, the previously underperforming crew began winning. The personnel had not changed. The leader had. The operational conclusion is precise and repeatable: leadership, not team composition, is the first variable to examine in team performance failure.

00.7.10Discipline equals freedom

Willink's operating philosophy: imposed structure, repeated practice, and strict SOP adherence free the operator for creative decision at the points where creativity matters, because the non-critical has been made reflex.

The mechanism is cognitive load. The operator has bounded attention. If attention is consumed by the non-critical — where the gear lives, how the debrief runs, how the movement formation spaces — none is available for the critical: the adversary read, the environmental anomaly, the decision under time pressure. The discipline of fixed SOPs on the non-critical reserves the attention budget for the moments that demand creative response. Undisciplined teams pay attention to everything equally and resolve nothing well. The operator's attention budget is the bottleneck; discipline on the non-critical is the tool that expands the budget where it matters.

00.7.11Taking the blame increases trust

The counter-intuitive finding in Extreme Ownership Ch 1. Taking structural ownership of a failure does not decrease the operator's credibility — in high-stakes organizations, it increases it. The inverse — blame-shifting, scapegoating, deflection — produces the operational failure the operator was trying to avoid.

The mechanism is observable trust-calculus. Team members and superiors read ownership behavior as diagnostic information about the leader's integrity under pressure. A leader who owns publicly is predictable under future pressure. A leader who deflects is unpredictable — the deflection now predicts more deflection later, and teams can no longer rely on truthful debriefs, honest planning, or accurate reports. In high-stakes organizations, unpredictable leadership is the most severe liability the team carries. Scapegoat behavior is a bigger red flag than the underlying failure; the failure can be corrected, the scapegoat behavior compounds.

00.7.12Install protocol

1. Run Personal Awareness as a continuous audit. Emotional, physical, cognitive, emitted-signal channels — all four, on every operational movement. 2. Install the Extreme Ownership default. On every failure, the first move is internal attribution and corrective-SOP identification. 3. Drill the after-action debrief protocol on every operational event. All hands present. Leader publicly owns. Subordinates self-assess. Root cause identified. SOP revised. Training scenario designed. Next iteration pre-empts the failure. 4. Run KIM drills on a weekly cadence. Progress through baseline, reduced exposure, distracted, delayed recall, and dual-task load. Track the trendline. 5. Run photographic self-evaluation on every new terrain. Measure against the Seven Target Indicators. Modify kit until the baseline zeroes at each tested range. 6. Audit the two engagement rings on a standing cadence. For each ring, detection, cover, and response. 7. Apply the no-bad-teams principle. On team-level underperformance, first diagnostic is the leader's own behavior. 8. Run discipline-equals-freedom on the SOPs that govern the non-critical. Reserve the attention budget for the critical. 9. Integrate with the Total Awareness System from 00.4 — Personal Awareness is the PA layer of the TAS stack. 10. Feed the self-assessment output into the OODA Orient stage in 00.8 and into the continuous situational picture in 00.9.

00.7.13Function indicators

The self-and-team diagnostic subsystem functions when the operator audits Personal Awareness on every operational movement and the four channels return clear reads. Debriefs produce corrective SOPs faster than the adversary learns. The identical failure does not recur twice. KIM drill trendlines show improvement toward baseline under distracted and dual-task conditions. Photographic self-evaluation shows zeroed target-indicator violations at each tested range. Close-ring and long-ring responses are defined and drilled. Team-level underperformance is diagnosed against the leader's own behavior first. Attention budget holds for the critical because the non-critical has been made reflex. Trust within the team and upward remains intact through failures because ownership is public and structural.

00.7.14Failure indicators

The subsystem fails on any of the following. Personal Awareness is skipped and the operator runs with fatigue, intoxication, emotional load, or anger uncorrected. Debriefs produce no SOP changes — blame is distributed, lessons are stated without structural follow-through, the identical failure recurs. The Excuse Cascade fires at any level of the team and lessons go unlearned. KIM drills are not run and observer accuracy under stress is unknown. Photographic self-evaluation is skipped and the operator deploys with target-indicator violations they cannot see. Engagement rings are not audited and threats appear inside the ring without detection. Team-level failures are diagnosed against subordinates first. The attention budget is consumed by non-critical hygiene, and the critical moments catch the operator saturated. Trust collapses because ownership is performative or absent.

Blame-shift is the terminal failure

The subsystem's most severe failure mode is not missing an audit — it is operationalizing blame-shift as the team's default response to failure. Once the cascade has fired twice without correction, trust is gone and no further diagnostic works. Recovery requires a leadership change or an external ownership reset.

00.7.15Feed-forward

The self-and-team diagnostic subsystem hands forward to two downstream installations and one lateral integration. OODA and decision architecture in 00.8 consumes Personal Awareness as the Orient input — the operator's own state shapes the interpretation of environment. The continuous situational picture in 00.9 integrates the team-and-self layer with every other subsystem into one running estimate. Lateral integration with 00.4: Personal Awareness is the PA channel of the Total Awareness System, and the self-audit runs continuously against the target-selection indicator catalog from 00.4.3.

The subsystem never turns off. The four Personal Awareness channels update continuously. The debrief protocol fires on every operational event. Trust compounds with every public ownership and collapses with every deflection.

SECTION 00.8

OODA, NDM, and modes of awareness

OODA STAGES4
AWARENESS MODES3
HABIT INTERVALS8 / 21 / 100 days
DECENTRALIZED SPAN3–6 direct reports
PRIORITIZE MNEMONIC3 steps
CHARLIE PLATOON FALL20 ft

Perception converts to action through decision loops. Escape the Wolf installs Boyd's OODA loop, Klein's Naturalistic Decision-Making, the Modes of Awareness cycle, and the habit-timing that gates automaticity. Extreme Ownership Chapters 7 and 8 install Prioritize and Execute and Decentralized Command. These frameworks are the engine that converts the perceptual subsystems in 00.1 through 00.7 into directed movement. Without the decision architecture, the perceptual subsystems run open-loop and produce no output.

This section installs the decision-loop subsystem. You load the OODA cycle and the faster-loop principle, the loop-quality trap that defeats speed alone, the three Modes of Awareness (Alert, Pre-Crisis, Crisis) with the return-transition failure mode, the Cooper's Colors critique, the NDM pattern-matching model of expert decision under time pressure, the Prioritize and Execute protocol for multi-problem load, the Charlie Platoon rooftop case as the textbook execution, the habit-formation timing that gates automaticity, the Decentralized Command span-of-control rule, Contingency Planning as pre-loaded decision load-shedding, and the install protocol, function indicators, failure indicators, and feed-forward handoffs. Sources: Escape the Wolf (OODA, NDM, Modes, habit timing, Cooper's Colors critique); Extreme Ownership Ch 7 (Prioritize and Execute, Charlie Platoon rooftop case); Extreme Ownership Ch 8 (Decentralized Command, span-of-control).

00.8.1The OODA loop

John Boyd's OODA cycle is the standard decision architecture for dynamic adversarial environments. Escape the Wolf carries the model forward and applies it to civilian operational contexts.

OODA — four stages
01OOBSERVE · Take in sensor data. What is happening.
02OORIENT · Integrate data against mental models, priors, cultural frames. What it means.
03DDECIDE · Select a course of action.
04AACT · Execute.

The cycle loops. The Act stage's consequences become new Observe data, and the next cycle runs. Boyd's central insight: the operator does not have to be smarter or stronger than the adversary. The operator has to cycle faster. If the operator's loop runs at one second and the adversary's runs at three seconds, by the time the adversary completes their first cycle the operator has already acted three times, and the adversary's second Observe is looking at the consequences of the operator's third Act. The adversary is perpetually behind. The faster loop wins by imposing reactive posture on the slower loop.

00.8.2The loop-quality trap

Speed is necessary but not sufficient. The OODA cycle's value is gated by the Orient stage's quality. If the Orient stage integrates against wrong priors, faster execution gets the operator to the wrong place faster. The loop-speed advantage becomes a liability.

Fast loop plus bad Orient equals catastrophic failure

Boyd's insight runs in both directions. A faster loop with correct Orient outpaces the adversary. A faster loop with incorrect Orient outpaces the adversary's ability to correct the operator, and the operator runs deeper into error before the feedback arrives. Loop quality matters as much as loop speed.

The operator maintains both. Observation discipline, pattern recognition, cultural and situational priors, and debrief-driven correction all refine the Orient stage over time. An operator who has run KIM drills, Area Study cycles, and Extreme Ownership debriefs has higher-quality Orient priors than an operator who has only drilled loop speed. The self-assessment subsystem in 00.7 feeds directly into Orient quality.

00.8.3Modes of Awareness — the three-state cycle

Escape the Wolf supplies the behavioral content that Jeff Cooper's color code under-specifies. The Modes of Awareness model partitions the operator's state into three modes and specifies the transition rules between them.

Modes of Awareness — three states
01ALERTAmbient baseline; scanning, not tasked; low heart rate; broad visual sweep; catalog-level attention.
02PRE-CRISISAnomaly detected; heart rate up; focus narrows; orientation underway; commitment to action not yet made.
03CRISISEvent unfolding; operator is acting; full engagement.

Transition rules are specified. Alert to Pre-Crisis on any baseline violation — person out of place, unusual sound or smell, anomalous behavior. Pre-Crisis to Crisis on threat confirmed at contact distance. Crisis back to Alert on event resolved, area cleared, team accounted for.

00.8.4The return-transition failure

The hardest transition in the cycle is Crisis back to Alert. Escape the Wolf identifies this as the common failure mode in under-trained operators and most civilians.

Post-crisis arousal

Operators stay in an elevated-arousal state for hours after the Crisis event resolves, pattern-matching the last event rather than the current one. The operator sees threats where there are none, misses genuine anomalies entirely, and produces both false positives and false negatives at the same time. The return to Alert requires explicit deceleration — physiological reset, environmental audit, team accounting — not a passive drift back.

The operational consequence is severe. An operator stuck in post-crisis arousal misreads the next ambient environment because they carry the prior event's priors forward. A robbery survivor sees robbers in every convenience store for weeks. A combat veteran reads civilian crowds as ambush geometry. The Modes of Awareness model names the failure and prescribes the reset: deliberate exhale, environmental catalog-scan, team count, mission state check. Getting back to Alert is not automatic; it is a protocol.

00.8.5Naturalistic Decision-Making — how experts decide under pressure

Gary Klein's NDM model, carried forward in Escape the Wolf, describes how expert decision-makers actually operate under time pressure. They do not compare alternatives. They pattern-match.

The protocol the expert runs: recognize the current situation as a pattern from prior experience; generate the first course of action that matches the pattern; mentally simulate the action to check for disqualifying problems; if the simulation surfaces a problem, move to the next pattern; if the simulation passes, execute. The expert does not produce a list of options and rank them. The expert produces one option at a time, each running through the simulation gate, and commits on the first option that passes.

The model has training implications. Pattern libraries are built through repeated exposure to varied scenarios, not through flowchart teaching. Case-based training, simulation-based training, and post-action review all build the library. An operator trained on a flowchart runs the flowchart under pressure; an operator trained on two hundred scenarios runs NDM against a deep pattern library. Under pressure, the expert simplifies further — fewer channels, higher-value channels, faster cycle. Adding data inputs slows the loop; the expert's discipline is to subtract inputs, not add them.

00.8.6Cooper's Colors — the insufficient frame

Jeff Cooper's color code (White, Yellow, Orange, Red, Black) sees broad civilian use. Escape the Wolf critiques the frame as under-specified for operational use.

Cooper's Colors as entry-point, not operational model

The colors describe arousal state but do not prescribe behavior. Yellow in particular under-specifies what the operator should attend to and how to transition between states. The model is serviceable as a self-check prompt — "am I in white right now?" is a valid diagnostic question — but as an operational cycle it fails the transition-rule test. The Modes of Awareness model supersedes it.

The critique is not dismissive. Cooper's Colors remains a reasonable entry-point for civilians building their first awareness model, and the question "am I in white right now?" catches the most dangerous civilian failure (ambient unawareness in public). The operational upgrade is the Modes of Awareness cycle from 00.8.3 — same awareness levels, plus the transition rules, plus the behavioral prescription, plus the return-transition discipline.

00.8.7Prioritize and Execute

Extreme Ownership Ch 7 installs the protocol for handling multiple problems presenting simultaneously. A leader attempting to solve all at once fails at all, and the team loses direction.

Prioritize and Execute — the sequence
01EVALUATEIdentify the highest-priority problem.
02STATEState the priority simply enough that every team member understands.
03DEVELOPSolicit input where time permits; develop the solution.
04DIRECTCommit the team; focus all energy on the priority.
05EXECUTERun the solution.
06SHIFTMove to the next priority; communicate the shift up and down chain.
07SCANWatch for new higher priorities emerging; target-fixation is the trap.

The verbal mnemonic: relax, look around, make a call. The relax is a deliberate exhale that breaks target-fixation. The look around is a sensor sweep of the real environment, not the imagined worst case. The call is commitment to the highest-priority action. Three beats, seconds to execute, and the protocol re-engages the team with the actual problem space instead of the cognitive overload that was freezing decision.

00.8.8Charlie Platoon rooftop — the reference case

Extreme Ownership Ch 7 documents the Charlie Platoon South-Central Ramadi rooftop incident as the textbook Prioritize-and-Execute run under overload.

The scenario. A fireteam had been BTF'd (brought-to-fight) into an apartment building and taken heavy fire throughout the day. An EOD element found an IED at the planned exit. The team breached through a concrete wall with a sledgehammer onto an adjacent rooftop. A SEAL fell through a dust-covered tarp and dropped 20 ft to the street below. The IED timer was running. The iron gate to the street below was locked. The team on the adjacent rooftop was fully exposed to surrounding higher buildings. Four simultaneous problems — fallen team member, active IED, locked gate, rooftop exposure — each of them urgent.

Willink's sequence. Set security first — guns up, covering all arcs — so the rooftop exposure was managed before any other action. Breacher up on the gate — the locked gate was the path to the fallen SEAL and had to be opened before recovery was possible. Head count — verify no one else was down, no one else was missing. Move down and recover the fallen SEAL. Clear to safe distance before the IED timer ran out.

The IED detonated on time. No friendly casualties. The sequence ran in under two minutes. The protocol worked because Willink resolved four problems into a strict priority order inside seconds and the team executed one at a time rather than splitting resources across all four. The load on the leader is the priority-sequencing decision; the load on the team is the focused execution.

00.8.9Habit formation — the 8 / 21 / 100 day timing

Escape the Wolf references the habit-formation schedule for installing awareness and decision behaviors until they run automatically under stress.

Habit formation — three intervals
018 DAYSConscious effort to execute the behavior decreases; the behavior becomes less disruptive to perform.
0221 DAYSThe habit is formed; the behavior executes without dedicated attention under normal conditions.
03100 DAYSThe behavior persists under stress; the habit holds through operational load, fatigue, and novelty.

The timing gates the subsystem's automaticity and applies to every decision-loop behavior installed in this section. An operator who practices the OODA cycle for one week performs it deliberately. At three weeks the loop runs by default. At 100 days the loop holds under operational stress — which is where the subsystem must run. The training schedule is structural: operational combat-readiness on a new behavior is measured in months, not in single sessions.

00.8.10Decentralized Command — the span-of-control rule

Extreme Ownership Ch 8 installs the structural principle that scales the OODA cycle past single-operator span. No leader cognitively manages more than three to six direct reports under chaos.

Decentralized Command

Senior leaders set commander's intent — the end state, the key tasks, the rules of engagement. Subordinate leaders execute with decision authority pushed down to the lowest level capable of making the call. The senior leader's cognitive load stays inside the three-to-six-direct-report band. Subordinates own their sectors and make their own decisions within commander's intent.

Willink's Task Unit Bruiser example. Thirty-plus SEALs were organized into fire teams of four to six, each with a designated leader. Willink's direct span of control was four to six fire-team leaders, not thirty-plus individual SEALs. Each fire-team leader ran their team's OODA cycle inside commander's intent, and Willink ran the task-unit cycle at his level. Decentralized command preserved loop-speed at scale because the decision was made by the nearest capable actor, not escalated to Willink's desk.

00.8.11Contingency Planning — pre-loaded decision load-shedding

Extreme Ownership Ch 8 also installs Contingency Planning as the discipline that pre-identifies likely failure modes, pre-maps responses, and pre-briefs the team.

The mechanism is cognitive load-shedding. When a failure occurs, a team without contingency plans must run the full OODA cycle on the failure — Observe the failure, Orient to the new situation, Decide on a response, Act. The cycle takes time, and in the interim the situation worsens. A team with a pre-briefed contingency plan runs a compressed cycle: Observe the failure, recognize it as the pre-planned case, Act. Orient and Decide have been pre-computed.

The cost of contingency planning is paid in the planning phase, when time is cheap. The savings are claimed in execution, when time is expensive. The principle: compute decisions when time is cheap, execute decisions when time is expensive.

00.8.12Install protocol

1. Install the OODA cycle as the default decision architecture. Observe, Orient, Decide, Act, loop. 2. Maintain loop quality alongside loop speed. Invest in Orient-stage refinement through KIM drills, Area Study cycles, and Extreme Ownership debriefs. 3. Run the Modes of Awareness cycle continuously. Alert as default; Pre-Crisis on any baseline violation; Crisis on threat confirmed at contact distance; deliberate return to Alert on event resolution. 4. Drill the post-crisis reset protocol — exhale, environmental catalog-scan, team count, mission state check — until it fires automatically. 5. Build NDM pattern libraries through varied-scenario training, case-based review, and post-action debrief. Add scenarios; do not add flowcharts. 6. Run Prioritize and Execute on multi-problem load. Relax, look around, make a call. Priorities are sequenced, not parallel. 7. Organize the team on Decentralized Command. Three-to-six direct reports maximum per leader. Push decision authority down. 8. Pre-load Contingency Plans for likely failure modes before operational movement. Brief the plans so the team recognizes the case when it occurs. 9. Commit to the 8 / 21 / 100 day schedule for every new decision-loop behavior. Conscious at 8, habit at 21, stress-durable at 100. 10. Integrate the subsystem with self-assessment in 00.7 (Orient input), adversary profile in 00.4 (pre-attack cascade detection), and continuous situational picture in 00.9 (full loop integration).

00.8.13Function indicators

The decision-loop subsystem functions when the operator's OODA cycle runs faster than the adversary's, the Orient stage integrates against correct priors, and the Act stage's consequences feed the next Observe without delay. The Modes of Awareness cycle transitions cleanly, including the return transition. Post-crisis arousal is recognized and reset within minutes, not hours. NDM pattern libraries are broad enough that first-option pattern-matches hold under simulation gate more often than they fail. Prioritize and Execute resolves multi-problem load into a sequenced priority stack under pressure. Span of control stays inside the three-to-six band. Contingency plans are pre-briefed and recognized when they fire. Decision authority distributes across the team so tempo holds even when the senior leader is saturated.

00.8.14Failure indicators

The subsystem fails on any of the following. Loop speed is prioritized over loop quality, and the operator executes fast against wrong priors. Post-crisis arousal persists for hours, producing pattern-matched threats that are not present and missed anomalies that are. Cooper's Colors is retained as the operational model and the transition behavior stays unspecified. NDM is replaced by flowchart decision-making and the operator freezes under novel scenarios. Prioritize and Execute fails because the leader attempts to solve multiple problems simultaneously. Span of control exceeds six direct reports and loops slow at the leader's saturation point. Contingency plans do not exist, or exist but are not briefed, and the team runs the full cycle on a failure that could have been pre-computed.

Span-of-control violation is the hidden failure mode

A leader managing eight or ten direct reports under chaos does not notice their own saturation. The team notices — decisions slow, guidance arrives late, priorities fragment. The leader attributes the problem to team performance. The actual failure is structural span-of-control. The fix is not better leadership; the fix is smaller direct-report count.

00.8.15Feed-forward

The decision-loop subsystem hands forward to one downstream installation and one full-system integration. The continuous situational picture in 00.9 runs against the OODA cycle as its operating engine — the picture updates every Observe, feeds every Orient, informs every Decide, and records every Act. Primary Systems in 01 consumes the decision architecture as standing input for every technique installed downstream — survival technique, movement, applied force, compound systems, sustainment, command, and field deployment all run their operational behavior through this loop.

The decision architecture is the gearbox between perception and execution. Without it, the perceptual subsystems in 00.1 through 00.7 run open-loop and produce no output. With it, every perception converts to directed movement inside the operator's OODA cycle.

SECTION 00.9

Continuous situational picture

PICTURE LAYERS6
HALT-SCAN5 / 25 m
IED PROTOCOL5 Cs
CLOSE-TERRAIN SPACING20 m
OPEN-TERRAIN SPACING50 m
MOVEMENT TECHNIQUES3
COUNTERTRACK DECEPTIONS4

The final section integrates every prior subsystem into one live running estimate. Area Intelligence Handbook's Area Study, Escape the Wolf's Total Awareness System, Combat Tracking Guide's running tracker read, Extreme Ownership's priority stack, and Essential Wilderness Navigation's map-first principle all converge on a single continuously updated operational mental model. The picture is the compound output of every subsystem installed in 00.1 through 00.8, and every observation updates at least one layer of the picture.

This section installs the integration subsystem. You load the six-layer picture model that compiles every prior subsystem into one estimate, the baseline-anchoring principle that makes detection possible, the 5-and-25-meter drill that runs on every halt, the 5 Cs for IED and booby-trap discovery, the movement formation spacing standards, the three movement techniques gated by threat level, the Report-Everything Protocol and its echelon discipline, the cardinal-direction comms standard, the four countertracking deceptions that appear on both offense and defense, the Red River Gorge SAR case as the integrated-picture proof-case, the gear-versus-picture operating principle, and the install protocol, function indicators, failure indicators, and feed-forward handoffs. Sources: Area Intelligence Handbook (integration, priority intelligence requirements, Report-Everything); Escape the Wolf (TAS integration, awareness stack); Combat Tracking Guide (running tracker read, movement formation, countertrack deceptions); Extreme Ownership Ch 7 (priority stack); Essential Wilderness Navigation (map-first SAR application, Red River Gorge case).

00.9.1The six-layer picture

The continuous situational picture compiles in six layers. Each layer is the output of a prior subsystem. Every new observation updates the relevant layer, and layer updates propagate to adjacent layers.

Picture layers — integration map
01AREA STUDY LAYERPolitical, military, economic, social, information, infrastructure state from 00.6.
02MODES-OF-AWARENESS LAYERCurrent decision state — Alert, Pre-Crisis, Crisis — from 00.8.
03TEAM-AND-SELF LAYERLast known status of each team member and asset from 00.7.
04ACTIVE SIGN LAYERGround, aerial, olfactory, and signature reads from 00.1, 00.2, 00.3.
05ADVERSARY MODEL LAYERHuman-threat posture from 00.4.
06TERRAIN MODEL LAYERArea association from 00.5.

The layers do not run independently. A single observation can update multiple layers and propagate across the picture. A single human track matching an unknown boot tread in a known-hostile direction updates the track log (active sign layer), triggers threat-actor model revision (adversary model layer), may escalate Modes of Awareness from Alert to Pre-Crisis (awareness layer), prompts posture adjustment in cover and route and comms (team-and-self layer), cues collection through a new NAI (Area Study layer), and revises the terrain model if the track indicates an unexpected route. One signal, six updates; the picture is a compound feedback architecture.

00.9.2Baseline — the integrated anchor

The detection threshold anchors on baseline. Baseline is the combined normal — visual, auditory, olfactory, behavioral, cultural — of a specific place at a specific time of day, established in the first two to fifteen minutes of entering an area through ambient observation.

Baseline

The combined normal across all awareness channels of a specific location at a specific time. Established through ambient observation in the first two to fifteen minutes in the area. Updated continuously as the operator remains in the area. Used as the reference against which all deviation is detected.

Disturbance detection measures against this internal baseline, not against a generic model. Two patches of ground two miles apart have different baselines; a generic "woods at dusk" baseline catches nothing. The discipline is to build the specific baseline before running the deviation-detection layer on top of it. An operator who skips baseline construction reports every observed signal as an anomaly because they lack the reference to distinguish normal from deviant. An operator who builds baseline cleanly reports only the genuine anomalies and the signal-to-noise ratio of their observation products runs high.

00.9.3The 5-and-25-meter drill

Combat Tracking Guide specifies the scan protocol that runs on every halt. The drill partitions the immediate environment into two concentric rings and establishes local security before any other task.

Halt-scan protocol — two rings
015 mScan immediate area around body or vehicle for booby traps and hostile close proximity.
0225 mScan for cover, threats, and next hide position.
03SECURITYEstablish local security (arcs assigned, overwatch posted) before any other task.
04TASKOnly then attend to map read, radio, casualty care, or equipment adjustment.

The discipline is the sequence. The operator who drops the pack and pulls out the map before running the 5-and-25 audit has skipped the security step and now carries out the map-read task in a space that has not been cleared. The halt is the moment the operator is most stationary, most visible, and most exposed; the drill is non-optional. Practiced to the 100-day standard, the drill runs on every halt without deliberate activation.

00.9.4The 5 Cs — IED and booby-trap response

Combat Tracking Guide specifies the five-step protocol for discovered devices. The protocol covers both explosive and non-explosive hazards and runs identically in both cases.

5 Cs — device discovery protocol
01CONFIRMConfirm the object is a threat. Visual identification from distance; do not approach.
02CLEARClear personnel from the hazard area. Minimum safe distance scales with device type.
03CORDONCordon a perimeter. Prevent re-entry.
04CHECKCheck for secondary devices. Adversaries plant a second near the first for responders.
05CONTROLControl traffic until EOD disposes of the device.

The Check step defeats the secondary-device trap that is the standard adversary tactic against responders. A device discovery draws immediate attention and response; a secondary device planted adjacent to the first targets the respondents. The operator who runs the Check step sweeps for the secondary before committing the response team, and the sweep catches the trap before it fires.

00.9.5Movement formation spacing

Combat Tracking Guide specifies standing spacing doctrine for team movement. The spacing scales with visibility, cover, and threat level.

Movement spacing — terrain-dependent
01CLOSE TERRAIN20 m between personnel · Forest, urban, restricted visibility.
02OPEN TERRAIN50 m between personnel · Fields, ridgelines, desert, open countryside.
03ADJUSTMENTScale up for reduced cover; scale down for higher visibility or dense brush.

The spacing serves a specific tactical function. A single indirect-fire round, a burst of automatic fire, or an IED blast has a limited effective radius; team members spaced beyond that radius take one casualty instead of two or three. The operator who walks close on the teammate's shoulder doubles or triples the casualty count on a single enemy action. The discipline is continuous — spacing drifts closed over time through conversation, fatigue, and terrain pressure, and the leader re-corrects it on a standing cadence.

00.9.6Movement techniques — three levels

Combat Tracking Guide specifies three movement techniques that scale to threat level. The team shifts technique as the threat picture updates, not on a schedule.

Movement techniques — threat-level gating
01TRAVELINGLow threat; full team moves continuously; standard spacing; maximum tempo.
02TRAVELING OVERWATCHPossible contact; lead element moves, trail element follows at increased distance with weapons ready; spacing extended.
03BOUNDING OVERWATCHImminent contact; one element moves while the other covers from static position; elements swap on each bound.

Bounding overwatch is the slowest and the most defensively postured technique. One element is stationary and covering; the other is moving. The stationary element holds sectors of fire on the movement. On completion of the bound, the elements swap. The technique trades tempo for survivability, and it runs when the threat picture indicates imminent contact. A team that stays in Traveling when the picture calls for Bounding Overwatch takes the contact standing up; a team that stays in Bounding Overwatch when the picture calls for Traveling moves at a third of the rate the situation allows. The leader's responsibility is to match the technique to the threat picture as the picture updates.

00.9.7The Report-Everything Protocol

Area Intelligence Handbook and Combat Tracking Guide both prescribe the same discipline. Raw detail pushes up through SALUTE and Tracker Nine-Line formats; senior integrates into the picture; decisions at appropriate echelon, not at observer level.

The protocol: observer reports raw observations using standardized formats. The observer does not filter for relevance — filtering introduces observer bias, and observer bias compounds. The senior receives the raw data, integrates against the picture, identifies which observations matter for which decisions, and acts or cues further collection. The cost of over-reporting is negligible; the cost of a missing data point at decision time can be catastrophic.

Better to record and not need than to need and not have. The corollary applies to information. A report that costs thirty seconds to transmit and turns out to be irrelevant costs nothing. A datum that was never reported and turns out to be the key to the puzzle costs the mission.

00.9.8Cardinal-direction comms

Combat Tracking Guide specifies the communications standard for directional callouts. The rule: refer to directions in cardinal form (N, S, E, W, compass-bearing), never in relative form (left, right, behind you).

The mechanism is frame-independence. Relative directions depend on the receiver's facing, and the receiver's facing may not match the transmitter's. "Enemy on your right" means different things when the receiver is facing east versus west. Cardinal directions are frame-independent — "enemy to the south" means the same thing regardless of who is facing where. Under stress, under fatigue, and under overlapping radio traffic, the cardinal-direction standard prevents the frame-mismatch error that relative directions almost always introduce.

00.9.9Countertracking deceptions

Combat Tracking Guide catalogs countertracking patterns that appear in the picture both as offensive tools (when the operator is the quarry) and as adversary behavior to anticipate (when the operator is the tracker).

Countertracking deceptions — four patterns
01FISHHOOKWalks forward, loops back, sets ambush on the back-trail.
02CIRCLEReturns adjacent to start; tracker ends up re-reading own team's tracks.
03BOXWalks a rectangle; creates ambiguity about which side is the exit.
04FIGURE-EIGHTRuns two overlapping loops; tracker must resolve which exit to commit to.

The offensive and defensive sides of the picture compose. The operator plans their own countertracking (when quarry) using these patterns, and the operator anticipates adversary countertracking (when tracker) by recognizing the same patterns in sign. The fishhook is the most dangerous pattern to track because the adversary sets the ambush on the observer's path. The tracker's counter is to detect the loop-back before committing to the forward trail. The pattern library runs both ways; the operator's awareness of the deception set is the same asset on offense and on defense.

00.9.10Red River Gorge — the integrated picture in a real SAR event

Essential Wilderness Navigation documents the Red River Gorge hiker recovery as the reference case for the integrated picture running in a real search-and-rescue operation.

The scenario. A 10 PM call reported two hikers lost. The first team's brief phone contact with the hikers, before cell coverage dropped, let the SAR lead discern the general area. The team's standing area knowledge from the 00.6 Area Study layer gave them the three possible entry points. Mutual aid teams were called. The hikers were located 1.5 miles in. One hiker had an ankle injury. A Stokes basket was brought in. The extraction ran on the known shortest route.

The picture integration. The Area Study layer produced the three-entry-point constraint that compressed the search space from the full gorge to three corridors. The continuous situational picture took the phone-contact input (active sign layer) and integrated against the standing entry-point list (Area Study layer) to produce the search plan. Prioritize-and-Execute from 00.8 sequenced the team's actions — locate, assess injury, stabilize, extract. Every layer the operator had installed from 00.1 through 00.8 was active in the recovery. The operation closed without a second casualty because the picture was compiled, not because any single subsystem produced the answer.

00.9.11Gear versus picture — the operating principle

The subsystem's operating philosophy. Situational awareness is the asset; gear is the force multiplier. The order does not reverse.

A superb operator with a stubby pencil, a 1:24,000 topo, a ten-dollar compass, and a practiced baseline-observation habit outperforms a lesser operator wearing five thousand dollars of kit with no situational picture.

The principle is load-bearing for every resource decision. Money spent on gear produces marginal returns once baseline adequacy is reached; money spent on training, area study, and picture-compilation habit produces compounding returns across every operational deployment. The operator's first investment is perception and decision architecture. Gear acquisitions come after the picture is compiled, not before.

00.9.12Install protocol

1. Compile all six picture layers on entry to the operational environment. Area Study, Modes of Awareness, team-and-self, active sign, adversary model, terrain model. 2. Build baseline in the first two to fifteen minutes through ambient observation across all awareness channels. 3. Run the 5 / 25 m drill on every halt. Security before task, always. 4. Apply the 5 Cs on any discovered device. Check for secondaries before committing response. 5. Maintain movement spacing to terrain-dependent standard. 20 m close, 50 m open, scaled for conditions. 6. Match movement technique to threat level. Traveling under low threat; traveling overwatch under possible contact; bounding overwatch under imminent contact. 7. Push raw observations up via SALUTE and Tracker Nine-Line. Do not filter at observer level. 8. Use cardinal-direction comms. N, S, E, W, compass-bearing. Never left, right, behind. 9. Run the countertracking deception set on both offense and defense. Fishhook, circle, box, figure-eight. 10. Invest in picture first, gear second. Training, area study, and baseline habit compound; gear does not. 11. Integrate the subsystem with every prior subsystem from 00.1 through 00.8; every observation updates at least one picture layer.

00.9.13Function indicators

The continuous situational picture subsystem functions when any team member can answer at any moment: where am I, what time is it, who is with me, who may be against me, what is my plan, what is my contingency, what do I need to know next. Baseline is compiled within fifteen minutes of entry to any new area. The 5 / 25 m drill fires on every halt without deliberate activation. Movement spacing holds to terrain standard without drift. Movement technique matches threat level and shifts as the picture updates. The Report-Everything Protocol runs without observer-level filtering. Cardinal-direction comms are the default. Countertracking patterns register on both offense and defense. Every observation updates at least one picture layer, and updates propagate across adjacent layers.

00.9.14Failure indicators

The subsystem fails on any of the following. A layer drifts out of date and the picture carries stale signal at high confidence. Observations get filtered at the observer level rather than pushed raw to the appropriate echelon. The map layer disappears and the operation degrades into walking rather than operating. Baseline is not built, and every observation reports as an anomaly because the reference is absent. The 5 / 25 m drill gets skipped under fatigue or schedule pressure. Movement spacing collapses under conversation or terrain. Technique mismatches threat level in either direction. Relative directions replace cardinal and frame-mismatch errors compound. Gear acquisition replaces picture compilation as the primary operational investment.

Map absence is the canary failure mode

Searching should always include map knowledge; operating without a map in your head or in your pocket is walking, not operating. When the map layer drops, every other layer degrades — the picture loses the anchor, terrain memory runs blind, the Area Study has no geography to attach to, and countertracking deceptions that only make sense against the map become invisible. The map is the integration surface.

00.9.15Feed-forward

The continuous situational picture subsystem is the full-system integration of every prior subsystem in sub-module 00. It hands forward to every downstream module. Primary Systems in 01 consumes the picture as standing input; every survival technique operates inside a compiled picture. Movement in 02 routes through the terrain layer and the adversary model layer. Applied Force in 03 engages threats inside the adversary model layer on ground surveyed by the terrain model layer. Compound Systems in 04 interlocks the picture layers into feedback loops that accelerate without the baseline in place. Sustainment in 05 logistics against the Area Study layer. Command in 06 runs on the decision architecture the picture drives. Field Deployment in 07 indexes condition-class triggers against the picture's current state.

The picture is the operator's running operational estimate. It never finalizes. Every observation updates it. The operator who runs the picture continuously outperforms every operator who runs subsystems in isolation, because the picture is the compound — and the compound is the asset.

Close — from baseline to primary systems

You now hold nine subsystems running in parallel and one integration layer binding them together. Ground sign, full-spectrum non-ground sign, full-spectrum signature detection, adversary profiling, terrain memory and area association, structured Area Study production, self-and-team diagnostic loops, OODA and NDM and Modes of Awareness, continuous situational picture. Each subsystem carries explicit install protocols, functioning indicators, and failure signatures. Each subsystem cross-feeds the others: signcut updates the adversary model, terrain reads update the Area Study, self-assessment updates the OODA Orient, and the continuous picture draws every input into one running estimate refreshed by every observation.

Baseline is the layer every downstream gain multiplies against. The error in your baseline read is the error every subsequent subsystem inherits.

This is the BASELINE LAYER of the RSI progression. Everything downstream compounds on it. Survival technique in 01 routes around terrain you have already read. Movement in 02 operates across ground you have already memorized and through adversary envelopes you have already profiled. Applied force in 03 engages threats you have already identified and on terrain you have already surveyed. The compound layer in 04 interlocks these subsystems into feedback loops that acceleration cannot generate without the baseline in place. Sustainment in 05 operates under area-study-informed logistics. Command in 06 runs on decision architectures already installed here. Field deployment in 07 indexes condition-class triggers into the subsystem activation matrix that 00 has already built.

00 baseline → downstream compound
**00.1–00.3Detection subsystems feed → 03 applied force (threat identification), 04 compound systems (signal-density feedback loops), 07 field deployment** (condition-class triggers).
**00.4–00.5Terrain and area memory feed → 01 primary systems (environmental survival), 02 movement (route selection, cover, concealment), 05 sustainment** (resource mapping).
**00.6Area Study** feeds → every downstream module, because every downstream module operates inside an operational environment that 00.6 has already structured.
**00.7–00.8Self-assessment and decision architecture feed → 06 command (Decentralized Command, Extreme Ownership, Prioritize and Execute) and 04 compound systems** (OODA-speed as the multiplier on every other subsystem).
**00.9Continuous picture** feeds → the operator's running estimate at all times, across all downstream modules. The picture never hands off. It persists.

The operator who runs 00 at operational standard carries a continuously calibrated sensor array, a continuously updated mental model, and a decision loop tight enough to outpace most adversaries and most environments. The operator who skips 00 runs every subsequent subsystem on unverified priors, and every downstream gain multiplies against the error in the baseline read.

00 NEVER TURNS OFF. Downstream modules install additional subsystems on top of 00; they do not replace it. When you run Primary Systems in 01, your scan continues. When you run Movement in 02, your picture continues. When you run Applied Force in 03, your self-assessment continues. Baseline is the layer that stays live during every other subsystem's execution. The moment baseline drops, every downstream subsystem degrades to the quality of an operator who is no longer reading the ground.

You land in a situation. You read what you are looking at. The ground truth comes first. Primary Systems installs next.

Sub-module 00 covers perception. Before any technique runs, you produce a working model of the ground, the air, the terrain, the adversary, the team, and the self. The sub-module integrates six primary sources. Combat Tracking Guide supplies the signcutting spine, the Seven Target Indicators, the SALUTE and Tracker Nine-Line reporting formats, the 5-and-25-meter halt drill, the movement spacing standards. Escape the Wolf supplies the Total Awareness System with its five stacked awarenesses, the Modes of Awareness cycle (Alert, Pre-crisis, Crisis), Grossman's sheep/wolves/sheepdogs typology, and the 8/21/100-day habit timing. Appear to Vanish contributes the signature-detection architecture across visible, UV, NIR, and LWIR bands, the Gray Man protocol, the S-Word Scents framework, and the self-assessment worksheet. By the end of this sub-module you have nine calibrated subsystems running in parallel: visual signcutting on the ground, non-ground signal detection in air and sound and smell, signature discipline across the full electromagnetic spectrum, adversary and predator recognition with behavioral priors, terrain memory and area association, standardized area-study production for any operational environment, self-and-team diagnostic feedback, the decision loops that convert perception to action, and the continuous situational picture that integrates all of it into one live running estimate. The arc from here is straight: you assess, then you survive, then you move, then you engage. The ground truth comes first.
