SECTION 01.1

Survival priorities and the Rule of Threes

RULE OF THREES3 min / 3 hr / 3 day / 3 wk
HYPOTHERMIA AT50°F WET + WIND
GLYCOGEN BURN90–180 min
CORE THRESHOLDS<95°F / <89.6°F / <82°F
CW CAL DEMAND~4,500 kcal/day
WATER RULE8 qt MOVE · 6 qt STATIC
TEN Cs10
PACE LAYERS4

The ground clock is not negotiable. Every decision in the primitive-systems stack orders against the Rule of Threes, the canonical time-to-death hierarchy that fixes triage priority across every downstream section. Advanced Bushcraft anchors the rule at the front of Chapter 1 and drives its Ten Cs kit architecture from it; the First Aid Manual TW-05 opens its WROL-aid introduction on the same figures and maps the sixteen aid-guideline ordering directly against the four time bands; wilderness-medicine canon runs the same spine.

This section installs the triage subsystem. You load the Rule of Threes tiered clock, the cascade-of-insults mechanism that explains why three hours is a ceiling for mild conditions only, the shivering-as-countdown correction that reframes the body's cold response as a depleting reserve, the inverse-difficulty / inverse-urgency principle that reorders effort against felt sensation, the Ten Cs kit scaffold and the FARMED blade criteria that operationalize redundancy into carry weight, the STOP decision-pause and the PACE four-layer redundancy per primitive, the ceiling-vs-clock case data that fixes the rule as heuristic rather than literal duration, and the install protocol, function indicators, failure indicators, and feed-forward handoffs. Sources: Advanced Bushcraft Ch 1, Ch 2, Ch 4 (Rule of Threes, Ten Cs, FARMED, cascade chain); First Aid Manual TW-05 (WROL intro, hypothermia staging, hydration rule, clothing COLD mnemonic); wilderness-medicine canon via both sources (core-temperature thresholds, glycogen-depletion timing).

01.1.1The tiered clock

The Rule of Threes partitions survival risk into four time bands, each ending in death if no intervention reaches the layer. Advanced Bushcraft Chapter 1 specifies the controlled figures.

Rule of Threes — time-to-death hierarchy
01AIR3 minutes · Airway compromise, toxic atmosphere, drowning, cardiac arrest.
02SHELTER3 hours · Severe thermal exposure — cold-wet, cold-wind, immersion, high altitude.
03WATER3 days · Dehydration at moderate activity and moderate temperature.
04FOOD3 weeks · Starvation in an otherwise-stable thermoregulated operator.

Each band fixes a different intervention priority, each subsystem in this sub-module maps onto a band, and TRIAGE ALWAYS ORDERS TOP-DOWN. An operator with a collapsed airway and a fourteen-day food cache is dead in three minutes. An operator with a full canteen and no hat is dead in three hours in the right weather. The clock is the ruler every kit, every protocol, and every decision in 01 measures against.

01.1.2Heuristic, not literal

The rule is an order-of-magnitude heuristic. Advanced Bushcraft Chapter 4 and the First Aid Manual TW-05 hypothermia chapter both document fatalities at ambient temperatures as high as 50°F under wet-and-wind conditions in under three hours, with the core-to-cardiac-arrest chain completing in under 90 minutes in the worst-case combination of immersion, wind exposure, and cotton clothing.

WARN

The 3-hour figure is a ceiling for mild conditions only. Wet, wind, and inadequate clothing compress it toward 90 minutes. Treat the rule as a category-scale, not a countdown timer.

The inverse also holds. In dry, windless, temperate ambient, the shelter layer may extend to a full day without thermal insult. The rule tells the operator which primitive to solve first, not how many minutes remain. The operational consequence: READ THE CONDITIONS, THEN SCALE THE CLOCK. A wet-cold scenario runs the three-hour band at 90 minutes; a warm-dry scenario runs it at several hours; an immersion scenario can run it at 20 minutes. The ordering holds. The duration flexes.

01.1.3The cascade of insults

The mechanism underneath the three-hour band is a chained physiological failure that one small insult initiates. Advanced Bushcraft Chapter 4 maps the full sequence.

Cascade of insults — cold-weather failure chain

WET CLOTHING (sweat or immersion) → EVAPORATIVE COOLING (540 cal/g latent heat removed per gram of water) → SHIVERING (metabolic heat attempt burning glycogen) → GLYCOGEN DEPLETION (90–180 min) → SHIVERING CESSATION → CORE DROP <95°F → DEXTERITY COLLAPSE → OPERATOR CANNOT BUILD FIRE OR SHELTER → FURTHER CORE DROP → VENTRICULAR FIBRILLATION at <82°F → CARDIAC ARREST.

One unzipped collar, one pair of wet socks, or one cotton base layer initiates the cascade hours before dehydration or starvation would register as threats. The cascade runs serially — each node feeds the next — and the system offers no intrinsic stopping point once dexterity collapses, because the operator at core <95°F can no longer execute the tool-based interventions that would reverse the chain. The window for voluntary correction closes before the operator's subjective experience of cold reaches peak intensity, because shivering masks the degradation of fine-motor capacity that the cascade is already driving.

01.1.4Shivering is a countdown

Layperson intuition reads shivering as the body "handling it." The actual physiology is opposite. TW-05 and Advanced Bushcraft Chapter 4 both frame shivering as the body burning its glycogen reserve at accelerated rate to generate metabolic heat.

Shivering is not a shield. It is a countdown on glycogen. When shivering stops, the body has not adapted — it has exhausted the fuel source that was holding the line.01.1.4 · The inversion

Glycogen reserves run 90–180 minutes depending on fitness, caloric state, and the severity of the thermal gradient. When the reserve depletes, shivering stops and the inflection is into severe hypothermia, never into recovery. The operational consequence reverses the layperson read: a shivering teammate is on a countdown with live reserves; a non-shivering teammate who was previously shivering is past the inflection and requires active rewarming protocol, not reassurance. The calm stillness the layperson reads as improvement is the transition into the most dangerous stage.

01.1.5Core temperature thresholds

Hypothermia stages across four bands, each with a protocol-defining threshold. Prepper's Medical Handbook and TW-05 converge on the figures.

Hypothermia stages — core-temperature bands
01NORMAL98.6°F / 37.0°C · Baseline function.
02MILD90–95°F / 32.2–35°C · Intense shivering, impaired fine motor, confusion. Passive rewarm: dry clothes, shelter, warm fluids if conscious.
03MODERATE82–90°F / 27.8–32.2°C · Shivering cessation, severe ataxia, stupor. Gentle handling (cardiac irritability); active rewarm.
04SEVERE<82°F / <27.8°C · Coma, ventricular fibrillation risk, apnea, apparent death. "No one dead until warm and dead."

The 82°F threshold is the cardiac-arrhythmia inflection: below this band the heart is electrically unstable and rough movement can trigger ventricular fibrillation. Cold-water submersion revivals are documented at 66 minutes submerged because cold preserves neural tissue while suspending function. ROUGH HANDLING OF A MODERATE-TO-SEVERE HYPOTHERMIC IS ITS OWN CAUSE OF DEATH.

01.1.6Caloric demand under cold

The food band is not the band that kills cold-weather operators. The TW-05 nutrition chapter and Advanced Bushcraft Chapter 4 specify the operational budget.

Caloric-demand budget

SEDENTARY BASELINE · ~2,000 kcal/day · Indoor, resting, thermoregulated. COLD-WEATHER OPERATIONAL · ~4,500 kcal/day · USMC cold-weather-ops figure cited by TW-05. RUCKING UNDER LOAD · 5,000–6,000 kcal/day · Backpack + movement + cold. EXTENDED BELOW-FREEZING WET · >6,000 kcal/day · Shivering tax plus movement plus load.

The operator at day five with a full food cache and no fire is not starving; they are freezing, because caloric intake cannot replace the heat loss that shivering is ledger-closing against. Cold multiplies the caloric deficit. A ration that sustains a warm operator starves a cold operator, because shivering is taxing the same budget that baseline metabolism draws from. The implication for the food section in 01.5 and the kit architecture in 01.9: fat-dense and caloric-dense reserves beat equivalent protein weight in cold climates by a wide margin.

01.1.7Water loss rates

The three-day band compresses under exertion and heat. Harvesting H2O Chapter 1 and TW-05 specify the graduated loss curve.

Water loss — daily operational bands
01RESTING ADULT~2 qt/day · Urine + respiration + perspiration baseline.
02MODERATE ACTIVITY~6 qt/day · Walking, light load, moderate temperature.
03HEAVY EXERTION OR HEAT~8 qt/day · Rucking, elevated ambient, load.
04EXTREME EXERTION ABOVE 85°F>12 qt/day · Alpine climbing, desert movement, fighting load in hot ambient.

The TW-05 field rule compresses the band-selection into a carry directive: 8 QT/DAY ON THE MOVE, 6 QT/DAY STATIC. The rule determines how fast the canteen empties, which determines when the water subsystem in 01.4 must activate. The three-day figure assumes moderate activity at moderate temperature; a summer desert march at exertion drops the band toward 36 hours, and an immersion or wound-hemorrhage scenario drops it further. Track the conditions; scale the band.

01.1.8The inverse-difficulty principle

The survival task that solves the most time-urgent problem is, by design, the easiest to execute. Advanced Bushcraft Chapter 1 and the TW-05 framing converge on this ordering.

Effort scales inversely to task difficulty and directly to time-to-death urgency. The hat costs nothing. The hunt costs a day.01.1.8 · Inverse-difficulty / inverse-urgency

Putting on a hat addresses the three-hour thermoregulation band in seconds. Zipping a collar addresses it in one motion. Sitting on a foot of dry debris rather than frozen ground addresses it in thirty seconds. These interventions have ~0 calorie cost and solve the band that kills fastest. Hunting large game to address the three-week food band costs ~3,000 kcal in pursuit energy, requires advanced skill, and solves the band that kills last. The operator who reads the principle backwards — hunting for food while shivering in wet cotton — consumes the last of the glycogen reserve on the task that solves the least urgent problem. Layperson error defaults to food first because hunger is the most felt sensation; first-level survivalist correction moves to water first; the fully installed ordering places shelter and fire above both.

01.1.9Canterbury's Ten Cs

Kit redundancy purchases time on the clock. Advanced Bushcraft Chapter 1 specifies ten replaceable field capabilities that, if carried, compress the time-and-calorie cost of primitive manufacture.

The Ten Cs — replaceable field capabilities
01CUTTING TOOLFixed-blade knife (FARMED-compliant).
02COMBUSTION DEVICEFerro rod, lighter, matches.
03COVERTarp, poncho, mylar blanket.
04CONTAINERMetal 32 oz Nalgene or single-walled steel bottle.
05CORDAGEParacord 550 or equivalent.
06COTTONBandanna or shemagh — tinder, bandage, filter, pre-filter, tourniquet pad.
07COMPASSBaseplate with declination adjustment.
08CANDLING DEVICEHeadlamp with fresh batteries.
09CARGO TAPEGorilla or duct tape for repair and medical.
10CANVAS NEEDLELarge-eye for cordage or stitching.

Canterbury's rule on the Ten Cs: every C can be re-manufactured from the environment, but every re-manufacture costs calories and time that are often priced from higher-priority tasks. A cutting tool takes ~30 minutes to knap from flint in skilled hands and ~8 hours untrained; a container takes ~6 hours to fire-harden from pitched bark. The kit imports the solved version of the problem so the clock stays available for the problems the operator cannot pre-solve.

01.1.10FARMED — blade criteria

The cutting tool dominates kit priority because it multiplies every other C. Advanced Bushcraft Chapter 2 specifies the six criteria.

FARMED — fixed-blade selection

F · FULL TANG · Steel runs through the full handle length; no partial-tang hollow handles. A · ABOVE 5" BLADE LENGTH · Enough to baton through 4–6" wood. R · RIGHT STEEL · High-carbon (1095, O1, 1084) for sparking and sharpenability; no stainless (poor sharpening at field-standard). M · MULTIPURPOSE · No serrations, no partial edges, no compound grinds. E · EDGE GEOMETRY · Scandi grind or high-saber grind for carving and batoning. D · DIMENSIONS · Overall ≤10"; blade 5–6" Goldilocks.

A FARMED-compliant knife throws sparks on a ferro rod (the M and R criteria interlock), batons through wood up to 6" (the A and E criteria), carves a bow-drill spindle (the E criterion), processes game without breaking (the F criterion), and survives use as a pry (the F and D criteria). ONE BLADE. FIVE JOBS. The knife earns its weight several times per operational day in a below-freezing deployment, which is why the FARMED criteria override preference on a serious carry.

01.1.11The STOP decision-pause

Panic movement kills more lost operators than starvation. Advanced Bushcraft Chapter 1 and the wilderness-survival canon specify the four-step decision pause.

STOP — decision-pause protocol
01SSTOP · Cease all movement immediately upon recognizing you are lost or stranded.
02TTHINK · Inventory what is on your person, in your pack, and within arm's reach.
03OOBSERVE · Survey terrain, weather, daylight remaining, injuries, teammates.
04PPLAN · Sequence against Rule of Threes: airway → shelter/fire if cold → water within 24 hr → signal/extraction → food.

The S step is the load-bearing one. "Keep walking to find a road" is the most common fatal error in lost-person cases — it burns glycogen, disorients, and strands the operator further from known landmark and from rescuers searching the last-known-point. The T and O steps generate the inventory the P step orders. The P step writes the sequence that the remaining sub-module sections execute.

01.1.12PACE per primitive

Single-point failures in any primitive are terminal. TW-05 equipment chapter formalizes the four-layer redundancy; Canterbury's Ten Cs imply it across the kit.

PACE — redundancy layers

P · PRIMARY · First-choice solution, fastest, most reliable. A · ALTERNATE · Direct backup, same-class tool. C · CONTINGENCY · Degraded option using a different mechanism. E · EMERGENCY · Last resort, primitive-manufactured or field-expedient.

Fire PACE: (P) Bic lighter → (A) ferro rod → (C) flint-and-steel with char cloth → (E) bow drill. Water PACE: (P) carried water → (A) filter pump → (C) boil → (E) solar still or distillation. Shelter PACE: (P) packed tent → (A) tarp-and-cordage A-frame → (C) natural debris hut → (E) tree well or snow trench or body-heat sharing. THREE-DEEP ACROSS THREE FAILURE MODES is the minimum for any primitive the operator's life depends on. The kit architecture in 01.9 builds every irreplaceable function to this standard.

01.1.13Food-before-shelter is the layperson error

Felt sensation drives layperson triage. Hunger is the loudest signal at day one of displacement, which places food first in the untrained intuition. Advanced Bushcraft Chapter 1 names the error and corrects it.

WARN

Food first is the wrong answer. Water first is the first-level correction. Shelter and fire above both is the full ordering.

Hunger registers as discomfort within hours; dehydration registers as fatigue within a day; hypothermia registers as cold within minutes but masks its own cascade under shivering. The sensation-to-threat mapping inverts exactly where it matters most. The most felt sensation is rarely the most immediate threat; the threat that can take the operator out in the next ninety minutes is the one that should be triaged first, regardless of which sensation is loudest. The fully installed ordering — shelter and fire, water, food, in that sequence — is the subsystem this section installs.

01.1.14The kit in your head weighs nothing

Canterbury's introduction specifies the overriding principle: equipment is a time-discount on rehearsed skill, not a substitute. Advanced Bushcraft opens on this claim before any gear recommendation.

The kit in your head weighs nothing. The river, the thief, and the bear cannot take it. Prioritize rehearsed skill over equipment hoarding; equipment discounts the time skill solves the problem in, but equipment alone solves no problem.01.1.14 · Knowledge as primitive asset

A ferro rod is a paperweight to an operator who has never started a fire in the rain with one. A tourniquet in sealed packaging has never been practiced under the stress of a bleeding partner. REHEARSAL COMPOUNDS. CARRY ALONE DOES NOT. The rehearsed skill runs when the gear is lost, when the gear fails, and when the conditions degrade beyond the gear's design envelope. The kit-plus-skill compound is the asset; the kit alone is a liability priced in carry weight.

01.1.15Ceiling-vs-clock — case data

Wilderness-medicine case files keep the rule honest. Advanced Bushcraft Chapter 4 and TW-05 hypothermia chapter both document the same class of fatalities across temperate-zone cases.

Case class — "mild-weather" hypothermia fatalities

Hikers dead of hypothermia at ambient temperatures as high as 50°F, wet and wind-exposed, in under 3 hours. Core-to-cardiac-arrest chain completes in under 90 minutes in worst-case wet + wind + cotton combinations. Spring and fall account for more hypothermia fatalities in temperate climates than mid-winter deep-cold events, because the operator dresses for the ambient without accounting for wet-and-wind transition.

The case class refutes the literal-clock read. Fifty-degree ambient is "mild" by ambient-only reading; it is "lethal in ninety minutes" by full-condition reading. The band does not care what the thermometer says — it cares what the combination of wet, wind, ambient, and clothing sets the heat-loss rate at. The operator in 01.2 installs the clothing-layer and shelter-siting discipline that keeps the band at its mild-conditions ceiling.

01.1.16Install, function, failure, feed-forward

INSTALL. You load the four-band ordering as the default triage every decision passes through. You carry the Ten Cs as kit scaffold and run a FARMED-compliant blade as the one-tool multiplier. You rehearse the STOP decision-pause until it runs automatically on recognition of a lost-or-stranded condition. You build PACE redundancy three-deep across every primitive your life depends on. You calibrate the rule as a category-scale, not a countdown — reading conditions to scale the band duration up or down from the canonical figures.

FUNCTION INDICATORS. The subsystem functions when your first response to any degraded-condition event is a silent triage pass through the four bands in order. Cold-wet conditions default to shelter-and-fire before water despite the felt urgency of thirst. The Ten Cs carry pattern shows no single-point failures in any irreplaceable function. Your STOP pause consumes 30 seconds of decision time and returns a sequenced plan. Every primitive has a named P, A, C, and E option carried or pre-rehearsed.

FAILURE INDICATORS. The subsystem fails when panic movement burns calories and strands the operator further from known landmark. It fails when food triage runs first because hunger is the loudest sensation. It fails when the shivering teammate is read as "handling it" and the inflection to cessation is missed. It fails when a primitive carries only one layer of redundancy, because a single gear loss collapses the subsystem. It fails when the kit runs without rehearsal — the ferro rod that has never started a rainy fire is no different from no ferro rod at all.

FEED-FORWARD. Shelter and thermoregulation install next in 01.2 — the subsystem that drives the three-hour band from ceiling-at-ninety-minutes back to ceiling-at-several-hours through clothing discipline, site selection, and primitive shelter geometry. The triage ordering this section installs is the ruler every subsequent section measures against.

theFIELD.run / CONSTRUCT_APPLICATIONS / 01 PRIMARY SYSTEMS / 01.2 Shelter systems and thermal regulation
SECTION 01.2

Shelter systems and thermal regulation

METABOLIC OUTPUT~100 W AT REST
GROUND CONDUCTION25× STILL AIR
UNDER-SLEEPER COMPRESSED≥4 in
HEAD RADIATION~40% CORE
COTTON WATER UPTAKE27× DRY WEIGHT
WOOL WET R-VALUE~80%
DEBRIS DEPTH≥3 ft UNCOMPRESSED → ~12 in COMPRESSED
LATRINE CLEARANCE≥200 ft FROM WATER · ≥3 ft ABOVE WATER TABLE
LATENT HEAT OF VAPORIZATION~540 cal/g

Shelter traps output; it does not generate heat. The human body radiates, convects, and conducts roughly 100 W of metabolic heat to the environment at rest, and a primitive shelter's entire function is to reduce the rate at which that heat escapes. Advanced Bushcraft Chapter 3 anchors the siting and construction spine, the First Aid Manual TW-05 cold-weather chapter and US Army cold-weather doctrine supply the COLD clothing-discipline mnemonic and the three-layer system, and Stewart's 365 Essential Survival Skills contributes the raised-bed frame and the wedge-canopy field variants.

This section installs the thermoregulation subsystem. You load the heat-retention container framing that corrects the laypersons's "warm the shelter" intuition, the four modes of heat loss (conduction, convection, radiation, evaporation) that govern every design decision, the ground-conduction inversion that puts insulation under the sleeper before insulation over, the Four Ws of site selection that screen every potential site before the first stake, the COLD mnemonic that compresses cold-weather clothing discipline into four audit points, the three-layer base-insulation-shell system, the cotton-kills / wool-works-wet fabric law, the minimum-volume principle that sizes shelter to the body, the debris-hut build sequence, the tarp configuration catalog, the raised-platform bed that eliminates ground conduction, the pit-latrine siting rules that route sanitation out of the watershed, the log-cabin permanent-primitive upgrade, and the install protocol, function indicators, failure modes, and feed-forward handoffs. Sources: Advanced Bushcraft Ch 3 and Ch 4 (Four Ws, debris hut, raised bed, log cabin, latrine siting, cascade chain); TW-05 (COLD, three-layer system, heat-loss modes, hypothermia staging); Stewart's 365 (wedge canopy, raised-frame variants, Yukon-stove coupling).

01.2.1The shelter is a heat-retention container

Primitive shelter produces zero heat. It lowers the rate at which your body's ~100 W of metabolic output leaks to the environment. Advanced Bushcraft Chapter 3 opens the shelter chapter on this correction because the common error — building the biggest shelter the timber allows — collapses the equilibrium temperature rise that the occupant's fixed heat source can drive against a variable-volume air sink.

The heat-retention container

A shelter that holds one operator at 100 W equilibrates its interior above ambient by a margin proportional to heat source ÷ interior volume × insulation R-value. Doubling interior volume roughly halves the equilibrium rise from body heat alone. Minimum-volume shelters are warmest.

The operational consequence reverses the layperson build: SIZE THE SHELTER TO THE OPERATOR, NOT TO THE TIMBER. You build to within inches of the body, with overhead clearance only as much as sitting upright demands, and with interior volume that one person's metabolic output can lift against the insulation of the walls. A shelter that feels "spacious" is a shelter that is thermally useless.

01.2.2Four modes of heat loss

The body loses heat through four physical channels, and every shelter decision targets one or more of them. TW-05 hypothermia chapter and Advanced Bushcraft Chapter 4 converge on the enumeration.

Heat loss — four modes with targeted intervention
01CONDUCTIONDirect contact with cold surface · Ground insulation ≥4 in compressed.
02CONVECTIONAir or water moving past skin · Wind shell, site windbreak, shelter-opening orientation.
03RADIATIONIR emission to cold sky or surroundings · Hat, scarf, enclosed shelter geometry.
04EVAPORATIONLatent heat carried away by vapor (~540 cal/g) · Shell venting, dry change, COLD discipline.

Conduction removes heat roughly 25× faster through wet soil than through still air of the same temperature. Wind at 20 mph over 20°F air drains more heat than still air at 40°F. Roughly 40% of core radiation exits from head, neck, and upper torso, which is why a hat and scarf delete more heat loss than any chest-layer upgrade. Each gram of water evaporating from skin carries ~540 cal of latent heat with it, which is why sweat-soaked insulation collapses into a conductive compress. Each mode requires its own intervention, and a shelter that addresses three of four still hemorrhages heat through the neglected channel.

01.2.3Ground conduction dominates

The ground drains heat at ~25× the rate of still air of equal temperature, and body weight compresses most sleeping pads to near-zero loft. Advanced Bushcraft Chapter 3 fixes the rule directly: the warmth comes from under you, not over you.

A 20°F night with 4 in of pine duff below you is warmer than a 40°F night with a bare tarp on frozen ground.01.2.3 · The under-rule

The operational rule: PUT THE INSULATION UNDER YOU FIRST. You measure insulation depth at compression, not at loft. Closed-cell foam and spruce boughs hold thickness under load; down bags collapse to near-zero R-value under sleeper weight. A down bag rated to 0°F fails to its rating on bare ground because its under-side is pinned. Canterbury's minimum is ≥4 in compressed underneath the sleeper. Cold-ground conduction is the single most underestimated fatal channel in primitive shelter, because the subjective experience of cold concentrates on the exposed upper body while the lethal drain runs through the pressure contact below.

01.2.4The Four Ws of site selection

Canterbury's mnemonic screens every potential site before a stake drives. Advanced Bushcraft Chapter 3 enforces all four as non-negotiable.

The Four Ws — pre-build site audit
01WINDDownwind of prevailing weather · Terrain or dense conifer windbreak · Opening oriented away from prevailing flow · Fire reflector opposite opening.
02WATER100–300 ft from source · Above flood line · Out of gullies and dry washes (flash-flood capture) · Off animal trails converging at dusk.
03WIDOWMAKERSCanopy scan for standing-dead trees, hanging branches, loose rock · A falling widowmaker kills more campers than cold.
04WOODAbundant deadfall for fire · Live standing trees for cordage and bough collection · Tinder trees (birch, cedar, cottonwood) within walking distance.

The audit runs in sequence: wind first because convective drain degrades every other subsystem, water second because proximity and flood geometry govern overnight survival, widowmakers third because a single canopy failure ends the operator outright, wood fourth because fuel scarcity forces a site relocation inside the same conditions. Skip any W and the shelter is conditional on luck rather than design.

01.2.5The COLD clothing-discipline mnemonic

Clothing is the first shelter. TW-05 cold-weather chapter and US Army cold-weather doctrine compress the discipline into four audit points.

COLD — four-point clothing audit

CLEAN · Dirty insulation loses loft; body oils and soot compress fibers. OVERHEATING AVOIDED · Sweat-soaked insulation is conductive and loses ≥90% of insulative value. LOOSE / in LAYERS · Dead-air space is insulation; tight cuffs, belts, boot laces defeat it. DRY · Wet insulation kills; change socks at halt; dry against skin if necessary.

The COLD audit runs at every halt. YOU ADJUST LAYERS BEFORE AND AFTER EXERTION, NOT DURING. Starting a climb overclothed produces sweat-soaked base layers that turn into an evaporative refrigerator when the pace drops at the ridge. Ending a halt in the damp layer you arrived in produces the same failure. The correct cadence: strip before starting a climb, add layers at the top before you cool, change socks at every halt that lasts over 30 min. Overheating in cold weather is a cold-weather injury in slow motion; the sweat it produces is the failure mode.

01.2.6The three-layer clothing system

The three-layer system assigns distinct physical functions to distinct garments. TW-05 and Advanced Bushcraft Chapter 4 converge on the architecture.

Three-layer clothing system — function per layer
01BASE / WICKINGMerino wool or synthetic · NEVER cotton · Moves vapor off skin before it condenses in insulation.
02INSULATIONFleece, down, synthetic fill · Traps dead air · Loft = warmth · Compression = failure.
03SHELLWind and water repellent · Breathable (Gore-Tex class) · Blocks convection and precipitation · Vents open at halts to dump moisture.

Each layer fails without the other two. A shell without insulation blocks wind but has no R-value to hold heat against. Insulation without shell wets out and collapses in any wind or precipitation. Base layer without wicking function holds sweat against skin and turns insulation into a wet compress. The system is a compound of three interdependent functions, and operators who skip one layer run a two-of-three kit that fails to the skipped mode first.

01.2.7Cotton kills; wool works wet

Cotton absorbs ~27× its dry weight in water, retains 0–10% of dry insulative value when wet, and dries slowly. TW-05 cold-weather chapter and wilderness-medicine canon fix cotton as a direct cause of hypothermia in cold conditions.

WARN

A cotton base layer in cold-wet conditions is the single fastest-acting kit failure in the primary-systems stack. The cascade of insults completes in under 90 min in immersion, wind, and wet cotton. Wool retains roughly 80% of insulative value wet; synthetic fleece retains ~70%.

The inversion holds in desert heat: wetted cotton becomes an evaporative cooler, the same property that kills in cold saves against heat stroke. The fabric choice is conditional on climate, and the same garment that solves the desert daytime problem is the garment that kills on the cold-wet slope after sunset. Operators who train in one climate and deploy to another carry forward a fabric assumption that turns lethal at the first climate inversion.

01.2.8Minimum-volume shelter principle

Doubling shelter interior volume roughly halves the equilibrium temperature rise that the occupant's body heat produces. Advanced Bushcraft Chapter 3 fixes the rule as a direct consequence of fixed heat source against variable heat sink.

The design consequence: BUILD TO WITHIN INCHES OF THE BODY. A debris hut interior runs barely larger than the occupant's sleeping envelope. A tarp plow-point wraps the operator in a conic volume barely exceeding sitting height. A snow trench compresses to shoulder width plus a few inches. The warmest shelters in the primitive catalog are the smallest shelters that allow sleep, because every cubic foot of additional air volume is a cubic foot of heat sink the operator's 100 W must lift. A shelter that looks comfortable is a shelter that has abandoned the thermal calculus; a shelter that looks cramped is a shelter that has been sized for survival.

01.2.9The debris hut sequence

The debris hut is the canonical emergency primitive. Advanced Bushcraft Chapter 3 and Stewart's 365 converge on the eight-step build.

Debris hut — ordered build sequence
01SITEFlat ground, overhead clearance (Four Ws screen).
02RIDGEPOLEBears several hundred pounds of debris weight · One end at ~3 ft in tree crotch or stump · Other end on ground · Length ~1.5× occupant height.
03RIBBINGLean sticks against ridgepole at ~45° · Spacing 6–8 in.
04CROSS-LATTICESmaller branches perpendicular to ribbing · Holds debris from falling through.
05DEBRISDry leaves, pine needles, grass · Pile ≥3 ft thick uncompressed → ~12 in compressed insulation.
06THATCHShingled bark slabs over debris if rain expected.
07INTERIOR BED≥12 in compressed boughs or grass · Raised off ground if possible.
08DOOR PLUGPre-built debris bundle to seal entrance after entering.

The dominant failure mode is DEBRIS TOO THIN. Layperson intuition underestimates depth by a factor of two to three; the pile looks excessive at the depth that compresses to adequate insulation. The second failure is ridgepole undersized: a ridgepole that bends under debris weight collapses into the occupant mid-night. The debris hut fails silently at the boundary of its insulation margin; the occupant feels cold an hour after lying down, when the compressed insulation proves inadequate and there is no recovery short of rebuilding in the dark.

01.2.10Tarp configurations

A tarp trades weight for speed and coverage across several geometric modes. Advanced Bushcraft Chapter 3 and Stewart's 365 catalog the primary configurations.

Tarp configurations — geometry vs. use case
01A-FRAME / RIDGELINEFast setup · Sheds precipitation well · Open on two ends (worst wind).
02PLOW-POINT / DIAMOND-FLYOne corner staked high, opposite pinned low · Omnidirectional wind · Single-person.
03LEAN-TO + FIRE REFLECTORTarp face toward reflector wall · Fire between reflector and shelter · Radiant heat returns to occupant.
04WEDGE CANOPY (Stewart)Shaped-wedge orientation exploits prevailing wind flow-over.

The lean-to configuration uniquely couples shelter with fire: the reflector wall returns IR that would otherwise radiate past the fire into cold sky, and the tarp face catches and re-radiates the return. This is the Yukon-stove coupling Stewart's 365 documents in the wedge variant. A tarp is the highest leverage item in the kit per ounce when the operator carries the configuration catalog in the head; without the catalog, it is a blue plastic rectangle.

01.2.11The raised-platform bed

A raised bed eliminates the conduction channel entirely by separating sleeper from ground. Advanced Bushcraft Chapter 3 and Stewart's 365 document the primary configuration.

The build runs four stakes or tree-forks, two longitudinal rails laid 12–24 in above ground, transverse ribs, and 4–6 in of compressed boughs or grass. The geometry delivers three compounding advantages. Ground conduction is gone — the 25× drain rate against air cannot reach the sleeper. Ground moisture is gone — morning dew and rain runoff pass beneath. Exit is easier — the sleeper sits up into boots at bed height rather than bending to ground-level.

NOTE

The raised bed trades construction time (1–2 hr additional) against recurring nightly insulation cost. On a stay longer than one night, the amortization strongly favors the raised build. On a single-night bivouac the debris-hut interior bed dominates.

The platform is the single highest-return shelter upgrade beyond the core weatherproof envelope; it converts a survivable shelter into a sleep-quality shelter, and sleep quality compounds into decision quality across every subsequent subsystem.

01.2.12Pit latrine siting

Sanitation is thermoregulation-adjacent because a camp-sourced illness degrades the operator's capacity to maintain every primitive. Advanced Bushcraft Chapter 3 fixes the siting rules.

Pit latrine siting — clearances and discipline
01WATER TABLEPit floor ≥3 ft above local water table.
02WATER SOURCE≥200 ft from any water source or shelter.
03GRADIENTDownhill of water sources, never uphill.
04COVERLid or dirt cover when not in use · Limits insect vector and scent signature.
05TREATMENTLime or ash sprinkle between uses.

Pathogen contamination of the watershed is the dominant failure mode. A latrine uphill of a spring contaminates the source; a latrine less than 200 ft from a shelter invites rodent and insect vectors into the sleeping zone. The discipline compounds with 01.4's water-procurement standard: every field water source assumes upstream contamination by default, and the camp's own latrine is the first contamination the operator controls. The operator who routes sanitation correctly at camp construction avoids a preventable illness layer that dominates the casualty load on long stays.

01.2.13The log-cabin permanent primitive

A log cabin extends the shelter subsystem to long-horizon deployment. Advanced Bushcraft Chapter 3 specifies the construction parameters.

Load walls run 8–10 in diameter logs notched at corners (saddle notch simplest). Chinking runs moss and clay packed between courses. Roof pitch runs ≥30° to shed snow load. Hearth sits on an earth or stone pad. Smoke vent runs a hole or primitive chimney. A two-person build of a sub-100 sqft cabin runs 2–4 weeks depending on tools and stock wood.

NOTE

The log cabin is the 05-Sustainment layer's shelter primitive, not the 01-Primary-Systems layer. It enters 01.2 as the upgrade path beyond debris hut and raised bed, and it hands forward to 01.9 integration and 05 infrastructure. Operators at the primary-systems layer execute to the debris-hut standard and plan forward to the cabin standard only when deployment horizon exceeds the 30-day threshold.

The upgrade path from debris hut to tarp plow-point to raised-platform lean-to to log cabin is a continuous series of compounding investments, and the operator who runs the series in order builds habitable infrastructure without ever executing a decision outside the current subsystem's caloric and time budget.

01.2.14The ground-to-air channel inversion

Layperson shelter intuition concentrates insulation above the sleeper (the heavy blanket, the thick sleeping bag). Physical reality concentrates the drain below the sleeper (ground conduction at ~25× the rate of air convection above).

The inversion holds across every configuration. A 40°F night under an uninsulated tarp on frozen ground is colder than a 20°F night with 4 in of pine duff under a minimal cover. A 0°F-rated sleeping bag on bare ground performs worse than a 20°F bag on a full closed-cell foam pad. A debris hut with inadequate interior bed is colder than a lean-to with a full raised-platform.

You do not need a warmer bag. You need a thicker pad. The warmth is under you, not over you.01.2.14 · The operational inversion

The rule compounds with every downstream primitive. Fire-craft prioritizes the heated-rock "bed warmer" for the under-sleeper zone because that zone drives the thermal accounting. Water procurement in cold weather prioritizes the morning snowmelt into a pot over collecting frost directly because frost on skin is an evaporation channel the operator cannot afford. Every cold-weather decision audits against the ground channel first; the air channel is subordinate.

01.2.15Install, function, failure, feed-forward

INSTALL. On arrival at any halt, you run the Four Ws in order before selecting the site. You run the COLD audit on the clothing system at the same time. You set ground insulation before vertical structure. You size the interior volume to the operator, not to the timber. You build toward the debris-hut standard as the floor, upgrade to tarp plow-point when cover is available, upgrade to raised-platform when stay exceeds one night, and plan forward to cabin when stay exceeds the 30-day horizon.

FUNCTION. The subsystem runs correctly when interior equilibrium rises above ambient by the margin the operator's 100 W output can drive against the wall R-value, when no heat-loss mode runs uncorrected, when the ground-to-air channel inversion is honored, and when the sanitation clearances protect the watershed from the camp.

FAILURE. The subsystem fails when a single channel leaks: cotton base layer under shell, bare tarp on frozen ground without ground insulation, shelter sized for appearance rather than occupant, opening oriented into prevailing wind, debris pile at the depth that looks adequate rather than the depth that compresses to adequate, or latrine sited where runoff reaches the water catchment.

FEED-FORWARD. Shelter traps the body's output. Fire supplements it. The lean-to with fire reflector couples the two primitives explicitly, and the next section installs the combustion subsystem that compounds with every shelter geometry you now hold.

theFIELD.run / CONSTRUCT_APPLICATIONS / 01 PRIMARY SYSTEMS / 01.3 Fire ignition and fire-craft
SECTION 01.3

Fire ignition and fire-craft

FERRO-ROD SPARK~3000°C · ~3000 STRIKES LIFE
CHAR-CLOTH CATCH~800°F
MAGNESIUM BURN~5000°F · 2–3 sec
BOW-DRILL DUST>800°F · 1/3 NOTCH RULE
SPINDLE1/4–1" DIAMETER · 6–12" LENGTH
CURFEW RECOVERY8–12 hr UNDER 3–4" ASH
GATHER RULETINDER / KINDLING / FUEL AT 3× EXPECTED
FIRE TRIANGLEFUEL + ~21% O₂ + HEAT
LATENT HEAT VAPORIZATION~540 cal/g
KMnO₄ + GLYCERIN30–60 sec SELF-IGNITE

Fire raises a tiny amount of easily-ignited fuel above its ignition temperature while oxygen flows across it, then chains the flame through progressively larger fuel sizes. Fire Skills 50 Methods anchors the mechanism catalog across twenty ignition modes; Advanced Bushcraft Chapter 2 supplies the tinder-kindling-fuel hierarchy and the fire-lay geometry catalog; Stewart's 365 Essential Survival Skills supplies the field-expedient compound tinders and the curfew-banking protocol.

This section installs the fire subsystem. You load the fire triangle as the three simultaneous conditions ignition requires, the tinder / kindling / fuel size hierarchy and the 3× gather rule, the ignition taxonomy across ferrocerium, flint-and-steel, magnesium, friction, solar, and chemical modes, the char-cloth manufacture that bridges spark-duration mismatches, the fire-lay geometry catalog matched to function, the curfew banking and fire-carry techniques that preserve heat across downtime, the Six P's discipline that sequences preparation before ignition, the tinder-bundle build and the blow-across-ember oxygen-delivery correction, the one-match-one-fire rule, and the install protocol, function indicators, failure modes, and feed-forward handoffs. Sources: Fire Skills 50 Methods (ignition catalog, char cloth, fire-carry); Advanced Bushcraft Ch 2 (tinder hierarchy, fire-lay geometry, Six P's); Stewart's 365 (curfew banking, compound tinders, blow discipline); TW-05 cold-weather chapter (fire as hypothermia-spiral interrupt).

01.3.1The fire triangle

Three elements must contact simultaneously for combustion. Fire Skills 50 Methods anchors the diagram at the front of its introduction.

Fire triangle — three simultaneous conditions

01 · FUEL · Combustible matter, sized in a hierarchy from tinder through kindling through fuel logs. 02 · OXYGEN · ~21% of ambient air suffices in any unrestricted environment. 03 · HEAT · Ignition source raising fuel surface above its ignition temperature.

Remove any one element and fire extinguishes. Smother a flame and you eliminate oxygen. Separate fuel from heat and you break the chain. Deny the heat of continued combustion through water absorption of latent heat at ~540 cal/g and the triangle collapses. EVERY FAILED FIRE IS A MISSING SIDE. The operational consequence: diagnose a failed ignition by checking which side of the triangle is absent — wet fuel is fuel-side failure, suffocated fire-lay is oxygen-side failure, cold-spark-to-unprepared-tinder is heat-side failure.

01.3.2Tinder, kindling, fuel — the size hierarchy

Fire chains through fuel sizes. Advanced Bushcraft Chapter 2 specifies the three classes.

Fuel hierarchy — ignition-to-sustain chain
01TINDERDry, fibrous, high-surface-area material ignitable by spark or ember. Birch-bark shavings, inner cedar bark, cottonwood fluff, dry grass, punk wood, fatwood shavings, char cloth, jute-twine fluff, cotton ball in petroleum jelly.
02KINDLINGPencil-lead through pencil-thickness dry twigs. Graded into two sub-classes — matchstick and pencil — stacked separately.
03FUELThumb-to-wrist for main fire. Wrist-to-leg for overnight sustaining burn. Split wood dries faster and burns hotter than round.

The 3× gather rule governs: you assemble three times the volume of each class you think you need before striking the first spark. Underestimation is the default field error; a tinder bundle that seemed adequate gives out at the kindling transition and the operator scrambles for more material while the ember dies. The fire that fails at minute two fails because the kindling pile was assembled at minute three rather than minute zero. Stacking discipline matches gather discipline — tinder on the dry platform, matchstick kindling at arm's reach, pencil kindling behind it, fuel split and stacked within the fire circle's perimeter.

01.3.3Ignition taxonomy — spark class

Ferrocerium, flint-and-steel, and magnesium partition the spark-ignition class. Fire Skills 50 Methods anchors the mechanisms.

Spark ignition — three mechanisms
01FERRO RODMicroscopic iron-cerium alloy shaved into air; friction heat ignites each particle mid-flight at ~3000°C for milliseconds per spark. Standard 3/8" × 5" rod lasts ~3000 strikes.
02FLINT-AND-STEELHigh-carbon steel shaved by sharp flint; microscopic carbon chips oxidize instantly, landing on char cloth that catches at ~800°F. Antiquity: millennia of field use.
03MAGNESIUMShavings ignite at ~5000°F for 2–3 sec flash, flash-drying marginal tinder. Rod form combines magnesium block with ferro-rod edge.

Sparks are hotter than flame, yet more tinders light from a match than from a ferro spark. IGNITION IS ENERGY TIMES TIME, NOT TEMPERATURE ALONE. A ferro spark delivers peak temperature for milliseconds; a match flame delivers lower temperature for seconds. Low-ignition receptors (char cloth, petroleum-jelly cotton ball) absorb the millisecond energy; natural tinders without preparation often do not. The counterintuitive consequence drives the fire PACE plan: you carry spark ignition as primary for weight and durability, and you carry char cloth or its equivalent as a non-optional companion.

01.3.4Ignition taxonomy — friction class

Bow drill is the rehearsed primitive that runs when every spark source is absent. Advanced Bushcraft Chapter 2 specifies the geometry.

Bow drill — rotational-friction ignition

SPINDLE · 1/4–1" diameter · 6–12" length · softwood (cedar, cottonwood, willow, yucca root, sotol stalk). FIREBOARD · 1/2–1" thick · matched species to spindle for matched hardness. NOTCH · Cut at 1/3 spindle width and 1/3 board depth at the edge of the spindle socket. BEARING BLOCK · Hardwood or stone with shallow depression; lubricated with earwax or pine pitch. BOW · Flexible branch ~24" with cordage loose enough to loop once around spindle.

Rotation raises wood dust in the notch above ~800°F; the dust blackens, coalesces into an ember, and the ember transfers to a tinder bundle. The 1/3 notch rule governs ember production: too shallow and dust scatters, too deep and the spindle wobbles. A bow drill in trained hands produces an ember in under a minute in dry conditions; in wet conditions no friction method works reliably, which is why the spark PACE layer sits above it. Hand drill and fire plow are lower-yield friction primitives carried as below-bow emergency redundancy.

01.3.5Ignition taxonomy — solar and chemical

The remaining ignition modes run from focused radiation or reagent reaction. Fire Skills 50 Methods catalogs the field variants.

Solar and chemical — alternative ignition modes
01FRESNEL LENSCredit-card-size page-magnifier focuses sunlight to ignition at mid-day solar elevation.
02MAGNIFIERAny convex lens above ~2" focal length.
03CLEAR-ICE LENSCarve convex lens from clear river ice; works below freezing in sun.
04POLISHED SODA-CAN BASEPolished with chocolate, toothpaste, or fine ash to mirror finish; concave base focuses to ignition distance.
05WATER-FILLED BALLOON OR CLEAR BAGActs as converging lens.
06KMnO₄ + GLYCERINPotassium permanganate crystals plus glycerin self-ignite in 30–60 sec.
079V BATTERY + STEEL WOOLFine #0000 steel wool across terminals flames on contact.
08CAR BATTERY + GRAPHITEJumper-cable arc across pencil-lead bridge ignites tinder.

Solar ignition fails without sun; chemical ignition fails without reagent carry. Both are contingency-layer capabilities that free the primary spark layer when the operator can pre-position reagents or exploit direct sunlight. Potassium permanganate double-books: fire-starter, water-disinfectant, wound-wash, and antifungal across four field functions, which is why 01.8 names it as a priority stocking item.

01.3.6Char cloth — the spark bridge

Char cloth bridges the spark-duration mismatch between ferro spark and natural tinder. Fire Skills 50 Methods specifies manufacture.

Char cloth — pyrolyzed cotton

MATERIAL · 100% cotton (bandanna, denim, duck canvas); synthetics melt rather than char. CUT · 2" squares stacked without compression. CONTAINER · Metal tin with single small vent hole (~1/16"). PROCESS · Set tin in existing coals; smoke emerges from vent for 5–10 min; seal tin when smoke ceases. COOL · Sealed, undisturbed, to ambient.

Opening the tin while hot admits oxygen and combusts the batch. ONE VENT. NO OPENING HOT. A correctly charred square blackens through its full thickness, stays flexible, and catches spark at ~800°F with a glowing ember propagating across the weave in seconds. The operator who carries ferro rod without char cloth carries half a subsystem; the operator who pairs char cloth with flint-and-steel carries the same compound capability with a lower-tech primary.

01.3.7Tinder-bundle architecture

The ember transfers from char cloth to tinder bundle to flame. Advanced Bushcraft Chapter 2 specifies the bundle build.

Tinder bundle — build geometry
01OUTER SHELLCoarse fibrous material (dry grass, cedar-bark strips) wrapped as a 6" × 3" football.
02MIDDLE LAYERFiner fibrous material (inner-bark shavings, cottonwood fluff, punk-wood crumbles).
03CORE DEPRESSIONGolf-ball-size indent in the center accepting the ember.
04STAGINGBundle held at mouth height, airflow path clear, kindling stack within arm's reach.

The ember drops into the core depression; the bundle folds closed; the operator raises to mouth height; the breath runs laterally across the ember, not onto it. Direct hard breath scatters heat and cools the ember; lateral airflow draws oxygen across the glowing surface and propagates the burn outward through the fibers. The bundle catches flame within ~15 seconds of correct blow technique, at which point it is laid into the fire-lay and the kindling cascade begins.

01.3.8Fire-lay geometry

Lay shape matches function. Advanced Bushcraft Chapter 2 catalogs the canonical geometries.

Fire-lay catalog — geometry by function
01TEPEEKindling tented over tinder; fastest ignition, tall flame, full-combustion heat; burns fuel rapidly.
02LOG CABINKindling stacked in squared layers around tinder core; medium duration, steady flame, solid coal bed.
03LEAN-TOSingle kindling spine propped at ~30° over tinder; wind-sheltered, one-match starts, low-profile.
04STARThree to five logs laid radially inward; minimum-wood overnight slow burn with the operator advancing logs as ends consume.
05LONG-FIRETwo parallel logs 3–4 ft long; sleeping parallel to fire gives radiant heat across body length. Pairs with reflector wall opposite sleeper.
06DAKOTA HOLETwo connected pits (~1 ft diameter, ~1 ft deep, joined by tunnel); concealed flame, wind-fed combustion, low smoke signature.

Selection orders against conditions. Rain runs lean-to for wind protection and rapid ignition. Cold bivy runs long-fire with reflector. Minimum-wood overnight runs star. Signaling runs tepee for maximum flame height. THE LAY IS DIAGNOSTIC. An operator who defaults to tepee regardless of condition burns through fuel budget and signals that the discipline layer is absent. Matched geometry is a fuel-economy decision that compounds across a multi-day deployment.

01.3.9Curfew banking

Overnight fire maintenance preserves coals without active tending. Stewart's 365 specifies the curfew protocol.

Curfew — overnight coal preservation

RAKE · Active coals into a compact mound at the fire center. ASH COVER · 3–4" fine dry ash evenly over the mound — thick enough to suppress flame-visible oxygen, thin enough to leave thermal gradient. FLANKING LOGS · Two small hardwood logs flanking the mound with ~1" airflow gap. SOIL SHOULDER · Mineral soil mounded around outer edges to contain spread. RECOVERY · 8–12 hr later: rake ash aside, apply gentle breath, feed tinder; live coals resume flame.

The technique saves the morning re-ignition cost. The fire curfew-banked at 2200 and recovered at 0600 spent zero calories on re-ignition; the operator who let it die spent glycogen on a rain-condition bow drill that may take several minutes to produce an ember. In freezing conditions the curfew is survival-critical: morning thermal gradient runs most hostile just before dawn, and a cold-dead fire-pit at that hour places the operator in the cascade-of-insults window during the hardest thermoregulation hour.

01.3.10Fire-carry — moving heat across distance

Portable embers save re-ignition time across movement. Fire Skills 50 Methods specifies three carriers.

Fire-carry — ember transport methods
01PUNK WOOD IN CANSmoldering punk wood in a vented metal can (~1/8" air holes on lid); carries hours with occasional gentle breath.
02FAT CIGARCommercial cigar smolders 30–60 min; stopgap carry for short repositioning.
03TINDER FUNGUSChaga or horseshoe fungus carries ember indefinitely with occasional air exposure; historical standard for coast-to-coast movement.

The carry mechanism depends on the ember's need for restricted oxygen. TOO MUCH AIR BURNS IT OUT. TOO LITTLE AIR SUFFOCATES IT. The vented can and the porous fungus both restrict airflow to the rate that sustains smolder without transitioning to flame. A fire-carry turns a single successful ignition into a multi-day heat asset; it operationalizes the first fire as the only fire the operator has to start across the deployment.

01.3.11The Six P's — preparation discipline

Ignition runs after preparation completes, never during. Advanced Bushcraft Chapter 2 names the discipline.

Proper Prior Preparation Prevents Poor Performance. The fire is built before the first spark — tinder gathered, kindling graded, fuel split and stacked, windbreak staked, dry platform laid. The strike is the last step, not the first.01.3.11 · Preparation is the ignition

Untrained operators strike first and gather after, losing the ember window while searching for kindling. The Six P's reverses the order. Every element of the lay assembles before the ignition source leaves its storage; the operator's hands are on the ferro rod only when every other variable is locked in. Rain doubles the discipline — the dry platform (split log laid flat, bark underside up), the windbreak (stacked rocks, pack, tarp corner), the tinder (kept dry inside a jacket), all stage before the strike. The fire that fails in rain fails because the platform was skipped; the fire that succeeds in rain succeeded because the P's ran in order.

01.3.12The one-match / one-fire rule

Every ignition gets one attempt. Fire Skills 50 Methods specifies the discipline.

One-match / one-fire

Treat every ignition as your last. Plan the lay, prepare the tinder, position the windbreak, stage the kindling, and commit to a single ignition attempt. Two matches is twice the failure rate; ten matches is a skill-absence signature.

The rule is a forcing function for the Six P's. An operator who expects a second attempt cuts corners on the first. An operator who commits to the one-match rule allocates preparation time proportional to the cost of failure. In cold-wet conditions the single-ignition discipline is survival-critical: every failed ignition consumes glycogen, tinder volume, and daylight, and the operator who runs ten matches is burning the reserve that later bands will need.

01.3.13Blow across, not onto

The instinctive breath scatters the ember. Stewart's 365 specifies the correction.

WARN

Do not blow onto the ember. Blow across it. Direct breath scatters heat laterally and cools the glowing surface; lateral airflow draws oxygen across the ember and propagates the burn outward through the fibers.

The error is muscle memory from candle-extinguishing reflex; the correction is deliberate redirection of the breath stream. LATERAL, NOT PERPENDICULAR. The bundle held at mouth height with the fold line horizontal and the breath directed past the ember toward the far edge of the bundle is the correct geometry. Every new fire-practitioner scatters at least one ember this way; the correction is built in the rehearsed session so the field attempt runs right.

01.3.14Fire as hypothermia-spiral interrupt

Fire is medical equipment in the cold-wet condition. TW-05 cold-weather chapter specifies the coupling.

In the cold-wet cascade, fire is the heat source that drives the hypothermia spiral backwards, the dryer that restores insulating capacity to wet clothing, and the cognitive anchor that holds decision function at the edge of the dexterity-collapse window.01.3.14 · Fire as clinical intervention

A lean-to with a reflector fire opposite restores operator core temperature in 30–60 min even under continued ambient cold exposure, by reversing the heat-loss ledger. Wet clothing dried on a frame at the fire's radiant edge returns to ~80% of dry R-value before hypothermia progresses past the mild stage. The medical read of fire, not the comfort read, is what puts fire second in the primitives ordering behind shelter; fire without shelter is a fire that burns out, and shelter without fire in cold-wet conditions is a container for a hypothermic operator.

01.3.15Install, function, failure, feed-forward

INSTALL. You gather tinder, kindling, and fuel at 3× expected volume before striking the first spark. You carry a three-deep PACE stack for ignition — lighter primary, ferro rod alternate, flint-and-steel-with-char-cloth contingency, bow drill emergency. You rehearse char-cloth manufacture until the batch runs reliably in an existing fire. You select the fire-lay geometry against the condition — lean-to in rain, long-fire in cold bivy, star for overnight minimum-wood, tepee for signaling. You run the Six P's in order before every ignition. You curfew the banking fire for any downtime over 2 hours.

FUNCTION INDICATORS. The subsystem functions when your first ignition sustains to full fuel in under 5 min across dry and wet conditions. The one-match rule holds — first-attempt success is the standard, not the exception. The fire-lay geometry matches the condition rather than defaulting to tepee. The curfew recovers live coals in 8–12 hr with gentle breath. The fire-carry moves heat across a camp repositioning without re-ignition cost.

FAILURE INDICATORS. The subsystem fails when the operator strikes with green tinder or gathered-too-little volume. It fails when char cloth is absent from a spark-only kit. It fails when the fire-lay is built in the wind opening rather than behind the break. It fails when hard breath extinguishes the ember that lateral breath would have propagated. It fails when the fire is allowed to die overnight in cold-wet conditions and the morning re-ignition runs inside the dexterity-collapse window.

FEED-FORWARD. Water procurement and purification installs next in 01.4 — the subsystem that rides on fire as the boil-kill primary method and on the heat-retention container shelter and fire jointly maintain. Fire couples with shelter through lean-to-and-reflector geometry; it couples with food through cooking and preservation; it couples with medical through hypothermia-spiral reversal and wound-cautery contingency. The next subsystem routes water through the boil-kill standard fire makes possible.

theFIELD.run / CONSTRUCT_APPLICATIONS / 01 PRIMARY SYSTEMS / 01.4 Water procurement, purification, storage
SECTION 01.4

Water procurement, purification, storage

MOVE RULE8 qt/day
STATIC RULE6 qt/day
WATER WEIGHT8.34 lb/gal
PATHOGEN CLASSES4
FILTER CUTOFFS0.2 µm BACTERIA · 1 µm CRYPTO · 0.02 µm VIRUS NEAR-CUT
BOIL185°F/10 min OR ROLLING 1 min · +2 min ABOVE 6500 ft
BLEACH FIELD DOSE2 drops/L · 30 min WAIT
IODINE 2%8 drops / half-gal · 30 min / 60 min COLD
US SURFACE-WATER FAILURE~90% POTABILITY
SOLAR STILL~1 pt/day
RAIN CATCH~600 gal/in PER 1000 ft²

Every field source is treated or proven safe, and clarity is not safety. Harvesting H2O anchors the pathogen taxonomy and the treatment hierarchy; the First Aid Manual TW-05 supplies the field hydration rule and the condition-class decision protocol; Canterbury's Ten Cs supply the container and the cordage that the procurement protocols run through.

This section installs the water subsystem. You load the four pathogen classes (bacteria, protozoa, helminths, viruses) and their size brackets, the treatment hierarchy ordered by reliability (distillation, boil, chemical, filtration, UV), the chlorine chemistry and the field bleach dose, the iodine contraindication catalog, the filtration cutoffs that separate filter classes, the solar still and transpiration bag as last-resort procurement, the rain-catchment yield formula, the 8 qt / 6 qt move-and-static rule, the snow-dehydrates counterintuitive that corrects the layperson "snow equals water" assumption, the pre-filtration-plus-definitive-treatment sequence, and the install protocol, function indicators, failure modes, and feed-forward handoffs. Sources: Harvesting H2O Ch 1 and Ch 2 (pathogen taxonomy, treatment hierarchy, still yields, rain catchment); TW-05 (8/6 rule, condition-class ordering, pre-filtration discipline); Stewart's 365 (field bleach mnemonic, solar still build); Advanced Bushcraft (boiling protocol, Ten Cs container integration).

01.4.1The four pathogen classes

Surface water loads four pathogen classes, each with a distinct size bracket and a distinct treatment profile. Harvesting H2O Chapter 1 maps the taxonomy.

Pathogen classes — size and treatment sensitivity
01BACTERIA0.2–5 µm · E. coli, Salmonella, Shigella, Vibrio cholerae, Campylobacter. Killed by boil, UV, chlorine, iodine, 0.2 µm filtration.
02PROTOZOA / PARASITES4–15 µm · Giardia lamblia, Cryptosporidium. Cryptosporidium resists chlorine; requires boil or 1 µm filtration.
03HELMINTHS>20 µm · Schistosoma, Ascaris, hookworm. Handled by any filter.
04VIRUSES20–300 nm · Rotavirus, hepatitis A and E, norovirus. Smaller than most filter pores; requires UV, chemical, or boil.

Roughly 90% of US surface water fails potability testing under Harvesting H2O's assessment. CLARITY IS NOT SAFETY. A clear alpine stream can carry any of the four classes, and the operator who drinks on clarity has not ruled them out. The treatment is chosen against the pathogen profile the source most likely carries — beaver-watershed runs Giardia-likely, agricultural runoff runs bacterial-likely, human-waste downstream runs viral-likely — and the treatment that covers every class in a single step is boiling.

01.4.2Treatment hierarchy — ordered by reliability

Methods order by how completely they reduce the pathogen load. Harvesting H2O Chapter 2 specifies the sequence.

Treatment hierarchy — reliability order
01DISTILLATIONBoil, capture vapor on cooled surface, collect condensate. Removes viruses, chemicals, heavy metals, radionuclides. Energy- and equipment-intensive.
02BOILING185°F for 10 min or rolling boil 1 min. +2 min above 6500 ft. Kills all four pathogen classes.
03CHEMICALChlorine or iodine oxidation of cell membranes and nucleic acids. Covers bacteria and viruses; Cryptosporidium resists chlorine.
04FILTRATIONPore-size exclusion. Covers bacteria, protozoa, helminths; does not reliably cover viruses above 0.02 µm.
05UV STERILIZATIONDisrupts nucleic acids. Requires clear water and batteries. Fast, battery-dependent.

No single method covers every class except boiling and, for clear water, distillation. BOIL IS THE UNIVERSAL. Every other method has a hole in its coverage. The operational consequence: when the source is unknown and the fire is up, the water goes in the pot. Filtration and chemical treatment are weight-and-time economies that apply when the source profile is characterized or when fire is not available.

01.4.3Chlorine chemistry

Chlorine oxidizes cell walls and nucleic acids. Harvesting H2O Chapter 2 and Stewart's 365 converge on the dose.

Chlorine — field doses

UNSCENTED HOUSEHOLD BLEACH · 5.25–6% sodium hypochlorite · 1/2 tsp / 5 gal clear water · 1 hr wait · double if cloudy · faint chlorine smell at end confirms dose. STEWART'S FIELD MNEMONIC · 2 drops / 1 L · 30 min wait · "drinking age 21." POOL CHLORINE (CALCIUM HYPOCHLORITE) · 65–75% granules · indefinite shelf life sealed dry. BLEACH SHELF LIFE · ~50% potency loss in 6–12 months after manufacture date.

The smell-test is the field check. No smell at the one-hour mark means under-dosed; re-dose and wait again. Pool chlorine stocks better than bleach by an order of magnitude in shelf life, which is why retreat caches run calcium hypochlorite granules and rehydrate at use rather than carrying degrading bleach. Cryptosporidium is the gap — chlorine does not kill it within useful field wait times, and boiling or filtration at ≤1 µm covers the gap.

01.4.4Iodine dosing and contraindications

Iodine covers what chlorine covers with a distinct contraindication profile. TW-05 and Harvesting H2O specify the dose and the contraindication catalog.

Iodine tincture 2%

DOSE · 8 drops / half-gallon (5 drops / qt) · 30 min wait · 60 min if cold (<40°F). CONTRAINDICATIONS · Pregnancy. Thyroid disorders (Graves', Hashimoto's). Iodine allergy. Cumulative long-term use above 6 weeks (thyroid suppression).

Iodine has the same Cryptosporidium gap as chlorine. NOT A UNIVERSAL. The contraindication catalog is non-trivial — a pregnant team member or a member with known Hashimoto's cannot run iodine for extended deployment, which puts bleach or boil on their personal PACE stack by default. Long-term use above six weeks suppresses thyroid function even in the absence of baseline disorder; the six-week window is the operational ceiling for any continuous-deployment iodine protocol.

01.4.5Filtration cutoffs

Pore size defines what a filter excludes. Harvesting H2O Chapter 2 catalogs the cutoffs.

Filtration cutoffs — pore size vs. pathogen
010.2 µm ABSOLUTEBacteria and protozoa. Standard hollow-fiber and ceramic field filters.
020.02 µm ULTRAFILTRATIONApproaches virus exclusion. Sawyer Mini class.
03<0.001 µm REVERSE OSMOSISExcludes viruses, dissolved salts, heavy metals. ~10% yield vs. ~90% brine reject. Pressure- or power-dependent.
04ACTIVATED CARBONNot a size filter. Adsorbs organics, chlorine, pesticides, some heavy metals. Saturates over use.

Activated carbon is a common layperson error — it pulls chemical load but does not reduce microbial count. CARBON IS NOT STERILIZATION. Pairing a 0.2 µm absolute filter with carbon post-treatment handles bacteria, protozoa, helminths, and chemical load, but still leaves viruses on the table. For the kit that runs filtration as primary, a chemical or UV virus-kill step layers behind the filter to close the gap.

01.4.6Solar still and transpiration

Two primitive procurement methods run when no liquid source is accessible. Harvesting H2O Chapter 3 specifies the yields.

Solar still and transpiration — procurement of last resort

SOLAR STILL · 3 ft × 3 ft pit under clear plastic sheet, collection container centered, sheet weighted at center to drip-point. Yield: ~1 pt/day. Green vegetation in pit doubles yield. TRANSPIRATION BAG · Clear plastic bag sealed over leafy branch of non-toxic tree. Yield: 1–2 cups/day per branch in temperate conditions, more in hot-dry.

Both methods trade time and plastic for water. A single three-by-three-foot still supplies one operator at the static rule if it runs continuously through the diurnal cycle; two stills plus a transpiration rig at the canopy supplies a two-person team. The methods preserve calorie budget over the alternative of foot-movement to a flowing source, which is why they appear in the desert and alpine procurement playbooks where source density is low.

01.4.7Rain catchment yield

Rainfall is the highest-yield field source when it runs. Harvesting H2O Chapter 3 specifies the formula.

Rain-catchment yield

~600 gal per 1 in of rainfall across 1000 ft² of catchment surface. A tarp strung at a slight grade to a metal container captures the field-expedient version; a permanent retreat runs gutters to a cistern.

A single 10 ft × 10 ft tarp at one inch of rain returns ~60 gal, enough to cover a 7-day deployment for a two-person team at static rate. RAIN IS THE CHEAPEST WATER. Procurement cost is zero once the tarp is rigged. The rain-water window is short and unpredictable; the operator who rigs the catch at the first cloud line captures the storm; the operator who waits for confirmation gets wet without catch. Bacterial load from roof or tarp runoff is non-trivial, so definitive treatment still runs — rain-caught water is not untreated by default.

01.4.8The 8 / 6 field rule

Hydration budget governs procurement tempo. TW-05 specifies the rule.

8 qt/day on the move. 6 qt/day static. The rule determines how fast the canteen empties, which determines when the procurement subsystem must activate.01.4.8 · The move / static rule

At 8 qt/day a single operator drains a 32 oz Nalgene every 4 hours of movement. The rule reframes the canteen from "drink when thirsty" to "drink on tempo": thirst is a lagging indicator, and the operator who drinks on the rule enters the next hydration window topped up rather than already in deficit. In hot-exertion conditions above 85°F the rule climbs to >12 qt/day, which makes the procurement layer the rate-limiting step rather than the carry layer.

01.4.9Water weight

Water is the heaviest per-ounce primitive the kit carries. TW-05 equipment chapter names the figure.

8.34 lb/gal — 2.1 lb/qt — one 32 oz Nalgene weighs ~2.1 lb full.

The weight forces a carry decision. CARRY PROCUREMENT, NOT RESERVE. A three-day move at 8 qt/day would mean ~50 lb of water carried; no operator carries that. The kit biases toward means of procurement and purification (filter, tablets, bleach, a pot for boil, a tarp for rain-catch) that weigh a fraction of the water they produce. The one-gallon cache on the ground at a pre-positioned resupply point is a better logistics answer than the one-gallon cache in the pack.

01.4.10The snow-dehydrates counterintuitive

Snow appears to be water. Functionally, it dehydrates the operator who eats it. Advanced Bushcraft Chapter 4 names the mechanism.

WARN

Do not eat snow. Melting snow on the tongue consumes more body heat than the water it yields, and an operator running below caloric budget is taxing glycogen on a net-loss process.

Snow is mostly air; 10 in of snow yields roughly 1 in of water. Latent heat of fusion at ~80 cal/g of ice and latent heat of vaporization at ~540 cal/g both draw from the body-heat budget if consumed directly. Melt snow in a pot over fire; never on the tongue. The pot runs with a small quantity of already-melted water to start — dry snow against hot metal scorches and the pot taste becomes bitter — so the operator keeps a half-cup reserve for re-start.

01.4.11Source-quality decision protocol

Pre-filtration and source-selection come before definitive treatment. Harvesting H2O and TW-05 specify the evaluation order.

Source evaluation — preferred order
01FLOWING CLEAR HEADWATERCreek at source, spring. Lowest pathogen load; pre-filter and boil.
02STILL CLEARPond, lake. Treat as flowing; pre-filter and boil; dipping in the middle beats the shoreline.
03MUDDY OR AGRICULTURAL STREAMPre-filter through cloth, settle 30 min, decant, definitive treat.
04RAIN CATCHTarp to container. Definitive treat (roof or tarp surface contamination).
05MORNING DEWCloth wipe from non-toxic vegetation. Sustains small operator volume.
06SOLAR STILL / TRANSPIRATIONLast-resort primitives. Still output is distilled and requires no further treatment.
07SEAWATERDistillation or reverse osmosis only. Ingestion of raw seawater accelerates dehydration.

Muddy water in a minimally-used watershed can be safer than clear water downstream of a beaver colony. Clarity is not a source-quality indicator; the upstream catchment is. A brown-water creek above dense forest is low-pathogen; a gin-clear creek below a pasture is high-pathogen. The operator reads the watershed, not the glass.

01.4.12Pre-filter → settle → definitive

Two-step treatment runs when the source is not headwater-clear. Harvesting H2O specifies the sequence.

Two-step treatment

01 · PRE-FILTER · Bandanna, shemagh, coffee filter, layered cloth. Removes coarse solids. 02 · SETTLE · 30 min undisturbed. Decant top 2/3. 03 · DEFINITIVE TREAT · Boil, chemical, or filter matched to pathogen profile.

The pre-filter extends the definitive step's lifetime — a 0.2 µm hollow-fiber filter clogs fast on un-pre-filtered muddy water, and a chemical treatment consumes more reagent in cloudy water. The two-step discipline also lets the operator visually verify clarity transition; decanted post-settle water that still runs cloudy signals a colloidal load that filtration alone will not remove.

01.4.13Container and storage tier

Water storage runs through matched containers. Canterbury's Ten Cs fixes the specification.

Water-storage tier
01METAL 32 oz NALGENE OR SINGLE-WALLED STEELPrimary. Fire-boil capable.
02COLLAPSIBLE 2 qt BLADDERReserve carry. Weight- and bulk-efficient.
03RETREAT-LEVEL BULK55-gal food-grade drums. Rotated annually; bleach-treated for storage (~1 tsp / 5 gal).
04ROUTE-CACHE CONTAINERSPre-positioned sealed containers on planned movement routes. Reduces carry budget.

BOIL-CAPABLE PRIMARY. A plastic Nalgene burns on a fire; a metal Nalgene or single-walled steel bottle doubles as a boil pot. The dual-use collapses two items into one and saves the weight of a dedicated cook pot at the individual-kit level. The cycle of fill-boil-cool-refill in the metal bottle is the canonical field purification loop; no additional equipment is required.

01.4.14Install, function, failure, feed-forward

INSTALL. You carry a three-deep PACE stack for water — filter primary, chemical alternate, boil contingency, solar-still or transpiration emergency. You rehearse the 2 drops bleach per 1 L, 30 min field dose as a muscle-memory sequence. You build the two-step pre-filter plus definitive treatment into every non-headwater source encounter. You read the upstream watershed before deciding source quality. You track hydration against the 8 / 6 rule on tempo, not thirst. You stage catchment at the first weather line, not after the storm passes.

FUNCTION INDICATORS. The subsystem functions when every field source receives a definitive treatment matched to its pathogen profile. No untreated water crosses the lips on the assumption that altitude or movement implies cleanliness. Hydration stays within the 8 / 6 window under movement and static conditions. The metal bottle doubles as boil pot when fire is up. The rain catch runs during every storm the camp sits through.

FAILURE INDICATORS. The subsystem fails when clear alpine water passes untreated. It fails when a filter runs without recognition that viruses pass through it. It fails when snow melts on the tongue instead of in a pot. It fails when thirst rather than tempo drives drinking, and the hydration deficit compounds across the deployment. It fails when iodine continues past six weeks in a continuous deployment and thyroid function suppresses.

FEED-FORWARD. Wild food and foraging economics install next in 01.5 — the subsystem governed by caloric-ROI mathematics where passive gear dominates active hunting and plant identification runs species-level or not at all. Water feeds the three-day layer of the Rule of Threes; food routes through the last and slowest layer, running against a baseline kept alive by the shelter-fire-water compound this section closes.
