SECTION 01.5

Wild food: foraging, fishing, trapping, basic hunting

CALORIC ROI RULEYIELD > COST OF LOCATE + HARVEST + PREP
EDIBLE PLANTS GLOBALLY~10%
PHOTO MIS-ID>50%
UET HOLD8 hr PER STAGE · SKIN / LIP / TONGUE / CHEW / SWALLOW / HANDFUL
LETHAL LOOKALIKE FAMILIESUMBELLIFERAE · SOLANACEAE
CICUTOXIN SEIZURE~60 min TO FATALITY
PROTEIN POISONING3–6 WK DEATH ON LEAN-ONLY
PURSLANEHIGHEST OMEGA-3 TERRESTRIAL GREEN
PAIUTE DEADFALL CLASS0.5–3 lb GAME
SNARE ARRAY30 SNARES > DAY OF HUNTING
CATTAIL5 EDIBLE PARTS ACROSS SEASONS

A wild food is worth harvesting only if caloric yield exceeds the caloric cost of locating, harvesting, and preparing it. This governing economic rule orders every decision in the food subsystem and dictates that passive gear (traps, trotlines, gill nets, weirs, snares) dominates active hunting in sustained survival. Warnock's 276 Edible Wild Plants supplies the plant catalog and lookalike architecture; Advanced Bushcraft Chapter 5 supplies the ITEM identification discipline; Stewart's 365 Essential Survival Skills supplies the trap and fishing primitives.

This section installs the food subsystem. You load the caloric-ROI law as the master economic rule, the ITEM species-level discipline (Identify, Time, Environment, Method), the Universal Edibility Test and the mushroom exception, the lethal-lookalike catalog across the carrot and nightshade families, the five nutrition classes (greens, roots, seeds-and-nuts, berries-and-fruits, inner bark), the protein-poisoning mechanism that makes fat non-optional, the passive-gear dominance principle, the Paiute deadfall and primitive fishing primitives, the scent-masking discipline for close-approach hunting, and the install protocol, function indicators, failure modes, and feed-forward handoffs. Sources: Warnock's 276 Edible Wild Plants (catalog, lookalikes, nutrition classes); Advanced Bushcraft Ch 5 (ITEM, UET, rabbit-starvation mechanism); Stewart's 365 (Paiute deadfall, gorge hook, stick-weir); TW-05 (caloric budget under cold).

01.5.1The caloric-ROI law

Food is energy accounting before it is nutrition. Advanced Bushcraft Chapter 5 anchors the rule.

A wild food is worth harvesting only if its caloric yield exceeds the caloric cost of locating, harvesting, and preparing it. The rule orders every food decision in the subsystem.01.5.1 · The economic governor

A squirrel at ~100 kcal does not pay for a three-hour stalk that burns ~900 kcal. NET-NEGATIVE FORAGING IS STARVATION WITH EXTRA STEPS. Passive gear rewrites the math — a trap line of thirty snares set once and checked daily costs ~30 min of morning labor and catches food on any timeline the animals move through the area, which is why passive gear dominates active hunting in every deployment longer than two days. The operator who reads the rule backward — hunting by foot for a single kill — burns the reserve that the compound subsystem is trying to preserve.

01.5.2ITEM — species-level discipline

Common names kill. Advanced Bushcraft Chapter 5 specifies the four-checkpoint identification protocol.

ITEM — identification discipline

I · IDENTIFY · To species, never by common name. Dozens of plants share names like "wild carrot" or "wild garlic." T · TIME OF YEAR · Fixes harvest window: greens in spring, shoots at emergence, roots in fall, seeds in late summer, inner bark best in spring flow. E · ENVIRONMENT · Authenticates site: chaga grows on white birch only, Queen Anne's lace tolerates disturbed soil, cattail requires standing water or saturated mud. M · METHOD OF PREPARATION · Governs consumption: pokeweed shoots require three water changes, acorns require tannin leach, cassava-class tubers require heat hydrolysis of cyanogenic glycosides.

SPECIES OR NOTHING. The four-checkpoint audit runs every plant decision before consumption; a plant that fails any of the four does not cross the lips. The operator who runs ITEM closes the identification before the harvest, not after the meal; a meal-time identification is a test run on the operator's liver.

01.5.3The Universal Edibility Test

Unknown plants run the UET only when known plants are unavailable and starvation risk is active. Advanced Bushcraft Chapter 5 specifies the staged hold.

UET — staged-exposure protocol
01SEPARATIONTest each plant part (leaf, stem, root, flower, fruit, seed) separately; many plants are edible in part and toxic in whole.
02SKIN CONTACT8 hr hold against inner elbow or wrist; watch for redness, burning, blistering.
03LIP8 hr hold against outer lip; watch for burning, numbness.
04TONGUE15 min hold on tongue without swallowing.
05CHEWChew small piece, hold in mouth 15 min without swallowing.
06SWALLOWSmall swallow, 8 hr hold for reaction.
07HANDFULEat handful, 8 hr hold for reaction.
WARN

The UET does not apply to mushrooms. Amatoxins in Amanita destroy the liver before symptoms appear, and the most lethal North American mushrooms present as unremarkable plain-looking specimens. Mushrooms require species-level positive identification, never staged-exposure testing.

The UET is a last-resort protocol that runs across a full day of no-other-food conditions; it is not a browsing tool for unfamiliar roadside plants. The separation discipline catches plants like elderberry (berries edible cooked, raw bark toxic) and pokeweed (young shoots edible leached, mature root lethal).

01.5.4Lethal lookalike families

Two plant families account for the majority of fatal misidentifications in North America. Warnock's catalog and Advanced Bushcraft Chapter 5 both name them.

Lethal lookalike families
01UMBELLIFERAE (carrot family)Wild carrot vs. poison hemlock vs. water hemlock. Umbels (flat-topped flower clusters) mask species differences.
02SOLANACEAE (nightshade family)Deadly nightshade, bittersweet, Jimson weed. Solanine and tropane alkaloids across the family.

THESE ARE THE FAMILIES THAT KILL. Wild carrot (Daucus carota) has hairy stem, a single dark-red central floret, carrot smell, and dense taproot. Poison hemlock (Conium maculatum) has smooth purple-blotched stem, no central floret, musty rodent smell, and the lethal alkaloid coniine. Water hemlock (Cicuta spp.) carries cicutoxin, one of the most lethal plant toxins in North America, with seizures progressing to fatality in ~60 min. The operator who defaults to "it looks like wild carrot" is one purple blotch from a funeral; the discipline is the four-point audit (stem texture, central floret, smell, taproot density), and a single ambiguity disqualifies the plant.

01.5.5The five nutrition classes

Wild-food nutrition partitions across five class profiles. Warnock's catalog organizes the tier.

Nutrition classes — field profiles
01GREENSAmaranth, lamb's-quarters, purslane, nettle, dandelion, chickweed. Low calorie, high vitamin and mineral load.
02ROOTS AND TUBERSCattail rhizome, wild onion, Jerusalem artichoke, burdock. Starch; real caloric payoff.
03SEEDS AND NUTSAmaranth seeds, acorns (leached), beaked hazelnut, black walnut, pine nuts. Fat and protein; long storage life.
04BERRIES AND FRUITSServiceberry, hawthorn, elderberry (cooked), rose hips, raspberry, blackberry. Sugars and vitamin C; perishable.
05INNER-BARK CAMBIUMPine, birch, willow. Emergency carbohydrate, best in spring flow.

Purslane carries the highest omega-3 content of any terrestrial leafy green. Cattail is the supermarket of the swamp: rhizome starch in fall, shoots in spring, pollen flour at emergence, immature flower spikes as a summer vegetable, and autumn fluff as insulation and tinder — five harvest products across seasons from one species. Inner-bark cambium scraped in strips in spring sustains caloric load when winter tubers are unavailable; summer and fall cambium is bitter and lower-yield.

01.5.6Protein poisoning — "rabbit starvation"

Lean-game-only diet is a slow fatality. Advanced Bushcraft Chapter 5 names the mechanism.

Protein poisoning — urea-cycle saturation

Lean game (rabbit, squirrel, winter deer) carries high protein and nearly no fat. The liver's urea cycle saturates on nitrogen load without fat or carbohydrate to buffer. Death follows in 3–6 weeks despite apparent caloric adequacy.

LEAN GAME ALONE KILLS. Signs progress from diarrhea through headache and fatigue to bradycardia and death. The fix is fat alongside protein — nuts, pine nuts, fatty birds (beaver tail, waterfowl), rendered tallow, organ meats (liver, kidney, brain), bone marrow. The operator who snares rabbits daily and eats nothing else is on the protein-poisoning countdown; the operator who pairs rabbit with rendered raccoon fat or beaver tail breaks the countdown. Mixed diet is survival-critical, not a nutritional nicety.

01.5.7Passive-gear dominance

Thirty snares outrun one hunter. Stewart's 365 and Advanced Bushcraft Chapter 5 converge on the principle.

Thirty snares work while you sleep. A day of hunting works only while you walk. Passive gear compounds across the deployment; active hunting drains glycogen on a single kill.01.5.7 · Passive over active

A snare line set on rabbit runs at sites of narrowing travel (fence corners, brush edges, log-over-stream crossings). Deadfalls work where snares cannot — Paiute deadfall handles game from 0.5–3 lb through a vertical post, horizontal bait stick, short trigger stick, tensioned cord, and deadfall rock or log; disturbance at the bait collapses the geometry. Passive gear runs at ~20:1 caloric ROI over active hunting because the operator's metabolic budget sleeps while the trap line works. Trotlines, gill nets, stick-and-stone weirs, and gorge hooks extend the same logic into the water column.

01.5.8Primitive fishing — methods catalog

Fish are the highest-yield protein source in most temperate watersheds. Stewart's 365 catalogs the primitives.

Primitive fishing — methods
01GORGE HOOKSliver of bone, wood, or thorn pointed at both ends, notched in middle, baited, swallowed whole; twists sideways when line pulled and lodges in throat.
02HAND-LINELine, bait, weight; cast and watch from shore or canoe.
03TROTLINECross-stream line with multiple baited hooks; checked morning and evening.
04STICK-AND-STONE WEIRV-shaped rock or stick fence funneling fish into narrowing chamber; standing the operator spears or nets the concentrate.
05GIGMulti-tine barbed spear for shallow-water or nighttime lamping with torch.
06BARK-FIBER NETImprovised net from inner-bark cordage; sweep or set-net deployment.

Gill net and trotline dominate caloric ROI. A gill net set across a narrows at dusk and recovered at dawn returns a day's protein at zero waking labor; the handful of minutes at rigging amortize across the entire deployment. Hand-line is a tempo-dependent active method that pays when fish are feeding and lies dormant when they are not.

01.5.9The Paiute deadfall

The Paiute geometry handles small game without complex trigger-work. Stewart's 365 specifies the build.

Paiute deadfall — small-game primitive

VERTICAL POST · Upright stake in ground, ~12" tall. HORIZONTAL BAIT STICK · Cross-stick with bait on the camp-facing end, balanced against the post. SHORT TRIGGER STICK · Vertical piece holding the deadfall angle, tensioned by cordage. DEADFALL · Flat rock or log ~5–15 lb angled above the bait. CAMOUFLAGE · Leaves, soil, or debris over the deadfall to reduce visual signature.

An animal disturbing the bait slips the trigger; the deadfall drops on the vertical post and rock-or-log inertia crushes the animal against the ground. The geometry is tunable — larger deadfall for raccoon-class, smaller for squirrel and rat — which is why the Paiute is the first deadfall most field-curriculums teach. Figure-four is the alternate geometry; Paiute tends to trigger with less disturbance, which increases catch rate in low-bait environments.

01.5.10Scent masking for close-approach hunting

Human volatile organics signal hunted species at hundreds of yards. Stewart's 365 specifies the three-layer mask.

Scent-masking stack
01CREEK BATHFull submersion in moving water strips skin and hair volatiles.
02CREEKBED MUDApplied to skin and clothing; absorbs remaining volatiles and matches local scent signature.
03FIREBED ASHDusted on dry areas (face, hands); further masks with local combustion signature.

The stack knocks back human scent enough to work downwind. THE THREE-LAYER STACK IS THE DIFFERENCE BETWEEN SPOTTED AT 100 YD AND APPROACHED WITHIN 20 YD. Wind discipline runs alongside scent discipline — approach downwind always, cross-wind if downwind is impossible, never upwind. The operator who skips the scent layer and expects to approach game on field craft alone is solving half the problem; game-class species run predator-detection on olfaction first and vision second.

01.5.11When in doubt, throw it out

Identification ambiguity is a cash-out. Advanced Bushcraft Chapter 5 names the rule.

WARN

No partial identification is ever good enough. A meal-time "I think this might be wild carrot" is a test run on the operator's liver. When in doubt, throw it out.

The rule closes the ITEM protocol. Every checkpoint that fails — species ambiguity, off-season harvest, wrong-environment specimen, unfamiliar preparation requirement — disqualifies the plant, and the disqualification has zero cost compared to the cicutoxin fatality it prevents. The psychology of hunger drives identification shortcuts; the discipline is the precommitment to the rule before hunger activates.

01.5.12Install, function, failure, feed-forward

INSTALL. You carry Warnock's catalog (or a regional equivalent) as field reference. You rehearse the ITEM protocol until the four-checkpoint audit runs automatically on every plant encounter. You deploy passive gear (snares, trotlines, deadfalls, weirs) as the primary protein-procurement layer, with active hunting as the contingency. You pair every lean-game protein source with fat (nuts, rendered tallow, organ meat, waterfowl) to break the protein-poisoning window. You rotate harvest across spring greens, summer berries, late-summer seeds, and fall roots. You run the three-layer scent mask before any close-approach hunt.

FUNCTION INDICATORS. The subsystem functions when your daily harvest clears its caloric cost under the ROI law. Species-level ID closes every plant decision before consumption. The protein-fat pairing holds across every day of game-only-access. The trap line runs at ~20:1 caloric ROI over active hunting. Mushrooms pass species-level positive identification or do not enter the camp.

FAILURE INDICATORS. The subsystem fails when a foraging fatality trails any unconfirmed identification. It fails when hunting on foot depletes calories for a single squirrel. It fails when rabbit-only diet runs into the protein-poisoning window. It fails when the UET is applied to a mushroom and the amatoxin has already committed to the liver before symptoms appear. It fails when hunger pressure overrides the ITEM audit and a purple-blotched stem enters the pot.

FEED-FORWARD. Trauma care installs next in 01.6 — the MARCH and PAWS protocols that stabilize the operator when injury degrades the capacity to execute the primitive-systems stack. Food closes the four primitives; the medical protocol runs through all four as stabilizer, and the next section loads the trauma layer that protects the operator's ability to keep executing.

SECTION 01.6

Trauma care: MARCH, PAWS, and the TCCC phases

PREHOSPITAL BATTLEFIELD FATALITY~90%
TOP PREVENTABLE CAUSEEXTREMITY EXSANGUINATION
PHASESCUF · TFC · TEC
PRIMARY SWEEPMARCH
SECONDARY SWEEPPAWS
TQ ISCHEMIA WINDOW2 hr IDEAL · 6 hr SALVAGE
WOUND-PACK PRESSURE3 min DIRECT
NCD NEEDLE14 GA × 3.25"
TBI SBP TARGET≥110 mmHg
TXA WINDOW1 g WITHIN 3 hr
COAGULATION TEMP FLOOR36–37°C
GOLDEN HOUR<60 min TO DEFINITIVE CARE

Ninety percent of battlefield fatalities die before reaching a medical treatment facility, and the top preventable cause is exsanguination from extremity wounds that a tourniquet addresses in seconds. This epidemiological fact drives the entire TCCC architecture. The TCCC Handbook anchors the three-phase structure, MARCH, PAWS, the lethal triad, and intervention thresholds; the First Aid Manual TW-05 supplies the civilian-adapted wilderness variants and the tightness standard.

This section installs the trauma subsystem. You load the three-phase architecture (Care Under Fire, Tactical Field Care, Tactical Evacuation Care) that partitions care by threat environment, the MARCH primary sweep that orders every intervention by time-to-kill, the PAWS secondary sweep that runs after MARCH stabilizes, the lethal triad (hypothermia, acidosis, coagulopathy) that dominates post-bleed mortality, the CAT tourniquet application sequence and the two-hour ischemia window, the wound-packing hemostatic protocol, the NPA and needle-chest-decompression and chest-seal interventions, the permissive-hypotension fluid-resuscitation rule, and the install protocol, function indicators, failure modes, and feed-forward handoffs. Sources: TCCC Handbook (phases, MARCH, PAWS, intervention thresholds); TW-05 (civilian-wilderness MARCH, tightness standard, triad prevention); Prepper's Medical Handbook (secondary-care cross-walk).

01.6.1The three TCCC phases

Care partitions by threat environment, not by injury severity. The TCCC Handbook anchors the phase model.

TCCC phases — environment-driven care
01CARE UNDER FIRE (CUF)Rounds still incoming. Priorities: return fire, move casualty to cover, control massive extremity hemorrhage with tourniquet applied high-and-tight over clothing. NO airway, NO breathing, NO further care.
02TACTICAL FIELD CARE (TFC)Relative cover, still hostile environment. Full MARCH executes. Reassessment, intervention escalation, documentation.
03TACTICAL EVACUATION CARE (TEC)Transport phase. Reassessment continues. Advanced interventions as platform permits.

GOOD MEDICINE IS BAD TACTICS IN THE WRONG PHASE. A perfect airway in the open kills the medic, the casualty, and the team. CUF is not triage paralysis — it is deliberate restriction of care to the one intervention (tourniquet) that addresses the dominant preventable cause (exsanguination) in the time the fire window permits. The phase determines what care runs, not the provider's skill level; a medic executing full MARCH under fire is a medic violating the phase rule.

01.6.2MARCH — the primary sweep

MARCH orders interventions by time-to-kill. The TCCC Handbook specifies the acronym and the sequence.

MARCH — primary trauma sweep

M · MASSIVE HEMORRHAGE · Extremity tourniquets, junctional tourniquets, wound packing with hemostatic gauze, pressure bandage. A · AIRWAY · Position (recovery), sit-up, jaw-thrust, nasopharyngeal airway, surgical cricothyroidotomy. R · RESPIRATIONS · Chest seals for penetrating chest wounds, needle chest decompression for tension pneumothorax, bag-valve-mask support. C · CIRCULATION · Rapid pulse and perfusion check, IV or IO fluids, tranexamic acid, permissive hypotension. H · HEAD INJURY AND HYPOTHERMIA · SBP ≥110 mmHg in TBI; active hypothermia prevention (Ready-Heat blanket, space blanket, hypothermia prevention kit).

The ordering is strictly time-to-kill. BLOOD BEFORE BREATH. A patient exsanguinates in minutes; a compromised airway kills in minutes but most airway compromise requires active positioning that MARCH has already sequenced. The triad of airway-breathing-circulation from civilian BLS reorders in combat medicine because the battlefield fatality distribution is dominated by extremity hemorrhage and tension pneumothorax, both of which require immediate intervention under the new acronym.

01.6.3PAWS — the secondary sweep

PAWS runs after MARCH stabilizes. The TCCC Handbook specifies the secondary acronym.

PAWS — secondary trauma sweep

P · PAIN · Acetaminophen + meloxicam combat pill pack · or oral transmucosal fentanyl citrate 800 µg lozenge · or ketamine 50 mg IM or intranasal. A · ANTIBIOTICS · Moxifloxacin 400 mg PO if able to swallow · or ertapenem 1 g IV/IM if not. W · WOUNDS · Clean, dress, splint, document. S · SPLINTING · Long bones, traction splint for femur.

SAMPLE history runs alongside PAWS: Symptoms, Allergies, Medications, Past medical, Last meal, Events. PAWS is not optional. The antibiotic delivered in the field reduces infection incidence enough to change the survival curve for penetrating abdominal and open-fracture wounds, and the pain control preserves the casualty's cognitive function for the transport phase. The casualty card records every drug, dose, route, and time to prevent re-dosing errors at handoff.

01.6.4The lethal triad

Three interacting failures dominate post-bleed trauma mortality. The TCCC Handbook names them.

Lethal triad — post-bleed physiological spiral
01HYPOTHERMIACoagulation enzymes require 36–37°C core temperature for normal function.
02ACIDOSISHypoperfusion drives lactic acid accumulation; pH drop impairs clotting factor activity.
03COAGULOPATHYHemodilution, factor consumption, acidosis, and hypothermia combine to block clot formation.

The three feed each other in a spiral. Hypothermia slows clotting; failed clotting extends bleeding; extended bleeding drops perfusion; low perfusion drives acidosis; acidosis slows clotting further. BREAK ONE NODE AND THE SPIRAL BREAKS. Active hypothermia prevention is trauma medicine, not comfort care; the space blanket goes on every casualty regardless of ambient temperature, because even a 75°F ambient pulls body heat faster than a shocky patient can generate it. Permissive hypotension (below) limits hemodilution; TXA within 3 hr limits coagulopathy directly.

01.6.5CAT tourniquet application

The Combat Application Tourniquet runs a fixed sequence. The TCCC Handbook and TW-05 converge on the protocol.

CAT — phase-dependent application
01CUF APPLICATIONSlap CAT high and tight over clothing, above the wound, on the first bone encountered (single-bone femur vs. paired radius-ulna).
02TFC RE-EVALUATIONMove to 2–3" above the wound on skin; NEVER over a joint.
03TIGHTENSelf-adherent band tight through buckle, route back, secure.
04WINDLASSTwist until distal pulse disappears AND bleeding stops.
05LOCKSecure windlass in clip.
06MARK TIMEPermanent marker on tourniquet itself AND on patient's forehead.

TW-05's rule: if you have not made the patient swear, it is not tight enough. A tourniquet that hurts is doing its job; a tourniquet that is comfortable is not controlling arterial flow.01.6.5 · The tightness standard

Under-tightened tourniquets kill by restricting venous return without arresting arterial flow — the wound continues to bleed while tissue swells downstream and the team reads "applied" as "effective." The pulse-and-bleed dual check at the end of tightening closes the error.

01.6.6The two-hour ischemia window

Tourniquet ischemia is time-bounded. The TCCC Handbook specifies the window.

TQ ischemia window

IDEAL · <2 hr from application to definitive care. SALVAGE · <6 hr with compartment syndrome and rhabdomyolysis risk rising. REMOVAL IN FIELD · Never after 2 hr has elapsed; reperfusion of ischemic tissue drives acidosis, hyperkalemia, and myoglobinuria that can crash the casualty.

YOU DO NOT REMOVE A TOURNIQUET IN THE FIELD AFTER TWO HOURS. A second tourniquet goes proximal if the first is not controlling; the original stays in place. The casualty arrives at definitive care with the tourniquet still on, time-marked, and the transition to hospital management runs under controlled reperfusion protocol — a field reperfusion attempt in a shocky patient drives the lethal triad directly. The 6 hr salvage ceiling is the outer limb-preservation window; beyond it, amputation probability rises sharply and systemic reperfusion injury becomes the dominant mortality driver.

01.6.7Wound packing with hemostatic gauze

When tourniquet cannot apply (junctional, torso, neck) or is not controlling, wound packing runs. The TCCC Handbook specifies the gauze classes and the technique.

Hemostatic gauze — mechanism by product class
01KAOLIN (QUIKCLOT COMBAT GAUZE)Activates factor XII on contact; accelerates intrinsic clotting cascade.
02CHITOSAN (CELOX, CHITOGAUZE)Binds red cells electrostatically, independent of clotting cascade; functions on anticoagulated patients.

Packing technique: pack gauze directly into the wound to the bleeding source (not over the top); three minutes of direct pressure by wristwatch; overwrap with pressure bandage. PACK TO THE SOURCE. THREE MINUTES. OVERWRAP. The pressure-bandage-without-packing failure mode is common and fatal; a bandage wrapped around external tissue compresses the wound edges but does not close the deep artery, and the casualty bleeds out under a neatly-wrapped dressing.

01.6.8Nasopharyngeal airway

The NPA maintains airway patency in an unconscious or semi-conscious patient. The TCCC Handbook specifies sizing and insertion.

NPA sizing and insertion

SIZE · Flange-to-nostril, tip-to-earlobe. LUBRICATE · Water-based lubricant. INSERT · Right nostril, bevel toward septum, along the nasal floor (not upward). CONTRAINDICATIONS · Awake patient (triggers laryngospasm and gag). Suspected basilar skull fracture (raccoon eyes, Battle's sign, CSF rhinorrhea or otorrhea).

RIGHT NOSTRIL, BEVEL TOWARD SEPTUM, ALONG THE FLOOR. The anatomically correct insertion path runs horizontally, not upward; upward insertion drives the tip into the ethmoid plate and, in a basilar fracture, into the brain. The NPA tolerates lower consciousness than the OPA; a casualty with gag reflex who expels the OPA retains the NPA, which is why the NPA is the MARCH airway default.

01.6.9Tension pneumothorax and needle chest decompression

Tension pneumothorax kills on the same timeline as arterial hemorrhage. The TCCC Handbook specifies the clinical presentation and the intervention.

WARN

Tension pneumothorax signs: decreased breath sounds on the affected side, tracheal deviation away from affected side, jugular venous distension, hypotension, combative patient. Untreated tension kills within minutes.

Needle chest decompression — NCD

NEEDLE · 14-gauge × 3.25-inch catheter. SITES (EITHER) · 2nd or 3rd intercostal space, midclavicular line. OR 4th or 5th intercostal, anterior axillary line (current TCCC preferred for reduced failure rate). INSERTION · Over the rib (neurovascular bundle runs under each rib), straight in, pop through pleura, remove needle leaving catheter.

The 4–5 ICS AAL site has lower failure rate than the classic 2–3 ICS MCL in obese patients because chest-wall thickness overwhelms the shorter needle at the MCL. The tension-to-simple-pneumothorax transition on successful NCD is audible — air releases through the catheter with a hiss — and the casualty's hemodynamics improve within seconds. Chest seal (vented Halo, HyFin, or Sam) covers every entry and exit wound after the full-chest sweep including axillae, back, and shoulders.

01.6.10Permissive hypotension

Fluid resuscitation is conditional, not reflexive. The TCCC Handbook specifies the target-based approach.

Withhold fluid resuscitation when radial pulse is palpable and mentation is normal. Target radial pulse return or SBP ~90 mmHg when radial is lost. Target SBP ≥110 mmHg in traumatic brain injury for cerebral perfusion.01.6.10 · Permissive hypotension

The reasoning is hemodilution. EXCESS CRYSTALLOID DILUTES CLOTTING FACTORS AND WORSENS COAGULOPATHY. A casualty with conscious mentation and palpable radial pulse has adequate perfusion to brain and kidney; pushing fluid raises blood pressure above the clotting threshold that the patient's own pressure was maintaining, tears existing clots, and restarts bleeding. TBI is the exception: cerebral perfusion pressure requires the higher 110 mmHg target because intracranial pressure rises post-injury and perfusion depends on the pressure gradient. Fluid choice runs whole blood preferred, plasma next, Hextend 500 mL with 1000 mL maximum, TXA 1 g within 3 hr of injury.

01.6.11The casualty card and documentation

Every intervention gets recorded. The TCCC Handbook mandates the casualty card.

Casualty card fields

Patient identifier · Mechanism of injury · Time of injury · Vitals at intervals · Interventions (drug, dose, route, time, provider) · Tourniquet placement and time · MARCH findings · PAWS administration.

The card prevents handoff error. UNDOCUMENTED DOSE IS A DOUBLE-DOSE WAITING TO HAPPEN. The receiving provider at TEC or hospital reads the card to avoid repeating interventions — a second fentanyl lozenge stacked on the first causes respiratory depression; a second dose of TXA administered outside the three-hour window changes the risk-benefit profile. Time markings on tourniquet and forehead both communicate to the receiving provider and create a visible audit trail when the card is lost.

01.6.12Install, function, failure, feed-forward

INSTALL. You carry the IFAK with MARCH inventory — CAT, combat gauze, pressure bandage, chest seals pair, NPA, decompression needle, permanent marker, nitrile gloves, trauma shears. You rehearse CAT application until the high-and-tight sequence runs under stress with eyes closed. You drill the phase rule — CUF is hemorrhage-only, TFC is full MARCH, TEC is reassessment. You run active hypothermia prevention on every casualty regardless of ambient temperature. You document every intervention on the casualty card.

FUNCTION INDICATORS. The subsystem functions when the casualty arrives at definitive care within the Golden Hour with the lethal triad interrupted at every node you can reach. The tourniquet is time-marked, the space blanket is applied, the TXA is administered within three hours. The fluid bolus is withheld from the conscious radial-pulse patient. The chest seal covers every entry and exit wound. The NPA runs in the unconscious patient without basilar-fracture signs.

FAILURE INDICATORS. The subsystem fails when the tourniquet goes on late. It fails when hypothermia prevention is treated as optional. It fails when the fluid bolus runs despite adequate perfusion signal. It fails when full MARCH is attempted under fire and the medic becomes the second casualty. It fails when the tourniquet is removed in the field to "check if it's still bleeding" and the casualty rebleeds or reperfusion drives the lethal triad. It fails when the NPA inserts upward in a basilar-fracture patient and drives the tip into the brain.

FEED-FORWARD. Non-trauma field medicine installs next in 01.7 — the protocols for environmental injury, CPR, fracture management, and the WROL sixteen aid guidelines that extend medicine beyond the acute-trauma window. MARCH stabilizes the event; the next section installs the medicine for everything else the field produces.

theFIELD.run / CONSTRUCT_APPLICATIONS / 01 PRIMARY SYSTEMS / 01.7 Field medicine beyond trauma
SECTION 01.7

Field medicine beyond trauma

HYPOTHERMIA BANDSMILD 90–95°F · MODERATE 82–90°F · SEVERE <82°F
FROSTBITE REWARM104–108°F × 40–60 min
ADULT RULE OF NINESHEAD 9 · ARM 9 · ANT TORSO 18 · POST TORSO 18 · LEG 18 · PERINEUM 1
PARKLAND4 mL × kg × %BSA / 24 hr · HALF IN FIRST 8 hr
BURN EVAC THRESHOLD>20% ADULT · >10% CHILD
ADULT CPR30:2 · DEPTH >2" · RATE 100–120/min
HELP POSITION~50% HEAT-LOSS REDUCTION
RESCUE HIERARCHYREACH · THROW · TOW · GO
FORGEY FEVER LAW~10 bpm PER 1°F ABOVE BASELINE
SNOW UV REFLECTED~85% · KERATITIS LATENCY 6–12 hr
COLD-WATER SUBMERSION REVIVAL66 min DOCUMENTED

Without-rule-of-law medicine runs on the assumption that the patient will not reach a hospital. You stabilize for days rather than minutes, assume infection, and reassess every hour. Forgey's Prepper's Medical Handbook anchors non-trauma field doctrine and the fever-heart-rate law; the First Aid Manual TW-05 supplies environmental-injury protocols, rewarming thresholds, and the rescue hierarchy; the TCCC Handbook supplies the SAMPLE history and the assessment tempo that integrates with MARCH from 01.6.

This section installs the non-trauma medical layer. You load the SOAP note that structures every encounter, the three-band hypothermia staging with the afterdrop mechanism that makes peripheral rewarming dangerous, the frostbite rewarm protocol at 104–108°F with the three never-rules, burn depth classification with the Rule of Nines and the Parkland formula, adult CPR with the hands-only variant, the choking algorithm for conscious and unconscious casualties, fracture splinting with the neurovascular sweep, the Kocher shoulder reduction sequence, RICE, the HELP position with the Reach-Throw-Tow-Go rescue hierarchy, Forgey's fever-heart-rate law that separates infection from covert hemorrhage, snow-blindness keratitis management, and the install protocol, function indicators, failure modes, and feed-forward handoffs. Sources: Prepper's Medical Handbook (non-trauma stabilization, fever law, drug cross-references); TW-05 (environmental injury, rewarming protocols, rescue hierarchy); TCCC Handbook (SAMPLE history, assessment cadence integration).

01.7.1SOAP note and the assessment tempo

Every encounter runs a common structure. Forgey's Prepper's Medical Handbook and the TCCC Handbook converge on SOAP for documentation and SAMPLE for history.

SOAP — documentation frame

S · SUBJECTIVE · Chief complaint, pain 1–10, onset, character, location, aggravating and relieving factors. O · OBJECTIVE · Vitals, physical exam, visible findings, measurements. A · ASSESSMENT · Clinical impression, differential, severity. P · PLAN · Treatment, observation schedule, evacuation or referral decision.

SAMPLE — history frame

S · SYMPTOMS · A · ALLERGIES · M · MEDICATIONS · P · PAST MEDICAL HISTORY · L · LAST MEAL · E · EVENTS LEADING UP

REASSESS ON SCHEDULE, NOT ON CRISIS. Reassessment runs every 15 min on active trauma, every 1 hr on stable casualty, every watch change in permanent camp. The casualty card persists across phases; the SOAP note extends the card into longitudinal care. Sanitation is medicine, and the handwash-clean-water-latrine-at-200 ft discipline prevents more field morbidity than any antibiotic corrects.

01.7.2Hypothermia — three-stage staging

Core temperature partitions intervention. TW-05 and Forgey converge on the three-stage model.

Hypothermia — stage-based presentation and rewarm path
01MILD 90–95°FIntense shivering, failing fine motor, confusion. Passive external rewarm: dry clothing, shelter, warm fluids if alert and swallowing.
02MODERATE 82–90°FShivering ceases, severe ataxia, stupor. Cardiac irritability rises; handle gently. Active rewarm with warmed fluids, warm inhaled air, space-blanket layer.
03SEVERE <82°FComa, apparent death, ventricular-fibrillation risk, apnea. Gentle handling. Core rewarm only. CPR continues until core >90°F.

"No one is dead until warm and dead." Cold-water submersion revivals are documented to 66 min of submersion because metabolic arrest in near-freezing water preserves brain tissue long past normothermic anoxic tolerance.01.7.2 · The warm-and-dead standard

ROUGH HANDLING KILLS A MODERATE HYPOTHERMIC. The cold myocardium is electrically irritable; jostling, vertical transport, or premature CPR compressions trigger ventricular fibrillation that does not convert until core temperature rises. Triage order for a multi-casualty cold-water event inverts normal priority — the still, silent, blue casualty gets worked first, because the screaming casualty is thermoregulating and has hours, while the quiet one has minutes.

01.7.3The afterdrop mechanism

Peripheral rewarming kills severe hypothermics. TW-05 and Forgey both specify the mechanism.

WARN

WARMING A SEVERELY HYPOTHERMIC PATIENT FROM THE OUTSIDE CAN KILL THEM. External heat dilates peripheral vessels; cold stagnant blood in the limbs returns to the core; core temperature drops further; ventricular fibrillation triggers.

Afterdrop — the physiological trap

MECHANISM · Peripheral vasodilation releases cold blood to the core. Core temperature drops 2–5°F below pre-rewarm level. Myocardium fibrillates. TRIGGER · Campfire exposure, hot-water bath, electric blanket, warm-shower rewarm of a severe hypothermic. COUNTER · Core-first rewarm — warm intravenous fluids (40–42°C), warm humidified oxygen, gastric or bladder lavage with warmed saline.

CORE FIRST. ALWAYS. Peripheral rewarming applies only to the mild hypothermic with intact thermoregulation. The moderate-to-severe casualty runs core rewarm with gentle handling and no direct external heat to the trunk or limbs until core is >90°F. The fireside-rewarm fatality is the classic preventable outcome — rescuers read shivering as the emergency, apply heat to the fastest pathway, and the casualty dies of afterdrop-induced VF in what looks like a successful rescue.

01.7.4Frostbite — rewarm protocol and the three never-rules

Tissue freezes below 28°F tissue temperature. Ice crystals in interstitial fluid damage cell membranes; thaw drives ischemia and necrosis. TW-05 specifies the rewarm protocol.

Frostbite rewarm — the water-bath protocol
01IMMERSEAffected tissue in 104–108°F clean water. Check with thermometer, not by hand.
02DURATION40–60 min until tissue is soft and pink to the core.
03PAINRewarming hurts. Oral analgesia tolerated; narcotic if available and evacuation is feasible.
04POST-THAWDry, elevate, sterile dressing between digits, no pressure, no blister debridement in the field.
WARN

THREE NEVER-RULES · Never rewarm with open fire (burns insensate tissue). Never rub with snow (abrades damage and refreezes the surface). Never thaw if refreeze risk exists (thaw-refreeze damage far exceeds continued freeze to evacuation).

WALKING ON FROZEN FEET OUTPERFORMS THAW-REFREEZE. The classic error runs a thaw at the trailhead hut followed by the final mile's march back into freezing conditions; tissue that would have survived continued freeze with viable limb-salvage loses amputation-level tissue to the second freeze cycle. The decision rule is definitive care or continued freeze, with no intermediate thaw unless the evacuation path is secured and heated through to hospital.

01.7.5Burns — depth classification and Rule of Nines

Burns partition by depth and by extent. TW-05 and Forgey converge on the classification.

Burn depth — classification and field read
01FIRST-DEGREEEpidermal only. Erythema, pain, no blister. Sunburn. Cool, aloe, oral hydration, analgesia.
02SECOND-DEGREE (PARTIAL)Dermal involvement. Blisters, severe pain, wet appearance, blanches. Dressing, fluid replacement if extensive, infection watch.
03THIRD-DEGREE (FULL)Full-thickness. Leathery, dry, painless (nerves destroyed). Requires grafting. Evacuation.
04FOURTH-DEGREEThrough fascia to muscle or bone. Definitive surgical care required.
Rule of Nines — adult body-surface estimation

HEAD · 9% (ant 4.5, post 4.5) · ARM · 9% each · ANTERIOR TORSO · 18% · POSTERIOR TORSO · 18% · LEG · 18% each · PERINEUM · 1% · PALM (patient's own) · ~1% for scattered burns.

EVAC AND FLUID TRIGGER AT 20% ADULT, 10% CHILD, OR ANY FACE-HAND-FOOT-PERINEUM-CIRCUMFERENTIAL BURN. Face, hand, foot, and perineum trigger on any depth because function loss and contracture drive morbidity; circumferential burns on extremities or torso trigger because eschar contracture compresses vessels and respiration. The patient's own palm is the field protractor for scattered burns — each palm-sized area is roughly one percent BSA, and the patch-counting method survives when you have no chart.

01.7.6Parkland formula and burn fluid resuscitation

Large burns drive plasma loss and hypovolemia. TW-05 specifies the Parkland formula.

Parkland formula — 24-hour crystalloid target

VOLUME · 4 mL × body weight (kg) × %BSA burned = total 24 hr crystalloid. DISTRIBUTION · Half in first 8 hr from time of burn (not time of presentation). Half over next 16 hr. FLUID · Lactated Ringer's preferred; normal saline acceptable. TARGET · Urine output 0.5–1 mL/kg/hr adult, 1–1.5 mL/kg/hr child.

Worked example: 80 kg adult with 30% BSA burn. 4 × 80 × 30 = 9600 mL over 24 hr. 4800 mL in first 8 hr (600 mL/hr). 4800 mL over next 16 hr (300 mL/hr). START FROM TIME OF BURN, NOT TIME OF IV. If the casualty presents 3 hr post-burn, the first-eight-hour half runs in the remaining 5 hr, which compresses the rate. The formula underestimates in inhalation injury, electrical burns, and delayed presentation, and urine output is the titration target that corrects the formula's blind spots.

01.7.7Adult CPR and the hands-only variant

Cardiac arrest runs a fixed sequence. TW-05 and Forgey align on the protocol.

Adult CPR — 30:2 standard
01SCENE SAFEUnresponsive → call for help → check pulse <10 s.
02COMPRESSIONSLower half of sternum, heel of hand. Depth >2", rate 100–120/min, full recoil between.
03RATIO30:2 compressions-to-breaths.
04BREATHSHead-tilt chin-lift airway. Two breaths over 1 s each with visible chest rise.
05CYCLEMinimize interruptions. Rotate compressors every 2 min to prevent quality decay.

HANDS-ONLY IS ACCEPTABLE IF YOU CANNOT OR WILL NOT VENTILATE. Continuous chest compression alone at 100–120/min maintains circulation for witnessed adult arrest long enough to bridge to defibrillation. AED application when available runs immediately because survival drops roughly ~10% per minute without defibrillation in shockable rhythms, and the time-to-shock is the dominant determinant of neurologically-intact survival. Cease CPR only on return of spontaneous circulation, arrival of advanced care, rescuer exhaustion with no relief, or a mass-casualty triage context where resources commit elsewhere.

01.7.8Choking — conscious and unconscious algorithms

Complete airway obstruction kills on minute-scale. TW-05 specifies the civilian algorithm.

Choking — by consciousness state
01CONSCIOUS ADULT5 back blows between shoulder blades → 5 abdominal thrusts (Heimlich). Alternate until expelled or casualty loses consciousness.
02UNCONSCIOUS ADULTBegin CPR compressions. Check mouth each cycle; remove visible obstruction only. NEVER blind finger-sweep.
03PREGNANT OR OBESEChest thrusts replace abdominal thrusts.
04INFANT (<1 yr)5 back blows head-down on forearm → 5 two-finger chest thrusts. No abdominal thrusts.

BLIND FINGER-SWEEP DRIVES OBSTRUCTIONS DEEPER. Look-before-sweep on the unconscious adult runs with a light source, direct visualization, removal of only what is seen. Chest compressions on the unconscious choking adult function as an improvised Heimlich through the intrathoracic pressure spike, which is why the algorithm converges on compressions rather than dedicated abdominal thrusts once consciousness is lost.

01.7.9Fracture splinting and neurovascular checks

Splinting preserves limb viability and reduces pain. TW-05 specifies the neurovascular sweep and the joint-above-joint-below rule.

Splint protocol — joint above, joint below
01EXPOSECut clothing away. Inspect for open-fracture signs.
02NEUROVASCULAR SWEEP (PRE-SPLINT)Distal pulse, capillary refill <2 s, sensation (light touch), motion.
03ALIGNLongitudinal traction to gross deformity only if distal pulse is absent; otherwise splint in position found.
04IMMOBILIZERigid support spanning the joint above and the joint below the fracture. SAM splint, rolled magazine, duffel, padded stick.
05PAD BONY PROMINENCESWrist, ankle, elbow, heel.
06NEUROVASCULAR SWEEP (POST-SPLINT)Recheck pulse, refill, sensation, motion. Loosen if any regressed.

OPEN FRACTURE = ANTIBIOTIC + EVAC. Moxifloxacin 400 mg PO per TCCC or cephalexin 500 mg four times daily per Forgey within 1 hr of injury. Gross contamination irrigates with pressurized clean water; sterile dressing seals; splint as closed. Compartment syndrome presents with pain out of proportion to injury, pain on passive stretch of the distal muscle group, tense muscle compartment, and late-stage pulselessness; it requires fasciotomy within 6–8 hr of onset or the limb is lost, and the pain-out-of-proportion signal is the earliest reliable indicator.

01.7.10Kocher shoulder reduction

Anterior shoulder dislocation reduces with a slow leverage sequence. Forgey specifies the Kocher maneuver.

Kocher — anterior shoulder reduction
01FLEX ELBOWTo 90° with casualty supine or seated.
02ADDUCTSlow adduction toward the body over 5–10 min.
03EXTERNAL ROTATESlowly until resistance felt. Hold against resistance 5–10 min; muscles fatigue and release.
04LIFT ELBOWAcross chest toward opposite shoulder.
05INTERNAL ROTATESlide hand toward opposite shoulder. Reduction felt as a clunk.
06IMMOBILIZESling and swathe post-reduction. Recheck distal neurovascular.

SLOW IS FAST. The Kocher maneuver reduces through muscle fatigue, not force; fast attempts fracture the humeral head or tear the rotator cuff. The earlier the reduction, the easier the reduction — a dislocated shoulder muscular-splints within hours, and a two-hour window between dislocation and reduction often converts a five-minute procedure into a ten-minute procedure, while a day's delay often requires anesthesia to break the splint. Confirm with gentle active motion and distal neurovascular check; document.

01.7.11RICE for sprains and strains

Soft-tissue injury runs a four-beat protocol. TW-05 specifies RICE.

RICE — sprain and strain protocol

R · REST · No weight-bearing on lower extremity; no loading on upper. 24–48 hr minimum. I · ICE · 20 min on, 20 min off. First 48 hr. Thin cloth between ice and skin to prevent frostbite. C · COMPRESSION · Elastic wrap firm but not restrictive. Recheck distal capillary refill. E · ELEVATION · Above heart. Reduces edema through the hydrostatic gradient.

GRADE II AND III SPRAINS REQUIRE IMAGING WHEN AVAILABLE. In the field, no-imaging sprain management defaults to RICE plus splinting if weight-bearing fails or if instability is gross. The Ottawa Ankle Rules flag likely fracture — inability to bear weight four steps immediately after injury and at exam, tenderness over the posterior edge of the distal 6 cm of either malleolus, tenderness at the base of the fifth metatarsal or the navicular — and trigger splinting and evacuation rather than simple RICE.

01.7.12Cold-water HELP and the Reach-Throw-Tow-Go hierarchy

Cold-water immersion kills on 10–60 min timescales depending on water temperature. TW-05 specifies the survival position and the rescue hierarchy.

HELP — Heat Escape Lessening Posture (solo)
01POSITIONKnees drawn to chest. Arms crossed over torso. Head back to keep airway above waterline.
02EFFECTReduces core heat loss ~50% versus swimming or treading water.
03GROUP VARIANT (HUDDLE)Small group interlocks arms chest-to-chest, lower bodies intertwined, children or weakest in center.
04SWIM RULESwim for rescue only within ~150 ft; beyond that, swimming accelerates heat loss and rarely reaches distant safety.
Rescue hierarchy — Reach, Throw, Tow, Go
01REACHFrom stable position with pole, oar, stick, extended limb.
02THROWRope, flotation, cooler lid. Victim holds; rescuer pulls.
03TOWGo to water only with flotation attached to rescuer via line held on shore.
04GOEnter water as absolute last resort, with flotation for self and for victim.

UNTRAINED RESCUERS DROWN ALONGSIDE VICTIMS ROUTINELY. The drowning casualty is panicked, strong, and will climb the rescuer to breach the surface; even a swimmer is submerged in seconds once the casualty makes contact. Lay-rescue fatalities almost uniformly violate the hierarchy by skipping to Go when Reach or Throw was available, and the discipline of the four-step escalation holds specifically to prevent the second fatality.

01.7.13Forgey's fever-heart-rate law

Heart rate scales with fever at a known rate. Forgey anchors the rule.

Fever-heart-rate law

BASELINE · Adult resting HR rises ~10 bpm per 1°F above normal body temperature. APPLICATION · A fever of 103°F (+4°F above 99°F baseline) predicts HR rise ~40 bpm above the patient's resting rate. DIAGNOSTIC VALUE · Tachycardia DISPROPORTIONATE to fever signals a second process — hemorrhage, pulmonary embolism, severe sepsis, myocardial ischemia, dehydration.

PULSE EXCEEDS EXPECTATION, LOOK FOR THE SECOND PROCESS. The 103°F patient with pulse 140 against resting 72 is running +68; expected +40 from fever alone leaves ~25–30 bpm unexplained. The law is prospective — it flags covert hemorrhage or early sepsis before hypotension sets in, and the field response is reassessment for occult blood loss, careful hydration, and a lower threshold for evacuation.

01.7.14Snow-blindness keratitis

UV reflection off snow burns the cornea. TW-05 specifies the exposure-to-symptom latency and the management protocol.

Snow blindness — UV photokeratitis

EXPOSURE · ~85% of UV reflected off snow. >4 hr unprotected exposure at altitude damages corneal epithelium. LATENCY · Symptoms present 6–12 hr post-exposure. The casualty is asymptomatic during the damaging exposure. SYMPTOMS · Intense pain, photophobia, tearing, foreign-body sensation, conjunctival erythema.

Keratitis management — 48-hour tempo
01DARK ENVIRONMENTBlindfold or dark shelter.
02COOL COMPRESSAgainst closed eyes.
03TOPICAL TETRACAINEShort-term pain relief only. Maximum 48 hr — prolonged use delays corneal healing.
04OPHTHALMIC ANTIBIOTICErythromycin ointment QID.
05ORAL ANALGESIAIbuprofen for systemic pain.

PREVENTION BEATS TREATMENT. Sunglasses with side shields or improvised slit goggles — cardboard with narrow horizontal slits — drop exposure below the damage threshold. The improvised-goggle principle runs narrow horizontal slits rather than mesh or clear plastic because slits allow ample central vision while filtering the diffuse UV reflection, and the design scales to snow, glacier, and high-altitude desert conditions.

01.7.15Install, function, failure, feed-forward

INSTALL. You carry the IFAK expanded for non-trauma work — SAM splint, elastic wraps, burn dressing, survival blankets, tetracaine, erythromycin ointment, oral analgesics, oral rehydration salts, antibiotic stock. You rehearse Kocher reduction on a willing partner and the CPR 30:2 cycle to autonomic tempo. You drill the hypothermia staging and the afterdrop rule until core-first rewarm is reflex. You document every encounter on SOAP and append to the casualty card.

FUNCTION INDICATORS. The subsystem functions when environmental injuries receive protocol-accurate rewarming or cooling, when fracture and dislocation management preserves distal neurovascular function, when Parkland targets urine output in the burn patient, when the fever-HR law flags covert hemorrhage before hypotension sets in, and when the rescue hierarchy prevents second-casualty drowning. Assessment tempo holds across active and stable phases.

FAILURE INDICATORS. The subsystem fails when the severe hypothermic warms by fireside and arrests. It fails when the frostbite thaws and refreezes on the march back. It fails when tetracaine stacks past 48 hr and the cornea ulcerates. It fails when the rescuer enters the water without flotation and the response doubles the casualty count. It fails when the tachycardia of covert hemorrhage reads as anxiety and the transfusion window closes.

FEED-FORWARD. Field pharmacology installs next in 01.8 — the drug ladders, antibiotic syndrome-mapping, the SLEP expiration data, the improvised-pharmacy herbal preparations, and the potassium permanganate four-function reagent that close the medicine layer. The assessment layer runs here; the pharmacy runs next.

SECTION 01.8

Field pharmacology and improvised pharmacy

FIVE RIGHTSDRUG · DOSE · PATIENT · ROUTE · TIME
IBUPROFEN200 mg q4h · MAX 3200 mg/24 hr
TCCC COMBAT PILLACETAMINOPHEN 1 g + MELOXICAM 15 mg
OTFC800 µg LOZENGE
KETAMINE50 mg IM/IN
DOXYCYCLINE100 mg BID · SINGLE-BEST-ANTIBIOTIC
SLEP≥90% POTENCY 5–15 yr PAST LABEL
EPIPEN~95% POTENCY 12 MO POST-EXPIRY
ACS PROTOCOLASA 324 mg CHEWED · NTG 0.4 mg SL q5 min × 3
EPI IM0.3 mg q5–15 min
IRRIGATION500–1000 mL/in @ ~7 psi
PED WT ESTAGE × 2 + 8 = kg (1–10 yr)
KMnO44 FIELD FUNCTIONS

Field pharmacy runs under degraded storage, absent monitoring, and irregular handoffs. The discipline that keeps the pharmacy safe under those conditions is the five-rights protocol with a casualty-card audit trail, syndrome-mapped antibiotic selection rather than broad-spectrum defaults, and rehearsed ladders for pain, allergy, and cardiac emergency. Forgey's Prepper's Medical Handbook anchors the drug ladders and dose thresholds; the First Aid Manual TW-05 supplies expiration data and the single-best-antibiotic heuristic; Canterbury's Advanced Bushcraft and Warnock's 276 Edible Wild Plants supply the herbal preparations that extend the pharmacy when manufactured drugs run out.

This section installs the pharmacology layer. You load the five-rights discipline with casualty-card documentation, the pain ladder from ibuprofen through the TCCC combat pill pack, antibiotic syndrome-mapping that matches drug to presentation, the single-best-antibiotic heuristic that names doxycycline as the one coverage you carry under weight constraint, the SLEP extension data that converts labeled expiry from absolute to conservative, the ACS cardiac protocol with aspirin-chew-first, the allergic reaction ladder with epinephrine as primary in anaphylaxis, the 7-psi wound irrigation standard, pediatric dosing by weight with the age-times-two-plus-eight estimator, the five herbal preparation methods, a medicinal plant index for yarrow, plantain, willow bark, elderberry, chaga, the potassium permanganate four-function reagent, and the install protocol, function indicators, failure modes, and feed-forward handoffs. Sources: Prepper's Medical Handbook (drug ladders, dose thresholds, ACS, anaphylaxis); TW-05 (SLEP expiration, single-best-antibiotic rule, wound irrigation pressures); Canterbury's Advanced Bushcraft (herbal preparation methods, wild medicinals); Warnock (edible-medicinal cross-over plants).

01.8.1Five-rights and documentation discipline

Every administration passes five checks. Forgey's Prepper's Medical Handbook and the TCCC Handbook converge on the protocol.

Five rights — every administration

RIGHT DRUG · Read the label twice before and once after. Different drugs share similar packaging. RIGHT DOSE · By weight for children; by indication for adults. RIGHT PATIENT · Confirm identity before administration. Critical in multi-casualty. RIGHT ROUTE · PO, IM, IV, IN, SL, PR, topical, ophthalmic. Many drugs carry different doses for different routes. RIGHT TIME · Absolute time of last dose, not "about two hours ago."

DOCUMENT ON THE CASUALTY CARD: DRUG, DOSE, ROUTE, TIME, RESPONDER. The receiving provider at handoff reads the card to prevent double-dose. Re-dosing errors at phase transitions are the dominant field medication-error pattern, and the casualty card plus a pen-on-forehead time mark for critical administrations — tourniquet, fentanyl, TXA — carries the record when paperwork is lost.

01.8.2The pain ladder

Pain control steps up by severity. Forgey and the TCCC Handbook specify parallel ladders.

Pain ladder — stepwise escalation
01MILDIbuprofen 200 mg PO q4h · max 3200 mg/24 hr short-term · 1200 mg OTC ceiling.
02MILD LONG-ACTINGMeloxicam 15 mg PO daily. Extended coverage without every-four-hour dosing.
03MODERATEHydroxyzine (Atarax) 25 mg PO q4–6h adds sedation for pain with anxiety.
04MODERATE-SEVEREButorphanol (Stadol) nasal spray ~10× morphine potency, rapid onset, dependence risk.
05SEVERENalbuphine (Nubain) 10 mg IM/IV — partial opioid agonist-antagonist with a respiratory-depression ceiling safer than pure agonists.
TCCC combat pill pack — parallel pain triad

PACK · Acetaminophen 1 g + Meloxicam 15 mg PO. First-line for casualties still fighting. OTFC · Oral transmucosal fentanyl citrate 800 µg lozenge. Moderate-to-severe. Duct-tape the lozenge stick to the casualty's finger so over-sedation drops the lozenge. KETAMINE · 50 mg IM or IN. Severe pain, especially with hemodynamic instability. Dissociative; preserves airway and blood pressure.

NSAID STACKING ON A DEHYDRATED CASUALTY DRIVES RENAL INJURY. The field ibuprofen ceiling holds only under adequate hydration. Ketamine is the hemodynamically-safe analgesic in shock because it maintains sympathetic tone and airway reflexes where morphine and fentanyl drop blood pressure and depress respiration, and the combat-trauma use case runs ketamine specifically when the patient can least afford the hypotension that pure opioids cause.

01.8.3Antibiotic selection by syndrome

Antibiotic selection maps to presentation, not to guess. Forgey supplies the syndrome table.

Antibiotic — syndrome mapping
01CELLULITISCephalexin 500 mg QID × 7–10 d or doxycycline 100 mg BID (MRSA coverage).
02COMMUNITY-ACQUIRED PNEUMONIALevofloxacin 500 mg daily × 7–10 d.
03STREP THROATAzithromycin Z-Pak.
04LYME PROPHYLAXISDoxycycline 100 mg BID × 3–5 d or amoxicillin 500 mg TID.
05DENTAL ABSCESSAmoxicillin 500 mg TID or clindamycin 300 mg QID.
06UNCOMPLICATED UTI (WOMEN)Bactrim DS BID × 3 d or nitrofurantoin 100 mg BID × 5 d.
07PENETRATING ABDOMINAL WOUNDErtapenem 1 g IV/IM or ciprofloxacin 500 mg + metronidazole 500 mg.
08OPEN-FRACTURE PROPHYLAXISMoxifloxacin 400 mg PO (TCCC).

MATCH THE DRUG TO THE SYNDROME, NOT TO THE WORST CASE. Broad-spectrum defaults drive C. difficile risk, disrupt gut flora, and waste a limited stock. Allergy documentation runs as critical as the prescription itself — a documented penicillin allergy redirects cellulitis from cephalexin to doxycycline, a documented sulfa allergy redirects UTI from Bactrim to nitrofurantoin, and undocumented-allergy anaphylaxis in an austere environment has poor salvage.

01.8.4The single-best-antibiotic rule — doxycycline

When the pharmacy reduces to one antibiotic, doxycycline is the choice. TW-05 anchors the rule.

Doxycycline covers tick-borne illness (Lyme, Rocky Mountain Spotted Fever, ehrlichiosis), MRSA skin, atypical pneumonia (mycoplasma, chlamydia), Vibrio, anthrax, and serves as malaria prophylaxis. No other single agent covers this spectrum at the cost and weight of 100 mg BID tablets.01.8.4 · Doxycycline — the one-drug coverage

WARN

OLD TETRACYCLINE FORMULATIONS DEGRADE TO NEPHROTOXIC FANCONI SYNDROME. Modern doxycycline is reformulated to avoid this. The SLEP expiration-extension applies to current doxycycline but NOT to expired pre-reformulation tetracycline.

ONE DRUG, SEVEN SYNDROMES. The calculus runs: if the team can carry only one antibiotic for a 30-d deployment across unknown exposures in tick-endemic terrain, doxycycline carries the broadest prophylactic and treatment coverage at minimal weight, and the redundancy-in-one-drug principle consolidates the kit without sacrificing function. Reservations: pregnancy (teratogenic), children under eight (tooth staining), photosensitivity requiring sun precautions.

01.8.5SLEP and drug expiration

Labeled expiration is conservative. The FDA and Department of Defense Shelf Life Extension Program documents most solid-dosage drugs retaining ≥90% potency for 5–15 yr past expiry.

SLEP — drug-class expiration behavior
01SOLID DOSAGE (TABLETS, CAPSULES)≥90% potency 5–15 yr past label when stored cool, dry, dark.
02LIQUID SUSPENSIONSDegrade faster. Check for color change, separation, odor.
03NITROGLYCERINOnce the bottle opens, potency drops. Replace every 6 MO.
04EPIPEN~95% potency at 12 MO post-expiration when stored properly.
05INSULINRefrigeration-dependent. Unopened vials 28 d at room temperature; degrades faster unrefrigerated.
WARN

EXPIRED NITROGLYCERIN IN ACS IS A DEAD DRUG. The aspirin in the ACS pack keeps for years; the nitroglycerin loses potency within months of bottle opening. Rotate NTG on a calendar, not on expiration date.

STORAGE BEATS LABEL DATE. Cool, dry, dark beats the printed expiry by nearly an order of magnitude on solid-dose drugs. The liability-labeled expiration is a manufacturer's conservative date; the SLEP pharmacokinetic data extends the operational shelf life but does not convert liquid or temperature-sensitive formulations, and the rule of thumb is solid-and-stored keeps, liquid-and-opened rotates.

01.8.6Cardiac emergency protocol — ACS

Suspected acute coronary syndrome runs a rehearsed sequence. Forgey specifies the protocol.

ACS field protocol
01ASPIRIN324 mg chewed (four 81 mg baby aspirin chewables). Platelet inhibition begins immediately.
02NITROGLYCERIN0.4 mg SL q5 min × 3 doses if SBP >100 mmHg. Withhold for hypotension or recent PDE5 inhibitor.
03CLOPIDOGREL (PLAVIX)300 mg loading dose, then 75 mg daily.
04METOPROLOL25 mg q6h if HR and BP tolerate.
05EVACUrgent transport to cath lab. Time-to-reperfusion is the outcome driver.

CHEW, DON'T SWALLOW. Chewed aspirin achieves platelet inhibition in minutes; swallowed tablets lag by 30+ min. The field ACS sequence prioritizes the cheap, fast, high-leverage interventions (aspirin chew, NTG SL, call for evac) over the later additions (clopidogrel load, metoprolol) because the mortality curve of ACS is time-to-reperfusion dominant, and the first 30 min carry more outcome weight than the next four hours combined.

01.8.7Allergic reaction ladder and anaphylaxis

Allergic reactions step up by severity. Forgey specifies the ladder.

Allergy ladder — stepwise intervention
01LOCAL TOPICALHydrocortisone 1% cream. Desoximetasone 0.25% for moderate.
02SYSTEMIC MILDDiphenhydramine 25 mg PO q6h. Non-sedating loratadine alternative for sustained use.
03MODERATEAdd oral prednisone 40–60 mg daily taper for contact dermatitis or reaction beyond local.
04ANAPHYLAXISIntramuscular epinephrine 0.3 mg (EpiPen) anterolateral thigh. Repeat q5–15 min if symptoms persist.
WARN

DIPHENHYDRAMINE IS ADJUNCT, NOT PRIMARY, IN ANAPHYLAXIS. Anaphylaxis runs epinephrine first. Benadryl does not reverse airway edema or cardiovascular collapse; it blunts post-epinephrine residual histamine. An anaphylactic patient given Benadryl as primary arrests.

EPI FIRST. ALWAYS. THEN EVERYTHING ELSE. The bi-phasic reaction risk — ~5–20% of anaphylaxis cases rebound within 6–12 hr — is the reason anaphylaxis trips mandatory observation or evacuation, and the follow-up epinephrine must be available because a casualty who appears stable after one EpiPen can relapse without warning. Prednisone and diphenhydramine both extend the epinephrine window, they do not replace it.

01.8.8Wound irrigation — the 7-psi standard

Irrigation pressure drives bacterial clearance. TW-05 specifies the threshold.

Wound irrigation — pressure-controlled lavage

VOLUME · 500–1000 mL clean water per inch of wound length. PRESSURE · ~7 psi minimum for bacterial reduction. Achieved with 18-gauge needle on 60 mL syringe. ANESTHESIA · Lidocaine 1% local infiltration if resources allow. CLOSURE · Primary closure within 6 hr for clean wounds. Delayed primary or secondary intention for contaminated, bite, or >6 hr wounds.

LOW-PRESSURE RINSE WITHOUT SYRINGE IS COSMETIC, NOT THERAPEUTIC. A bottle pour at <1 psi moves visible debris but does not drive bacterial count down. The 7 psi floor is the documented bacterial-reduction threshold below which irrigation produces cosmetic improvement without measurable infection-rate drop, and the 18-gauge-on-60-mL-syringe is the cheap field mechanism to cross that threshold. Pressure above ~15 psi risks forcing debris deeper into tissue.

01.8.9Pediatric dosing

Adult doses are lethal in small children. Forgey specifies the weight-based approach.

Pediatric dosing — weight-based
01DOSE BY WEIGHTMilligrams per kilogram for every drug.
02WEIGHT ESTIMATION NO SCALEBroselow tape (color-coded by length); or formula: age (yr) × 2 + 8 = kg, valid 1–10 yr.
03AGE ADJUSTMENTSInfants (<1 yr) carry different dosing than older children for many drugs.
04PEDIATRIC-SPECIFIC CONTRAINDICATIONSDoxycycline <8 yr (tooth staining); aspirin in viral illness (Reye's syndrome); fluoroquinolones generally avoided.

IF YOU DO NOT KNOW THE WEIGHT, DO NOT GIVE THE DOSE. Pediatric medication errors in the field cluster on adult-dose substitution and on misread decimal points in milligram-per-kilogram calculations, and the Broselow tape reduces both error modes by color-coding the dose against measured length rather than estimated weight. Write the calculation on the casualty card before administration; verify with a second responder when one is available.

01.8.10Herbal preparations — five methods

Herbal extension of the pharmacy runs five preparation methods. Canterbury specifies the techniques.

Herbal preparation — five methods
01INFUSIONSoft parts (leaves, flowers) in just-off-boiling water 10–15 min covered. Yarrow, plantain, chamomile tea.
02DECOCTIONHard parts (roots, bark, seeds) simmered 20–45 min. Willow-bark decoction (salicin — aspirin precursor), burdock root.
03FOMENTATIONCloth soaked in hot infusion applied externally as compress.
04WASHCool infusion applied externally to wounds, eyes, skin.
05POULTICEMashed or chewed plant applied directly to wound. Plantain poultice draws venom from insect stings; yarrow leaf poultice stops bleeding.

INFUSE SOFT, DECOCT HARD. The preparation method matches plant anatomy — leaves and flowers release their active compounds at sub-boiling steep, while roots and bark require sustained simmer to extract, and a decoction attempt on a flower burns the active fraction while an infusion of bark extracts nothing. Consistent preparation preserves dose predictability across batches.

01.8.11Medicinal plant index

A small field formulary scales across climates. Canterbury and Warnock converge on the core set.

Field formulary — common medicinal plants
01YARROW (Achillea millefolium)Soldier's woundwort. Hemostatic poultice. Febrifuge infusion.
02PLANTAIN (Plantago major)Insect stings, cuts, burns. Chew-and-apply poultice.
03WILLOW BARKPain, fever. Decoction. Salicin precursor to aspirin; same contraindications.
04ECHINACEAImmune support.
05ELDERBERRY SYRUPFlu, cold. Modern studies support antiviral activity.
06CHAGA (on white birch)Antioxidant tea.
07PINE NEEDLE TEAVitamin C, ~5× orange juice per gram.

DO NOT SUBSTITUTE WITHOUT CONFIRMED ID. Yarrow and plantain carry lethal lookalikes in other plant families; the foraging discipline from 01.5 applies to medicinal plants with the same ruthlessness. Herbal preparation as adjunct to manufactured drugs extends the pharmacy window, but a plantain poultice does not replace a tourniquet, and echinacea tea does not replace doxycycline in a tick-exposure prophylaxis window; the rule is augment, not substitute.

01.8.12Potassium permanganate — four-function reagent

A single reagent covers four field needs. Canterbury specifies the concentrations.

Potassium permanganate — four field functions
01WATER DISINFECTIONLight-pink solution. Dissolves until barely tinted. Drink after 30 min contact.
02WOUND WASHLight-pink solution. Antiseptic flush.
03ANTIFUNGAL SKINMedium-pink solution. Foot soak for athlete's foot, trench foot, fungal infection.
04FIRE STARTERDry crystals + glycerin. Self-igniting reaction in 30–60 s.

ONE CHEMICAL, FOUR FUNCTIONS, CONCENTRATION-DEPENDENT. The concentration controls the function — overconcentrated for water or wound wash burns tissue; underconcentrated for fungal treatment fails. KMnO4 illustrates the consolidated-reagent principle of the austere pharmacy: a single cheap stable crystal carries four functions that would otherwise require four separate purpose-specific chemicals, and the weight savings free caloric budget for other primitives.

01.8.13Install, function, failure, feed-forward

INSTALL. You carry the single-best-antibiotic (doxycycline) plus syndrome-specific extensions where weight and caloric budget allow. You rotate nitroglycerin on a 6 MO calendar and EpiPens on a 12 MO calendar. You carry the ACS pack (aspirin 324 mg chewables, sublingual nitroglycerin, clopidogrel load), the anaphylaxis pack (EpiPen, diphenhydramine, prednisone), and the wound-care pack (lidocaine 1%, 18-gauge needle, 60 mL syringe, saline). You rehearse EpiPen deployment, aspirin-chew-for-ACS, and casualty-card documentation until the sequence runs autonomically.

FUNCTION INDICATORS. The subsystem functions when the right drug reaches the right patient at the right dose, route, and time with the documentation trail intact. Antibiotic selection matches syndrome rather than defaulting to broadest coverage. NTG is in-date and potent. The EpiPen deploys on anaphylaxis with diphenhydramine and prednisone as adjunct. Herbal preparations augment manufactured drugs without substituting where substitution is unsafe.

FAILURE INDICATORS. The subsystem fails when expired nitroglycerin is trusted in ACS. It fails when ibuprofen stacks past maximum in a dehydrated patient and triggers renal injury. It fails when an anaphylactic casualty receives diphenhydramine as primary rather than epinephrine. It fails when antibiotic "gut reset" disrupts flora and drives diarrhea dehydration in a casualty who needed the stock for a real infection. It fails when pediatric dosing defaults to adult-by-eye and the child arrests from overdose.

FEED-FORWARD. System integration installs next in 01.9 — the Ten Cs kit scaffold mapped onto the Rule-of-Threes layers, the three-tier kit architecture (EDC, IFAK, team), the 72-hour / 7-day / 30-day cache, the first-24-hour sequence, the calorie-water-heat budget, signaling primitives, long-term sanitation, and the reassessment tempo. The pharmacy closes the medical tier; integration closes the sub-module.
