System integration: kit, sequence, extended deployment

TEN CsCUTTING · COMBUSTION · COVER · CONTAINER · CORDAGE · CANDLING · CARGO TAPE · COTTON · COMPASS · CANVAS NEEDLE
KIT TIERSEDC · IFAK · TEAM/VEHICLE
CACHE72 hr · 7 d · 30 d
PACEPRIMARY · ALTERNATE · CONTINGENCY · EMERGENCY
COLD-WX STEADY STATE4500 kcal/d · 6–8 qt WATER · ~100 lb GREEN WOOD (~50 lb SEASONED)
72-HR BUG-OUT WATER18 qt OR WATER + FILTER
DISTRESS SIGNALS3 FIRES · 3 SMOKE · 3 WHISTLE · V = ASSISTANCE · X = UNABLE
MIRROR RANGE~10 mi CLEAR
LATRINE SITING>200 ft FROM WATER · >3 ft ABOVE WATER TABLE
REASSESS TEMPO15 min ACTIVE · 1 hr STABLE · WATCH-CHANGE CAMP

Sub-module 01 installs nine subsystems. Integration is the thesis — shelter, fire, water, food, and the medical stabilizer interlock as a compound, and the weight of the sub-module is in the handoffs between them. Canterbury's Advanced Bushcraft supplies the Ten Cs kit scaffold; TW-05 supplies the three-tier kit architecture (EDC, IFAK, team) and the equipment inventories; Harvesting H2O supplies the long-horizon water infrastructure that anchors the 30-day cache; Stewart's 365 Essential Survival Skills supplies the signaling primitives and the field-expedient extensions that carry the subsystem through unplanned-duration events.

This section installs the integration layer. You load the Ten Cs scaffold that maps gear to function, the Ten Cs-to-Rule-of-Threes mapping that routes each item to the time-to-kill layer it supports, the three kit tiers (EDC, IFAK, team/vehicle) that scale the architecture to operational tempo, minimum-viable redundancy with PACE planning that runs three-deep across three failure modes per irreplaceable function, the 72-hour / 7-day / 30-day tiered cache that extends across time-scales, the first-24-hour sequence that enforces priority order under stress, the calorie-water-heat steady-state budget that quantifies daily throughput, signaling primitives with the international distress code, long-term sanitation and sick-call discipline that prevents camp-sourced illness from dominating the casualty load, the reassessment tempo that preserves medical vigilance across watch changes, the rehearsal-beats-hoarding principle, and the install protocol, function indicators, failure modes, and feed-forward handoffs. Sources: Advanced Bushcraft (Ten Cs, redundancy philosophy, cold-weather budgets); TW-05 (three-tier kit, IFAK inventory, sanitation discipline); Harvesting H2O (long-horizon water infrastructure); 365 Essential Survival Skills (distress codes, signaling, field-expedient extensions).

01.9.1The Ten Cs scaffold

Canterbury's Ten Cs partition gear by function. Advanced Bushcraft anchors the inventory.

The Ten Cs — function-indexed kit
01CUTTING TOOLFixed-blade knife. The one item that earns its weight daily.
02COMBUSTION DEVICEFerro rod primary; lighter alternate; char tin for ember preservation.
03COVERTarp, poncho, bivy. The 3-hour layer's anchor.
04CONTAINERMetal 32 oz Nalgene-class. Boil-capable; holds the water system.
05CORDAGEParacord, bankline. Shelter rigging, snares, fishing, lashings.
06CANDLING DEVICEHeadlamp primary; candle alternate.
07CARGO TAPEGorilla or duct. Repair, wound closure in emergency, improvised glove.
08COTTONBandanna, shemagh, cotton balls for char-cloth stock.
09COMPASSBaseplate or lensatic. The traverse layer's anchor (02).
10CANVAS NEEDLEHeavy needle + waxed thread. Gear repair, wound suture in extremity.

EACH C SERVES A TIME-TO-KILL LAYER. The function indexing is the point — the Ten Cs are not a shopping list, they are a kit audit against the Rule of Threes. The scaffold fails when the operator carries duplicate knives and three lighters but omits the metal container, because the kit passes a gear-enthusiast check while failing the 3-day water layer, and the first rain-soaked night exposes the asymmetry.

01.9.2Ten Cs mapped onto the Rule-of-Threes layers

The Ten Cs cross-index the Rule of Threes. Advanced Bushcraft and the TCCC Handbook converge on the mapping.

Ten Cs × Rule of Threes — layer mapping
013 MIN AIRWAYCPR training (no item cost). IFAK-level NPA kit.
023 HR THERMOREGULATIONCOVER (tarp). COTTON (bandanna, shemagh). COMBUSTION (ferro rod). CANDLING (headlamp for dark-hour work).
033 DAY WATERCONTAINER (metal Nalgene). Purification tabs. Sawyer Squeeze filter. CORDAGE (solar-still and condensation rigs).
043 WEEK FOODCANVAS NEEDLE. CORDAGE (snares, fishing). Small-game kit.
05UBIQUITOUSCUTTING TOOL. CARGO TAPE. COMPASS. COTTON (char-cloth stock).

THE MAP REPLACES THE CHECKLIST. The operator does not pack ten items; the operator packs coverage across four layers with redundancy at each. A kit that weighs the same as another kit but covers all four layers outperforms the heavier kit that triples the 3-day water and skips the 3-week food, because survival time is bounded by the shortest-covered layer, not by the total weight of the pack.

01.9.3Three kit tiers — EDC, IFAK, team

The kit scales in three tiers by role and tempo. TW-05 specifies the tier architecture.

Three kit tiers — scaled architecture
01EDC (EVERYDAY CARRY)Knife, lighter, tourniquet, trauma shears, light, multitool, permanent marker, small bleed kit.
02IFAK (INDIVIDUAL FIRST AID KIT)CAT tourniquet, combat gauze, pressure bandage, chest seals pair, NPA, decompression needle, permanent marker, nitrile gloves, trauma shears.
03TEAM / VEHICLECrystalloid + tubing, IO kit, SAM splint, hypothermia kit (Ready-Heat, HPMK), full antibiotic cache, extraction gear, litter.

THE EDC CARRIES THE FIRST-MINUTE CAPABILITY. EDC runs the interventions the operator can deploy immediately without returning to the pack or vehicle. The IFAK is worn on the body, not stored in the pack, because the MARCH inventory addresses the time-to-kill window that the pack fails to reach; a tourniquet in a ruck at 50 ft has the same mortality profile as no tourniquet at all for an arterial bleed. Team kit extends coverage to the casualties EDC and IFAK stabilize.

01.9.4Minimum-viable redundancy and the PACE principle

Redundancy runs three-deep across three failure modes per irreplaceable function. Advanced Bushcraft and the TCCC Handbook converge on PACE planning.

PACE — four-level redundancy

PRIMARY · Preferred method. Carried as first reach. ALTERNATE · Independent second method. Different failure mode than primary. CONTINGENCY · Field-expedient third method. Lower capability, broader availability. EMERGENCY · Last-resort method. Functions when first three fail simultaneously.

Minimum-viable redundancy — three irreplaceables
01IGNITIONFerro rod (mechanical) → lighter (chemical) → char tin (ember preservation) → bow-drill training (no-tool).
02WATERBoil (heat) → bleach (chemical) → Sawyer (mechanical) → solar still (evaporation).
03AIRWAYPosition (recovery) → NPA (device) → surgical cricothyroidotomy (skill + scalpel) → bag-valve-mask (ventilation-only).

THREE DEEP ON THREE DIFFERENT FAILURE MODES. A kit that carries three lighters is not redundant — it is three instances of the same chemical-ignition failure mode sharing a fuel dependency, and a cold-soaked pack kills all three simultaneously. Three-deep with mode-diversity crosses the single failure-mode gap that concentrated redundancy leaves open.

01.9.5The 72-hour / 7-day / 30-day tiered cache

The cache extends across time-scales. TW-05 and Harvesting H2O converge on the tiered architecture.

Tiered cache — time-scale architecture
0172-HR BUG-OUT18 qt water or water + filter. Shelter tarp + insulation. Redundant ignition. 3-day dense food. Complete IFAK.
027-DAY EXTENDEDFilter + chemical backup. Secondary tent shelter. Cook kit. Expanded pharmacy. Communications (radio, beacon).
0330-DAY HOME OR RETREATStored water + drilled well or rain catchment. Fuel cache. Long-term food (grains, beans, canned). Chickens and garden. Antibiotic reserves. Tool redundancy.

EACH TIER IS INFRASTRUCTURE, NOT INVENTORY. The 30-day tier is not a larger version of the 72-hr tier; the scaling is architectural. Stored water at 30-day scale exceeds practical carry weight, so the tier shifts to drilled well, rain catchment, or riparian siting — the cache's center of gravity moves from what fits in the pack to what is installed in the terrain, and the operator's role shifts from carrier to siter.

01.9.6The first-24-hour sequence

The first 24 hr enforce the priority order. Advanced Bushcraft and TW-05 converge on the hour-block sequence.

First 24 hours — hour-block sequence
01HR 0STOP. Inventory. MARCH on self and team.
02HR 0–1Fire and dry layer if cold-wet.
03HR 1–3Shelter oriented for wind, water, widowmakers, wood (the four Ws).
04HR 3–6Water procurement plan. If none feasible in 24 hr, signal plan.
05HR 6–24Signal (ground-to-air markers, signal fire, mirror). Begin low-priority passive food (snares, trotlines).
06HR 24+Shift to sustained subsistence.

THE FIRE-SHELTER-WATER TRILEMMA ORDERS BY TIME-TO-KILL. At dusk in 40°F rain, the sequence runs tarp first (fastest shelter preserves capacity for everything else), fire second (stops the hypothermia spiral), water in the morning. Trying for all three simultaneously and accomplishing none is the classic preventable fatality — the operator who attempts a bow-drill fire in the rain while still un-sheltered hypothermics before ignition, and the subsystem fails at hour two of an event that should have run 72 hr to rescue.

01.9.7The calorie-water-heat steady-state budget

Steady-state operation runs a known throughput. Advanced Bushcraft specifies the cold-weather budget.

Cold-weather steady-state — daily budget

CALORIES · ~4500 kcal/d for active work in cold conditions. WATER · 6–8 qt/d (higher end under load and at altitude). FIREWOOD · ~100 lb green / ~50 lb seasoned per day for 2 cook fires + 1 overnight sustain. WOOD COLLECTION · 2–3 hr with cutting tool; 6–10 hr without.

THE CUTTING TOOL EARNS ITS WEIGHT DAILY. Each unpowered day the saw-and-axe pair saves 4–7 hr over by-hand wood procurement, which is caloric and thermoregulatory dividend compounded. The FARMED criteria for kit selection (Functional, Affordable, Repairable, Multi-use, Effective, Durable) reframe under steady-state as caloric accounting — the heavy tool that halves daily wood-collection time returns its weight in calories saved and body heat preserved within the first cold week, and the weight-optimized ultralight kit that doubles the collection time runs a caloric deficit that depletes reserves by day ten.

01.9.8Signaling primitives

The international distress code runs standardized signals. 365 Essential Survival Skills specifies the primitives.

Signaling — international distress code
01FIRES3 fires in triangle or line at night.
02SMOKE3 smoke columns by day. Green foliage on coals produces white smoke visible against dark forest; dry tinder produces black smoke visible against snow.
03MIRROR / HELIOGRAPHFlash at aircraft. Visible to ~10 mi in clear air.
04WHISTLE3 blasts. Carries farther than voice with less caloric cost.
05GROUND-TO-AIR PANELSV = ASSISTANCE REQUIRED · X = UNABLE TO PROCEED · SOS spelled out in high-contrast material.

THREE IS THE UNIVERSAL DISTRESS NUMBER. Three fires, three smoke columns, three whistle blasts, three mirror flashes — the rule of three distinguishes distress from random signal across every modality. Signaling is the highest-leverage low-caloric activity in the first 24 hr — a mirror flash at an aircraft costs seconds and returns potential rescue, while building a redundant shelter consumes hours and returns incremental comfort, and the sequencing places signaling above food procurement for precisely this reason.

01.9.9Long-term sanitation and sick-call discipline

Camp-sourced illness dominates long-deployment morbidity. TW-05 specifies the sanitation architecture.

Long-term sanitation — infrastructure
01LATRINESingle dedicated pit. >200 ft from water source. >3 ft above water table. Cover soil or lime after use.
02HANDWASH STATIONAt camp entry. Soap, clean water, drying surface.
03SURFACE SEPARATIONFood-prep surfaces distinct from wound-care surfaces.
04DAILY SICK CALLPriority order: new trauma → worsening conditions → chronic.
05ISOLATIONSuspected contagious illness isolated from camp population.
06TRASHBuried or burned to suppress scent signature.

CAMP-SOURCED ILLNESS OUTPACES TRAUMA ON LONG DEPLOYMENTS. The 30-day casualty ledger is dominated by diarrhea, respiratory infection, and wound infection from contaminated care — none of which require hostile action, all of which are prevented by sanitation infrastructure. The discipline erodes predictably when fatigue sets in and the latrine walk feels excessive; the preventive architecture compensates by making the sanitary path shorter than the shortcut, with the handwash station at the camp entry and the food surface closer than the latrine.

01.9.10Reassessment tempo

Reassessment runs on schedule regardless of apparent stability. TCCC Handbook and Forgey converge on the tempo.

Reassessment — three cadences

ACTIVE TRAUMA · Every 15 min. MARCH sweep, vitals, intervention status. STABLE CASUALTY · Every 1 hr. Vitals, mental status, drainage or dressing check. PERMANENT CAMP · Every watch change. Sick-call round, medication log, environmental check.

REASSESS ON SCHEDULE, NOT ON CRISIS. The casualty who appears stable at hour two crashes at hour four when the TXA window closes, the bleed resumes under the pressure dressing, or the hypothermic rewarm plateaus. Documentation on the casualty card or SOAP format carries the trend — the single measurement is weakly informative; the delta across three measurements flags the deterioration before the hemodynamic collapse, and the scheduled reassessment is what produces the delta.

01.9.11Rehearsal beats hoarding

Gear rehearsed under stress outperforms gear stored new. Advanced Bushcraft anchors the principle.

A ferro rod is a paperweight to someone who has never started a fire in the rain with one. A tourniquet in sealed packaging has never been practiced under the stress of a bleeding partner. Fitness beats gear: a fit person with a knife outlasts an unfit person with a full pack because caloric reserve, cold tolerance, and decision-making under fatigue all scale with baseline conditioning.01.9.11 · The rehearsal principle

PATIENCE IS THE UNDER-WEIGHTED PRIMITIVE. Most survival fatalities are not skills failure but premature action — moving when waiting would bring rescue, eating an unknown plant for quick calories, crossing a river rather than a day's detour. When you do not know, wait. MARCH in the backcountry extends civilian wilderness medicine beyond ABCDE because uncontrolled extremity bleeding kills faster than airway compromise in any environment where firearms, chainsaws, large game, vehicles, or roadsides are present, and the rehearsed tourniquet-first sequence replaces the defaulted ABCDE that fails in any non-clinical setting.

01.9.12Install, function, failure, feed-forward

INSTALL. You carry the Ten Cs against the Rule-of-Threes mapping, tiered across EDC, IFAK, and team/vehicle. You build PACE redundancy three-deep on ignition, water, airway, and shelter. You stage the 72-hr / 7-d / 30-d cache with each tier's architecture rather than scaling inventory. You rehearse the first-24-hr sequence under cold-wet conditions until it runs autonomically. You quantify the 4500 kcal, 6–8 qt water, ~100 lb wood daily budget against expected exertion. You install the sanitation infrastructure before the casualty count demands it.

FUNCTION INDICATORS. The subsystem functions when kit maps onto the Rule-of-Threes layers without gap, when the first-24-hour sequence executes in priority order under cold-wet stress, when minimum-viable redundancy crosses three failure modes on each irreplaceable function, and when the medical protocol stabilizes any trauma that degrades operator capacity to run the other primitives. Reassessment tempo holds across the event. Signaling runs as the highest-leverage low-caloric activity.

FAILURE INDICATORS. The subsystem fails when redundancy concentrates in one primitive at the expense of coverage across four. It fails when unrehearsed gear sits in the pack during the first real ignition attempt in rain. It fails when the sanitation discipline erodes and camp-sourced illness dominates the casualty load. It fails when the operator attempts all of fire, shelter, and water simultaneously at dusk in cold rain and accomplishes none. It fails when signaling is deferred in favor of extra shelter construction and the rescue window closes.

FEED-FORWARD. Sub-module 01 closes the primary-systems layer. Sub-module 02 (TRAVERSE) installs movement across terrain — routing, navigation, alpine, conditioning — on the ground that 01 now keeps survivable. The medical stabilizer threads forward into every subsequent sub-module as the capacity-preserver when trauma or illness degrades operator function under movement, applied force, compound operations, long-horizon sustainment, command, and field deployment. The primitive that is ignored is the one that kills — fatalities cluster on the gap, not the redundancy, and 01's compound integrity depends on coverage across all four primitives with the medical stabilizer live through every one.

Close — from primary systems to traverse

You now hold nine interlocking subsystems running as the foundational architecture layer — Rule-of-Threes triage, shelter systems and thermal regulation, fire-craft and ignition, water procurement and purification, wild food and foraging economics, MARCH and PAWS trauma response, non-trauma field medicine, field pharmacology and the improvised pharmacy, and the integrated kit-sequence-sanitation architecture. Each subsystem carries explicit install protocols, functioning indicators, and failure signatures. Each subsystem cross-feeds the others: shelter reduces the fuel burden fire would otherwise shoulder, fire enables the boil-kill standard water purification assumes, water purification protects against the dehydration that accelerates hypothermia and degrades every other primitive, food ROI economics dictate passive gear that frees caloric budget for shelter maintenance and signaling, and the medical protocol threads through every primitive as the stabilizer that preserves operator capacity when trauma or illness degrades it.

The primitive that is ignored is the one that kills. Fatalities cluster on the gap, not the redundancy. The subsystem is a compound, and its integrity depends on coverage across all four primitives with the medical stabilizer live through every one.

This is the FOUNDATIONAL ARCHITECTURE LAYER of the RSI progression. Everything downstream compounds on it. Movement in 02 routes across ground that 01 keeps survivable. Applied force in 03 scales from hand to small unit on the ground that 01 keeps you alive on and 02 lets you move through. The compound layer in 04 interlocks 00, 01, 02, and 03 into feedback loops that require the foundation in place. Sustainment in 05 scales 01's primitives to long-horizon infrastructure. Command in 06 runs decision architecture over the teams that 01 stabilizes medically. Field deployment in 07 indexes condition-class triggers into the subsystem-activation matrix, and 01's subsystems populate the majority of first-call activations because the primary-systems layer runs under every operational condition.

01 foundational → downstream compound
**01.1–01.5Shelter, fire, water, food primitives feed → 02 traverse (cold-weather movement, water-crossing discipline), 04 compound systems (environmental-stress feedback loops), 05 sustainment (long-horizon infrastructure scaling), 07 field deployment** (condition-class environmental triggers).
**01.6–01.8Trauma response, non-trauma medicine, pharmacology feed → 02 traverse (alpine medicine, load-injury prevention), 03 applied force (casualty stabilization mid-engagement), 06 command (casualty-driven decision tempo), 07 field deployment** (medical readiness by condition class).
**01.9System integration** feeds → every downstream module, because every downstream module runs the kit, sequence, and sanitation discipline that 01.9 has already standardized.

The operator who runs 01 at operational standard carries a body maintained, a team stabilized, a kit rehearsed, and a compound system that holds integrity across the first 24 hr through the first 30 d and beyond. The operator who skips 01 runs every subsequent subsystem on a body that is cold, dehydrated, underfed, and untreated, and every downstream gain multiplies against that degradation.

01 COMPOUNDS THE SUBSYSTEMS. Sub-module 01 is not a collection of skills; it is a compound in which each primitive protects the operator's capacity to run the others. The shelter that survives the night preserves the body that runs the traverse. The fire that heats the water prevents the hypothermia that would collapse the trauma intervention. The trauma protocol that stabilizes the casualty preserves the team that signals for rescue. When any single primitive drops out, the rest lose leverage — not because any one primitive is sufficient, but because the compound is the asset, and gaps transmit through the entire chain.

You survive the ground. You stabilize the team. You keep the primitives compounding through the first twenty-four hours and forward. Primary Systems is installed. Traverse installs next.

SUB-MODULE 01 · HEARTH · FOUNDATIONAL ARCHITECTURE (1/3)

PRIMARY SYSTEMS

Survival primitives and the medical interlock — foundational architecture of the ground operator

9

02/08
POSITION

You survive the ground before you move across it. Sub-module 00 built the perceptual substrate; sub-module 01 installs the primitive subsystems that keep the operator breathing, warm, hydrated, fed, and patched through the first critical hours and the sustained days that follow. This is the first beat of foundational architecture in the RSI progression, and every later sub-module assumes that fire, water, shelter, food, and trauma response are already running as default subsystems rather than improvised responses. Install these badly and the sharpest signcutter in the woods dies of hypothermia in wet cotton on the second night. Install them well and the operator's attention is free for terrain, adversary, and command.

The sub-module integrates seven primary-anchor sources and one supporting. Canterbury's Advanced Bushcraft supplies the survival-priorities spine, the Ten Cs, the FARMED blade criteria, the Four Ws of shelter siting, the wild-plant ITEM discipline, and the primitive-shelter building sequences. The TCCC Handbook supplies the three-phase tactical casualty framework, the MARCH algorithm, PAWS secondary sweep, the lethal triad, permissive hypotension, and specific drug and dose protocols. Fire Skills 50 Methods supplies the full ignition taxonomy across mechanical, chemical, electrical, solar, and friction methods with their temperature and duration physics. Harvesting H2O supplies the waterborne-pathogen taxonomy, the treatment hierarchy, well and rain-capture infrastructure, and the chemistry of chlorine, iodine, and distillation. 276 Edible Wild Plants supplies the foraging catalog and the lookalike-hazard architecture. The First Aid Manual TW-05 supplies the WROL aid doctrine, hypothermia staging, burn protocols, cold-weather clothing discipline, and the equipment-tier framework. Forgey's Prepper's Medical Handbook supplies non-trauma field medicine, the pain ladder, antibiotic syndrome-selection, cardiac emergency protocols, and drug-expiration data. Stewart's 365 Essential Survival Skills supplies the field-expedient variants across shelter, fire, and foraging.

Field-medicine scope disclaimer at module level: the protocols in 01.6, 01.7, and 01.8 apply to without-rule-of-law conditions where hospital care is hours to weeks away. Doses and sequences cite TCCC standards, wilderness medicine consensus, and the specific source directly. Inside each section the framework claims stand firm as operational guidance for the scope they address.

By the end of this sub-module you install nine interlocking subsystems: Rule-of-Threes triage, shelter and thermoregulation, fire-craft, water procurement and purification, wild food and foraging economics, trauma response under MARCH and PAWS, non-trauma field medicine, field pharmacology with improvised pharmacy, and the integrated kit-and-sequence architecture for extended deployment. The compounding is the thesis. Shelter without fire stalls; fire without shelter bleeds heat into the sky; water without purification becomes illness; food without cordage and tools becomes calorie loss; and every one of them fails fast if a preventable trauma is not addressed in the first minutes. The medical protocol is the stabilizer that runs through all four primitives. That interlock is the sub-module's central claim.

theFIELD.run / CONSTRUCT_APPLICATIONS / 02 TRAVERSE / 02.1 Map systems — datum, grid, scale, symbology
SECTION 02.1

Map systems — datum, grid, scale, symbology

THREE MAP-LANGUAGE STACKSDATUM / GRID / SCALE+SYMBOLOGY
DATUMSNAD 27 / NAD 83 / WGS 84 / NATRF 2022
NAD 27 → WGS 84 SHIFT~500 ft / ~160 m
UTM60 zones × 6° LAT 80°S – 84°N
USGS HIKER'S QUAD1:24,000 · 7.5 min · 1 in = 2,000 ft
CONTOUR INTERVAL40 ft TYPICAL
INDEX CONTOUREVERY 5th LINE
THREE NORTHSTRUE / MAGNETIC / GRID
MAGNETIC DRIFT~55 km/yr

The map is an instrument, not a picture. Before the operator takes a bearing, before the team commits a leg, before the GPS reports a fix, every map encodes the ground through three independent language stacks: the datum (the mathematical model of Earth's shape the map assumes), the grid (the coordinate system painted onto that model), and the scale and symbology (how ground distance and ground features render on paper or screen). Caudill and Trimble's Essential Wilderness Navigation Ch 1 supplies the taxonomy; Mountaineering: Freedom of the Hills Ch 5 supplies the alpine sidebar; Kjellström's Be Expert with Map & Compass anchors the stack for the compass user. Mix any two of these across map, compass, GPS, or PLB and the operator installs systematic error before the first bearing.

This section installs the map-language stack as operational primitive. You load the three-stack decomposition and the rule that every layer is independent, the datum catalog with NAD 27, NAD 83, WGS 84, and NATRF 2022 plus the ~500 ft shift that destroys field coordination, the grid hierarchy across lat/long, UTM, USNG, and MGRS, the USGS quad scales with contour-interval mechanics, the color code that turns line art into terrain, the three norths that "go north" can ambiguously reference, the grid-convergence correction for UTM at zone edges, the orient-at-every-halt protocol that cross-checks terrain against paper, the marginalia principle that marks declination, datum, and revision date as load-bearing, the datum-mismatch case class that kills SAR segments before they start, and the install / function / failure / feed-forward handoff to compass craft. Sources: Essential Wilderness Navigation Ch 1 (three stacks, datum, grid, scales, contours, colors, orient protocols, margin discipline); Mountaineering: Freedom of the Hills Ch 5 (coordinate systems, grid convergence, G-M angle); Be Expert with Map & Compass (declination diagram, scale, margin authority); Fundamentals of Search and Rescue (datum-mismatch operational consequences).

02.1.1The three stacks

Every topographic map resolves position through three orthogonal layers. Each layer is a choice made by the map's publisher, and none is implied by another. Essential Wilderness Navigation Ch 1 and FOTH Ch 5 both open their navigation chapters on this decomposition.

The three map-language stacks

DATUM · The mathematical model of Earth's shape. Controls what latitude and longitude mean on this sheet. GRID · The coordinate system painted on top of the datum. Controls how position is named — decimal degrees, UTM zone + easting + northing, MGRS letter-letter + digits. SCALE + SYMBOLOGY · The compression ratio from ground to paper plus the visual language of colors, contour intervals, and feature icons. Controls how distance and terrain render.

A shift in any one layer, unmatched across instruments, produces position error that compounds down every downstream navigation decision. THE LAYERS ARE INDEPENDENT. A map in NAD 27 with a UTM grid at 1:24,000 is a different map than the "same" sheet rendered in WGS 84 with MGRS at 1:24,000, even when the topographic content is identical. The operator's first map act is not taking a bearing but confirming which stack the paper represents — datum in the margin, grid in the margin, scale on the legend.

02.1.2Datum — the model underneath

The datum is the Earth-shape model the map's coordinates project onto. Essential Wilderness Navigation Ch 1 and FOTH Ch 5 enumerate the working set for North American operators.

North American working datums
01NAD 27North American Datum 1927. Underlies most older USGS quads.
02NAD 83North American Datum 1983. Current USGS-product refinement.
03WGS 84World Geodetic System 1984. Default GPS datum; functionally identical to NAD 83 at consumer GPS precision.
04NATRF 2022Emerging North American Terrestrial Reference Frame. Supersedes NAD 83 over time.

The NAD 27 to WGS 84 shift averages ~500 ft or ~160 m at the same stated latitude and longitude — larger than any practical SAR segment, larger than most map features the operator is trying to resolve, and large enough to place one team in the wrong drainage while command tracks them in the right one. The map's datum is printed in the lower-left margin. The GPS receiver's datum is a menu setting. SET THE RECEIVER TO THE MAP. NEVER THE REVERSE. The map is the fixed reference on the ground; the receiver is the flexible instrument that conforms.

02.1.3Grid — how position gets named

The grid is the coordinate language overlaid on the datum. Four systems dominate North American field work.

Coordinate grid systems
01LAT/LONGDegrees, minutes, seconds (or decimal degrees) from equator and Prime Meridian. Global coverage. Longitude degrees compress toward the poles. Plotting is slow.
02UTMUniversal Transverse Mercator. 60 vertical zones each 6° wide, between 80°S and 84°N. Position as zone number, easting in meters, northing in meters. Metric, rectangular, SAR-preferred.
03USNGUS National Grid. USGS subset of MGRS for civilian domestic use.
04MGRSMilitary Grid Reference System. NATO variant using 100,000-m grid squares labeled by letters; 1-m precision in a 15-character string.

UTM, USNG, and MGRS share the same underlying Transverse Mercator projection, which makes them interoperable with unit conversion. Lat/long is global but slow to plot and requires explicit sign or hemisphere letter to avoid ambiguity. A 10-digit UTM report of 10 550145mE 4185730mN is unambiguous at 1-m precision. A lat/long report of 37.6°N 121.4°W requires the datum and the direction sign to be named out loud, and field teams who skip those qualifiers seed errors the base station cannot recover.

02.1.4Scale — the compression from ground to paper

Scale is the ratio of map inch to ground distance. USGS standardizes several bands; orienteering runs tighter; regional planning runs looser.

Standard scale bands
011:24,0007.5-minute USGS quad — "the hiker's quad." 1 in = 2,000 ft, roughly 0.38 mi. Covers 7.5′ × 7.5′ of latitude and longitude.
021:62,50015-minute quad — legacy, ~1 in = 1 mi. Still in circulation in Alaska.
031:100,000Metric — 1 cm = 1 km.
041:250,000Regional — ~1 in = 4 mi. Planning only, not field navigation.
051:15,000Orienteering-event standard.
061:10,000 / 1:5,000Sprint and school orienteering.

The 7.5-minute 1:24,000 quad is the operational default for North American ground work. It renders a trail junction, a drainage head, and a ridge inflection clearly enough for leg-level route planning and detailed enough for SAR segment assignment. The 1:250,000 band is too coarse for anything but trip-scale corridor work; trails often do not appear at all. Match scale to operational phase: 1:24,000 or tighter for on-the-ground navigation; 1:100,000 or looser only for corridor planning.

02.1.5Contour intervals and slope reading

Contours encode the third dimension on a flat sheet. The interval — the elevation change between adjacent lines — varies by scale and terrain.

Contour intervals by scale
011:24,000 QUAD40 ft typical in moderate terrain, 20 ft or 10 ft in flat country, 50 ft in steep relief.
021:62,500 QUAD80 ft or 100 ft.
03METRIC QUADS5 m / 10 m / 20 m / 40 m depending on terrain roughness.
04INDEX CONTOUREvery 5th line bolded, labeled with elevation.

Contour spacing reads slope directly. Tight lines mean steep ground; wide lines mean gentle ground; lines touching mean cliff. The V-shape of a single contour names the feature: V pointing uphill marks a drainage or gully because water flows downhill across the V's apex; V pointing downhill marks a ridge or spur because the ridgeline points toward lower ground. Closed concentric loops mark a summit, or a depression if rendered with hachures (small tick marks pointing inward). A saddle between two summits prints as two closed-loop sets joined by a waist of open contours. The contour fingerprint of every feature — drainage, ridge, saddle, cirque, bench — can be rehearsed on a training quad until the operator reads slope, aspect, and feature type in the same glance that reads a city street grid.

02.1.6The color code

USGS conventions assign meaning to color at a glance. Essential Wilderness Navigation Ch 1 enumerates the set.

USGS topographic color conventions
01BROWNContour lines; sand features.
02BLUEWater — perennial solid, intermittent dashed; glaciers and permanent snowfields.
03GREENVegetation — forest, orchard, dense canopy.
04BLACKCultural features — buildings, roads, trails, boundaries, benchmarks.
05REDMajor roads; public-land-survey township and range grid.
06PURPLEPhotorevised features added after last ground survey.
07WHITEOpen terrain without canopy — tundra, meadow, bare rock.

The color-coding lets the operator filter terrain at a glance: green zones mean canopy-attenuated GPS signal and slower bushwhack travel; white zones mean exposed terrain with clear sightlines; blue zones mean water obstacle, water resource, or both. COLOR READS FASTER THAN SYMBOL. The operator who internalizes the code extracts drainage pattern, vegetation density, and route feasibility from a thirty-second scan before any bearing or pace calculation begins.

02.1.7The three norths

"North" names three distinct directions on any map sheet. Confusing them introduces angular error that scales with distance.

The three norths

TRUE NORTH · TN · Geographic pole. Fixed axis of Earth's rotation. Star symbol on the declination diagram. MAGNETIC NORTH · MN · The pole the compass needle tracks. Drifts ~55 km/yr and migrates across years. GRID NORTH · GN · Projection artifact — the direction "up" on the grid lines of UTM, USNG, or MGRS. Diverges from true north at zone edges.

USGS maps print the declination diagram in the lower-left margin, three arrows showing TN, MN, and GN diverging from a common origin at the angles in effect at the map's last update. "GO NORTH" IS AMBIGUOUS. The instruction is 0° relative to which north, and the answer matters because MN can sit 15°–25° off TN on the West Coast or in Alaska, and GN can sit up to 3° off TN at a UTM zone edge. Name the north every time: "bearing 045 true," "bearing 060 magnetic," "heading 030 grid." Every navigation conversation on the ground runs in explicit reference frame, or the operator fails silently.

02.1.8Magnetic drift and stale margins

Magnetic north is a moving pole. The declination printed on a map freezes the angle at a moment in time, and that moment ages.

WARN

Magnetic north drifts at ~55 km/yr. A 1992-print USGS quad in North America is several degrees stale on magnetic declination by 2026. Pull current declination from NOAA before every serious trip. Never trust the margin diagram of a map more than a few years old.

The magnetic pole's drift has accelerated since 1990, crossing from Canadian Arctic territory toward Siberia. The US agonic line of zero declination passed through Minnesota, Iowa, Missouri, Arkansas, and Louisiana in 2015 and has since drifted westward. East of the agonic runs west declination (typically 10°–17° on the East Coast); west of the agonic runs east declination (10°–20° on the West Coast, >25° in Alaska). CURRENT DECLINATION BEFORE EVERY TRIP. The correction runs through a NOAA calculator or a current-edition topo; the margin diagram on an old quad is a historical artifact that confirms the map's datum far better than the current magnetic field.

02.1.9Grid convergence — when grid north drifts

UTM grid lines are not parallel to lines of longitude except at each zone's center meridian. At the east or west edge of a zone, grid north diverges from true north by as much as 3°.

G-M angle on military maps

Military maps print a Grid-Magnetic angle — the full correction from grid north to magnetic north, combining both true-north declination and grid-convergence offset. Civilian USGS maps print only the true-to-magnetic declination and leave grid convergence implicit.

The consequence reaches the navigator at UTM zone boundaries (the West Coast transitions between UTM Zone 10 and Zone 11; the Gulf Coast transitions between Zones 14, 15, and 16). A bearing plotted from UTM grid lines at a zone edge without grid-convergence correction introduces 2°–3° of angular error that compounds down every leg. At zone edges, convert UTM bearings through grid-convergence before applying declination, or plot bearings from true-north lines drawn through the target point rather than the grid itself.

02.1.10Orienting the map

A map held flat on the hood of a truck is useless until the symbols align to the ground. Orientation is the first field action at every halt.

Orient-by-terrain protocol
01IDENTIFYPick one visible ground feature with certainty — peak, lake, road bend, obvious ridge.
02ROTATERotate the map physically until that feature's symbol aligns to the feature on the ground.
03CROSS-CHECKConfirm with a second visible feature. Two-feature confirmation rules out false alignment on a symmetric ridge.
04LOCKNote the direction the map's north arrow now points. That is your true-north reference for the halt.

The compass-assisted variant sets declination on the compass, lays the compass along a map north-south line, and rotates map and compass together until the needle points to map north. ORIENT AT EVERY HALT. The map-to-ground alignment lapses every time the operator moves, turns, or sets the map down. Thirty seconds of re-orientation per halt costs nothing against the hour of back-tracking a mis-oriented leg generates.

02.1.11The marginalia is the map

Every working layer of map information sits in the margins. Trimming them to save pack weight destroys the instrument.

Scale, contour interval, datum, declination, grid designation, magnetic-declination diagram, revision date, legend, publisher — the sheet without margins is a picture of terrain, not a navigation instrument.02.1.11 · The margin is load-bearing

Kjellström's rule anchors the discipline: an operator who carries the body of a map without the margins carries a collectible illustration. The scale sets distance estimation; the contour interval sets slope reading; the datum sets coordinate interoperability; the declination sets compass correction; the revision date sets whether the magnetic correction can be trusted at all. KEEP THE MARGINS. FOLD, DO NOT CUT. A weatherproof map case carries the full sheet; a map in a pocket gets folded along the creases so that the working area sits face-up without severing the margin strip.

02.1.12The "free map" trap

Default hiker and trail apps render street-tile base maps, not topographic. A trail that looks passable on a default screen may hide a cliff band the app has no contour data to draw.

WARN

A "free" app map without the topographic layer active is a road-network illustration. Always verify the contour/topo layer is enabled before planning a leg. A 2,000-ft cliff band that does not render is still there.

The street-tile base is optimized for urban navigation: road centerlines, building footprints, intersection names. The topographic overlay is a separate data layer that must be explicitly enabled on most consumer apps. An operator who plans an alpine route on the default tile set misses every relief feature that would normally determine the leg's feasibility. The topo layer is the deliverable; the street tile is the wrapper. On any serious trip, the paper USGS quad or the offline-cached topographic map is the primary, and the screen runs as confirmation.

02.1.13Same coordinate, different ground — the datum-mismatch case

The load-bearing failure mode of sub-module 02 is a datum mismatch between map and GPS. Fundamentals of Search and Rescue and Essential Wilderness Navigation converge on the case class.

Case class — the 500-ft offset

A field team reads a coordinate off a NAD 27 paper quad and relays it by radio to command. Command enters the same numeric coordinate into a WGS 84–based rescue-management GIS. True positions differ by ~500 ft. The field team searches one grid cell; command plots them in another. The mismatch is resolved only after hours of wasted sweep coverage, with POD values logged against the wrong segment.

The case is not an edge case. Many SAR operations run mixed-vintage paper maps alongside current-vintage GPS and GIS. The discipline that blocks the failure is simple and non-negotiable: DATUM ON THE RADIO. Every coordinate transmission names its datum: "UTM Zone 10, NAD 83, five-five-zero-one-four-five East, four-one-eight-five-seven-three-zero North." The one-line datum tag at the head of a coordinate string is the simplest unit of SAR-coordination hygiene and the one most commonly dropped.

02.1.14Install, function, failure, feed-forward

INSTALL. You load the three-stack decomposition — datum, grid, scale and symbology — as the first three questions asked of any map. You read the margin before the body: datum, grid type, scale, contour interval, declination, revision date. You match GPS receiver datum to paper-map datum before the trip starts. You run the orient-at-every-halt protocol as automatic reflex. You name declination in current NOAA terms, not the print on the quad. You transmit every coordinate with its datum and grid tag attached.

FUNCTION INDICATORS. The subsystem functions when the operator reads slope, aspect, and feature type from contour fingerprints inside thirty seconds of opening the map. Color coding filters terrain at a glance. GPS and map agree on position within the receiver's rated accuracy. Radio coordinate transmissions carry datum tags. Orientation cross-checks confirm with at least two features before committing a bearing. The map's margin remains intact.

FAILURE INDICATORS. The subsystem fails when a default hiker-app tile set substitutes for topographic data. It fails when "go north" is said without naming true, magnetic, or grid. It fails when a radio coordinate transmission drops the datum tag and command plots to the wrong grid cell. It fails when the margin diagram's declination is treated as current despite a stale map date. It fails when grid convergence at a UTM zone edge is ignored and the bearing drifts several degrees per leg. It fails when the map is held in one hand and the ground is read with the other, never cross-checked.

FEED-FORWARD. Compass craft installs next in 02.2 — the subsystem that converts the map stack this section installs into a ground-heading under magnetic and declination correction. Every bearing the compass produces assumes the map's datum, grid, and declination are read and applied correctly; the map stack is the scaffold the compass stands on.

theFIELD.run / CONSTRUCT_APPLICATIONS / 02 TRAVERSE / 02.10 Physical conditioning — FITT, AeT/LT, periodization, altitude
SECTION 02.10

Physical conditioning — FITT, AeT/LT, periodization, altitude

FITTFREQUENCY / INTENSITY / TIME / TYPE
SMARTSPECIFIC / MEASURABLE / ACHIEVABLE / RELEVANT / TIME-BOUND
MHR ≈ 220 − AGE (±10–20 bpm)
AEROBIC ZONE65–95% MHR
AeT ≈ +1 mMol/L LACTATE ≈ ~75% MHR NOSE-BREATHING PACE

Z1–Z5 ARCHITECTURE

Conditioning underwrites everything above. The operator who cannot move the terrain at the rate navigation prescribes is an operator for whom every map becomes aspirational, every Naismith estimate becomes a lie, and every aiming-off leg runs late into last light. Steve House and Scott Johnston's Training for the New Alpinism and its sister volume Training for the Uphill Athlete (House, Johnston, Jornet) anchor the endurance-physiology architecture; Mountaineering: Freedom of the Hills Chapter 4 supplies the FITT, SMART, and seasonal periodization frames. Physical conditioning is the aerobic engine beneath the navigation stack, and every subsystem in 02 degrades in the operator whose engine is undertrained.

This section installs physical conditioning as the movement-rate underwriter for the entire module. You load the FITT framework structuring every session, the SMART goal architecture anchoring training cycles to specific mountain objectives, the seasonal periodization running post / off / pre / in-season blocks, the Z1–Z5 intensity architecture with AeT and LT definitions, the polarized 80 / 20 distribution preferred for endurance-dominant sport, the aerobic-engine mechanism of mitochondrial density, capillary density, and slow-twitch lactate clearance, the Aerobic Deficiency Syndrome failure mode from threshold-heavy training, the baseline fitness test of 5 mi round-trip / 13 lb / 2,000 ft / under 2.5 hr, the nose-breathing AeT field test and heart-rate-drift AeT test, the altitude-acclimatization rules of ≤ 1,000 ft/day sleeping gain above 8,000 ft with rest day every 3,000 ft, the AMS / HACE / HAPE escalation and descend-descend-descend rule, the CGM master principles (Continuity, Gradualness, Modulation), the TINSTAAFL discipline refusing shortcuts at physiology level, and the install / function / failure / feed-forward handoff closing the sub-module. Sources: House / Johnston Training for the New Alpinism (Z1–Z5 architecture, aerobic-engine mechanism, ADS, periodization); House / Johnston / Jornet Training for the Uphill Athlete (endurance specificity, altitude integration); Mountaineering: Freedom of the Hills Ch 4 (FITT, SMART, seasonal periodization frame).

02.10.1FITT — the four-variable session frame

Every training session gets specified on four variables.

FITT
01FREQUENCYDays per week. 3–6 typical for endurance athletes; progression runs from lower to higher across a training cycle.
02INTENSITY% MHR, % AeT, % LT, or RPE 1–10. Intensity zone dictates physiological adaptation.
03TIMESession duration in minutes or hours. Aerobic-engine sessions run longer than threshold sessions by roughly 3 : 1.
04TYPECardiovascular, strength, flexibility, skill-specific. Type matches the mountain specificity of the objective.

Maximum heart rate approximates 220 − age, with individual variation of ±10–20 bpm that operator-specific field testing narrows over training cycles. The optimal aerobic-training zone runs 65–95% MHR, subdivided by AeT and LT thresholds into Z1–Z5 (02.10.3). EVERY SESSION IS A FITT RECORD. The operator who logs FITT religiously produces a training-load trend line that identifies overtraining, undertraining, and plateau before symptoms force a rest cycle; the operator who trains by feel alone plateaus once, plateaus twice, and then injures.

02.10.2SMART goals and seasonal periodization

Training without a specific mountain objective drifts.

SMART goal anchor

Specific · Measurable · Achievable · Relevant · Time-bound. Applied: "climb Rainier standard route in 3 days by June 20 with 15 kg pack."

Seasonal periodization breaks the year into four blocks.

Seasonal periodization
01POSTSEASON1–2 weeks active recovery after the season's objective. Cross-train, sleep, decompress.
02OFF-SEASON8–12 weeks baseline rebuild. Cross-training, strength base, low-intensity aerobic volume. No peak pressure; no race-pace work.
03PRESEASON8–16 weeks sport-specific loading. Higher-intensity intervals, weighted pack carries, altitude exposure if available.
04IN-SEASONVariable. Maintenance volume during objectives; taper 1–3 weeks before the priority climb.

SEASONS SHAPE THE YEAR. The operator who runs year-round threshold training burns out by mid-season; the operator who runs the seasonal cycle accumulates a deeper aerobic engine each year without injury spike.

02.10.3The Z1–Z5 intensity architecture

The five-zone model structures every intensity prescription.

Intensity zones
01Z1 RECOVERYBelow AeT. Conversation pace. Post-workout and between-interval volume.
02Z2 AEROBICAt or just below AeT. Nose-breathing pace. Workhorse zone. Builds aerobic engine.
03Z3 TEMPOBetween AeT and LT. Feels like training; physiologically ambiguous. Overused, triggers fatigue plateau.
04Z4 THRESHOLDAt LT. Interval durations 8–20 min.
05Z5 VO₂MAXAbove LT. Interval durations 30 s → 5 min.
AeT · Aerobic Threshold

Intensity at which blood lactate rises ~1 mMol/L above resting baseline. Field-approximated as pace sustainable with nose-breathing for 2 hours, roughly ~75% MHR for most athletes.

LT · Lactate Threshold

Intensity at which blood lactate reaches ~4 mMol/L. Field-approximated as one-hour race pace, roughly ~88% MHR.

AeT AND LT ARE THE RAILS. Every endurance prescription references AeT and LT as the intensity rails; training below AeT builds aerobic engine, training at LT shifts the threshold upward, and training between AeT and LT (the Z3 dead zone) feels productive and delivers the least return.

02.10.4Polarized distribution and the Z3 trap

Endurance-elite data converges on polarized distribution.

Intensity distribution models
01POLARIZED 80 / 2080% Z1–Z2 + 20% Z4–Z5 + minimal Z3. Preferred for elite endurance athletes.
02PYRAMIDALZ1–Z2 > Z3 > Z4–Z5. Preferred for sub-elite athletes with smaller training volumes.
03THRESHOLD-HEAVYZ3–Z4 dominance. Classic error; produces plateau and Aerobic Deficiency Syndrome.

The Z3 trap runs on perceived effort. Z3 feels like real training — sweat, breathing, tempo — but sits too high for aerobic-engine building and too low for threshold shift. The athlete who stays in Z3 accumulates fatigue without adaptation. Z3 IS THE TRAP. The discipline of going easy enough in Z1–Z2 is counterintuitive for athletes who associate training quality with effort; the polarized model works because most of the volume is easier than feels productive, and the hard volume is harder than feels sustainable.

02.10.5The aerobic engine mechanism

Z2 volume builds the engine at the cellular level.

Aerobic-engine mechanism

Long low-intensity work stresses slow-twitch fibers. Cellular adaptations follow: mitochondrial density increase, capillary density increase, aerobic-enzyme upregulation, cardiac stroke-volume increase. Slow-twitch mitochondria function as a metabolic vacuum, absorbing pyruvate from working muscle and preventing lactate accumulation. Larger aerobic vacuum = higher AeT = higher sustainable pace without anaerobic debt.

Fuel economics stack on the mechanism. Aerobic metabolism uses fat preferentially, preserving glycogen (roughly 2,000 kcal stored) for higher-intensity efforts; a lean athlete carries about 100,000 kcal of fat, so aerobic pace becomes effectively unlimited when the engine can use it. FAT IS THE INFINITE TANK. The operator who trains the aerobic engine runs long missions on fat; the operator who trained only threshold runs out of glycogen mid-route and hits the wall with 100,000 kcal of unusable fat still on the body.

02.10.6Aerobic Deficiency Syndrome — the threshold-heavy failure

Z3–Z4 dominance breaks the system.

ADS · Aerobic Deficiency Syndrome

Glycolytic byproducts accumulate faster than aerobic metabolism can clear them. The athlete plateaus, then declines. Symptoms: resting HR elevated, training HR suppressed (the body cannot hit the zone), mood flat, sleep shortened, illness frequency rising, performance at fixed RPE dropping.

Recovery from ADS runs on 6–12 weeks of Z1–Z2 volume with almost no Z3–Z4 work, which athletes resist because the program feels like detraining. ADS IS A CELLULAR STATE, NOT A MOOD. The ADS diagnosis is a system-level reset, and the athlete who accepts the recovery block returns in 3 months with AeT lifted; the athlete who pushes through ADS injures or illnesses out of the season entirely.

02.10.7Volume progression — the 5–15% weekly increase

The progression rule prevents overuse.

Weekly volume rule

5–15% weekly volume increase on the main aerobic modality. Past 15%, overuse injury and overtraining syndrome trend up sharply.

Deload weeks run every 3–4 weeks at ~60–70% of the preceding peak week. RAMP, DON'T SPIKE. The mountain-fitness build is a multi-year arc, and the operator who compounds 5–10% weekly with deloads every fourth week carries a deeper engine in year three than the operator who spiked early and plateaued.

02.10.8Baseline fitness test and AeT field tests

Numbers anchor the training program.

Baseline and AeT field tests
01BASELINE FITNESS5-mile round-trip with 13-lb pack and 2,000 ft gain, under 2.5 hours. Sets the entry line for alpine-objective training; re-run every 3–6 months to track progression.
02NOSE-BREATHING AeTClose mouth on sustained uphill. Pace at which comfortable nose-breathing breaks down approximates AeT.
03HR-DRIFT AeT60-minute steady run at suspected AeT pace. HR drift under 5% across the run indicates sub-AeT; drift above 5% indicates the pace was above AeT.
04LAB TESTBlood-lactate threshold test in a lab confirms AeT and LT within ±1 bpm when field tests conflict.

NUMBERS CORRECT FEEL. Field testing every 6–12 weeks keeps AeT calibrated as the engine grows; the operator who trains to last year's AeT number loses the gain of every intervening adaptation.

02.10.9Altitude physiology — the acclimatization rules

Above 8,000 ft the body initiates significant acclimatization response.

Altitude rules
01RESPONSEVentilatory response in hours (faster and deeper breathing). Renal bicarbonate excretion in days (pH balance). Hematologic EPO-driven red-blood-cell mass increase over days to weeks.
02ASCENT RATESleeping altitude gain ≤ 1,000 ft/day above 8,000 ft. Exceeding the rate forces the body to operate under cellular hypoxia it has not had time to compensate for.
03REST DAYRest day every 3,000 ft gained.
04CLIMB HIGH, SLEEP LOWDay exertion can exceed the night's sleeping altitude; acclimatization tracks sleeping altitude, not peak exertion altitude.

SLEEPING ALTITUDE IS THE DIAL. The acclimatization curve responds to sleeping altitude across days; the climber who pushes camp faster than the rule compresses acclimatization and runs under hypoxia margin on summit day.

02.10.10AMS · HACE · HAPE — the escalation chain

Altitude illness runs on a recognizable escalation.

Altitude illness
01AMSAcute Mountain Sickness. Headache, nausea, fatigue, disturbed sleep. Common above 8,000 ft. Halt ascent; hydrate; consider descent if symptoms worsen.
02HACEHigh-Altitude Cerebral Edema. Ataxia (loss of coordination), confusion, altered mental status. Life-threat. Descend immediately.
03HAPEHigh-Altitude Pulmonary Edema. Shortness of breath at rest, productive cough (pink froth in late stages), cyanosis. Life-threat. Descend immediately.

Pharmacological support (acetazolamide, dexamethasone, nifedipine) buys time but does not substitute for descent. DESCEND, DESCEND, DESCEND. The rule is absolute on HACE and HAPE; the climber who hesitates at first signs in favor of pharmacology alone arrives at the next camp non-ambulatory, and the rescue downgrades from self-evacuation to technical extraction.

02.10.11CGM and TINSTAAFL — the master principles

The framework condenses to master principles.

Continuity · Consistent training over months and years. Missed weeks cost months. Gradualness · 5–15% volume progression. Ramping faster invites injury. Modulation · Intensity and volume modulated across macro-cycles; no single zone dominates. TINSTAAFL · There Is No Such Thing As A Free Lunch. No shortcut at the physiology level; every adaptation costs time and training volume.02.10.11 · CGM and TINSTAAFL

Specificity holds alongside: running builds running, climbing builds climbing. THE BODY OBEYS THE LOAD. The operator who internalizes CGM plus TINSTAAFL runs a training program that looks conservative week-to-week and shows decisive adaptation year-to-year; the operator who trains for shortcuts plateaus and re-plateaus until the body forces a stop.

02.10.12Install, function, failure, feed-forward

INSTALL. You log every session on FITT variables (frequency, intensity as zone and HR, time, type). You define the next mountain objective on SMART. You structure the year in post / off / pre / in-season blocks. You build the aerobic engine through Z1–Z2 volume at 80 / 20 polarized distribution. You test AeT with nose-breathing and HR-drift every 6–12 weeks. You run the baseline fitness test every 3–6 months. You ramp volume at 5–15% weekly with deload every 3–4 weeks. You apply altitude rules above 8,000 ft: ≤ 1,000 ft/day sleeping gain, rest day every 3,000 ft, climb-high-sleep-low, descend on HACE or HAPE.

FUNCTION INDICATORS. AeT pace rises over months on logged volume. Baseline-test time drops cycle over cycle. Resting HR trends down. Sleep deepens. Altitude exposures run clean through the acclimatization curve. In-season objectives close inside planned windows.

FAILURE INDICATORS. Slow-pace discipline breaks, and the program drifts into Z3 tempo. Threshold training dominates, and Aerobic Deficiency Syndrome appears (elevated resting HR, suppressed training HR, illness frequency up). Weekly volume spikes above 15%, and overuse injury follows. Altitude rules get compressed, and AMS turns into HACE on summit day.

FEED-FORWARD. Physical conditioning closes the movement sub-module. The compound of 02.1 → 02.10 installs the navigation, routing, search, tracking, and conditioning architecture that every downstream sub-module — Applied Force in 03, compound systems in 04, sustainment in 05, command in 06, field deployment in 07 — assumes is live on the operator. The CLOSE synthesizes the ten subsystems into the foundational-architecture layer for movement; Applied Force installs next.

SECTION 02.2

Compass — declination, bearings, field technique

FOUR DIRECTIONAL TERMSAZIMUTH / BEARING / HEADING / BACK-AZIMUTH
SCALE360° OR 6,400 MIL

LENSATIC BEZEL120 CLICKS × 3°/CLICK

The compass is a single-purpose instrument and a load-bearing one. It points to magnetic north and nothing else; every navigational value it produces emerges from integration with a map that shares a coordinate system, a known starting fix, or a sighted reference. Kjellström's Be Expert with Map & Compass anchors the doctrine through the Red Fred in the Shed mnemonic and the adjustable-declination rule; Essential Wilderness Navigation Ch 2 supplies the ground-to-map and map-to-ground field protocols, the resection geometry, and the cross-track error math; Mountaineering: Freedom of the Hills Ch 5 supplies the alpine variants for mirror sighting and clinometer; Wilderness Navigation from the Mountaineers confirms the tier hierarchy of baseplate, lensatic, and electronic instruments. The compass converts a read map into a heading the feet can walk.

This section installs compass craft as an executable second subsystem on the map-systems scaffold. You load the anatomy tiers from baseplate through lensatic, the Red Fred in the Shed protocol as the universal find-a-heading primitive, the four directional terms with their operational distinctions, the declination mechanism and the agonic-line geography, the east-least-west-best correction rule and its one-set adjustable-declination substitute, the lensatic 120-click night protocol for zero-light sighting, the take-a-bearing-from-the-ground and take-a-bearing-from-the-map drills run to reflex, the three-landmark resection for position fix, the dead-reckoning discipline of bearing-plus-pace-plus-time, the metal-deflection failure set naming rifle, vehicle, belt buckle, and radio, the cross-track math at ~92 ft/°/mi that destroys SAR segments on small declination oversights, the trust-the-instrument rule when feet and compass disagree in whiteout, and the install / function / failure / feed-forward handoff to GPS and PLB. Sources: Kjellström (declination rules, Red Fred, anatomy); Essential Wilderness Navigation Ch 2 (field technique, resection, dead reckoning, cross-track math); FOTH Ch 5 (alpine variants); Wilderness Navigation (tier hierarchy).

02.2.1Compass anatomy by tier

Three compass classes serve field work, and each tier trades weight and complexity for feature capacity. Wilderness Navigation and Essential Wilderness Navigation Ch 2 rank them for the operator.

Compass tiers
01BASIC BASEPLATETransparent base, direction-of-travel arrow, rotating bezel, magnetic needle. Entry-level. No declination adjustment; every correction is mental.
02FULL-FEATURED BASEPLATEAdds declination-adjustment screw, sighting mirror with notch, and clinometer scale inside the housing. Operator standard.
03LENSATICMetal case, hinged lens and sight wire, rear sight, 120-click audible bezel calibrated to 3°/click. Military issue. Engineered for precise sighting and night work.
04DIGITALGPS receiver, phone app, or altimeter-watch compass. Software-corrected for declination; dependent on power and calibration.

You carry full-featured. The sighting mirror extends useful range from chest-height sling to mirror-and-eye alignment that reads bearings off distant ridge features with lower angular error. The clinometer converts any snow-slope sighting into a slope angle reading that feeds the avalanche assessment in 02.9. The declination screw removes the largest single source of field-calculation error. Digital compasses belong in confirmation role, never in primary; a magnetized steel needle remains functional after a dropped phone, a drained battery, or a wet screen.

02.2.2Red Fred in the Shed

The universal find-a-heading primitive resolves into a single sentence. Kjellström's mnemonic anchors the operator's reflex.

Red Fred in the Shed

Rotate your body until the red north end of the magnetic needle sits inside the orienting arrow engraved in the bezel housing. The direction-of-travel arrow on the baseplate now points your heading.

The mnemonic encodes the physics. The bezel's orienting arrow is a mechanical reference frame the operator sets; the magnetic needle tracks Earth's field independently; when the operator aligns the needle into the orienting arrow by rotating the compass-and-body together, the direction-of-travel arrow locks onto the bearing encoded in the bezel. RED FRED, SHED. The four-word call is the atomic unit of compass use, and every other field protocol in this section assumes the operator runs it without thinking.

02.2.3Azimuth, bearing, heading, back-azimuth

Four directional terms name related but distinct quantities. Mixing them breeds errors the map will not reveal until the leg lands in the wrong drainage.

Directional terms

AZIMUTH · Clockwise angle from a chosen reference north, 0° to 360° or 0 to 6,400 mils. Full-circle. BEARING · Civilian synonym for azimuth. Some traditions use a four-quadrant form (N 45° E); modern SAR defaults to full-circle (045°). HEADING · Your current direction of movement, measured as azimuth. BACK-AZIMUTH · Reciprocal azimuth, computed as azimuth + 180° when azimuth < 180°, else azimuth - 180°. Used to sight back to a known origin for position verification.

NAME THE REFERENCE FRAME EVERY TIME. A 045 magnetic reads ~17° off a 045 true on the East Coast, ~20° off on the West. Radio calls carry the frame attached to the number: "bearing zero-four-five magnetic, back-azimuth two-two-five magnetic." Back-azimuth is the operator's simplest position check: at any halt, sight back to the last known point and confirm the reading matches original bearing plus 180°; a mismatch flags a mis-walked leg before it compounds.

02.2.4Declination — mechanism and geography

Declination is the load-bearing correction of compass work. Essential Wilderness Navigation Ch 2 and Kjellström converge on the operator's reading.

Declination

The horizontal angle between true north and magnetic north at a specific location. East when magnetic north sits right of true north, west when left. Units: degrees. Sign convention: east positive, west negative.

The agonic line of zero declination crossed the continental US through Minnesota, Iowa, Missouri, Arkansas, and Louisiana around 2015 and has since drifted westward. Current declination is location-specific and date-specific, not trip-invariant. East of the agonic, west declination: 10°–17° common on the East Coast. West of the agonic, east declination: 10°–20° on the West Coast, >25° in Alaska. THE MARGIN DECLINATION DIAGRAM AGES. A 1992-print quad reports a value off from 2026 field truth by several degrees, and the operator who reads the margin without cross-checking NOAA plants systematic error into every leg.

02.2.5East is least, west is best

The mental-arithmetic rule converts between true and magnetic bearings. Essential Wilderness Navigation and Kjellström use identical phrasing.

Correction rules

From map-to-compass (true → magnetic): east is least (subtract east declination); west is best (add west declination). From compass-to-map (magnetic → true): east is least (add east declination); west is best (subtract west declination). The rule reverses direction depending on which way you are translating.

The correction is error-prone under cognitive load, cold, and night. A flipped sign introduces exactly the error you were trying to prevent, doubled. An operator who plots 045 true on a West Coast quad with 15° E declination converts cleanly to 030 magnetic in a classroom and wrong roughly as often as right under fatigue. The operational answer is not faster arithmetic; the operational answer is to remove the arithmetic.

02.2.6Adjustable declination — one setting, zero math

Full-featured baseplate compasses carry a declination screw that rotates the orienting arrow away from the bezel index by the declination angle. Once set, compass-to-map and map-to-compass read the same bezel number with no further correction.

Set-declination protocol

PRE-TRIP · Look up current declination for the trip area (NOAA geomagnetic calculator). Rotate the declination screw until the orienting arrow offsets from index by the declination angle, east-positive or west-negative per instrument marking. Confirm visually. Lock. IN-FIELD · Set the bezel to a bearing read directly from the map. Hold compass level. Rotate body until Red Fred sits in the Shed. The direction-of-travel arrow now points the bearing, corrected for magnetic, with no mental arithmetic.

The trade is one thirty-second pre-trip setup against zero field arithmetic. SET DECLINATION ONCE, PER TRIP. A multi-state traverse may require resetting at region borders; NOAA's calculator cues the operator when the delta exceeds a degree or two. The adjustable-declination compass is the single most error-reducing piece of navigation hardware the operator can carry after the map itself.

02.2.7Lensatic 120-click night protocol

The USMC lensatic compass resolves night navigation through a mechanically audible bezel. Essential Wilderness Navigation Ch 2 specifies the protocol.

120-click night protocol
01COMPUTEDerive desired azimuth from map and declination.
02DIVIDEDivide azimuth by 3. Round to nearest integer. That is the click count.
03ROTATERotate the bezel that many clicks from the index. Each click is 3°, felt through the thumb.
04ALIGNIn darkness, align the luminous line on the bezel cover with the luminous needle-north dot through the rear sight.
05WALKAny time the dot sits inside the line, you are on bearing. Sight the next feature through the hinged lens, walk to it, re-check.

Night operation scales the error cost. A 3° bezel-setting error produces ~90 ft cross-track at one mile, and visible landmarks vanish in darkness. The click protocol makes the bezel settable by touch alone. Carry lensatic for dedicated night work, or a full-featured baseplate with tritium needle and bezel markings. The red-filter-flashlight-on-the-instrument method that works in training fails in moonless forest at four a.m.

02.2.8Taking a bearing from the ground

The first operational drill reads bearing off a visible feature. Essential Wilderness Navigation Ch 2 specifies the procedure.

Ground-to-bearing
01HOLDCompass level at chest height, forearms braced, direction-of-travel arrow on target.
02ROTATERotate the bezel until Red Fred sits in the Shed.
03READRead the index line on the bezel. That is the magnetic bearing to the target (or true bearing if declination is pre-set).
04SIGHTOn a full-featured compass, flip up the sighting mirror; hold at eye level; sight the target through the notch; rotate bezel until Red Fred sits in the Shed as seen in the mirror. Mirror sighting reduces angular error by a factor of 2 or more over chest-held.

The drill produces a bearing to any visible feature: a peak, a ridge tree, a structure, a waypoint flag. On long-range sightings through clean mountain air, the compass resolves a ridge a mile distant inside 1°. Operators who practice ground-to-bearing until it takes under fifteen seconds have a navigation primitive available every time a landmark comes into view, and field navigation converts to "sight, bearing, walk" instead of "map, stare, guess."

02.2.9Taking a bearing from the map

The second drill converts a map-measured bearing into a heading the operator can walk.

Map-to-bearing
01PLACELay the compass on the map with one long baseplate edge along the line from start to destination, direction-of-travel arrow toward destination.
02ROTATE BEZELRotate the bezel until the orienting lines inside the housing sit parallel to the map's north-south lines (meridians, UTM grid easting lines, or neat line).
03LIFTRemove the compass from the map. The bezel holds the bearing.
04WALKHold compass level, rotate body until Red Fred sits in the Shed. Direction-of-travel arrow points your heading. Sight a landmark on line; walk to it; re-sight.

The lift-and-walk sequence severs map-work from ground-work and transports the bearing from sheet to world. With adjustable declination set, map-to-bearing returns a magnetic-corrected reading directly. The operator who masters ground-to-bearing and map-to-bearing has a two-way translator between world and sheet; every other compass technique in this section is a specialized application of those two primitives.

02.2.10Resection — position fix from three landmarks

Resection solves the inverse problem: given three visible features of known map position, find the operator's position. Essential Wilderness Navigation Ch 2 supplies the cocked-hat geometry.

Three-landmark resection
01SELECTThree visible landmarks of known map position, separated in azimuth by 60°–120° for geometric strength (avoid three within a narrow wedge).
02SIGHTTake ground-to-bearing on each.
03BACK-AZIMUTHCompute back-azimuth of each.
04PLOTDraw each back-azimuth line on the map from the corresponding landmark.
05COCKED HATThe three lines form a small triangle. Operator position sits inside.
06FIXCocked-hat centroid inside 200 m on clean sightings is typical field accuracy.

A cocked hat larger than 200 m flags an error: misidentified landmark, declination error, metal deflection, or map-datum mismatch. Two landmarks define a line of position, not a point; three is the minimum for a fix; four is better. When four are available, plot all four back-azimuths and drop the one with the largest residual — typically a misidentified feature or a near-axial bearing with weak geometry.

02.2.11Dead reckoning — bearing plus pace plus time

When landmarks vanish (fog, night, featureless terrain), dead reckoning reconstructs position from heading, pace, and time. The compass holds bearing; the feet hold pace; the watch holds time. Essential Wilderness Navigation Ch 2 and Ch 4 integrate on the protocol.

Dead-reckoning leg

From a known fix: record start time, record compass bearing, walk on bearing counting paces. At a nominal end point (distance or time), record end time and pace count. Convert pace to distance with your calibrated pace-per-100-m figure. Plot the vector from the last fix on the map at the recorded bearing for the recorded distance. That is your estimated position. Cross-check with any visible feature or altimeter reading.

Every error in bearing, pace, or time compounds down every leg. The operator re-calibrates at every halt, re-fixes at every visible landmark, re-sets at every drainage or terrain transition. DEAD RECKONING DEGRADES. A dead-reckoned position after six legs without a landmark fix can sit a kilometer from reality; the technique is a bridge between fixes, not a substitute for them. In featureless terrain with no landmarks for an hour, commit to a baseline that lies across the line of travel (road, river, long ridge) and aim-off deliberately rather than trying to navigate point-to-point.

02.2.12Metal deflection and the field-strip

The compass needle is a magnet. Any ferrous object, any electrical current, any active electronics within a meter deflects the needle and throws every bearing off.

WARN

Step away from rifles, vehicles, steel helmets, belt buckles, handheld radios, cell phones, GPS receivers, magnetic watch closures, and metal pack frames before any bearing. Deflection from a rifle held across the chest can reach 10°. Deflection from a truck hood reaches 30° at close range.

Field-strip rule: drop pack, move three steps from any metal, hold compass flat at chest, shoot bearing. Rifles set down. Vehicles walked away from. The compass rides in its own pouch away from the radio, because a radio transmit pulse deflects the needle transiently and introduces intermittent error that surfaces only when the key is pressed mid-sighting. THE NEEDLE DOES NOT LIE. Every reading that seems off matches the geometry of some nearby metal the operator failed to account for.

02.2.13Declination error scales — the 92-ft/°/mi case

A small declination error compounds catastrophically over distance.

Cross-track error

For small angular errors, cross-track off the intended line grows approximately as tan(error) × distance. Simplified: roughly 92 ft per degree per mile, or ~17 m per degree per kilometer.

A 15° declination oversight (operator forgets to correct for 15° E on a West Coast trip) produces ~1,400 ft of cross-track at one mile and >7,000 ft at five miles. The team lands in the wrong drainage on a SAR segment, past the catching feature with no cue which way to turn, or off the ridge onto a cliffed face. A 10° error at 3 mi computes as 10 × 92 × 3 = 2,760 ft — over half a kilometer laterally. SMALL DECLINATION NUMBERS MAKE LARGE GROUND ERRORS. The cross-track math is the strongest argument for the adjustable-declination compass: correction cost is zero, error cost when skipped is measured in kilometers.

02.2.14Trust the instrument — the whiteout rule

When feet disagree with compass, trust compass. The rule survives countless near-misses in whiteout, fog, moonless forest, and featureless desert.

The compass does not get disoriented. Feet do. When vestibular and visual systems lose reference, humans rotate in closed loops without noticing, drift downhill without noticing, and veer toward the dominant hand without noticing. The needle points to magnetic north regardless of what the body believes.02.2.14 · Instrument over instinct

The whiteout case is diagnostic. On a snow-covered ridge in fog, the operator sets a bearing, walks, and within minutes feels strongly that the correct direction is left or right of what the compass shows. The feeling is real; the direction is wrong. The operator who trusts feet rotates in a circle and arrives back at the start, or lands in the wrong drainage exhausted. The operator who trusts the instrument walks a straight line to the next fix. COMPASS > FEET. The rule extends to any featureless terrain: fog, heavy snow, dense swamp, night forest, dust storm, sandstorm. If you cannot see the landmark, hold the instrument's heading and walk.

02.2.15Install, function, failure, feed-forward

INSTALL. You carry a full-featured baseplate with adjustable declination, sighting mirror, and clinometer; lensatic is an option for dedicated night work. You set current NOAA declination before departure. You drill Red Fred in the Shed to reflex. You name azimuth, bearing, heading, and back-azimuth with reference frame attached in every field call. You take bearings from the ground with mirror when range warrants. You take bearings from the map with baseplate edge along the travel line. You resect from three landmarks with 60°–120° separation. You dead-reckon only between fixes. You field-strip metal at every bearing. You trust the instrument over feet when they disagree.

FUNCTION INDICATORS. Ground-sightings converge inside 1° on repeated shots at the same feature. Map-to-bearing and back-to-map round-trip closes cleanly. Resection cocked-hats sit under 200 m. Leg plans land at the catching feature inside pace-count error. Night lensatic operation reads azimuth through luminous sights without flashlight on the instrument.

FAILURE INDICATORS. Declination gets read off the stale margin diagram rather than current NOAA. Red Fred sits outside the Shed because the compass rides on a steel tabletop. Back-azimuth gets computed wrong because the ± 180° branch is miscalled. The operator forgets to set adjustable declination and then applies manual correction anyway, correcting twice. Cross-track compounds past the catching feature because nobody aimed off. The compass sits in a radio pouch adjacent to a handheld in transmit mode.

FEED-FORWARD. GPS and PLB install next in 02.3, extending the compass's heading primitive to absolute-position-on-demand under open sky. Every GPS fix passes back through the compass: a waypoint bearing gets walked on compass, not by staring at the screen. Every PLB transmit reports a GPS coordinate whose accuracy rests on the datum discipline installed in 02.1. The electronic layer extends, not replaces, the map-and-compass stack.
