theFIELD.run / CONSTRUCT_APPLICATIONS / 02 TRAVERSE / 02.3 GPS, GNSS, PLB — electronic position and distress
SECTION 02.3

GPS, GNSS, PLB — electronic position and distress

GNSS CONSTELLATIONSGPS (US) / GLONASS (RU) / GALILEO (EU) / BEIDOU (CN) / QZSS (JP)
GPS CORE24+ SATS / 6 ORBITAL PLANES / ~20,200 km ALT
MULTI-GNSS ACCURACY3–5 m HORIZONTAL OPEN SKY / 1–2 m WITH DUAL-FREQ OR RTK
ELEVATION ACCURACY~1.5× WORSE THAN HORIZONTAL
PLB BAND406 MHz / COSPAS-SARSAT
PLB BATTERY24–48 hr TRANSMIT
TRACK-LOG CADENCE1 fix / 10 s OR 1 fix / 30 m
THREE DATA STRUCTURESWAYPOINT / ROUTE / TRACK
DEFAULT GPS DATUMWGS 84

Electronic position is the third navigation subsystem and the one that attracts the most operator error. A modern handheld receiver pulls signal simultaneously from GPS, GLONASS, Galileo, BeiDou, and QZSS, resolves position to 3–5 m horizontal accuracy under open sky, and offers a menu of coordinate displays and datums that, when mis-set, produces a confidently-displayed but systematically-wrong fix. Essential Wilderness Navigation Ch 3 anchors the constellation stack and the trip-start protocol; Mountaineering: Freedom of the Hills Ch 5 supplies the alpine-context PLB doctrine and the coordinate-display discipline; Fundamentals of Search and Rescue supplies the command-side failure class when GPS coordinates arrive with mismatched datum tags. The electronic layer extends the map-and-compass stack; it does not substitute for it.

This section installs GNSS and distress beacons as extenders of the map-and-compass primitive. You load the constellation stack with GPS, GLONASS, Galileo, BeiDou, and QZSS plus the multi-GNSS accuracy envelope, the datum-and-display alignment rule that sets receiver to map before a trip starts, the signal-degradation set covering canopy, canyon, cold, and multipath, the three data structures of waypoint, route, and track log, the track-log-always-on habit that retroactively answers where you went and computes SAR segment coverage, the PLB versus satellite-communicator distinction with the 406 MHz COSPAS-SARSAT infrastructure, the trip-start protocol from datum match through trailhead-mark, the in-field discipline of using GPS for fix and compass for heading, the PLB activation threshold of life-or-limb-or-severe-cold, the register-or-lose-30-minutes rule on NOAA beacon registration, the screen-over-terrain failure mode that puts the operator's eyes on the device instead of the ground, and the install / function / failure / feed-forward handoff to natural navigation as redundant backup. Sources: Essential Wilderness Navigation Ch 3 (constellations, data structures, PLB doctrine); FOTH Ch 5 (alpine-context PLB, coordinate display); NASAR Fundamentals of SAR (datum-mismatch operational consequences); manufacturer documentation (Garmin, InReach, ACR PLB-400).

02.3.1The GNSS constellation stack

Five operational constellations feed a modern multi-GNSS receiver. Each was designed and deployed independently; interoperability happens at the receiver chip.

Operational GNSS systems
01GPSUnited States. 24+ satellites in 6 orbital planes, ~20,200 km altitude. Full global coverage since 1995. Baseline for every receiver.
02GLONASSRussia. 24+ satellites. Better high-latitude coverage than GPS alone due to orbital inclination.
03GALILEOEuropean Union. 24+ operational satellites, civilian-first design with published control plane and no intentional degradation.
04BEIDOUChina. Global coverage since 2020. Includes regional short-message service for Asia-Pacific.
05QZSSJapan. Regional augmentation over Asia-Oceania; high-elevation orbits compensate for urban-canyon blockage in Tokyo and Seoul.

A receiver that tracks GPS alone sees 4–12 satellites in open sky. A multi-GNSS receiver tracks 16–30+, which reduces dilution-of-precision and holds fix in partial sky-mask conditions that would drop a GPS-only unit. The operational implication is simple: any new receiver carries multi-GNSS by default, and the multi-GNSS option gets enabled before the first trip. Dual-frequency receivers (L1 + L5 or equivalent) cut multipath error in dense canopy and near rock walls, and the feature justifies the price on a dedicated navigation handheld.

02.3.2Datum and display — set the receiver to the map

Handheld GPS defaults to WGS 84 datum and lat/long display. A paper USGS quad may run NAD 27 or NAD 83. A SAR command GIS may run WGS 84 with UTM display. The three configurations mis-aligned produce confident coordinates that do not match ground truth.

WARN

The ~500 ft offset between NAD 27 and WGS 84 (covered in 02.1.2) is produced by a datum-mismatched GPS-to-map handoff. A receiver in WGS 84 sending coordinates to a command station reading NAD 27 paper places the team one grid cell off, every time.

Before the trip: set receiver datum to match the paper map's margin; set coordinate display to match the radio-call convention used by the team or the command structure; confirm both with a known point at the trailhead. SET RECEIVER TO MAP. NEVER THE REVERSE. The map is the fixed reference; the receiver is the flexible instrument. If the command station runs a different datum than the team's map, the datum conversion happens in one place with one person, ideally at command with a conversion tool, not at six field teams on radio calls under stress.

02.3.3Signal degradation — where GNSS fails

GPS failures are predictable. Most are environmental; the largest single cause is operator error on datum and setup.

GNSS failure set
01SKY MASKSlot canyons, urban canyons, dense overhanging terrain drop the visible sky below 30% and push tracked-satellite count below the 4 needed for a 3D fix.
02CANOPYDense conifer canopy attenuates the L1 signal; fix wanders by 20–50 m. L5 dual-frequency improves significantly.
03MULTIPATHRock walls, water surfaces, ice faces reflect GPS signal; the receiver sees direct and reflected simultaneously and resolves position off.
04COLDAlkaline batteries crash below 0°F (-18°C); lithium cells hold.
05WATERScreen-touch failure with wet fingers; internal water intrusion disables the unit.
06OPERATOR ERRORWrong datum, wrong coordinate display, missed trailhead mark, disabled track log. Outpaces hardware failure as a cause of lost fix capacity.

The operator-error band is the actionable one. Hardware failures are rare; setup failures are common. Every trip-start checklist (covered in 02.3.7) directly addresses the operator-error set. Every trip without the checklist re-opens the same failure modes.

02.3.4The three data structures — waypoint, route, track

Every GPS receiver stores navigational data in three structures. Mastering their semantics converts the device from position-display to full navigation instrument.

GNSS data structures

WAYPOINT · A single stored coordinate with a name and optional elevation. Examples: trailhead, camp, found clue, subject location. The atomic data unit. ROUTE · An ordered list of waypoints. Examples: planned hike from trailhead through summit to camp, return path from emergency extraction point. TRACK LOG · A timestamped breadcrumb of fix points recorded continuously during travel. Cadence set by time interval (1 fix / 10 s) or distance interval (1 fix / 30 m).

Waypoints are the data entered and retrieved manually: mark the trailhead as START, mark camp as overnight, mark a found clue with time and photo reference. Routes are planned waypoint sequences the operator follows. Track logs record reality: where the feet actually went, not where the plan said. The track log is the highest-return single habit on any navigation receiver: it retroactively answers "where did I go," lets you retrace to the trailhead in fog, and on SAR computes segment coverage after a search pass.

02.3.5The always-on track log

Track logging converts the receiver from position-display to full-coverage record. The cost is battery; the benefit is retrace capability and SAR-segment auditability.

Track-log protocol

Enable track logging at trip start. Set cadence: 1 fix / 10 s for moving subjects; 1 fix / 30 m for minimum battery on long trips. Clear old logs before the trip so the new log is easy to isolate. Download the log at trip end for the mission record.

Battery cost is modest on modern receivers with efficient chipsets (15–20% additional drain over display-only use). The retrace application is lifesaving: in dense fog, failing light, or disorientation, enable "TrackBack" or the equivalent function and the receiver generates turn-by-turn instructions to reverse the recorded path. TRACK EVERY TRIP. The SAR application converts the track log into a segment-coverage report: overlay all team tracks on the segment polygon, compute the covered fraction, and apply the POD calculation from 02.7 directly to measured coverage rather than estimated coverage.

02.3.6PLB versus satellite communicator

Two distinct emergency-beacon products share the one-button-SOS convention. Their operational profiles differ.

Emergency-beacon classes
01PLB (Personal Locator Beacon)Transmits 406 MHz through COSPAS-SARSAT government satellite network. One-button activation. No subscription. Global coverage. GPS coordinate broadcast since 2003 on modern units. 24–48 hr battery. Owner registration required with NOAA.
02SATELLITE COMMUNICATORGarmin inReach, Spot, ZOLEO. Two-way text messaging plus SOS via Iridium or Globalstar commercial networks. Subscription required. Battery lasts days to weeks. SOS routes through private monitoring center (GEOS IERCC) to local authorities.
03OBSOLETEOlder radio-homing PLBs without GPS coordinate broadcast. Require aircraft or ground search to home in on the signal. Rescue time doubles or triples over GPS-equipped PLBs.

The PLB is the primary emergency beacon. The satellite communicator adds two-way messaging, which lets you confirm injury details, request non-emergency extraction, and receive weather forecasts; the PLB broadcasts one bit ("I need help, here") with no return channel. For serious trips, carry both: PLB as the primary distress guarantee, satellite communicator as the operational-communication layer. A dead satellite-communicator subscription does not cancel the PLB.

02.3.7Trip-start protocol

Every GPS-equipped trip begins with a checklist. Essential Wilderness Navigation Ch 3 supplies the standard sequence.

GPS trip-start checklist
01DATUMSet receiver datum to match paper map margin.
02DISPLAYSet coordinate display to match radio-call or command-station convention.
03BATTERYConfirm battery state; carry spare lithium cells; re-check temperature-performance curve for expected conditions.
04CLEARClear old track logs. Memory slots freed for current trip.
05STARTEnable fresh track log. Log cadence set.
06TRAILHEADMark the trailhead as START waypoint with name, time, elevation reference.
07ALTITUDECalibrate altitude at a known-elevation reference (trailhead benchmark, published elevation). Altimeter drift without calibration reaches 100 ft/day on a barometric-aided unit.
08FIRST-LEG BEARINGTake a magnetic bearing to the first leg on the compass with declination applied, before moving.

The checklist runs under two minutes and eliminates the operator-error band covered in 02.3.3. CHECKLIST BEFORE FIRST STEP. Skipped trip-start is the single most common failure mode on GPS-equipped expeditions, because the device appears to work correctly even when datum and display are wrong; the error surfaces only when the first coordinate goes over the radio.

02.3.8In-field discipline — GPS for fix, compass for heading

The GPS fix is absolute position. The compass heading is direction of travel. Using the GPS as both produces the screen-over-terrain failure that kills more trips than signal degradation does.

GPS → compass handoff

At a halt: GPS reports current position; operator selects next waypoint; Go-To function returns distance and bearing. Transfer the bearing to the compass. Apply declination (or rely on pre-set adjustable declination). Sight a landmark on the bearing line. Walk to the landmark with eyes on terrain, not the screen. At the landmark, re-check GPS for position; re-shoot bearing to next landmark.

The pattern preserves terrain awareness. Eyes stay on the ground, feet find their own placement, hazards surface before the operator is on top of them. GPS FOR FIX, COMPASS FOR HEADING, EYES ON GROUND. The alternative — walking with the GPS screen in hand and the Go-To arrow guiding each step — produces a subject who hits tree branches at head level, misses drop-offs, and steps on snakes. The screen is not a map; the ground is the map.

02.3.9PLB activation — threshold and procedure

PLB activation is a one-way decision with wide downstream consequences. The threshold is set carefully.

WARN

Activate the PLB when the situation is life-threatening, limb-threatening, or severe cold without shelter. Never "tired." Never "lost but warm and fed." Never "inconvenienced." Unnecessary activations tie up real SAR resources and reduce deployment rate for genuine emergencies.

PLB activation procedure
01DECISIONConfirm the situation meets the threshold. If uncertain, work the problem for 30 more minutes with shelter and signaling; most "maybe" situations resolve.
02OPEN SKYMove to the most open overhead sky available without exposing the casualty to further hazard.
03DEPLOYExtend antenna fully skyward. Hold vertical if possible.
04ACTIVATEPress and hold the activation button per unit instructions. Verify the strobe or LED confirming transmission.
05LEAVE ONContinuous transmission for a minimum of 24 hours unless rescue arrives earlier. The beacon is the primary signal; do not turn it off.
06VISUALSupplement with signal panel, signal mirror, fire. Beacon gets the direction; visual gets the final approach.
07REMAINDo not move from the activation site except to improve shelter within a short radius; rescue is vectoring to the reported coordinate.

Registration is non-negotiable. NOAA's beacon registry (beaconregistration.noaa.gov) lets SAR controllers identify the owner, contact emergency contacts, and verify trip plan before tasking assets. An unregistered 406 MHz activation adds 30 minutes or more to response time while controllers attempt to identify the beacon and confirm the activation is genuine. Register at purchase; update at every trip plan.

02.3.10Install, function, failure, feed-forward

INSTALL. You carry a multi-GNSS handheld or phone with offline topographic maps cached, plus a registered PLB, plus optionally a satellite communicator. You set receiver datum to match paper map before every trip. You run the trip-start checklist without shortcuts. You enable track log at START. You mark trailhead, clues, camps, and return points as waypoints. You use Go-To for fix-and-bearing, transfer to compass for heading, walk on compass with eyes on terrain. You reserve PLB activation for life-or-limb-or-severe-cold-without-shelter.

FUNCTION INDICATORS. GPS, compass, and map agree on position inside the receiver's rated accuracy. Track log captures the full trip. Retrace works at any halt. Radio coordinate transmissions carry datum and grid tags. Battery holds reserve through the planned trip plus margin.

FAILURE INDICATORS. The receiver becomes the only navigation tool and the map stays folded. Track log is disabled to save battery and the team loses retrace capability at the worst moment. Datum mismatch produces a ~500 ft offset that command discovers mid-operation. Operator walks with screen in hand and misses hazards the eye would have caught. PLB is activated for cold-and-hungry and SAR deploys a helicopter for a hike-out case.

FEED-FORWARD. Natural navigation installs next in 02.4 as the redundant backup running continuously when batteries die, canopy blocks signal, and the lensatic compass is still in the bottom of the pack. Every GPS fix is temporary; the sun, the stars, the wind, and the swell do not require power or subscription.

theFIELD.run / CONSTRUCT_APPLICATIONS / 02 TRAVERSE / 02.4 Natural navigation — sun, star, wind, swell
SECTION 02.4

Natural navigation — sun, star, wind, swell

SUN RATE15°/hr
SOLAR-NOON SHADOWSHORTEST OF THE DAY, N-S LINE
SHADOW-STICK INTERVAL15–30 min
POLARIS OFFSET FROM TRUE NORTH<0.7°
DUBHE-MEREK POINTER×5 TO POLARIS
SOUTHERN CROSS POINTER×4.5 TO SOUTH CELESTIAL POLE
ORION'S BELTDUE EAST AT RISE / DUE WEST AT SET EVERYWHERE
DIPPER STAR-CLOCK15°/hr COUNTERCLOCKWISE AROUND POLARIS
MOSSUNRELIABLE

Every natural phenomenon carries directional information. The compass industrialized one signal out of many; sun, moon, stars, wind, clouds, dew, trees, moss, sand dunes, sea swells, bird flight, and insect behavior all broadcast heading continuously to the operator who has learned to read them. Harold Gatty's Finding Your Way Without Map or Compass supplies the thesis and the master catalog; Essential Wilderness Navigation Ch 6 converts Gatty's catalog into modern field protocols; the US Army FM 3-25.26 and the Polynesian voyaging tradition (Mau Piailug, Nainoa Thompson, the Polynesian Voyaging Society) confirm the ocean-cue set. Natural navigation is the redundant subsystem that runs when batteries die, canopy blocks signal, and the compass is still in the pack.

This section installs natural navigation as the always-on backup to the instrument stack. You load the sun-based primitives of sunrise/sunset azimuth, solar noon, shadow stick, and analog watch, the star-based primitives of Polaris, Cassiopeia, the Southern Cross, the Big Dipper as star clock, and Orion's belt, the wind-encoded signals of tree flagging, krummholz, cornice, dune, and sastrugi, the moss myth rejection with the bias-reversal rule for shaded-and-damp indicators, the ocean cue set of swell direction, rebound patterns, stationary cumulus, and water coloration, the three-cue confirmation rule that never commits to a heading on a single signal, the pre-trip audit of prevailing wind, sunrise azimuth, and drainage direction, and the install / function / failure / feed-forward handoff to distance-pace-and-time. Sources: Gatty (full catalog, watch method, Polynesian wayfinding); Essential Wilderness Navigation Ch 6 (field protocols, shadow-stick, tree flagging, moss rejection); FOTH Ch 5 (alpine natural cues).

02.4.1Sun azimuth — sunrise and sunset

The sun rises and sets on azimuths that shift seasonally. The folk rule "sun rises due east" holds only on the equinoxes.

Sunrise/sunset azimuth

EQUINOX (Mar 21, Sep 22) · Sunrise 090° (due east); sunset 270° (due west). Everywhere on Earth. NORTHERN-HEMISPHERE SUMMER · Sunrise deflects north of due east (toward 060° at mid-latitudes on June 21); sunset deflects north of due west (toward 300°). NORTHERN-HEMISPHERE WINTER · Sunrise deflects south of due east (toward 120° on December 21); sunset deflects south of due west (toward 240°). SOUTHERN-HEMISPHERE · The deflection direction inverts by season.

The summer-winter deflection at mid-latitudes reaches 25°–30° off the equinox azimuth. SUNRISE IS NOT DUE EAST. The operator who cross-references date plus latitude against a sunrise-azimuth table (or the NOAA solar calculator) gets the correct reference direction; the operator who assumes equinox geometry plants a seasonal error of up to 30°. Modern ephemeris apps give you sunrise azimuth to the tenth of a degree for the trip date and location; memorize the value at pre-trip and use it as a fallback reference at dawn and dusk.

02.4.2Solar noon — the shortest shadow

At solar noon the sun sits at its highest angle in the sky, and its azimuth reads due south in the northern hemisphere above the Tropic of Cancer, due north in the southern hemisphere below the Tropic of Capricorn.

Solar-noon heading

The shortest shadow of the day marks the north-south line. In the northern hemisphere, the shadow points due north. In the southern hemisphere, the shadow points due south. Between the tropics, the sun crosses overhead twice a year and the rule breaks; confirm latitude before applying.

Solar noon is not clock noon. Daylight saving time, longitude offset within the time zone, and the equation of time together shift solar noon from clock noon by up to 30 minutes. The shortest-shadow method is self-calibrating: the operator marks shadow tip every five minutes through the midday window; the shortest is solar noon and points the N-S line directly. The shortest-shadow technique does not require a clock. It requires only a vertical stick and the patience to mark shadow tips through noon.

02.4.3The shadow-stick method

Gatty's foundational daylight technique uses the sun's motion to mark east-west in minutes, not hours.

Shadow-stick protocol
01DRIVEPlant a vertical stick 1–3 ft tall in level ground.
02MARK 1Mark the tip of the shadow with a pebble or scratch.
03WAITWait 15–30 min.
04MARK 2Mark the new shadow tip.
05LINEDraw a straight line between the two marks. The line runs approximately west-to-east.
06PERPENDICULARA line perpendicular to the west-east line runs north-south.

The physics: Earth rotates at 15°/hr; the shadow tip traces an arc perpendicular to the sun's path. The first mark sits west of the second mark in both hemispheres because the sun always moves east-to-west overhead. A third mark confirms linearity and flags non-solar-noon peculiarities. The technique requires no instrument, works with any vertical object (a trekking pole, an upright branch, even the operator standing still with a recorded head-shadow tip), and produces a heading reference inside 30 minutes from a cold start.

02.4.4The analog-watch method

An analog watch used with the sun produces a quick southbound (or northbound) reference. Gatty popularized it; Essential Wilderness Navigation refines the correction.

Analog-watch method (northern hemisphere)

Point the hour hand at the sun. South sits halfway between the hour hand and 12 o'clock, on the smaller arc. In the southern hemisphere: point 12 at the sun; north sits halfway between 12 and the hour hand.

The method requires solar time, not clock time. Subtract one hour for daylight saving. Correct for longitude within the time zone (4 min/° of longitude east or west of the zone central meridian). An uncorrected watch at the eastern edge of a time zone in DST runs almost 90 min off solar time; the resulting direction reads 22° off south, which is not a direction you want to walk. The analog-watch method works beautifully when the operator runs the correction explicitly. It produces large error when the correction is skipped.

02.4.5Polaris — the northern anchor

Polaris sits within 0.7° of true celestial north at all clock times, all dates, all northern latitudes. No star-clock correction, no seasonal offset.

Finding Polaris
01BIG DIPPER METHODIdentify the pointer stars at the outer lip of the Big Dipper's bowl (Dubhe and Merak). Extend the Dubhe-Merak line about ×5 the Dubhe-Merak distance toward the bright star on that line — Polaris.
02CASSIOPEIA METHODIf the Big Dipper sits below the horizon (common at high northern latitudes in winter), use Cassiopeia. The W opens toward Polaris; Polaris sits roughly opposite the open side of the W.
03ALTITUDEPolaris sits at an altitude above the horizon roughly equal to your latitude. At 40°N, Polaris is 40° above the horizon. Confirms the correct star vs. a nearby competitor.

The Polaris altitude trick serves as celestial backup for latitude: measure the angle from horizon to Polaris with a makeshift sextant (outstretched hand: pinky-to-thumb spans ~20° at arm's length) and that is your approximate latitude. POLARIS NEVER MOVES ENOUGH TO MATTER. Finding Polaris is the single most valuable natural-navigation skill for northern-hemisphere operators; the sky rotates around it nightly, and the star is visible any clear night.

02.4.6Southern Cross, Big Dipper star-clock, Orion's belt

Three secondary celestial references extend the set.

Other celestial references
01SOUTHERN CROSSFour-star asterism visible throughout the southern hemisphere and as far north as the Tropic of Cancer in certain months. Extend the long axis of the cross about ×4.5 beyond the foot star; drop perpendicular to the horizon; that point is approximately the south celestial pole, marking true south.
02BIG DIPPER STAR-CLOCKThe Big Dipper rotates 15°/hr counterclockwise around Polaris. Used at twilight to estimate time of night when clock is unavailable.
03ORION'S BELTThe three belt stars rise due east and set due west everywhere on Earth, on any night Orion is visible (roughly October through March for evening observation in the northern hemisphere).

Orion's belt is the cross-hemisphere reference: it works from the Arctic Circle to Tierra del Fuego with no latitude correction. ORION RISES DUE EAST. The asterism is conspicuous; any clear winter night in either hemisphere yields the reference direction from a thirty-second glance skyward. Natural navigators cross-check Polaris with Orion: if they disagree on "east," something is wrong with the identification of Polaris.

02.4.7Wind-encoded signals — trees, snow, dunes

Prevailing wind shapes everything it blows on. The signals persist for days, months, or years.

Wind indicators
01TREE FLAGGINGIsolated trees develop fuller foliage on the leeward side; branches on the windward side die back. The "flag" points downwind.
02KRUMMHOLZHigh-elevation stunted conifers grow with trunks bent away from prevailing wind. The bend points downwind.
03SNOW CORNICECornices form on the lee side of ridges. The overhang points downwind.
04SAND DUNEWindward face is gentle (10°–15°); leeward slipface is steep (~33°, the angle of repose). Barchan dune horns point downwind.
05SASTRUGIWind-carved snow ridges align parallel to prevailing wind direction. The sharp edges point windward.

Wind direction is not universal. Local topography funnels, reverses, and cross-couples the regional pattern; mountain-valley wind cycles reverse twice daily. The operator who memorizes pre-trip prevailing wind for the region gets a reliable reference; the operator who infers wind direction from a single isolated tree on a wind-channeled pass gets a misleading one. Cross-check across three indicators (tree flagging, cornice orientation, dune shape) before committing a heading to wind signal alone.

02.4.8The moss myth

The folk rule "moss grows on the north side of trees" is wrong in general, often wrong locally, and reversed in the southern hemisphere.

WARN

Moss grows where it is shaded and damp. In the northern hemisphere, that correlation weakly favors the north side of an isolated tree on an open slope. In dense canopy, moss grows everywhere the ground is damp. Under prevailing moisture-bearing winds (windward aspects of Pacific coastal ranges), moss grows preferentially on the windward side regardless of compass direction.

The reliability of moss as a compass is low enough that Gatty explicitly rejects it. MOSS IS NOT A COMPASS. Shaded-and-damp indicators (moss, lichen, fern, spider-web concentration on north-facing surfaces) work as weak inputs when cross-referenced with sun, wind, and terrain, and fail entirely as single-cue commitments. The general rule for any shaded-damp indicator: use it only when the other natural cues agree, and never as the primary heading source.

02.4.9Ocean cues — swell, rebound, stationary cumulus

The Polynesian voyaging tradition navigated thousands of miles of open ocean without instruments. Their cue set extends the catalog.

Ocean navigation cues
01SWELL DIRECTIONPrevailing swell runs from a predictable direction for days at a time. Felt through the hull at night after wind dies.
02REBOUND PATTERNSwells reflect off island coasts and refract around islands; the composite wave pattern reveals land over the horizon before visual contact.
03STATIONARY CUMULUSA single cumulus stack holding position over a single point indicates an island below. Lagoon reflection colors the cloud base green-blue.
04WATER COLORATIONLightening over reefs and shoals; muddying near river mouths; upwelling zones at current boundaries.
05BIRD PATTERNPelagic seabirds fly out to forage at dawn and return toward roost at dusk. Following terns or noddies to roost at dusk finds land.

The ocean cue set complements the celestial set. Night navigation in the open ocean uses stars; dawn transitions to swell direction; bird flights vector the final approach to land. The natural navigator works a layered reference: celestial primary, wind secondary, swell tertiary, biological confirmation. Each layer runs independent of the others.

02.4.10Three-cue confirmation

Single-cue commitments fail. The rule across every natural-navigation tradition is to confirm heading from three independent sources before committing.

Sun plus wind plus terrain. Star plus swell plus cloud. Polaris plus Orion plus wind-flagged trees. Any three independent cues converge on the same heading or one of the three is misread.02.4.10 · Three independent cues

Independence matters. Three cues that all trace back to the same signal (tree flagging on a wind-channeled pass plus cornice on the same pass plus dune orientation on the same pass) are one cue repeated three times. Three cues from different domains (celestial plus meteorological plus biological; or sun plus wind plus drainage geometry) carry independent error and agreement across them is informative. The natural navigator walks forward only when three independent cues agree on the direction. When two agree and one disagrees, stop and resolve the disagreement before moving.

02.4.11Pre-trip audit

Natural navigation works best when it is loaded before the trip starts, not improvised during a crisis.

Pre-trip natural-navigation audit

01 · Memorize prevailing wind direction for the region and season. 02 · Memorize sunrise and sunset azimuth for the trip date (NOAA solar calculator). 03 · Identify a distinctive back-stop terrain feature (baseline) from the trip plan. 04 · Memorize drainage flow direction at the start point. 05 · Identify local magnetic declination (see 02.2). 06 · Note local sunrise and sunset time with DST correction. 07 · Confirm Polaris or Southern Cross visibility for latitude and season.

The audit converts natural navigation from a recall task under stress to a reference lookup. A lost operator under fatigue and cold cannot reliably reconstruct sunrise-azimuth calculations or derive prevailing wind from memory; a pre-trip audit written on a trip card is available at the moment it matters. MEMORIZE BEFORE YOU NEED IT. Natural navigation is the redundancy layer; redundancy loaded after the primary fails is too late.

02.4.12Install, function, failure, feed-forward

INSTALL. You run the pre-trip audit: prevailing wind, sunrise/sunset azimuth, drainage direction, declination, back-stop feature. You find Polaris in under ten seconds from a clear night sky. You drive a shadow stick at any sunlit halt to confirm heading. You cross-reference three independent cues before committing to a natural-navigation heading. You reject moss as a compass. You treat natural navigation as the always-on redundancy, not the primary.

FUNCTION INDICATORS. You recover heading from sun angle, tree flagging, or shadow-stick inside 30 seconds. Your pre-trip audit values match field observations at the trailhead. Three-cue confirmation gives converging heading. Dawn and dusk sightings cross-check against the prevailing-wind reference.

FAILURE INDICATORS. "Sun rises in the east" drives a heading without seasonal correction. Moss gets treated as a compass. Analog-watch method is used without solar-time correction. A single cue commits the operator to a long leg. Shaded-and-damp indicators get read in dense canopy where they run omnidirectional.

FEED-FORWARD. Distance, pace, and time install next in 02.5, converting whatever heading the operator is holding — instrument or natural — into a measured rate of ground displacement. A heading without pace is a direction, not a position; pace converts direction into arrival.

← PREVIOUS02.3 GPS, GNSS, PLB — electronic position and distressNEXT →02.5 Distance, pace, time — Naismith, pace count, triangulation

theFIELD.run / CONSTRUCT_APPLICATIONS / 02 TRAVERSE / 02.5 Distance, pace, time — Naismith, pace count, triangulation
SECTION 02.5

Distance, pace, time — Naismith, pace count, triangulation

PACEDISTANCE BETWEEN SAME-FOOT STRIKES = 2 STEPS
ADULT-MALE LEVEL PACE~5 ft · ~65 PACES / 100 m
CALIBRATION COURSE100 m OR 330 ft
NAISMITH'S RULE1 hr / 3 mi + 30 min / 1,000 ft ASCENT
LANGMUIR DESCENT-10 min / 1,000 ft GENTLE, +10 min / 1,000 ft STEEP
SAR DEFAULT2× NAISMITH OFF-TRAIL
TERRAIN MULTIPLIERSUP +10–30% · DOWN +5–15% · SAND/SNOW +20–40% · NIGHT +10–20% · BRUSH +25–50%
TALLY-PERSON ROLEPACE HOLDER ONLY

Distance is time in disguise. On the ground, distance has operational meaning only as time-to-arrival, and the operator who tracks time against a map arrives on schedule while the operator who tracks distance arrives late, tired, or benighted. Essential Wilderness Navigation Ch 4 supplies pace count and Naismith; Mountaineering: Freedom of the Hills Ch 6 supplies the alpine-context planning factor and Langmuir descent correction; NASAR's Fundamentals of SAR Ch 15 supplies the tally-person role and re-calibration discipline; Taylor's Fundamentals of Mantracking supplies the stride-measurement protocol used in tracking. Pace and time are the feet-side of the navigation loop: the map tells where to go, the compass tells which direction, and pace-and-time tell when you will arrive.

This section installs pace, time, and distance as the third measured dimension of the navigation stack. You load the pace definition (same-foot-to-same-foot), the personal calibration protocol on a 100 m or 330 ft course over representative terrain, the terrain-multiplier table for uphill, downhill, sand, snow, brush, night, and load, the fatigue-compound rule that forces re-calibration at every long halt, the Naismith time-budget rule at 1 hr/3 mi + 30 min/1,000 ft, the Langmuir descent correction, the SAR-doubling convention for off-trail work, the tally-person role that isolates pace-counting from navigation and radio, the triangulation geometry kit of Pythagoras, sine rule, and 30-60-90 plus 45-45-90 ratios, the stride-measurement protocol that scales personal pace from leg length rather than population average, the time-on-target rule that treats arrival time as the commitment, not linear distance, and the install / function / failure / feed-forward handoff to route craft. Sources: Essential Wilderness Navigation Ch 4 (pace count, Naismith, triangulation); FOTH Ch 6 (alpine context, descent correction); NASAR Fundamentals of SAR Ch 15 (tally-person, search-team pace); Taylor Mantracking (stride measurement).

02.5.1The pace — definition and population baseline

A pace is the distance between successive strikes of the same foot. Two steps. Essential Wilderness Navigation Ch 4 and Taylor's Mantracking converge on the measurement.

Pace, step, stride

PACE · Distance between successive strikes of the same foot (left-to-left or right-to-right). Equals 2 steps. STEP · Single footfall. Approximately ½ pace. STRIDE · In tracking doctrine, the heel-to-heel distance of successive same-foot prints. Equivalent to a pace.

The adult-male population baseline on level clear ground averages ~5 ft per pace, which converts to ~65 paces per 100 m or ~66 per 100 yd. Adult-female baseline sits slightly shorter. The baseline is a starting estimate, not a usable personal figure. COUNT PACES, NOT STEPS. Counting every same-foot strike halves the cognitive load of the count across a long leg; the operator who counts every footfall fatigues the counter and loses fidelity after 300 m. Short operators carry more paces per 100 m, not fewer, because stride scales with leg length. Height is a rough proxy: pace in feet runs approximately 0.41 × height.

02.5.2Personal calibration — the 100-m course

Your personal pace count is a measured figure, not an estimate. The calibration course makes it measurable.

Pace-calibration protocol
01LAY OUTMark a 100 m or 330 ft course on level, representative terrain.
02WALKWalk at natural SAR pace (not a casual stroll, not a forced march — the pace you would hold for hours).
03COUNTCount same-foot strikes from start to end.
04REPEATThree passes. Average.
05RECORDWrite the figure on your trip card. "Level clear, loaded, day: 66 paces / 100 m."
06EXTENDRe-calibrate on uphill, downhill, brush, snow, sand, night, loaded, unloaded. Build a personal table covering representative terrain classes.

The personal figure beats every population estimate. An operator whose level-clear pace is 62 per 100 m and whose brush pace is 95 per 100 m tracks ground displacement to within 5% on a calibrated leg. The personal pace table is a trip-card entry, not a memorization task; copy the table at every trip prep, and the operator walks with a quick reference rather than a recall burden.

02.5.3Terrain multipliers

Pace count drifts with terrain class. The rough multipliers apply over the level-clear personal baseline.

Terrain multipliers over level-clear
01LEVEL CLEAR×1.0 baseline.
02UPHILL×1.10–1.30 depending on grade.
03DOWNHILL×1.05–1.15 (strides shorten on braking).
04SAND OR SNOW×1.20–1.40.
05NIGHT×1.10–1.20.
06HEAVY PACK×1.05–1.10.
07DENSE BRUSH×1.25–1.50.
08TRACKED OR SNOWSHOE×1.10–1.20 over unbroken snow.

Multipliers stack. Uphill at night under heavy pack through brush runs ×1.25 × 1.15 × 1.10 × 1.35 = ×2.13: a level-clear 65 paces / 100 m becomes ~140 paces / 100 m, more than doubling the count. The multiplier stack is the reason personal calibration on a single terrain class is insufficient: the operator who walks 300 paces expecting ~450 m of displacement and gets ~210 m under stacked multipliers plants a position error of 240 m that compounds every leg.

02.5.4Fatigue compound

Pace count increases through a long day. The operator's stride shortens with fatigue; pace count rises to compensate for shorter individual strides.

Fatigue compound

A calibrated 65 paces / 100 m at mile 1 becomes ~70 at mile 5 and ~72 at mile 10. Cumulative effect: a 10% drift in pace count from a cold start to a full day's end.

The rate depends on load, fitness, terrain, and hydration. The operational consequence: every long halt (meal break, gear adjustment, team regroup) is a recalibration opportunity. Re-walk a known short distance at current fatigue state; recount pace; update the trip card. An operator who calibrates once at the trailhead and never again tracks position increasingly off reality through the day, and the error surfaces at the catching feature that fails to appear because the team overshot by a quarter mile.

02.5.5Naismith's rule — the time budget

W. W. Naismith's 1892 rule converts travel to time. The rule remains the dominant planning heuristic in anglophone mountain navigation.

Naismith's rule

Allow 1 hour per 3 miles or 5 km of horizontal travel. Add 30 minutes per 1,000 ft or 300 m of ascent. Assumes fit adult, daylight, moderate load, moderate terrain.

A 10-mile route with 2,000 ft of ascent: 10 ÷ 3 = 3.33 hours horizontal + 2 × 0.5 = 1.0 hours ascent = 4.3 hours total. The base rule does not account for descent, rest stops, navigation halts, meals, or terrain degradation. NAISMITH IS A STARTING ESTIMATE, NOT A COMMITMENT. Experienced parties run Naismith-plus-context: add 15 min/hour for rest, add an hour for a major navigation decision point, degrade by the appropriate SAR factor for off-trail work.

02.5.6Langmuir descent correction

Naismith ignored descent. Eric Langmuir's refinement addresses it.

Langmuir descent

For descent on gentle slope (less than ~12°): subtract 10 min per 1,000 ft of descent. (Gravity assists.) For descent on steep slope (greater than ~12°): add 10 min per 1,000 ft of descent. (Braking slows the descent, ankles and knees absorb load.)

The gentle-steep transition matters in practice. A 2,000 ft descent on a smooth trail at 10% grade runs ~20 min faster than flat equivalent; the same descent on a 40% scree slope with a 50 lb pack runs ~20 min slower than flat equivalent, and the pace drops to 1 mph or lower because every footfall absorbs impact through quads and ankles. On mixed descent, segment the descent by grade and apply Langmuir to each piece; do not average across grades.

02.5.7The SAR-doubling default

SAR planners and experienced alpine parties routinely apply a ×2 factor to Naismith for off-trail or difficult terrain.

WARN

Default to 2× Naismith for off-trail SAR work, bushwhack, deep snow, night, injured subject, heavy load, or inexperienced team. A 10-mile off-trail route with 2,000 ft gain calculates as 8.6 hours doubled from Naismith's base 4.3 hours. Empirically matches field team report times.

The doubling is not a safety margin; it is a realistic rate estimate. Teams operating under Naismith-base numbers routinely benight themselves, miss casualty-evacuation windows, and run out of daylight. DOUBLE UNTIL PROVEN OTHERWISE. The single most common time-estimation error in field navigation is under-application of the SAR-doubling factor on terrain that has degraded the team's rate.

02.5.8The tally-person role

On an organized search line, one team member holds the pace count exclusively. Fundamentals of SAR Ch 15 specifies the role.

Tally person

The team member assigned to hold pace count for the leg. Isolated from radio traffic, navigation decisions, and clue-scan duties. Announces the count at pre-agreed intervals (every 100 m, every 500 m, at major landmarks).

Pace count is cognitively incompatible with radio work, terrain scan, or compass reading. A team leader who runs navigation and radio and pace simultaneously drops pace accuracy within one long leg. PACE IS A DEDICATED ROLE. The tally person trades breadth for depth; other team members carry the search scan, the radio, the compass, and the navigation authority. Rotate the tally role every 2–3 hours to prevent fatigue-driven count drift; the rotation point is also a recalibration opportunity.

02.5.9The triangulation geometry kit

A small kit of eighth-grade geometry resolves distance-to-feature problems that the operator cannot measure directly.

Field geometry set
01PYTHAGORASa² + b² = c². Computes diagonal across a rectangular detour.
02SINE RULEa/sin(A) = b/sin(B) = c/sin(C). Unknown side from two known angles and one known side.
0330-60-90Side ratios 1 : √3 : 2. Quick estimation.
0445-45-90Side ratios 1 : 1 : √2. Quick estimation.
05TANGENTtan(θ) = opposite/adjacent. Computes distance to an inaccessible feature from an angle and a baseline.

For distance to an inaccessible feature: stand at point A, shoot bearing to feature; walk a known baseline perpendicular to the first bearing to point B; shoot a second bearing to feature from B; solve the triangle by sine rule. Distance-to-feature precision runs inside 5% with careful bearings. The kit is not advanced math; it is elementary geometry held in working memory for field application. The operator who memorizes the set extracts distance-to-feature estimates from any two-point observation.

02.5.10Tracking stride versus navigation pace

The tracker's stride measurement and the navigator's pace count measure the same quantity with different purposes. Taylor's Mantracking integrates the concept.

Stride as subject signature

In tracking, a subject's stride (heel-to-heel distance on successive same-foot prints) is a personal signature. Measured at first confirmed track pair, stride: — Calibrates the sign-cutting stick used to search for the next print (covered in 02.8). — Rejects false tracks outside the subject's stride range. — Infers subject height via stride ≈ 0.41 × height for adults on level ground. — Flags fatigue (stride shortens), injury (stride asymmetric), load (stride shortens and deepens print).

For the navigator, pace is self-calibrated for self-displacement. For the tracker, stride is subject-measured for subject-profiling. The two measurements share a definition and diverge in application; both feed the operational decision stack. A tracker who knows the subject's measured stride has a personalized search instrument; a navigator who knows their own measured pace has a personalized displacement sensor.

02.5.11Time-on-target over linear distance

The planning unit of field navigation is arrival time, not linear distance. Distance is a consequence of time-on-target, not a parallel metric.

The operator commits to a summit by 1400, a camp by 1800, a trailhead by dusk. The commitment is a time. The pace and distance arithmetic reconstructs what speed and what heading need to hold for that time to be met.02.5.11 · Time is the commitment

The practical implication: every trip plan carries a turnaround time, not a turnaround distance. An alpine ascent with a hard turnaround at 1200 is an operator who starts descent at noon regardless of how close the summit is. A SAR segment with a hard turnaround at 1700 is a team that reverses course at 1700 regardless of uncovered ground. TIME BINDS DISTANCE. The operator who tracks linear distance independent of time arrives at all the places they planned, at times later than they can afford, and the resulting benighting becomes its own emergency.

02.5.12Install, function, failure, feed-forward

INSTALL. You calibrate personal pace count on 100 m course over representative terrain. You build a personal pace table across uphill, downhill, sand, snow, brush, night, and load. You apply terrain multipliers when conditions stack. You re-calibrate at every long halt. You plan with Naismith's rule with SAR-doubling for off-trail work. You apply Langmuir for descent. You assign a tally person on team navigation. You commit to turnaround time, not turnaround distance.

FUNCTION INDICATORS. Time-and-pace estimates converge on ground truth inside 10% through a full day. Arrival at the catching feature matches pace-count prediction. Turnaround time is observed absolutely. The tally person calls pace at pre-agreed intervals without missing a count.

FAILURE INDICATORS. Pace count is treated as a population figure, not a personal calibration. Terrain transitions go unrecognized and multipliers are not applied. Naismith gets used at base rate for off-trail work and the team benights themselves. Descent gets planned without Langmuir correction and the steep descent eats hours. The tally role gets combined with radio and navigation, and pace drifts by 15%. Turnaround time gets pushed because the summit is close.

FEED-FORWARD. Route craft installs next in 02.6 — handrails, baselines, catching features, and aiming off. Every pace count lands somewhere; route craft chooses where that somewhere is. The map stack tells the operator where features are; the compass converts to bearing; pace converts bearing to displacement; route craft chooses which features to lean on so that pace and compass arrive where they were supposed to.

theFIELD.run / CONSTRUCT_APPLICATIONS / 02 TRAVERSE / 02.6 Route craft — handrails, baselines, catching features, aiming off
SECTION 02.6

Route craft — handrails, baselines, catching features, aiming off

FOUR PRIMITIVESHANDRAIL / BASELINE / CATCHING FEATURE / AIMING OFF
POSITION-FIX CADENCEEVERY 15 min OR EVERY TERRAIN TRANSITION
AIMING-OFF DEFLECTION5°–15°
LEAPFROG SIGHT DISTANCE~50 m DENSE FOREST / ~200 m OPEN
TEN COMMANDMENTSPRE-TRIP PLAN / CARRY MAP AND COMPASS / SET DECLINATION / ORIENT AT EVERY HALT / HANDRAIL WHERE POSSIBLE / CATCHING FEATURE EVERY LEG / RE-CALIBRATE PACE / SIGNAL FROM HIGH GROUND / COMMUNICATE POSITION / STOP WHEN UNCERTAIN

Staying found is cheaper than getting found. The cost of noting your position every fifteen minutes is trivial compared to the cost of reconstructing it after an hour of distraction, and route craft is the set of tactics that hold position continuously at low cognitive cost. Mountaineering: Freedom of the Hills Ch 5 and Kjellström's text converge on the four primitives — handrail, baseline, catching feature, aiming off — and Essential Wilderness Navigation's closing appendix supplies the Ten Commandments that bind them into doctrine. Route craft is the fourth navigation subsystem and the one that converts the other three into a team-sustainable rate of forward progress.

This section installs route craft as the decision layer on top of map, compass, and pace. You load the handrail primitive as linear-feature travel reference, the baseline primitive as area-transecting fallback target, the catching-feature primitive as the beyond-destination overshoot indicator, the aiming-off primitive as deliberate-error-for-certainty technique, the leapfrog protocol for zero-landmark travel, the line-target-over-point-target rule that replaces unforgiving point navigation with forgiving line navigation, the position-fix cadence at 15-min or terrain-transition intervals, the trail-as-liar rule that treats faint paths as game trails until proven otherwise, the Ten Commandments as doctrinal summary, the trip-card preparation that names handrail plus catching feature plus baseline before departure, the STOP protocol when uncertain, and the install / function / failure / feed-forward handoff to SAR search patterns. Sources: FOTH Ch 5 (four primitives, alpine context); Kjellström (handrail and baseline doctrine); Essential Wilderness Navigation Ch 5 and closing appendix (Ten Commandments, trip-card discipline); Wilderness Navigation (aiming-off technique).

02.6.1The handrail — linear-feature travel reference

A handrail is a linear feature that parallels your intended route and offloads lateral tracking onto a single visible cue.

Handrail

A linear terrain or cultural feature (ridge, drainage, fenceline, road, lakeshore, forest edge, powerline) you can travel alongside while remaining visually connected to it. Frees compass and pace attention for hazard-scanning, terrain-reading, and companion welfare.

The navigational logic: precision bearing navigation demands continuous attention to compass, feet, and terrain, and the operator's attention budget is finite. A handrail replaces continuous compass-and-pace tracking with occasional cross-checks against a feature the eye confirms passively. The operator walks along the ridge line; the ridge does the lateral navigation; the compass re-enters the loop only when the ridge inflects. HANDRAIL IS FREE LATERAL NAVIGATION. On complex legs, the operator chains handrails: ride the ridge until it drops to the drainage, ride the drainage until it crosses the trail, ride the trail until it reaches camp. Chained handrails convert a multi-bearing leg into a sequence of follow-the-feature segments.

02.6.2The baseline — area-transecting fallback target

A baseline is a linear feature that transects your entire route area and that you will reach on any bearing within the area. It is the lost-operator's guaranteed fallback.

Baseline

A linear feature — road, river, coastline, long ridge, pipeline, powerline — that extends across the full extent of the area you might plausibly be in. Reachable on any heading from anywhere inside the area.

The lost-operator protocol: when position is unrecoverable, pick a cardinal heading toward the baseline, walk it on compass, and arrive at the baseline. Once on the baseline, the operator walks the baseline (either direction from a random hit) until reaching a known point — the road to a known junction, the river to a known bend, the ridge to a known saddle. BASELINE GUARANTEES RE-ACQUISITION. The baseline converts an unknown-position problem into a walk-until-you-hit-it problem, which is solvable where the original is not. Every trip plan names a baseline for the area; the baseline appears on the trip card; the operator commits the baseline's direction to memory before the first step.

02.6.3The catching feature — beyond-destination overshoot flag

A catching feature is a distinctive terrain feature past your destination that flags overshoot. Essential Wilderness Navigation Ch 5 specifies the technique.

Catching feature

A distinctive linear or point feature located beyond the intended destination, orthogonal to the line of travel, such that the operator cannot pass it without noticing. Examples: stream crossing the ridge past a campsite, trail junction past a summit, vegetation-type change past a saddle, cliff band past a bench.

The catching feature answers the question "how do I know I've gone too far." A leg planned with no catching feature has no overshoot detection, and the operator who misses the intended destination walks past it into terrain that is no longer on the trip plan. A leg planned with a catching feature has a built-in stop signal. CATCHING FEATURE EVERY LEG. The operator who names the catching feature before the first step knows, at every moment during the leg, what the "gone too far" look is. The operator who skips this step gambles on recognizing the destination by sight alone, which works well on a clear day and fails on a foggy one.

02.6.4Aiming off — deliberate error for certainty

Aiming off is the counterintuitive move that introduces certainty through deliberate angular bias.

Aiming-off scenario

Destination: a cabin on the north bank of a river. Direct bearing from camp: 045°. Small drifts in compass or pace place you upstream or downstream of the cabin with no cue which way to turn. Apply aiming-off: bias the bearing 10° left, walk 035°. On hitting the river, the cabin sits downstream with certainty. Walk the bank downstream. Arrive at the cabin.

The deflection range runs 5°–15°. Smaller deflections risk hitting the point exactly (or very slightly off on the wrong side). Larger deflections add walking distance without adding certainty. Typical aiming-off deflection scales with leg length: 5° for short legs, 10° for medium, 15° for long or difficult. AIM LEFT OR AIM RIGHT. NEVER AIM AT. The operator who refuses to aim off gambles on bearing and pace precision that the field rarely delivers; the operator who aims off trades a quarter-mile of sideways walking for a guaranteed find.

02.6.5Line target over point target

A line target is a feature you cannot miss on any reasonable bearing. A point target is a feature you hit only with precision. The operator selects line targets for coarse navigation and reserves point navigation for the final approach.

Navigate to a line target (the river, the ridge, the road, the forest edge) for the coarse leg. Switch to point navigation (the cabin, the trailhead, the pass) only on the final approach from the line.02.6.5 · Line over point

The technique pairs with aiming-off and handrail. The operator aims at the baseline with a deliberate deflection, walks onto the baseline, then uses handrail-plus-pace to find the point. A 10-mile leg to a specific cabin decomposes into a 9.5-mile aimed-off walk to the river (line), followed by a 0.5-mile walk downstream on the handrail (river bank) to the point. Each sub-leg is solvable with field-grade precision. The alternative — 10-mile direct bearing to the point — demands <1% combined bearing-and-pace error, which is not what field conditions deliver.

02.6.6Leapfrogging — zero-landmark travel

Fog, whiteout, dense forest, and featureless desert present the zero-landmark case: the operator cannot sight a reference more than tens of meters ahead. Leapfrogging resolves the problem with two team members.

Leapfrog protocol
01MEMBER AStays on bearing at the current position, compass held level, sighting forward on the planned heading.
02MEMBER BWalks forward on bearing until barely visible to A. Stops.
03SIGNALA hand-signals B left or right until B sits exactly on the bearing line.
04B PLANTSB marks the position with a pole, a pack, or simply stands.
05A WALKSA walks past B, continuing on the original bearing, until barely visible to B.
06REVERSEB signals A left or right until aligned; A plants; process repeats.

Sight distance sets leg length. In dense forest: ~50 m. In open terrain: ~200 m. In whiteout: 10–30 m. The technique produces straight travel when no landmark exists to sight on. LEAPFROG IS SLOW BUT STRAIGHT. Leapfrogging doubles the leg time compared to landmark-based navigation, and the time cost is worth it because the alternative is circular drift that wastes hours and returns the team to the start.

02.6.7Position-fix cadence

Route craft works because position gets confirmed at regular intervals, not because the operator trusts a cold start to deliver a warm end.

Fix cadence rule

Fix position every 15 minutes or every terrain transition, whichever comes first.

At each fix the operator confirms: current heading against map-plotted heading; current pace count against expected distance covered; current terrain against mapped feature; any cross-checks with altimeter, GPS, or natural cues. A fix takes 30–60 seconds at a halt. Across a full day, fixes accumulate to 15–30 minutes of total halt time, which is trivial against the hours of backtracking one missed terrain transition generates. FIX CADENCE IS CHEAP INSURANCE. The operator who skips fixes "because nothing has changed" discovers at the catching feature that several things changed, all of them wrong, and now the fix reconstruction takes an hour.

02.6.8Trails can lie

A faint trail on the ground may not match the trail printed on the map. Humans pattern-match to any linear scrape.

WARN

A faint footpath may be a game trail, a historical logging track, a deer thoroughfare to a wallow, a seasonal poacher route, or an abandoned road. It can parallel, intersect, or replace the mapped trail. Trails fade, re-route after storms, get rerouted by land managers, and get flagged misleadingly by previous lost parties.

The map is the authority, not the ground scrape. The operator reads bearings off map plus compass, fixes position at the cadence, and treats the trail on the ground as confirmation when it matches map, not as primary when it diverges. THE MAP IS THE TRAIL. Game trails are the subtle failure: a faint path with moderate use through brush is often a deer route; following it produces an hour of walking that ends at a wallow or a bedding site with no further path forward. The operator who commits to trails-on-ground without map verification gets lost on trails the map never showed.

02.6.9The Ten Commandments of Wilderness Navigation

Essential Wilderness Navigation's closing appendix condenses route-craft doctrine into ten rules.

Ten Commandments
01PRE-TRIP PLAN a bail route off the planned route, at every decision point.
02CARRY physical map and compass always, regardless of GPS and phone.
03SET DECLINATION before departure, from current NOAA value.
04ORIENT the map at every halt.
05STAY on a handrail where one exists.
06PLAN a catching feature for every leg.
07RE-CALIBRATE pace at terrain transitions.
08SIGNAL from high ground so aircraft and distant searchers can see you.
09COMMUNICATE position at agreed intervals to base or team.
10WHEN UNCERTAIN, STOP — do not move until the position is resolved.

The commandments are cumulative. Each one prevents a different failure mode; skipping any raises failure probability for its specific mode. DOCTRINE IS A CHECKLIST, NOT AN ASPIRATION. The trip-card preparation in 02.6.10 is the operational expression of the Ten Commandments: if the card is filled out, the commandments are loaded.

02.6.10The trip card

Pre-trip preparation loads route-craft primitives onto a physical card carried on the operator's person.

Trip card contents

— Planned legs with bearing (true and magnetic), distance, expected time. — Handrail named per leg. — Catching feature named per leg. — Baseline named for the overall area. — Turnaround time per leg and for the trip. — Bail route from every decision point. — Personal pace calibration table. — Current NOAA declination for the area. — Emergency contacts, PLB serial, trip plan filer, expected return.

The card is paper, laminated or in a pocket sleeve, resistant to rain and tearing. It gets referenced at every halt. It gets updated in pencil when the plan adjusts in the field. THE TRIP CARD IS THE PLAN. An operator who carries the trip card walks with the full route-craft decision tree at arm's reach; an operator who carries the plan "in my head" loses access to it the moment fatigue, cold, or stress degrades recall.

02.6.11The STOP protocol

When uncertain, stop. When lost, stop. When the ground does not match the map, stop.

Stop · Halt motion immediately. Think · What was the last confirmed position? What has changed since? Observe · What is actually on the ground right now? Which bearings do landmarks run? Plan · What is the safest move? Backtrack? Climb for a view? Wait for light? Activate PLB?02.6.11 · STOP

The STOP protocol reverses the natural lost-operator impulse, which is to keep walking in the hope that something familiar appears. Walking when lost compounds the error: the operator's unknown position becomes an unknown position offset by an unknown distance in an unknown direction. Stopping preserves the information the operator still has. STOP, THINK, OBSERVE, PLAN. A stopped operator with a map, compass, and watch can reconstruct position from first principles; a walking lost operator destroys the reconstruction with every additional step.

02.6.12Install, function, failure, feed-forward

INSTALL. You name handrail, catching feature, and baseline for every leg before the first step. You write them on the trip card. You aim off for every line-target approach. You fix position every 15 min or at every terrain transition. You treat trails on the ground as confirmation, not primary. You follow the Ten Commandments. You STOP when uncertain.

FUNCTION INDICATORS. Legs land at the catching feature within pace-count expectation. Handrails reduce navigation cognitive load to scheduled cross-checks. Fix cadence holds without skipping. The trip card stays current through plan adjustments. No leg commits without all three primitives named.

FAILURE INDICATORS. A leg commits without a catching feature and the operator walks past the destination into unknown terrain. The trip card stays in the pack and the plan lives only in the operator's head. A trail on the ground gets trusted over the map, and the operator follows a game trail to a wallow. The operator keeps walking while lost because stopping feels passive.

FEED-FORWARD. SAR search patterns install next in 02.7 — the systematic methods for finding a subject who has run out of route craft. Every concept in 02.6 (handrail, baseline, catching feature, aiming off) reappears in 02.7 as search-team doctrine: search teams travel on handrails, post containment at baselines, report at catching features, and aim off destination points to guarantee coverage. Route craft is operator-side; search is responder-side; both run the same primitives.

← PREVIOUS02.5 Distance, pace, time — Naismith, pace count, triangulationNEXT →02.7 SAR search patterns and lost-person behavior
