theFIELD.run / CONSTRUCT_APPLICATIONS / 02 TRAVERSE / 02.7 SAR search patterns and lost-person behavior
SECTION 02.7

SAR search patterns and lost-person behavior

FOUR PLANNING TYPESTHEORETICAL / STATISTICAL / DEDUCTIVE / COMBINATION
CORE VOCABULARYIPP / PLS / LKP / POA / POD / COVERAGE
COVERAGE C = Z/A = W/S
SWEEP WIDTH W5–15 m DENSE / 15–30 m LIGHT / 30–100+ m OPEN
COVERAGE FACTOR0.25 HASTY → 2.0 FINAL GRID
PATTERNSHASTY / PARALLEL SWEEP / GRID / TRIANGLE / CHOKE-POINT / TRACK-TRAP
DEMENTIA 50% FOUND<1.9 hr IF SEARCH STARTS IMMEDIATELY
HIKER MEDIAN1–3 mi FROM IPP
HUNTER MEDIAN1–4 mi
CHILD 1–30.1–0.5 mi · HIDES
DESPONDENT0.5–1 mi · CONCEALMENT SEEKING

Search is Bayesian. Prior probability of area gets distributed over segments; search action generates probability of detection; cleared segments update the posterior; subsequent resources get allocated to segments with highest residual probability times feasibility. NASAR's Fundamentals of Search and Rescue anchors the doctrine; Essential Wilderness Navigation Ch 7 supplies the SAR-application framing; Robert Koester's Lost Person Behavior corpus supplies the statistical distance-from-IPP tables and subject-category priors; the US National SAR School's Inland SAR Planning Course and the Virginia Department of Emergency Management's Managing Search Operations formalize the Bayesian update cycle. Search is the responder-side subsystem that activates when the operator-side route craft in 02.6 fails or the subject has no route craft to begin with.

This section installs SAR search patterns and lost-person behavior as the fifth navigation-stack subsystem. You load the four planning types of theoretical, statistical, deductive, and combination, the core vocabulary of IPP, PLS, LKP, POA, POD, and coverage, the six primary search patterns of hasty, parallel sweep, grid, triangle, choke-point, and track-trap, the Bayesian update cycle that converts search effort into posterior POA, the coverage arithmetic relating effort, area, sweep width, and track spacing, the hasty-first rule that commits fast teams to highest-probability routes in the first 1–3 hours, the containment discipline that locks the search envelope at zero motion cost, the Koester subject-category table with distance medians by hiker, hunter, child, dementia, and despondent, the clue consciousness protocol where every searcher reports every anomaly, the mission priority triage from mobile live through deceased recovery, the survival-window integration connecting hypothermia and trauma timelines to search-pattern selection, and the install / function / failure / feed-forward handoff to tracking and sign-cutting. Sources: NASAR Fundamentals of SAR (full doctrine); Essential Wilderness Navigation Ch 7 (SAR framing for wilderness); Koester Lost Person Behavior (statistical tables); US National SAR School Inland SAR Planning (Bayesian planning); Virginia DEM MSO (managing operations).

02.7.1The four planning types

Every search plan draws on a mix of four analytical approaches. Fundamentals of SAR enumerates the set.

Search planning types
01THEORETICALTreat the subject as mobile in any direction at a reasonable terrain speed. Expand probability-of-area rings as elapsed time × terrain speed. Default when no information narrows the problem.
02STATISTICALDraw on Koester's historical data by subject category for probable distance and direction from the IPP.
03DEDUCTIVEExamine clues (last-seen point, intended destination, phone ping, vehicle location, known skills, weather at time of loss) to eliminate areas.
04COMBINATIONThe default. Weights across the three update as clues arrive.

The four types coexist in the plan. A search for a missing hunter might start with statistical (Koester hunter-category median at 1–4 mi) and theoretical (elapsed 6 hours × terrain speed), narrow by deductive (truck at trailhead X, last phone ping at location Y), and update the combination as tracks get cut at a trail junction. PLANNING IS UPDATE, NOT DECLARATION. The plan the command staff writes at 0600 gets revised by 0800 clue arrival, revised again at 1200 team-report debrief, revised again at dusk. A plan that does not update is a plan running on stale priors.

02.7.2The core vocabulary

SAR runs on a set of defined terms that carry specific operational meaning. Casual vocabulary collapses critical distinctions.

Core SAR vocabulary

IPP · Initial Planning Point. The anchor point for planning — typically the trailhead, vehicle location, or last-reported waypoint. May or may not equal the subject's actual last position. PLS · Point Last Seen. The last location a witness saw the subject. LKP · Last Known Point. The most recent evidence of subject presence: footprint, GPS ping, cell tower ping, witness sighting, found clue. POA · Probability of Area. The prior probability that the subject is within a given segment or ring. POD · Probability of Detection. The probability that a search of a given segment, with a given effort, finds the subject if present. COVERAGE · C = Z / A where Z is search effort (person-hours, aircraft-hours) and A is the area searched. Equivalent to W/S: sweep width over track spacing. SWEEP WIDTH (W) · The effective detection lane of a searcher, varying with vegetation, subject detectability, light, and weather.

The distinction between IPP, PLS, and LKP matters. An IPP is chosen for planning convenience; a PLS is witnessed; an LKP is physically evident. A search plan anchored on an IPP that is not the actual PLS generates probability rings centered on the wrong point. The command staff's first investigative task is resolving which of IPP, PLS, and LKP is load-bearing for this specific case, and updating as information arrives.

02.7.3Hasty search — first 1 to 3 hours

The first hours after a reported loss have the highest POD per unit hour, and hasty search exploits that window.

Hasty search

Small fast teams (2–3 members) deployed to highest-probability routes — trails, drainages, known destinations, prior campsites. Minimal equipment. Maximum rate. Visual scan only. The goal: find the subject or narrow the area before the subject moves further or conditions degrade.

Hasty teams run at twice or three times the rate of grid teams, with lower POD per segment but much higher POD per unit of deployment time. The hasty window closes as the subject moves, as night falls, or as weather degrades mobility. HASTY FIRST. A mobile subject missed in the hasty window becomes a geometrically larger search problem later: 2 hr at 2 mi/hr produces a 50 km² ring; 6 hr produces a 450 km² ring. Hasty search is not a compromise on quality; it is a recognition that the operational value of search declines with time, and the first team out the gate moves through the highest-value territory at the highest return rate.

02.7.4Parallel sweep and grid — systematic coverage

After hasty, systematic patterns take over. The two primary systematic patterns differ in track spacing.

Systematic search patterns
01PARALLEL SWEEPTeam marches abreast across a segment, compass-spaced (typically 10–50 m apart), maintaining parallel tracks. Sweep width W set by vegetation, subject size, and conditions.
02GRID (SQUARE)Shoulder-to-shoulder spacing (2–5 m). Highest POD. Highest labor cost. Reserved for segments with high residual POA after lower-coverage passes.
03TRACK SPACING (S)Distance between parallel tracks. Smaller spacing = higher coverage = higher POD.

Coverage arithmetic: C = W/S. Sweep width 5–15 m in dense forest, 15–30 m in light forest, 30–100+ m in open terrain with human-sized daylight subject. Track spacing equal to sweep width gives C = 1.0, which corresponds roughly to 50% POD for a single pass. Track spacing half of sweep width gives C = 2.0 and ~90% POD. The SAR manager allocates sweep width and track spacing per segment based on terrain, subject, and resource availability; tight spacing on high-POA segments, wide spacing on low-POA buffer zones.

02.7.5Triangle, choke-point, and track-trap

Three specialized patterns supplement parallel sweep and grid.

Specialized patterns
01TRIANGLEFor a stationary subject in limited area. Legs at 120° apart around a datum point, producing concentric coverage radiating from the datum.
02CHOKE-POINT / CONTAINMENTTeams posted at trail junctions, road crossings, pass saddles, river crossings, egress points. Catches a moving subject attempting to exit the search envelope.
03TRACK-TRAPSmoothed earth, raked snow, or mud strips laid across suspected egress routes. Inspected periodically. POD approaches 1.0 for subjects who cross.

Containment runs before full assembly finishes. The command staff posts choke-points at the earliest possible minute because containment locks the search envelope at zero motion cost; every minute of containment reduces the probability that the subject walks out of the searched area before systematic teams arrive. CONTAINMENT FIRST, SEARCH SECOND. Track-traps are the tracker's force multiplier: a few strips of raked earth across likely egress routes convert the trail-cutting problem from continuous work to scheduled inspection.

02.7.6Bayesian update — the probability cycle

Search planning runs a continuous Bayesian cycle. Each search pass updates posterior POA based on measured coverage and POD.

Bayesian update

PRIOR POA · Probability the subject is in segment S at the start of the pass. POD · Probability this pass detects the subject if present. POSTERIOR POA · Prior POA × (1 - POD). If the pass did not find the subject, the residual probability in S drops by the searched fraction.

Example: segment has prior POA 0.4 (40% probability subject is here). Pass covers with POD 0.5 (50% detection if subject is there). Pass returns no subject. Posterior POA: 0.4 × (1 - 0.5) = 0.2 (20%). The 20% that dropped out gets redistributed across other segments proportionally to their priors, updating the whole probability map. SEGMENTS NEVER HIT ZERO. A single pass at POD 0.5 leaves residual probability; two passes at 0.5 each leave 0.25. Only at POD → 1.0 (grid with full overlap) does a segment approach clearance. The Bayesian cycle is why search plans keep resources on high-residual-POA segments across multiple passes rather than declaring a segment "clear" after one sweep.

02.7.7The coverage arithmetic

Coverage C is the operational scalar that converts effort into POD.

Coverage factor → POD
01C = 0.25 (HASTY)POD ~20–30%. Fast, route-focused, single-pass.
02C = 0.5POD ~40%. Light parallel sweep.
03C = 1.0POD ~50–60%. Sweep width equals track spacing.
04C = 1.5POD ~75%. Tight sweep.
05C = 2.0 (FINAL GRID)POD ~90%. Shoulder-to-shoulder or double-pass.

The relationship is not linear. Doubling coverage from 1.0 to 2.0 does not double POD; it pushes from ~55% to ~90%, approaching but not reaching saturation. Tripling coverage from 1.0 to 3.0 adds ~5% POD for 200% more effort. DIMINISHING RETURNS ON OVERLAP. The SAR manager gets more POD per resource hour from covering two segments at C = 1.0 than from covering one segment at C = 2.0. Overlap saturates; extent does not.

02.7.8Koester subject categories — the statistical priors

Robert Koester's Lost Person Behavior corpus maps statistical priors for distance from IPP, survival behavior, and hiding tendency by subject category.

Koester category snapshots
01HIKERMedian 1–3 mi from IPP. Tends to continue in direction of travel. Responds to name. Moves toward trail or road on recognition of being lost.
02HUNTERMedian 1–4 mi. May travel further; often prioritizes return to vehicle; may stay on game trails.
03CHILD 1–3Median 0.1–0.5 mi. Moves short distances. Hides when scared. Does not respond to strangers' voice.
04CHILD 4–6Median 0.5–1.5 mi. More mobile. May hide from strangers.
05CHILD 7–12Median 1–2 mi. More navigational intent. May follow downhill or follow water.
06DEMENTIA WALKAWAYMedian 0.5–1 mi. Follows path of least resistance. Does not respond to name. Seeks enclosure (bushes, culverts, porches). 50% found within 1.9 hours when search starts immediately.
07DESPONDENTMedian 0.5–1 mi. Seeks privacy and concealment. High self-harm risk. Short search window for live recovery.

Category selection at the start of the mission drives the prior POA map. A missing 3-year-old gets a 0.5-mi probability ring centered on PLS with enclosure-search discipline; a missing hunter gets a 1–4-mi probability ring with game-trail and drainage emphasis. CATEGORY DRIVES POA. The command staff's first category assignment is provisional; clues update category as investigation proceeds (a despondent hiker behaves differently from a fit hiker).

02.7.9Clue consciousness

Every searcher is a clue collector. Every anomaly gets reported.

Clue consciousness protocol

Every searcher reports every anomaly: broken twig, candy wrapper, faint print, fabric fragment, compressed ground, disturbed leaf litter, audible response to call. Photograph if possible. Record location and time. Radio to command. Command tracks clues as data points. Each clue updates posterior POA and vectors resources.

The failure mode is over-filtering by the searcher. A candy wrapper "looks old" and gets left; a faint print "could be anyone" and gets dismissed. The searcher's filtering decision is made with less context than command's, and the clue that command would have weighted highly never arrives. REPORT EVERY ANOMALY. LET COMMAND FILTER. Clue consciousness is the team's single highest-leverage behavior; a single well-reported clue converts a 100 km² theoretical search into a 10 km² deductive one.

02.7.10Mission priority — triage to pattern

Mission priority determines which pattern and which pace a segment gets.

Priority triage
01MOBILE LIVEConfirmed responsive subject. Hasty to highest-probability routes. Survival-window math drives urgency.
02IMMOBILE LIVEInjured or incapacitated subject. Grid within the survival window for the hazard (hypothermia 4–24 hr depending on conditions; trauma 1–6 hr; dehydration 12–72 hr).
03UNKNOWNDefault to mobile-live-hasty until clue arrival updates.
04DECEASED OR EVIDENCE RECOVERYSlow systematic. No time pressure. Prioritize evidence integrity.

The survival window integrates with conditions. A subject lost overnight in winter with no shelter has a survival window measured in hours, which drives hasty-aggressive even in high-terrain-risk segments; a subject lost in summer with water access has a window measured in days, which permits systematic grid. Mission priority updates as search progresses: a 24-hour mobile-live search that has produced no evidence shifts toward immobile-live triage, then toward recovery triage as the window closes.

02.7.11The search-planner's morning cycle

Every morning of a multi-day search runs a planning cycle that applies the Bayesian update to the previous day's results.

Morning planning cycle

01 · CONSOLIDATE · Gather all team reports, clue reports, coverage logs from the previous operational period. 02 · UPDATE POA · Apply Bayesian update to each segment: posterior = prior × (1 - POD_achieved). Redistribute dropped probability. 03 · RE-RANK · Sort segments by residual POA × feasibility. 04 · ASSIGN · Allocate teams to highest-rank segments at appropriate pattern (hasty for residual mobile, grid for residual immobile). 05 · COMMUNICATE · Plan out by 0600. Teams briefed and moving by 0700. Dark-hour prep the previous evening.

The cycle is the operational expression of the Bayesian architecture. Every day is an iteration; every team-hour produces data that updates the probability map; every planning cycle re-commits resources to the highest-value next action. SEARCH IS ITERATED, NOT SCHEDULED. A multi-day search that runs the same segment assignments every day without Bayesian update is running priors that no longer hold, and the operational expression is wasted coverage on segments that were already cleared.

02.7.12Install, function, failure, feed-forward

INSTALL. You load the four planning types and default to combination. You run the core vocabulary (IPP, PLS, LKP, POA, POD, coverage) in every command-to-team communication. You commit hasty teams to highest-probability routes in the first 1–3 hours. You post containment before assembly finishes. You select search pattern by mission priority and survival window. You apply Koester categories to prior POA. You practice clue consciousness. You run the Bayesian update cycle every operational period.

FUNCTION INDICATORS. Hasty search produces a find or a significant area narrowing in the first window. Coverage logs match POD assumptions. Clue reports arrive from every team every operational period. POA map updates as clues arrive. Containment holds the envelope. Mission priority matches subject state and hazard.

FAILURE INDICATORS. Search launches with slow-and-thorough before hasty is complete, and the mobile subject walks out of the envelope. Containment gets skipped and the subject exits the search area. Searchers over-filter observations and clue reports drop. The Bayesian cycle gets skipped and teams re-cover cleared segments while residual-POA segments sit idle. A child's tendency to hide gets underestimated and enclosure search is missed.

FEED-FORWARD. Tracking and sign-cutting install next in 02.8 — the subsystem that converts "any anomaly" clue consciousness into systematic extraction of directional, temporal, and behavioral information from ground sign. Every SAR search produces sign; the tracker reads it; the search planner integrates the track into the posterior POA map.

SECTION 02.8

Tracking and sign-cutting — step-by-step and cutting-for-sign

THREE SIGN CLASSESGROUND / AERIAL / INTANGIBLE
STEP-BY-STEP SIGN-CUTTING STICK~40 in WITH O-RINGS AT STRIDE AND PRINT LENGTH
STRIDE-TO-HEIGHT~0.41 × HEIGHT ADULT LEVEL GROUND
ADULT-MALE BOOT PRINT11–12 in L
ADULT-FEMALE BOOT PRINT9–10 in L
YOUTH BOOT PRINT7–9 in L
SWEEP ARC10 o'clock → 2 o'clock, 20 s
TRACK-TRAP POD→ 1.0 FOR SUBJECTS WHO CROSS
LOW-ANGLE LIGHT WINDOWSDAWN / DUSK / HANDHELD LED

Every step leaves sign. Every human or animal footfall transfers, compresses, or displaces material, and the only question is whether the tracker sees the sign, not whether it exists. David Scott-Donelan's teaching lineage via Joel Hardin and Robert Taylor anchors the Fundamentals of Mantracking step-by-step method and the sign-cutting stick; NASAR's Fundamentals of SAR Ch 13 supplies the operational protocols integrating tracking into SAR command structure; the US Army and Border Patrol combat-tracking tradition supplies the cutting-for-sign doctrine at desert and tactical scale. Tracking is the sixth navigation subsystem and the one that converts ground disturbance into directional, temporal, behavioral, and physiological intelligence about the subject.

This section installs tracking and sign-cutting as the intelligence extraction layer on top of search patterns. You load the three sign classes of ground, aerial, and intangible, the step-by-step method using the sign-cutting stick with O-rings at stride and print length, the print-signature measurements converting boot length to demographic profile, the stride-height relationship allowing height estimation from a single stride measurement, the cutting-for-sign protocol that moves the tracker perpendicular to travel at pursuit-exceeding rates, the aging chain that reads edge sharpness, moisture equalization, debris settling, and weather overprint to place the trail in time, the low-angle-light advantage from dawn, dusk, and handheld LED, the print-deformation vocabulary translating heel-pressure, toe-pressure, and drag into load, ascent, descent, fatigue, and injury, the track-trap POD at near-1.0 on crossed substrates, the lost-spoor concentric protocol preventing random search, the sign-of-absence principle reading silence, missing insects, and unexpected bird response as tracking input, and the install / function / failure / feed-forward handoff to mountaineering travel. Sources: Taylor/Scott-Donelan/Hardin Fundamentals of Mantracking (step-by-step, sign-cutting stick); NASAR Fundamentals of SAR Ch 13 (operational tracking integration); US Army and Border Patrol combat-tracking doctrine (cutting-for-sign at scale); Ab Taylor Fundamentals of Mantracking monograph (print aging).

02.8.1The three sign classes

Sign partitions into three fidelity tiers. Fundamentals of Mantracking and NASAR Ch 13 align on the taxonomy.

Sign classes
01GROUND SIGNPrints, partial prints, stride disturbances, bent grass, disturbed leaf litter, scuff marks, broken roots, overturned stones, compressed moss. Highest fidelity. Easiest to age. Plottable on the map.
02AERIAL SIGNBroken branches above knee height, abraded bark, cleared spider webs, transferred mud or moss, bent weed tops, scuffed bark at pack-strap height. Medium fidelity. Tells direction and passage; aging harder.
03INTANGIBLE SIGNScent (wood smoke, sweat, urine, cooking odor), silence (absence of expected bird calls), animal alarm behavior, insect activity disruption. Low fidelity. Cannot be plotted; confirms presence-in-area only.

Ground sign drives step-by-step tracking. Aerial sign confirms direction when ground sign is ambiguous (walking through a creek bed, on rock). Intangible sign triggers increased search intensity in an area without defining a specific line. A competent tracker reads all three classes simultaneously: ground for the primary trail, aerial for direction confirmation, intangible for presence cues.

02.8.2The step-by-step method

The core mantracking discipline moves one stride at a time between confirmed prints.

Step-by-step protocol
01MEASUREAt first confirmed track pair, measure the subject's stride heel-to-heel between successive same-foot prints. Measure print length and width.
02MARKSlide O-rings on the sign-cutting stick (~40 in length) to match stride length and print length.
03SETFrom the last confirmed print, place the stick tip at the estimated next-print location.
04SWEEPSweep a 10 o'clock to 2 o'clock arc of vision for 20 seconds at the stick tip.
05WIDENIf no print found, widen the arc and sweep again, slower.
06ANCHOROn finding the next print, re-anchor the stick tip at the new print and repeat.

The stick is the tracker's measurement instrument. Stride-length O-ring calibrates where the next print should sit; print-length O-ring calibrates what the next print should look like. False tracks outside the measured stride get rejected automatically; the tracker does not chase every disturbance. ONE STRIDE AT A TIME. Step-by-step is slow and certain. The tracker who skips ahead to "obvious" sign loses the thread and walks past the cut where the subject changed direction; the tracker who works stride-by-stride catches every direction change as it occurs.

02.8.3Print signature — demographic profile from print

Print dimensions carry subject-demographic information.

Print-length signature
01ADULT MALE BOOT11–12 in length typical, sometimes up to 13–14 in.
02ADULT FEMALE BOOT9–10 in.
03YOUTH BOOT (AGES 8–14)7–9 in.
04CHILD (AGES 4–7)5–7 in.
05TODDLER4–5 in.

Width ratios vary by boot manufacturer but typical adult-male width runs 4–5 in, adult-female 3.5–4.5 in. Tread pattern identifies boot type (Vibram, Continental, specific manufacturer), which cross-references against the subject's known footwear at trailhead or home. A single confirmed print with clear tread pattern, length, and width narrows subject demographics and confirms subject identity when matched against known footwear; combined with stride measurement (02.8.4), the print plus stride produce height estimate and identity confirmation from a single track.

02.8.4Stride-to-height relationship

Adult stride scales approximately linearly with height on level ground.

Stride-height relation

Stride (heel-to-heel same-foot distance) ≈ 0.41 × height for adults on level ground.

A measured stride of 30 in suggests a 73-in (6 ft 1 in) subject; 25 in suggests 61-in (5 ft 1 in). The relationship breaks on uphill (stride shortens), downhill (varies with technique), and with load (stride shortens under heavy pack). STRIDE IS HEIGHT, ON LEVEL GROUND. A tracker who measures stride at first confirmed track pair has a height estimate from the track alone; combined with boot length, gender, build, and approximate age, the subject profile emerges before any sighting.

02.8.5Cutting for sign — perpendicular interception

Cutting for sign inverts step-by-step. Rather than follow a trail, the tracker crosses perpendicular cuts across the assumed direction of travel and intercepts sign at whichever cut picks up the trail.

Cutting-for-sign protocol

Assume direction of travel (from intelligence, deductive planning, or subject habit). Identify a perpendicular line — road, trail, clearing, natural clearing — that the subject must cross. Cut that line: walk slowly along it examining every inch for track disturbance. On finding sign, switch to step-by-step tracking.

Apache Scouts for the US Army tracked border crossers across hundreds of square miles of Sonoran desert by cutting roads perpendicular to northbound travel. Border Patrol sign-cutters exceed subject travel rate because cutting runs at road-walk speed while the subject moves at cross-country foot speed. CUTTING BEATS FOLLOWING FOR SPEED. Cutting for sign is the tracker's long-range strategy. The tracker who follows step-by-step from the IPP covers one line; the tracker who cuts ten parallel roads perpendicular to assumed travel intercepts any of a hundred possible subject paths, at pursuit rate.

02.8.6The aging chain

Print age determines search urgency and resource allocation. The causal chain is known.

Print aging
01FRESH (MINUTES)Sharp edges. Moist soil exposed. Green plant material cleanly broken and still green. Disturbed insects still fleeing.
02HOURS OLDEdges rounded by dew, wind, or settled soil. Moisture equalizing. Cut plant edges browning. Insect activity resumed.
03DAYS OLDDebris settling. Leaf and needle fall accumulated. Rain or dew crust on print surface. Plant cuts browned or wilted.
04WEATHEREDRain disruption. Frost-thaw deformation. Animal over-printing. Original edge blurred.

Aging is weather-dependent. A print in wet clay holds edge sharpness for longer than a print in dry sand; a print in snow ages in hours as the snow surface sublimes. The tracker calibrates aging by comparing the subject's print against a known reference print made in similar substrate at known recent time. AGE CALIBRATES TEMPO. A fresh print means the subject may be within earshot; an hours-old print means pursuit at walking pace; a days-old print means cold trail requiring escalation to scent dogs, aerial search, or deductive refinement. The aging chain is the temporal axis of tracking; without it, a found print tells direction only, not urgency.

02.8.7Low-angle light and the handheld LED

Light angle determines what sign the tracker sees.

Light discipline

LOW-ANGLE LIGHT (dawn, dusk) · Shadows cast into prints. Subtle disturbances visible. Prime tracking window. OVERHEAD LIGHT (noon) · Flat illumination. Sign washes out. Difficult tracking. HANDHELD LED · Held at near-ground angle (knee height) pointing along the line of print, recreates low-angle light at any time of day or night.

Night tracking with a low-angle LED often outperforms daytime tracking on fresh trails, because the tracker controls light angle absolutely and casts shadows into every print regardless of time or sky condition. LOW-ANGLE LIGHT REVEALS PRINT. The experienced tracker who starts at dawn, works through midday, and returns to the contested segment at dusk with handheld LED extracts multiple intelligence passes from a single trail; the tracker who works noon only and declares "no sign" misses three-quarters of what is there.

02.8.8Print-deformation vocabulary

The way a print deforms tells the tracker load, terrain, fatigue, and injury.

Deformation reads
01DEEP HEELDescending slope, braking, or heavy pack on the back.
02DEEP TOEAscending slope, accelerating, or front-load (backpack waist-strap tight plus front pouch).
03DRAGToe-drag between prints indicates fatigue, injury, or improperly fitting footwear.
04ASYMMETRIC STRIDEOne stride shorter than the other; suggests injury on the longer-stride side (favoring the intact leg).
05SCUFF MARKSSideways displacement indicates slipping, hasty footing, or avoidance of a surface.
06IRREGULAR SPACINGRunning, stopping, hiding, or confused pathfinding.

The deformation vocabulary converts the track from "who was here" to "what state were they in." A subject whose tracks show drag, asymmetric stride, and decreasing stride length is fatiguing or injuring; search urgency increases. A subject whose tracks show regular stride and confident direction is intact and likely traveling intentionally; search can shift from urgent to systematic. Print deformation is the tracker's physiological assessment at a distance; it updates mission priority (02.7.10) without any visual contact with the subject.

02.8.9Track traps — zero-motion POD

Track traps convert continuous trail-cutting into scheduled inspection with near-perfect POD.

Track trap

Smoothed soft substrate (raked earth, graded sand, damp clay, trampled and brushed snow) laid across a suspected egress path. POD approaches 1.0 for any subject who crosses. Inspected periodically; between inspections, the trap runs autonomously.

Track traps get placed at trail junctions, natural funnels, water crossings, road margins, and expected camp approaches. The trap's substrate is engineered for print retention: soft enough to record detail, firm enough to preserve until inspection. TRAPS ARE ZERO-COST CONTAINMENT. The traps in a search area form a perimeter that detects subject egress without requiring continuous team presence; the tracker who places traps correctly converts the egress-detection problem from 24-hour-manned to schedule-inspected.

02.8.10Lost spoor — the concentric protocol

When the step-by-step method loses the trail, the tracker does not walk onward looking for sign. The protocol is concentric.

Lost-spoor protocol
01MARKMark the last confirmed print.
02INITIAL SPIRALSpiral outward from the mark at 5-ft intervals, searching for the next disturbance.
03WIDENIncrease spiral radius to 10 ft, then 20 ft.
04RETURNReturn to the last confirmed print. Re-check for deliberate direction change (stream entry, rock hopping, walking backward, leaping).
05ANTI-TRACKCheck for anti-tracking: walking on rock ridges, walking in water, brushing out prints. Subject may have deliberately broken the trail.
06ESCALATEWiden search to 50 ft and then 100 ft concentric circles. Bring in additional trackers to work parallel arcs.

The concentric protocol preserves the last known data point. Random walking in hopes of re-finding sign destroys the spatial anchor the tracker still has. PRESERVE THE LAST POINT. The lost-spoor protocol is the tracker's STOP rule from 02.6.11, applied to the trail: when the data runs out, work the known anchor systematically rather than improvising.

02.8.11Sign of absence

The most diagnostic sign is often absence. The experienced tracker reads silence, missing insects, and unexpected bird behavior as primary input.

Silence where birds should call, at an hour they normally vocalize, indicates recent disturbance. Tracks stopping at a water crossing without continuing on the far bank indicate in-water travel or a diversion. Missing insect activity on a carcass, morning after a kill, indicates something is regularly disturbing the scene. Alarm behavior from deer, squirrels, or corvids in a specific direction indicates disturbance in that direction.02.8.11 · Absence as sign

Sign of absence is non-intuitive for the novice tracker, because the eye searches for presence (a print, a broken branch) rather than absence. The experienced tracker runs both scans simultaneously: what is here that should not be, and what is not here that should be. ABSENCE IS DATA. Bird silence at dawn is the tracker's early-warning radar; the subject in the area is announced by the birds before the subject announces themselves.

02.8.12Install, function, failure, feed-forward

INSTALL. You measure stride and print length at first confirmed track pair. You mark the sign-cutting stick with O-rings at stride and print. You work step-by-step on the thread. You cut perpendicular to assumed direction when long-range pursuit is warranted. You age prints through the edge-moisture-debris-weather chain. You work dawn and dusk and carry handheld LED for low-angle light at will. You place track traps at egress points. You run the lost-spoor concentric protocol when the thread breaks. You read sign of absence alongside sign of presence.

FUNCTION INDICATORS. Step-by-step tracking reconstructs the subject's path across hours or days. Demographic profile (height, age, gender, load) emerges from print and stride measurements. Aging correctly places the trail in time, and search tempo matches the age. Track-trap inspections find crossings or confirm non-passage. Lost-spoor protocols recover the thread without destroying the anchor.

FAILURE INDICATORS. The tracker skips ahead to "obvious" sign and walks past the direction change. Stride calibration drifts across a long trail and false tracks get chased. Aging gets inferred from a single print without reference calibration. Lost-spoor triggers random walking rather than concentric protocol. Sign-of-absence inputs (bird silence, alarmed deer) get ignored because they are not "prints."

FEED-FORWARD. Mountaineering travel installs next in 02.9 — the vertical and glaciated-terrain toolkit that opens segments of the search area that foot travel cannot reach without rope, axe, crampon, and avalanche training. Some subjects go where only technical rescuers can follow; tracking finds the direction, mountaineering opens the reach.

← PREVIOUS02.7 SAR search patterns and lost-person behaviorNEXT →02.9 Mountaineering travel — snow, ice, glacier, avalanche, LNT, YDS, Ten Essentials

theFIELD.run / CONSTRUCT_APPLICATIONS / 02 TRAVERSE / 02.9 Mountaineering travel — snow, ice, glacier, avalanche, LNT, YDS, Ten Essentials
SECTION 02.9

Mountaineering travel — snow, ice, glacier, avalanche, LNT, YDS, Ten Essentials

TEN ESSENTIALS SYSTEMS FRAMEWORK
YDS CLASSES1–6 WITH 5.0–5.15 / A0–A5 SUBDIVISION
LNT 7 PRINCIPLES · 200 ft = ~70 paces FROM WATER
ROPE-TEAM MINIMUM3 ON TECHNICAL / 2 × 2 ON GLACIER
ICE AXE60–90 cm SIZED TO USER
CRAMPONS10 / 12 POINT STEEL OR ALUMINUM
AVALANCHE TRIADTRANSCEIVER 457 kHz / PROBE 240–320 cm / METAL SHOVEL
SLAB RELEASE WINDOW30–45° · STATISTICAL PEAK 38°
SURVIVAL WINDOW90% @ 15 MIN → 30% @ 35 MIN
Z-PULLEY `31 / DROP-LOOP 6 : 1`

Vertical, glaciated, and overhanging terrain demands a distinct tool set, because the foot-travel navigation subsystems in 02.1 through 02.8 stop working the moment the route runs out of walkable ground. Mountaineering: Freedom of the Hills anchors the full canon — Ten Essentials, Yosemite Decimal System, Leave No Trace, rope-team composition, snow-travel tools, the avalanche safety triad, self-arrest, and crevasse rescue. Steve House and Mark Twight's alpine philosophy, amplified in House / Johnston's Training for the New Alpinism, converges on the rule that speed is safety because objective hazards — rockfall, serac collapse, thunderstorm, avalanche, altitude degradation — scale with time on route. The mountaineering subsystem is the vertical axis of navigation; it opens segments of the search area that foot travel cannot reach without rope, axe, crampon, and avalanche training.

This section installs mountaineering travel as the technical-terrain layer on top of the foot-travel navigation stack. You load the Ten Essentials systems framework, the Yosemite Decimal System classifying terrain from Class 1 trail walking through Class 6 aid climbing, the Leave No Trace seven principles with the 200-ft camp / cook / latrine rule, the rope-team composition rules (3 minimum on technical, 2 × 2 on glacier), the snow-travel tool set of axe, crampons, MICROspikes, harness, helmet, shovel, and snow anchor, the avalanche safety triad of transceiver, probe, and shovel plus slope-angle assessment at 30–45° with statistical peak 38°, the beacon-probe-shovel sequence targeting the sub-15-minute survival window, the self-arrest mechanics driving pick into snow with bodyweight plus crampon-up posture, the crevasse rescue kit with Z-pulley 3 : 1 and drop-loop 6 : 1 and Texas prusik self-rescue, the glacier-travel spacing at 10–15 m on taut rope with pre-rigged prusiks, the SERENE anchor standard, the speed-is-safety doctrine, and the install / function / failure / feed-forward handoff to physical conditioning. Sources: Mountaineering: Freedom of the Hills (Ten Essentials, YDS, LNT, snow and ice travel, crevasse rescue); House / Johnston Training for the New Alpinism (alpine philosophy, time-on-route doctrine); House / Johnston / Jornet Training for the Uphill Athlete (endurance integration).

02.9.1The Ten Essentials — pre-trip audit run aloud

The Ten Essentials are the minimum-systems framework. Freedom of the Hills shifted the list from ten items to ten systems in its ninth edition, because the systems formulation better captures the redundant-layer logic that keeps an operator alive when any single item fails.

Ten Essentials systems
01NAVIGATIONMap, compass, altimeter, GPS, PLB.
02HEADLAMPPrimary plus extra batteries.
03SUN PROTECTIONSunglasses, sunscreen, sun hat, UPF layers.
04FIRST AIDKit matched to trip length and group, insect repellent included.
05KNIFE + REPAIRFolding knife plus multi-tool plus repair kit matched to gear (tent-pole sleeve, ski-strap patch, ski-skin glue, duct tape).
06FIREPrimary ignition plus redundant; waterproofed tinder.
07SHELTEREmergency shelter independent of primary tent — bivy, tarp, space blanket.
08EXTRA FOODBeyond planned consumption for the planned trip duration.
09EXTRA WATER + TREATMENTBeyond planned need; purification method that works cold.
10EXTRA CLOTHESInsulation beyond the minimum predicted need, including vapor-barrier or waterproof layer.

The audit runs aloud at every trailhead, because silent inventory misses the gap that verbal enumeration catches. OMISSIONS KILL. Statistical review of alpine fatalities clusters the preventable deaths on navigation failure, avalanche, and missing-layer hypothermia, and the Ten Essentials framework is the structural defense against all three. The operator who runs the Ten Essentials aloud at the trailhead carries the alpine subsystem as a rehearsed compound; the operator who trusts to memory arrives at the bivy with the fire kit still in the car.

02.9.2The Yosemite Decimal System — terrain class calibrates the tool set

YDS classifies ground and dictates the protection kit the route will demand.

YDS classification
01CLASS 1Trail walking. No hand use. Boots, trekking poles, standard hiking kit.
02CLASS 2Off-trail hiking with occasional hand use for balance. Scramble boots; poles optional.
03CLASS 3Scrambling. A fall could injure. Hands required on rock. Helmet advised; rope for exposed moves.
04CLASS 4Exposed scrambling. A fall could kill. Rope often used. Helmet mandatory. Harness, protection, belay.
05CLASS 5Technical rock climbing. Rope, protection, and belay mandatory. Subdivided 5.0 → 5.15; protection density and crux severity scale with decimal.
06CLASS 6Aid climbing. Progress on placed gear rather than holds. A0 → A5 subdivides protection reliability, A5 being a pitch where every placement may fail in a fall.

The route is classified before departure, not on contact. A Class 3 segment that the team planned as Class 2 triggers equipment return; a Class 4 segment without rope triggers turnaround. TERRAIN CLASS IS A GEAR COMMITMENT. YDS calibration at trip-planning stage prevents the underequipped-at-the-crux failure; the operator who reads the guidebook ratings and stages rope and protection accordingly arrives at each class boundary already dressed for what follows.

02.9.3Leave No Trace — the 200-ft rule and the seven principles

LNT is environmental doctrine that doubles as operational discipline, because the same habits that protect alpine ecology preserve the search area for the tracker who follows.

Leave No Trace
01PLAN AHEADTrip card (02.6.10), group size capped at local regulation, permits confirmed.
02DURABLE SURFACESTravel and camp on rock, sand, gravel, snow, or established trail; avoid vegetation and crypto-biotic soil.
03WASTEPack out all trash; bury human waste 6–8 in deep and 200 ft from water, trail, and camp; pack out in alpine zone and on glacier.
04LEAVE WHAT YOU FINDNo carving, no cairning beyond established markers, no collecting.
05CAMPFIRESStove preferred; if fire is used, established fire ring only, small, out cold, ash dispersed.
06WILDLIFEObserve at distance; never feed; store food in bear canister or hang at 12 ft high and 6 ft from trunk.
07OTHER VISITORSYield on trail, minimize noise, respect other parties' lines.

The 200-ft rule converts to ~70 paces using the pace-count calibration installed in 02.5.2. Camp, cook, and latrine siting each get measured by pacing from water and from each other. The LNT discipline also degrades tracking sign: a camp sited at 200 ft with faeces buried and trash packed out leaves a search signature the following party has to work to find, which in a tactical context is force protection and in a recreational context is ethical minimum.

02.9.4Rope-team composition — 3 on technical, 2 × 2 on glacier

Team size is a structural defense against single-point failure.

Rope-team math

TECHNICAL TERRAIN · Minimum of 3, because an injured climber leaves 1 to attend and 1 to descend for help. A team of 2 with an injury has the uninjured party splitting between stabilization and evacuation, and either function collapses. GLACIER · Minimum of 2 rope teams of 2 (4 total), because crevasse rescue needs rescuers outside the fall and a single-team-of-two leaves a single rescuer to arrest, build anchor, set Z-pulley, and haul alone.

The team-size rule gets overridden only on carefully rehearsed partnerships where the individual climbers can demonstrate solo rescue under load, and even then the guide and professional-alpine literature converges that 2 × 2 is the minimum operational standard on glacier. SIZE IS INSURANCE. The team that launches under minimum is insuring against no failure at all; the incident consumes the entire reserve and leaves no margin for the evacuation the team now has to run.

02.9.5The snow-travel tool set

Snow and ice travel runs a distinct kit from rock and scramble.

Snow / ice tools
01ICE AXE60–90 cm sized to user: standing with arm relaxed at side, axe head in hand, spike reaches ankle bone. Head, shaft, spike. Self-arrest grip with pick forward. Leash optional; tethered tool resists loss, untethered tool resists injury on fall.
02CRAMPONS10-point for general mountaineering; 12-point with front points for steeper ice and technical routes. Steel for glacier-ice; aluminum for snow-only routes because weight savings are significant and aluminum points wear fast on rock.
03MICROSPIKESShort teeth on elastic harness; adequate for icy trails and low-angle hard-snow approach short of glacier. Not a substitute for crampons on technical or steep ground.
04HARNESSUIAA-rated seat harness. Self-arrest, glacier travel, and crevasse rescue all route through the harness.
05HELMETRockfall, pendulum, icefall, and self-arrest head-strike protection. UIAA or CE rated for climbing.
06SHOVELMetal blade. 1 per tent or rope team in summer; 1 per person in winter. Plastic blades shatter in dense avalanche debris.
07SNOW ANCHORSnow picket, deadman, bollard. Used for belay, rappel, and crevasse-rescue haul-system anchors.

The crampon-off discipline runs on glissade: crampons stay on for travel, come off for any glissade, because catching a front point in glissade tumbles the climber at high speed and destroys ankles, knees, and skulls. CRAMPONS OFF TO GLISSADE. The operator who owns this kit and drills it in training finds the kit obvious on route; the operator who has read about the kit drops one item at the trailhead and discovers the missing piece on the crux pitch.

02.9.6The avalanche safety triad and slope-angle assessment

Avalanche safety runs on a triad of gear plus a discipline of terrain read.

Avalanche triad
01TRANSCEIVER457 kHz international standard. Transmit / receive modes. Battery fresh at trailhead. Pre-departure function check running transmit-receive on every member of the party.
02PROBECollapsible, 240–320 cm length. Aluminum or carbon shaft. Marked in 10-cm increments for burial depth.
03SHOVELMetal blade. Extendable shaft. D-grip or T-grip per preference; D-grip preferred for high-angle chopping.

The statistical terrain window for slab avalanche release runs 30° through 45°, with the peak around 38°. Any slope in that window is a candidate, and the clinometer read runs on every approach. Below 30° the slab rarely releases; above 45° snow sloughs before consolidating into a releasing slab. Decision-making doctrine stacks avalanche-forecast level, recent weather (new snow, wind loading, rapid warming, rain-on-snow), slope aspect, terrain-trap presence (below-slope tree, gully, cliff), group discipline (one at a time across, spotters in safe zone), and the operator's honest assessment of competence to rescue if the slope releases. The terrain read is mandatory; the gear is not a pass to enter terrain that should not be entered.

02.9.7Beacon-probe-shovel sequence — the 15-minute survival window

The survival curve collapses fast. Swiss and Canadian avalanche data converges on ~90% survival at 15 minutes buried, dropping to ~30% at 35 minutes, because asphyxia and CO₂ poisoning in the ice mask around the buried subject's face drive the mortality curve after the initial trauma pass.

Beacon-probe-shovel sequence
01WITNESSWatch the slide. Note last-seen point. Mark the point on a reference feature.
02SCENE CHECKConfirm no secondary slide. Designate uphill spotter.
03BEACON TO RECEIVEEvery survivor switches transceiver transmit → receive.
04COARSE SEARCHWalk or ski a grid with 40-m spacing if slide is wider than 40 m. Follow directional arrow on transceiver.
05FINE SEARCHWithin 3 m, lower transceiver to snow surface. Follow signal minimum, bracketing orthogonally.
06PROBEAt signal minimum, probe orthogonal grid at 25 cm spacing until strike. Leave probe in place at strike.
07SHOVELExcavate downslope of strike, wider than the subject, clearing snow rapidly. Airway first; dig toward the face.
08AIRWAYClear mouth and nose immediately. Check breathing. Treat for trauma and hypothermia. Evacuate.

15 MINUTES IS THE GATE. The entire sequence has to be rehearsed to the sub-15-minute mark, because the team that rehearses only the beacon pass and skips the probe-shovel integration arrives at the subject at minute 8, then takes 20 more minutes to dig out a buried subject the team was supposed to have already surfaced by minute 12. The survival curve is the training target, not the beacon-search subcomponent.

02.9.8Self-arrest — pick, torso, crampons up

A slip on snow becomes a terminal fall in seconds without self-arrest.

Self-arrest mechanics
01ROLLRoll onto chest, face into slope.
02PICKDrive ice-axe pick into snow with both hands, one on head, one on shaft.
03BODYWEIGHTDrive the pick deeper with chest and shoulder weight.
04FEET UPKeep feet off the snow. Crampons on the slope in a slide catch a point and tumble the climber headfirst.
05SPIKEDig knees into the slope for additional friction if legs are above feet level.

The self-arrest drill runs on firm snow at a safe runout before the approach segment that would need it. REHEARSE BEFORE YOU NEED IT. The technique is muscle memory; the climber who has never rehearsed self-arrest flails the axe sideways in panic and loses the tool. The climber who has rehearsed it 10 times on a training slope drops into the posture without thought and arrests within seconds.

02.9.9Crevasse rescue — Z-pulley 3 : 1, drop-loop 6 : 1, Texas prusik

Crevasse rescue runs on mechanical advantage.

Crevasse rescue kit
01Z-PULLEY3 : 1 mechanical advantage. Rescuer loads one pull for 3 units of lift on the victim. Standard on most two-team glacier rescue.
02DROP-LOOP / C-PULLEY6 : 1 mechanical advantage. Used when a single rescuer needs to haul a weighted victim out of a deep crevasse. Lower pulley doubles line.
03TEXAS PRUSIKSelf-rescue kit when alone in a crevasse. Two prusik hitches on the fixed rope — foot-loop and waist-loop — alternating weighted hitches climb the rope.
04ANCHORSnow picket or deadman or bollard, set 3–5 m back from the crevasse lip, SERENE standard (Solid, Equalized, Redundant, Efficient, No Extension).
05EDGE PADPack or padded jacket at the crevasse lip, to prevent rope cutting over the edge on haul.

Glacier-travel spacing runs 10–15 m, rope kept taut, each climber carrying pre-rigged prusik loops on the harness so arrest plus self-rescue can initiate within seconds. SPACING IS ARREST TIME. A slack rope lets the victim fall 2–3 m before arrest loads, enough to injure on the fall or destroy the anchor when arrest finally catches. Taut rope arrests within the first meter of fall, and the rescue then runs on a victim who is hanging upright rather than tumbled and injured.

02.9.10SERENE anchors — the five-element test

Anchors fail through predictable vectors. The SERENE mnemonic covers the five.

SERENE anchor
01SOLIDEach component placed so any single component would hold the load alone.
02EQUALIZEDLoad distributes across components; equalized sling or cordelette geometry directs load to the master point through distributed legs.
03REDUNDANT≥ 2 independent components; the total anchor survives any single component failure.
04EFFICIENTMinimal gear, minimal rope, rapid to build and rapid to strike.
05NO EXTENSIONIf any component fails, the master point does not shock-load by dropping; equalization geometry locks the remaining legs without slack.

EVERY ANCHOR PASSES SERENE. An anchor that fails SERENE on any element is scheduled for failure; the only question is whether the failure takes a load before the climber notices the flaw. The test runs aloud on build, because the belayer who verbally confirms S, E, R, E, N catches the "equalized but extensible" trap that silent review misses.

02.9.11Speed is safety — the time-on-route doctrine

The House / Twight / Jornet alpine philosophy resolves into one operational rule.

Objective hazards scale with time on route. Rockfall frequency peaks mid-morning as insolation thaws frozen debris. Serac collapse runs on daily cycles. Thunderstorm windows open mid-afternoon in continental ranges. Avalanche hazard rises with daytime warming. The route that takes 12 hours exposes the team to more objective hazard than the route that takes 8 hours on the same ground.02.9.11 · Speed as safety

Speed is not aggression; speed is efficiency — of motion, of protection, of pitch management, of route-finding, of nutrition, of communication. The fast team is the team that never wastes a minute, not the team that runs the crux recklessly. FAST AND CLEAN, NOT FAST AND LOOSE. The training prescription in 02.10 exists because speed is a conditioning problem before it is a skill problem; the climber who cannot sustain the pace the route requires loses time on every pitch, and the time loss compounds into hazard exposure.

02.9.12Install, function, failure, feed-forward

INSTALL. You run the Ten Essentials aloud at every trailhead. You classify the route by YDS class and stage kit accordingly. You measure camp, cook, and latrine siting at 200 ft from water using the ~70 paces conversion from 02.5.2. You launch on glacier only with two rope teams of two, rope spaced 10–15 m and kept taut, prusiks pre-rigged on every harness. You read slope angle with clinometer on every approach crossing 30–45°. You rehearse beacon-probe-shovel to the sub-15-minute mark. You drill self-arrest on firm snow before the approach that would demand it. You build anchors to SERENE aloud. You crampons-off before glissade.

FUNCTION INDICATORS. Route runs at planned pace and finishes with daylight margin. Objective-hazard exposure stays inside planned windows. No single-point-of-failure anchor or transceiver or tool. Rehearsed responses trigger on first cue — self-arrest fires within a meter of slip, beacon-probe-shovel closes on the buried subject under 15 minutes, crevasse rescue builds Z-pulley without pause.

FAILURE INDICATORS. Ten Essentials audit skipped, and a missing item becomes the gap on which the trip fails. YDS classification mistaken, and the crux turns out to be rope-and-protection ground the team did not stage for. Two-person glacier team treated as glacier-competent. Crampons left on for glissade. Beacon search rehearsed without probe-shovel integration. Anchor built without SERENE read. Route planned slow, and objective hazards close the window mid-route.

FEED-FORWARD. Physical conditioning installs next in 02.10 — the endurance physiology that underwrites every movement rate in this sub-module and every subsystem in 02 as a whole. The mountaineering kit in 02.9 opens the vertical axis of the search area; the conditioning architecture in 02.10 underwrites the rate at which any operator can carry the kit across the ground.

← PREVIOUS02.8 Tracking and sign-cutting — step-by-step and cutting-for-signNEXT →02.10 Physical conditioning — FITT, AeT/LT, periodization, altitude

CLOSE

Close — from traverse to Applied Force

You now hold ten interlocking subsystems running as the second beat of the foundational architecture layer — map systems encoding ground into datum, grid, scale, and symbology; compass converting map to bearing under corrected declination; GPS / GNSS / PLB extending fix and distress capacity across constellations and satellite relays; natural navigation running sun-shadow, star, wind, and swell as redundant backups; pace, time, and triangulation converting intent into ground truth through Naismith, Langmuir, and the SAR-doubling rule; route craft keeping you found through handrails, baselines, catching features, and aiming-off; SAR search patterns directing force on lost-person probability with POD-governed coverage arithmetic; tracking extracting directional, temporal, behavioral, and physiological intelligence from sign; mountaineering travel opening vertical and glaciated terrain through the Ten Essentials, YDS, LNT, rope-team doctrine, and avalanche-triad discipline; and physical conditioning underwriting every movement rate across the Z1–Z5 architecture and the altitude acclimatization curve. Each subsystem carries explicit install protocols, functioning indicators, and failure signatures. Each subsystem cross-feeds the others: a compass bearing corrects through terrain-read, a Naismith time estimate corrects through pace calibration, an aiming-off deflection corrects through catching-feature hit, an avalanche assessment corrects through clinometer read, a POD coverage gap corrects through secondary tracker cut, a tracking thread reopens under handheld LED in low-angle light, and a Z2 training block raises AeT and raises every subsequent movement rate on the ground.

Navigation resolves position and heading. Terrain-reading tunes the route in real time. Conditioning sets the permissible rate. The compound is the asset; any single subsystem failing drops the permissible pace across the entire stack, and the team that ignored the weak subsystem pays the rate difference in daylight, margin, and capacity to rescue.

This is the FOUNDATIONAL ARCHITECTURE LAYER for movement in the RSI progression. Sub-module 00 installed perception. Sub-module 01 installed the survival primitives that keep the operator alive on the ground. Sub-module 02 installs the movement architecture that traverses that ground. Sub-module 03 installs Applied Force and scales engagement from personal defense through small-unit tactics, marksmanship under stress, and evasion tradecraft. Every subsequent capability compounds on the movement layer installed here. You cannot engage a threat you cannot reach. You cannot evade pursuit on terrain you cannot read. You cannot maneuver a team you cannot pace. You cannot close a distance your engine cannot sustain.

02 foundational → downstream compound
**02.1–02.6Map, compass, GPS, natural, pace, route craft feed → 03 applied force (route to and from contact, break-contact on terrain), 04 compound systems (navigation under environmental stress), 06 command (team routing, mission tempo), 07 field deployment** (condition-class navigation triggers).
**02.7–02.8SAR patterns and tracking feed → 03 applied force (evasion, counter-tracking, cutting-for-sign against pursuit), 05 sustainment (long-horizon scouting, perimeter tracking), 06 command** (search-tempo and clue-weight decision architecture).
**02.9–02.10Mountaineering and conditioning feed → 03 applied force (load-carry capacity under engagement), 04 compound systems (multi-day terrain compounding), 05 sustainment (multi-year conditioning arcs), 07 field deployment** (altitude and glaciated-terrain condition-class triggers).

The operator who runs 02 at operational standard carries a calibrated navigation stack, a conditioned engine matched to the terrain, the route-craft discipline to stay found across days of field time, and the tracking and search-pattern doctrine to put force on the subject at POD-governed rates. The operator who skips 02 arrives at every engagement late, tired, lost, and unable to read the sign that the subject left for anyone trained to see it.

02 COMPOUNDS THE SUBSYSTEMS. Sub-module 02 is not a collection of techniques; it is a compound in which each subsystem corrects the error modes of the others. The compass that fails on iron-mineral ground corrects through GPS fix; the GPS that degrades in canyon corrects through natural navigation; the natural navigation that runs ambiguous on overcast corrects through pace-and-baseline dead reckoning; the dead reckoning that drifts across a long leg corrects through the catching-feature hit; the catching-feature miss corrects through aiming-off geometry; the geometry that fails on fatigue corrects through the conditioning that raised AeT in the first place. When any single subsystem drops out, the rest hold the line — because the compound is the asset, and the redundancy is the design.

You assessed. You survive. You move. Applied Force installs next.

SUB-MODULE 02 · LAND · FOUNDATIONAL ARCHITECTURE (2/3)

TRAVERSE

Foundational architecture — movement across terrain

10
SECTIONS
02
MODULE
03/08
POSITION

You hold a read on the ground from sub-module 00 and an installed set of primary-systems protocols from sub-module 01. TRAVERSE installs the second of three foundational layers: the capacity to move across that ground with intent. Movement is where navigation, conditioning, and terrain-reading compound into a single operator function. The subsystems in this sub-module turn a static read into directed displacement: map and compass, GPS and PLB, natural signals, pace and time, route craft, SAR search method, tracking, mountaineering travel, and the physical engine that powers all of it. Skip any one of them and the others degrade. Install them together and you gain ground at the speed your body, your map, and your terrain permit.

The sub-module integrates nine primary sources. Caudill and Trimble's Essential Wilderness Navigation supplies the map-first methodology, the three map-language stacks, the Ten Commandments, and the SAR-oriented search framework. Mountaineering: Freedom of the Hills supplies the Ten Essentials, the Yosemite Decimal System, the full snow-ice-glacier tool set, avalanche assessment, and periodization. Gatty's Finding Your Way Without Map or Compass supplies the natural-navigation catalog: sun, star, wind, swell, flora, fauna, water. Kjellström's Be Expert with Map & Compass supplies the compass anatomy and declination correction rules. Training for the New Alpinism and Training for the Uphill Athlete supply FITT, periodization, AeT and LT, polarized versus pyramidal distributions, altitude protocols, and the Continuity-Gradualness-Modulation spine. NASAR's Fundamentals of Search and Rescue supplies POD, POA, sweep width, coverage, lost-person behavior categories, and Koester's distance-from-IPP tables. Taylor's Fundamentals of Mantracking supplies the step-by-step method and the sign-cutting stick. The Combat Tracking Guide supplies the cutting-for-sign doctrine.

The sub-module runs on a three-subsystem compound. Navigation resolves where you are and where you are going. Terrain-reading tunes the route you take to get there in real time. Conditioning sets the permissible movement rate and sustains it under load, under altitude, under fatigue. The feedback architecture runs cleanly: navigation error corrects through terrain-read, conditioning limits what routes navigation can commit to, terrain-read updates both. Pull any subsystem and the other two run open-loop.

By the end of this sub-module you have ten calibrated subsystems running in parallel. Map systems encode the ground. Compass converts map to bearing. GPS and PLB extend your fix capacity and your distress envelope. Natural navigation runs a redundant backup anytime instruments fail. Pace and time convert intent to ground truth. Route craft keeps you found. SAR patterns direct search action on lost-person probability. Tracking extracts intelligence from sign. Mountaineering travel opens vertical and glaciated terrain. Conditioning underwrites all of it. You assessed the ground in 00; you survive on it in 01; now you traverse it.

02.1
Map systems — datum, grid, scale, symbology
ENTER →
02.2
Compass — declination, bearings, field technique

theFIELD.run / CONSTRUCT_APPLICATIONS / 03 APPLIED FORCE / 03.1 Predator/prey dynamics and threat indexing
SECTION 03.1

Predator/prey dynamics and threat indexing

ROOT TAXONOMYSOCIAL / ASOCIAL
FIVE SOCIAL SCRIPTSMD / GMD / EBD / SSS / TERRITORY
ASOCIAL PREDATORSRESOURCE / PROCESS
CLOSING STRATEGIESCHARM / BLITZ
INTERVIEW RANGE5–15 ft
TACTICAL MATRIX2 × 2 SURPRISE × FORCE-LEVEL
FOUR ASSAULT TRUTHSCLOSER · FASTER · MORE SUDDEN · MORE FORCE
HIERARCHY OF RESPONSEABSENCE → ESCAPE → EVASION → DE-ESCALATION → FORCE
LOCATION-2 RULERESIST AT LOCATION 1
CLASSIFICATION WINDOW< 2 s

You classify the attacker before the first blow, because the wrong classification routes force selection to the wrong rung of the continuum and compliance to the wrong predator extends the event rather than ends it. Rory Miller's Meditations on Violence and Facing Violence install the taxonomy that governs every downstream decision in this sub-module; Miller and Kane's Scaling Force layers the legal consequences of each classification onto the same frame. The rest of 03 assumes the read is already running in your head as the adversary closes, because the decision cycle installed in 03.2, the force continuum in 03.11, and the evasion doctrine in 03.10 all route on whichever classification you named inside the first two seconds of detection.

This section installs predator/prey classification as the upstream instrument on which every applied-force decision depends. You load the social / asocial root taxonomy, the five social-violence scripts (monkey dance, group monkey dance, educational beat-down, status-seeking show, territory defense), the resource / process predator distinction with the Location-2 rule, the charm / blitz closing strategies and the physical-non-compliance filter, the Miller tactical matrix sorting surprise against force-level into four response quadrants, the Four Truths of Assault — closer, faster, more sudden, more force — that invert every training assumption, the interview-to-attack cascade tracing the predator's six-step close from crowd-scan to contact, the ambush-zone reading that mirrors squad terrain analysis on civilian ground, the hierarchy of response placing absence, escape, and evasion ahead of force itself, and the install / function / failure / feed-forward handoff to the decision-cycle subsystem. Sources: Miller Meditations on Violence Ch 1–7 (taxonomy, matrix, four truths, freeze and break); Miller Facing Violence Ch 3–4 (scripts, predator classes, charm / blitz, hierarchy, ambush-zone); Miller / Kane Scaling Force (continuum legal-gate overlay).

03.1.1The social / asocial root taxonomy

Violence partitions into two root categories, and every downstream decision routes off this split.

The root taxonomy

SOCIAL · Ritualized, audience-present, rules-bound. Participants follow a script; submission typically ends the event without death. ASOCIAL · No audience, no script. Target is interchangeable, chosen for utility (resource) or for the act itself (process). Submission does not reliably end the event.

Miller's rule on the split governs survival directly: social-violence response sets (de-escalation, submission, back-down) extend asocial attacks rather than ending them, and asocial-violence response sets (maximum counter-violence at the first blow) escalate social encounters into criminal liability. The classification is pre-force work — the sentence that names the category runs before the first strike, not after. CLASSIFICATION IS UPSTREAM. The operator who walks into contact without the social / asocial read has already lost the first decision of the engagement; every technique downstream runs on the assumption that this sentence was said first.

03.1.2Five social-violence scripts

Social violence runs on five dominant civilian scripts. Miller's Facing Violence Ch 3 catalogs each with its canonical step-sequence.

Social-violence scripts
01MONKEY DANCE (MD)Male dominance contest. Five-step: eye contact → verbal challenge → closing with posturing → first contact (shove, finger-poke) → dominance blow (looping right). Submission ends it.
02GROUP MONKEY DANCE (GMD)In-group violence on an outsider to affirm identity. Far more dangerous; no off-ramp; members watch each other; escalates toward maiming; increased by visible pain or submission.
03EDUCATIONAL BEAT-DOWN (EBD)One-sided instructional violence. Controlled, non-lethal; stops when the lesson is delivered. Often authority-to-subordinate.
04STATUS-SEEKING SHOW (SSS)Violence as performance before a third-party audience. Attacker cannot abort without losing the point of the act.
05TERRITORY DEFENSEAssertion of ownership or right-of-transit over a space (block, bar, tier).

Each script has an expected response set; breaking the script either collapses the ritual or escalates it abruptly into asocial violence. SCRIPT SORTS SCRIPT. The group monkey dance is the single most dangerous social script, because submission feeds it; the rule "break contact, abort the social frame entirely, treat any further approach as asocial" is the only workable counter, and it runs against every civilian instinct to negotiate.

03.1.3Resource vs. process predator — the Location-2 rule

Asocial predation partitions into two classes, and the distinction drives the go / no-go on lethal force.

Asocial predator classes
01RESOURCE PREDATORWants a thing. If cost of taking exceeds value of thing, the predator disengages. Compliance usually ends the event.
02PROCESS PREDATORWants the act (beating, rape, murder, captive-for-torture). Victim is a vehicle. Submission extends rather than shortens the event.

If the attacker is trying to move you to a second location, the encounter is a process attack. Submission extends it. Survival rates at Location 2 collapse. You resist at Location 1 even at poor odds.03.1.3 · The Location-2 rule

RESIST AT LOCATION 1. The Location-2 rule is absolute; the statistics that anchor it run across decades of criminal-case review, and no variant of "comply and hope" has produced survival advantage against process predators once the victim has been moved. The operator pre-commits to this response before the encounter, because in-the-moment cognition under chemical cocktail will not reason to it fresh.

03.1.4Charm vs. blitz — the physical-non-compliance filter

Closing strategy sorts into two modes.

Closing strategies
01CHARMInterview at 5–15 ft. Friendly approach, benign opener, tests compliance through proximity request. Target compliance opens the attack window. Physical non-compliance ends or reveals the attempt.
02BLITZNo interview. First awareness is the strike itself — from behind, side, or vehicle. Bypasses OODA because there is no Observe phase.

Against charm, the counter is failing the interview: physical non-compliance rather than verbal. Turning the body at angle, answering from distance, refusing the small favor, and visibly checking the hands all route the target out of the charm frame without triggering social-script escalation. Against blitz, the counter is pre-engagement: 360° awareness and tempo-holding at rest defeat it before initiation. Once a blitz has initiated, it has become an aftermath problem, not a combat problem. PHYSICAL NON-COMPLIANCE IS THE FILTER. The civilian who answers the benign question from inside conversational range has already failed the interview; the operator who answers from angle, at distance, with hands visible, ends the attempt without performing visible defense.

03.1.5Miller's tactical matrix — surprise × force-level

Miller's 2 × 2 matrix crosses surprise against force-level to produce four response quadrants.

Tactical matrix quadrants
01LO-FORCE / NOT-SURPRISEDSocial conflict (MD, drunk). Continuum Levels 1–3. Time to apply verbal and posture tools.
02LO-FORCE / SURPRISEDLate-revealed charm, shove from blind side. Recovery-focused. Levels 2–4.
03HI-FORCE / NOT-SURPRISEDYou saw the knife. Time to draw, create distance, take cover. Levels 5–6. Max defender advantage.
04HI-FORCE / SURPRISEDAmbush. First warning = first blow or round. Defender 1–3 s behind, possibly already injured. Only counter is pre-drilled response, not decision.

The hi-force / surprised quadrant is the ambush, and Miller's rule on it forces the operator out of cognitive response into operant-conditioned motor pattern. AMBUSH IS DRILL, NOT DECISION. The training prescription in 03.3 through 03.5 exists because the fourth quadrant is where decisions are too slow; the stimulus-response motor pattern that the operator has rehearsed to repetition-saturation is the only thing that fires fast enough, and the "decision" that installs it happened in training, not on contact.

03.1.6The Four Truths of Assault

Miller's rule separating a fight (two-way negotiation) from an assault (one-way execution).

Four Truths of Assault

A real assault is: (1) closer, (2) faster, (3) more sudden, (4) with more force — than expected.

Each truth alone defeats a trained fighter at training tempo. The compound of all four defeats everyone who has not trained against all four. Dojo partners start in range, move slow, telegraph entry, and calibrate force; the training-reality inversion is the central problem in 03.3 and the reason the combatives prescription there routes on power-generation and closing-distance drills rather than on technique catalogs. TRAINING LIES. CONTACT TELLS THE TRUTH. The operator who has trained for "faster and more sudden" with closer-than-arm's-length entry drilled to repetition has compressed the four truths into practice; the operator who has drilled technique at conventional dojo tempo carries an identity of competence into an encounter that will not honor it.

03.1.7Interview-to-attack cascade

Charm attacks follow a six-step cascade with filter points at every step.

Interview-to-attack cascade
01SELECTPredator scans crowd for gait, gaze, gear, focus, fitness, companions. Target selection runs on victim-signaling.
02APPROACHMove to interview range (5–15 ft).
03OPENBenign opener (time of day, directions, lighter) tests compliance and proximity.
04CLOSEContinue conversation while closing to contact range (< 6 ft).
05CONTROLEstablish grip, display blade or weapon, or isolate target from exit.
06ATTACKProper assault initiates.

Every step is a filter point. The target breaks the cascade by breaking protocol: a hard no at step 03, a fast directional change at step 02, a visible hand-check at step 03, a turn-and-leave at step 04. BREAK THE CASCADE EARLY. The discipline of treating the question as the strike — the social answer already given in body position and distance before the verbal answer forms — routes the operator out of cascade step 03 every time, and the attempt fails before step 05 can establish the control the attacker needs.

03.1.8Ambush-zone reading — civilian terrain analysis

The predator seeks terrain that mirrors small-unit ambush criteria.

Civilian ambush-zone indicators
01KILL ZONEVictim trapped or exposed with reduced movement options.
02COVERConcealment for the predator's approach; blind corner, pillar, vehicle, doorway.
03ISOLATIONLow witness density; low-light hours; reduced foot-traffic window.
04EGRESSPre-planned exit the predator can use and the victim cannot easily duplicate.

Canonical civilian ambush zones: stairwells, elevator approaches, the 10–15 ft car-to-building stretch, parking-garage pillars, ATM recesses, sidewalk corridors between parked trucks, restroom-vestibule offsets. The read mirrors Hopkins's terrain analysis in 03.8 and the concentric-ring defense in 03.9; the civilian ambush-zone discipline is the same doctrine operating on a smaller scale. THE TERRAIN IS THE ADVERSARY'S WEAPON. The operator who pre-routes around these zones on every movement is running squad terrain analysis at operator scale; pre-trip route planning flags the zones before contact, and the zone that was avoided is the ambush that never had a chance to fire.

03.1.9The hierarchy of response

Miller's Facing Violence Ch 4 fixes the preference order for response to a recognized predator.

Hierarchy of response to a predator
01ABSENCEDon't be there. Route plan, time shift, companion routing. Cost: hours. Benefit: 100%.
02ESCAPEAlready in pre-attack location — leave. Cost: looking scared. Benefit: ~95%.
03EVASIONExit blocked — break LOS, create cover, create time, leave.
04DE-ESCALATIONWorks on social and resource predators; worthless on process predators.
05FORCELast resort. Levels 1–6 per Miller / Kane continuum, per jurisdictional legal posture.

Each step is roughly an order of magnitude more costly and more risky than the one above. STEP 5 MEANS STEPS 1–4 FAILED. The hierarchy is why 03.10 installs evasion before 03.11 installs the integration; the operator who defaults to Force at every contact carries unnecessary legal exposure and unnecessary physical risk, and the operator who runs Absence / Escape / Evasion as the first three instruments wins most encounters before they turn into encounters at all.

03.1.10"Not being there" — the pre-threat fieldcraft multiplier

Every minute of pre-threat fieldcraft compounds against downstream cost.

Every minute of route-planning, time-shifting, companion-selection, vehicle parking, and situational awareness is worth ten minutes of technique drilling and one hundred minutes of legal and medical aftermath.03.1.10 · The multiplier

The principle scales from civilian street through small-unit patrol; "not being there" on patrol means not walking the predictable road and not basing in the obvious draw, mirroring the ambush-zone discipline at squad scale. PRE-THREAT WORK IS THE HIGHEST-LEVERAGE FORCE MULTIPLIER. The operator who invests in pre-threat fieldcraft buys down the probability of needing any subsequent subsystem in 03 — empty-hand, weapons, movement, ambush, defense, evasion — and when those subsystems do need to fire, they fire on ground the operator chose rather than ground the adversary chose.

03.1.11Install, function, failure, feed-forward

INSTALL. You build classification as a real-time read rather than a retrospective analysis. Pre-trip route planning flags ambush-zone analogs at every transit. You treat every approach within interview range as a potential charm opener. Physical non-compliance — turn, directional change, hard no, hand check — is the filter you run by default, not by decision. You pre-commit to the process-predator response before encounter: resist at Location 1, no transport accepted under any circumstance, any attempt to move you reads as lethal-intent signaling. You rehearse the hi-force / surprised response as drilled motor pattern, not reasoned decision.

FUNCTION INDICATORS. You classify attacker category, closing strategy, and matrix quadrant inside 2 s of detection. Interview-to-attack cascades break at step 02 or 03 without you entering combat. Ambush-zone routing occurs automatically on transit. The hierarchy of response runs Absence → Escape → Evasion before Force in every eligible encounter.

FAILURE INDICATORS. You pattern-match asocial violence to social scripts and attempt de-escalation on a process predator. You submit at Location 1 and accept transport. You answer the interview from inside conversational range. You walk a pre-routed ambush zone on autopilot. You train the techniques of 03.3 through 03.5 without the classification that routes them.

FEED-FORWARD. Reality-based decision cycle installs next in 03.2 — the Color Code, OODA, Hick's Law, and chemical-cocktail architecture that converts the classification named here into applied force at adrenaline-dump tempo. The taxonomy is the input; the decision cycle is the conversion; every section from 03.3 forward assumes both are running.
