SECTION 03.10

Evasion and escape — the four steps before Force

HIERARCHY OF RESPONSEABSENCE → ESCAPE → EVASION → DE-ESCALATION → FORCE
ABSENCE DELIVERS 100% · ESCAPE ~95%
BREAK-LOS PROTOCOLFIRST BREAK 2–3 s LEAD · SECOND BREAK 20–30 s
SERE CHECKPOINTS200 m · 1 km · 5 km
COUNTER-TRACKHARD SURFACE · DECEPTION · SIGNATURE · TIMING
BREAK-CONTACT BOUNDS30–75 m
RETURN INDIRECT · BACKTRACK AMBUSH
E&E KITON-PERSON · EDC BAG · VEHICLE
WARRIOR DIES ONCE · WINNING IS LIVING

Force is the last rung, not the first, and the hierarchy of response places four steps ahead of it. Miller's Facing Violence Ch 4 installs the hierarchy — Absence, Escape, Evasion, De-escalation, Force — in preference order, with each step costing or risking an order of magnitude more than the one above. The Air Force SERE Handbook supplies the E&E checkpoint architecture and counter-tracking doctrine. Miller and Kane's Scaling Force positions Presence and Voice as E&E instruments rather than Force instruments, because the stance and voice that deter engagement avoid the engagement entirely. Dolio's Scouting & Patrolling TW-04 supplies the break-contact drill as team-level E&E primitive.

This section installs the Miller hierarchy of response as preference order, the break-line-of-sight protocol for active-contact evasion, the SERE checkpoint architecture across 200 m / 1 km / 5 km, counter-tracking doctrine across hard surface / deception / signature / timing, Dolio's team break-contact drill as E&E primitive at small-unit scale, the indirect return with backtrack ambush, the E&E kit stratified across on-person / EDC / vehicle, the pre-trip route briefing that converts preparation minutes into execution seconds, the winning-is-living discipline, and the install / function / failure / feed-forward handoff into solo-to-unit integration. Sources: Miller Facing Violence Ch 4 (hierarchy of response, Absence, Escape, Evasion); Air Force SERE Handbook (E&E checkpoints, counter-tracking); Dolio Scouting & Patrolling TW-04 (team break-contact, indirect return, backtrack ambush); Miller / Kane Scaling Force (Presence and Voice as E&E).

03.10.1The Miller hierarchy of response

Miller's Facing Violence Ch 4 fixes the preference order for response to a recognized predator.

Hierarchy of response
01ABSENCEdon't be there. Route plan, time shift, companion routing. Cost: hours. Benefit: 100%. The attack that never occurred is the attack with zero consequence on every axis.
02ESCAPEalready in the pre-attack location — leave. Cost: looking scared. Benefit: ~95%.
03EVASIONexit blocked — break LOS, create cover, create time, leave.
04DE-ESCALATIONworks on social and resource predators. Worthless on process predators (submission extends rather than ends).
05FORCElast resort. Levels 1–6 on Miller-Kane continuum, per jurisdictional legal posture.

Each step costs or risks an order of magnitude more than the one above. STEP 5 MEANS STEPS 1–4 FAILED. The best self-defense technique is not being there; the hierarchy is the reason 03.1 classification, 03.2 decision cycle, and 03.10 evasion precede 03.3 through 03.9 in operational weight — every step earlier in the hierarchy prevents the need to execute later ones, and the operator who defaults to Force at every contact carries unnecessary legal exposure and unnecessary physical risk across every encounter he could have avoided.

03.10.2The break-line-of-sight protocol

The core evasion sequence under active contact.

Break-LOS protocol
01DETECTattacker identified in attack posture.
02FIRST BREAKmove toward nearest corner, wall, vehicle, or door that denies direct LOS.
03SPRINT WINDOWonce behind the break, accelerate maximum effort for 3–5 s (the window before attacker re-acquires).
04SECOND BREAKturn a second corner within the sprint window.
05CONTINUEthird and fourth breaks typically reduce pursuit probability to near zero.

The first break gives 2–3 s of lead; the second converts that into 20–30 s because the attacker now searches rather than chases; third and fourth breaks reduce pursuit probability catastrophically. Hiding without subsequent movement is not evasion; it is delay, and delay that allows the pursuer to close search loops back onto the hider. TWO BREAKS, NOT ONE. The operator who takes a single corner and stops has installed himself as a stationary target inside the attacker's progressive search; the two-break rule is the minimum execution of the protocol, and every additional break compounds against pursuit probability.

03.10.3SERE checkpoint architecture and counter-tracking

SERE structures E&E over distance; counter-tracking reduces the signal the pursuer can follow.

SERE checkpoints
01200 mbreaks immediate pursuit. Assess, reorient, move.
021 kmconsolidate, reorient, navigation fix, kit check.
035 kmsustained evasion. Established route, cached resources, communication plan.
Counter-tracking discipline
01HARD-SURFACE ROUTINGroad, rock, stream-bed, game trail. Reduces track sign.
02DECEPTIONbackward walking in short stretches, fishhooks, counter-angles, intersecting trails.
03SIGNATURE DISCIPLINEno dropped wrappers, no disturbed spider webs in return direction, no urine or feces near route.
04TIMINGhigh wind, rain, or pre-dawn degrades track quality.

Weather covers noise; terrain covers sign. WEATHER AND TERRAIN ARE FREE. The evading operator who moves in rain at dusk across stream-bed onto rock carries a signature that a competent tracker cannot recover; the operator who moves at midday in dry conditions across soft soil leaves a trail that a mediocre tracker can follow at walking pace — and the time-of-movement choice is usually the operator's to make if he has paid the hours of patience that the Absence-preferring hierarchy builds into his discipline.

03.10.4Dolio's team break-contact and the indirect return

At small-unit scale, evasion runs as a rehearsed bounding-withdrawal drill.

Team break-contact
01CONTACT [DIRECTION] called.
02Team in contact drops, runs RTR (suppress, cover, effective fire).
03Team leader decides BREAK CONTACT (civilian default).
04Bounding overwatch rearward, each element calling MOVING / SET, each bound 30–75 m, until contact breaks.
05Post-break: indirect return. Team heads general direction rather than directly to base. Base element sets ambush on backtrack route. Team doubles back. Waits to see if pursuit develops.

The indirect return exists because the direct return vector is the vector the pursuer expects. The backtrack ambush converts pursuit into the pursuer's last decision. NEVER RETURN DIRECT. The team that returns direct to base after break-contact has installed the base as a secondary target for a pursuer who may not have known the base existed; the indirect route with ambush fallback is the protocol that keeps the base off the pursuer's path and converts the pursuit into an opportunity rather than a continuing threat.

03.10.5E&E kit stratification and the pre-trip route briefing

Kit is stratified across three levels; the briefing converts route-planning into usable seconds-of-execution.

E&E kit stratification
01ON-PERSONknife, lighter, headlamp, map or paper compass, cash, ID copy, cell phone or HAM handheld, water-purification tabs, 550 cord.
02EDC BAGexpanded medical, food, water, additional ammunition, hardshell, comms, light, multitool.
03VEHICLEfurther expanded — shelter, food, water, fuel, redundant comms, weapons, medical, maps.

The pre-trip briefing runs before every transit: primary and alternate routes, ambush-zone analogs (parking lot, car-to-entrance stretch, ATM, stairwells), safe-haven points (police, fire, busy business, neighbor), rally points for companions ("if X, meet at Y"), and return-route options. BRIEF THE TRIP BEFORE THE TRIP. The pre-trip briefing converts minutes of preparation into seconds of execution; the operator who has named the alternate route and the safe haven in advance executes on the first break rather than deciding on the first break, and under cocktail the difference between execution and decision is the difference between evasion and capture.

03.10.6Install, function, failure, feed-forward

INSTALL. You pre-plan primary and alternate routes before every trip, identify ambush-zone analogs, identify safe-haven points, and brief companions on rally points. You carry the E&E kit on-person, expanded in EDC bag, further expanded in vehicle. You drill the break-LOS protocol as reflex — two breaks minimum, three or four preferred. You pre-commit to winning-is-living: a warrior dies only once and cannot throw his life away on ego, on misplaced obligation, or on a fight that did not have to happen. You run the hierarchy of response as routing, with Force as the fifth option and never the first.

FUNCTION INDICATORS. Route planning converts minutes of preparation into seconds of execution. The first break produces a second break within the sprint window. Break-contact returns run indirect with backtrack ambush set. Counter-tracking discipline holds across hard surface, deception, signature, and timing. The hierarchy of response runs Absence / Escape / Evasion before every Force decision.

FAILURE INDICATORS. Hiding substitutes for movement. Route planning is absent or cursory. The team returns direct to base after break-contact. The first break is the only break and the pursuer closes search loops before the operator moves again. Counter-tracking discipline collapses because signature control was never rehearsed.

FEED-FORWARD. Solo-to-unit integration installs next in 03.11 — the 6 × 4 matrix crossing the Miller-Kane continuum against Dolio's solo / buddy / fire-team / squad axis, the force-multiplier progression, tempo stacking, the Dempsey-Sajnog-Miller unified power model, and the integrated scaling decision protocol. Where 03.1 through 03.10 installed each subsystem in isolation, 03.11 is the architecture that selects which rung and which scale to run against which threat.

SECTION 03.11

Solo to unit integration — the `6 × 4` matrix and the unified power model

INTEGRATION MATRIX6 × 4 (MILLER-KANE RUNG × DOLIO SCALE)
CONTINUUMPRESENCE · VOICE · TOUCH · EMPTY-HAND · LESS-LETHAL · LETHAL
SCALESSOLO · BUDDY · FIRE TEAM · SQUAD
FORCE MULTIPLIER1.0 / 2.5–3.0 / 6–8 / 12–20
TEMPO CYCLESSOLO 1 · BUDDY 2 · FT 4 · SQUAD 8–12
UNIFIED POWER MODELDEMPSEY · SAJNOG · MILLER
PRE-COMBAT AUDITAWARENESS · INITIATIVE · PERMISSION · TECHNIQUE · TEAMWORK · AFTERMATH
RULEMASTER EACH SCALE BEFORE UP-LEVELING
UNIFYING LAWPOWER × TARGETING × TIMING

Every level of applied force runs on the same three-factor product — Power Generation × Targeting × Timing — applied against an adversary's OODA at the rung of the continuum matched to the threat. The Miller-Kane six-level vertical axis (Presence, Voice, Touch, Empty-Hand, Less-Lethal, Lethal) crosses Dolio's horizontal axis (Solo, Buddy, Fire Team, Squad) into an integration matrix, and every real engagement occupies one cell. Miller, Kane, Dempsey, Sajnog, Hopkins, and Dolio converge on this integration: the rung is the instrument, the scale is the force-multiplier, and the product of the two is the actual capacity the operator brings to contact.

This section installs the 6 × 4 integration matrix as the routing device across all prior sections, the force-multiplier progression across solo / buddy / fire team / squad, tempo stacking that compounds OODA cycles with scale, the Dempsey-Sajnog-Miller unified power model cross-mapping the three primary power frameworks into one, the integrated scaling decision protocol that runs the matrix live, the Miller pre-combat audit across Awareness / Initiative / Permission / Technique / Teamwork / Aftermath, the training-integration program across weekly / monthly / quarterly / annual rehearsal cycles, and the install / function / failure / feed-forward handoff into the module close. Sources: Miller Meditations on Violence Ch 8 (pre-combat audit); Miller / Kane Scaling Force (continuum, IMOP, Presence-through-Lethal integration); Dempsey Championship Fighting (power model); Sajnog Navy SEAL Shooting (shooting-platform power model); Hopkins Small Unit Infantry Ambush Tactics (small-unit integration); Dolio TW-02 / TW-03 / TW-04 (solo-to-squad integration, civilian scale).

03.11.1The 6 × 4 integration matrix

Every engagement occupies one cell in the matrix; the matrix itself is the routing device for which subsystem fires.

Miller-Kane rungs × Dolio scales
ROWS (rungs)1 PRESENCE2 VOICE · 3 TOUCH · 4 EMPTY-HAND · 5 LESS-LETHAL · 6 LETHAL.
COLUMNS (scales)SOLOBUDDY · FIRE TEAM · SQUAD.
Every cell has distinct protocol. Rung-1 / Solo differs from Rung-1 / Squad (a single operator's stance vs. a squad's posture); Rung-6 / Buddy differs from Rung-6 / Solo (paired shooters with overwatch vs. a single shooter alone).

The matrix is the routing device for every prior section. 03.1 taxonomy routes the rung; 03.7 formation routes the scale; 03.10 hierarchy routes the "none of the above" fifth option. ONE CELL PER ENGAGEMENT. The operator who cannot name the cell he is in at the moment of engagement cannot coordinate the rung-specific technique with the scale-specific coordination, and under cocktail he defaults to the cell he has most rehearsed — which is the argument for drilling the cell that matches the most probable encounter first, rather than the cell that matches a fantasy encounter.

03.11.2The force-multiplier progression and the master-before-up-leveling rule

Scale multiplies capacity, but only if each lower scale is mastered first.

Force-multiplier progression
01SOLO1.0 force output. Baseline.
02BUDDY PAIR (well-drilled)2.5–3.0 through one-suppresses-while-other-moves, one-watches-while-other-shoots, mutual aftermath medical.
03FIRE TEAM (4, well-drilled)6–8 through two mutually-supporting pairs and formation discipline.
04SQUAD (8, well-drilled)12–20 through two teams maneuvering as a unit with dedicated roles.

The rule runs inverse: a squad whose operators cannot execute solo fundamentals degrades to less than a fire team's output; a fire team of bad buddies is worse than a single solo. Coordination cost exceeds coordination gain when the underlying scale is not mastered. MASTER SCALE N BEFORE SCALE N+1. The civilian error runs toward assembling a squad without first having drilled the buddy pair the squad is made of; the resulting squad fights as four uncoordinated solos with overlapping fire sectors, which is worse than one coordinated solo with a clear sector of his own.

03.11.3Tempo stacking across scales

Tempo compounds with scale, when the scale is drilled.

OODA cycles by scale
01SOLO1 cycle. Operant conditioning drops cycle time from 1.5 s baseline to ~0.5 s under drilled response.
02BUDDY PAIR2 decorrelated cycles. One acts while the other observes; the cycle one operator is in is uncorrelated with the cycle the other is in.
03FIRE TEAM4 cycles through formation rotation.
04SQUAD8–12 active cycles through fire-and-movement.

The enemy's OODA, running a single cycle, cannot keep up. Tempo dominance is the product of individual skill × team rehearsal × unit coordination; missing any factor collapses tempo to the slowest link. TEMPO IS MULTIPLICATIVE, NOT ADDITIVE. The squad with four fast operators and four slow ones does not run eight cycles at average speed; it runs at the speed of the slowest, because coordination requires each operator to wait for the lagging one, and the squad's aggregate tempo degrades to the lag.

03.11.4The Dempsey-Sajnog-Miller unified power model

Three primary power frameworks describe the same phenomenon.

A power source (body mass or propellant), conditioned through structural alignment (Power Line or shooting platform), released with precise timing (trigger press or falling-step initiation), onto a precisely chosen target (the line or the threat). Violation of any axis zeros the output.03.11.4 · The unified power model

Dempsey's four methods of weight-in-motion instantiate the model for empty-hand; Sajnog's SEAL Seven instantiates it for shooting; Miller's Power × Targeting × Timing states the model in most general form. Empty-hand, pistol, rifle, ambush, defense — the rule is universal. ONE MODEL, MANY INSTRUMENTS. The operator who understands the model as a single structure rather than as three separate doctrines carries a transfer-learning advantage: drills that improve trigger-press timing improve Falling-Step timing, because the nervous system is learning the same skill (precise release under structural alignment), not three different skills.

03.11.5Integrated scaling decision and the Miller pre-combat audit

The live protocol that runs the matrix in the field.

Integrated scaling decision
01CLASSIFYthreat through 03.1 (social / asocial, resource / process, charm / blitz).
02ASSESSown state through 03.2 (Cooper color, OODA readiness, cocktail estimate, HR estimate).
03SELECT RUNGper threat + Disparity of Force + IMOP.
04SELECT SCALEper rung + availability (who is with you, and what have they drilled).
05EXECUTEwith full commitment.
06RE-ASSESSevery 2–3 s. Step up, step down, or transition to E&E.
07DISENGAGEand run aftermath: consolidation, ACE, SITREP, medical, legal.
Miller pre-combat audit (post-engagement)
AWARENESSdid I see it in time?INITIATIVE · did I act first? · PERMISSION · had I pre-settled it? · TECHNIQUE · did the motor pattern fire? · TEAMWORK · did the coordination hold? · AFTERMATH · did medical / legal / comms run?

The audit runs post-engagement as debrief, and the failure mode surfaced in any category becomes the training focus for the next cycle. AUDIT EVERY ENGAGEMENT. The operator who debriefs every encounter — verbal dispute, close call, near-miss, actual contact — against the six-category audit builds a drift-detection system across his own capacity; the operator who only debriefs "real fights" never catches the drift that shows up in the low-stakes engagements first and predicts the high-stakes failure later.

03.11.6Training-integration program

The cadence that keeps the matrix firing.

Training integration
WEEKLYdry-fire 100+ reps fundamentalsempty-hand Falling Step + Miller decision stick, 15 min · scenario review, 15 min.
MONTHLYweakness-biased live-fire (80% on weakest fundamental)formation rehearsal · RTR drill.
QUARTERLYforce-on-force with layered cognitive load (simunitions or airsoft, full continuum)patrol / ambush / defensive rehearsal · route planning refresh.
ANNUALlegal review with attorneyTCCC refresher · witness-statement drill · E&E route audit.

The program is the minimum cadence for the matrix to fire at tempo. Gaps in the cadence show up as gaps in the matrix, and the cell that has not been drilled in six months is the cell that will fail on contact. CADENCE IS THE SYSTEM. The operator without training cadence is running the matrix on memory rather than on conditioned motor pattern; memory fails under cocktail, and the cadence exists to convert memory into reflex before the cocktail does the conversion-destruction the operator cannot recover from.

03.11.7Install, function, failure, feed-forward

INSTALL. You name the matrix cell you are in at every engagement — rung × scale — before executing. You run the integrated scaling decision protocol as a sequenced cognitive routine: classify, assess, select rung, select scale, execute, re-assess every 2–3 s, disengage, aftermath. You run the Miller pre-combat audit post-engagement on every encounter, not just on "real" ones. You hold training cadence across weekly / monthly / quarterly / annual tiers. You refuse to up-level a scale before the lower scale is drilled to reliability.

FUNCTION INDICATORS. Every scale from solo through squad cycles OODA faster than any probable adversary. The continuum rung matches the threat without over-escalation or under-escalation. Integrated scaling runs as a cognitive routine rather than as in-the-moment improvisation. Training cadence holds across all four tiers. The pre-combat audit surfaces weaknesses before they manifest as failures.

FAILURE INDICATORS. Integration skips a scale — fire team assembled without buddy-pair mastery, squad assembled without fire-team mastery. Weapons outpace mindset — the operator acquires rung-6 instruments without having drilled rungs 1 through 4. Rung selection ignores Disparity of Force or IMOP. Cadence collapses, and the matrix cells decay as drilled motor patterns revert to unconditioned memory. The pre-combat audit is run only on catastrophic engagements rather than on every encounter.

FEED-FORWARD. Sub-module 03 closes with the CLOSE section — the hand-off to Sub-module 04 THE COMPOUND, which activates the Acceleration layer of the RSI progression. Where 01 installed survival, 02 installed traverse, and 03 installed applied force as three solo-to-unit subsystems, 04 composes them into feedback loops that exceed the arithmetic sum of their parts. Tracking + navigation + evasion composes detection-counter-detection. Medical + herbal + homestead composes self-sufficient pharmacy. Force + leadership + strategy composes command under fire. Fitness + combatives + mountaineering composes the operator physical specification. The foundational architecture is installed; the acceleration layer interlocks it.

SECTION 03.2

Reality-based decision cycle — Color Code, OODA, Hick's Law, chemical cocktail

COLOR CODEWHITE / YELLOW / ORANGE / RED / BLACK
DEFAULT POSTUREYELLOW
OODAOBSERVE · ORIENT · DECIDE · ACT
ORIENT IS WHERE IT FAILS
HICK'S LAWlog₂(n + 1)
DECISION STICK > DECISION TREE
HR THRESHOLDS< 80 bpm BASELINE / 115–145 bpm FINE-MOTOR DEGRADE / 145–175 bpm OPTIMAL GROSS / > 175 bpm SUB-CORTICAL
TUNNEL VISION20–30° CONE
CLASSIFICATION-TO-ACT WINDOW< 2 s

Perception converts to applied force through a decision loop that must survive adrenaline dump, tunnel vision, auditory exclusion, and fine-motor collapse, and the operator who trains the technique without the decision cycle carries force capacity that cannot fire on contact. Miller's Meditations on Violence and Facing Violence install the cognitive architecture — Cooper's Color Code as passive posture, Boyd's OODA loop as tempo, Hick's Law as the reason decision trees collapse under stress. Sajnog's Navy SEAL Shooting supplies the shooting-specific OODA compression, Dolio's Fieldcraft TW-02 anchors the civilian baseline, and the chemical-cocktail physiology common to all three sources fixes the operating envelope every downstream subsystem runs inside.

This section installs the Cooper Color Code as five-tier mental-state ladder with Yellow as passive default, the Boyd OODA loop with Miller's Orient-failure correction, Hick's Law and the decision stick vs. decision tree distinction that is the single most operationally consequential choice in all of 03, the chemical cocktail architecture fixing heart-rate thresholds and fine-motor collapse windows, operant conditioning as the installation method for motor patterns that must survive cocktail, the pre-loaded go-button compressing OODA to Observe→Act, the pre-settled permission question that decides whether the defender freezes or fires, and the install / function / failure / feed-forward handoff into the combatives subsystem. Sources: Miller Meditations on Violence Ch 6 (chemical cocktail, freeze, OODA); Miller Facing Violence Ch 5 (go-button, permission, operant conditioning); Sajnog Navy SEAL Shooting Ch 3–4 (OODA compression, dry-fire doctrine); Dolio Fieldcraft TW-02 (civilian posture baseline).

03.2.1Cooper's Color Code — passive posture, not active effort

The color code runs as default state rather than conscious monitoring.

Cooper Color Code levels
01WHITEUnprepared, off-task, phone-absorbed. Civilian default. Incapable of response within the reaction window.
02YELLOWRelaxed awareness. Head up, hands free, peripheral scan running, 360° bias. Sustainable indefinitely as posture rather than effort.
03ORANGEAlertness to a specific probable threat vector. Preparation to act underway. Hands moving, angles opening, exit identified.
04REDAction mode. Response begun or imminent. Go-button criteria satisfied or within a tick.
05BLACKCognitive collapse. Orange skipped, Red entered without preparation. Freeze, tunnel, dissociation.

The operator defaults to Yellow so Orange stimulus registers at all. White-to-Red is the Black pathway, and Black is where untrained civilians die. YELLOW IS POSTURE, NOT EFFORT. The operator who installs Yellow as default body-position and scan-cadence rather than as conscious effort carries zero ongoing cognitive cost; the civilian who tries to "pay more attention" burns cognitive fuel, fatigues, and defaults back to White inside twenty minutes.

03.2.2OODA loop and the Orient-failure correction

Boyd's OODA governs tempo; Miller's correction locates where it breaks.

OODA loop

OBSERVE · sensor data in, attention allocated, field-of-view scanned. ORIENT · data parsed against mental models, priors, training, genetics, cultural frame. DECIDE · option selected from available set. ACT · motor output executed. LOOP · new sensors, re-orient, re-decide, re-act.

Boyd's central claim: the faster cycler renders the adversary's last observation stale, so every adversary action arrives against a defender who has already moved. Miller's correction sharpens the rule. Most OODA failures occur at Orient, not Observe — the observation is correct, but it is parsed against the wrong frame, with normalcy bias holding longer than physics allows. Sajnog's shooting doctrine compresses OODA further by pre-conditioning the trigger press to the sight picture, bypassing conscious Decide. ORIENT IS THE BOTTLENECK. The operator who has pre-loaded Orient through the 03.1 classification drill collapses OODA to Observe→Act; the operator who Orients live burns the 1.5 s window that decides whether first-contact lethality lands on the attacker or on the defender.

03.2.3Hick's Law — decision stick vs. decision tree

Reaction time scales logarithmically with choice count, and the scaling law dictates the architecture of every drilled response.

Reaction time grows as roughly log₂(n + 1) with n options. More options, slower response under stress. Under chemical cocktail, selection collapses entirely. Thirty techniques against a punch yields zero under stress. One good option beats thirty.03.2.3 · The Hick's Law rule

A decision tree asks the operator to classify the input and branch — "if jab, do A; if cross, do B." The tree collapses under cocktail because classification requires cognition that cocktail suppresses. A decision stick runs a single drilled response against a class of inputs — "if surprised and assaulted, drop weight, close, deliver five forward-moving strikes to the line." The stick survives cocktail because no classification is required. ONE STICK BEATS THIRTY TREES. The operator who drills two or three gross-motor decision sticks against class inputs has usable force under cocktail; the operator who has memorized thirty technique branches has zero usable force under cocktail, and will experience that zero as a freeze the first time the cocktail dumps.

03.2.4The chemical cocktail — physiological operating envelope

Adrenaline, cortisol, and noradrenaline dump on life-threat perception and rewrite the body's performance specification in real time.

Cocktail effects and HR thresholds
01< 80 bpmCognitive baseline. Fine motor and speech normal.
02115–145 bpmFine-motor degrades. Complex finger movements (precise trigger reset, small-button manipulation) begin to fail.
03145–175 bpmGross motor optimal. Fine motor largely gone. Tunnel vision collapses to 20–30° cone. Auditory exclusion begins.
04> 175 bpmCognition sub-cortical. Only deeply-trained motor patterns fire reliably. Memory fragmentation. Tachypsychia (time dilation).

Every technique, drill, and weapon manipulation installed in 03.3 through 03.9 must survive cocktail-degraded performance. The rule is non-negotiable: a protocol that depends on fine motor above 145 bpm without having been drilled to automaticity will fail in live contact. THE COCKTAIL IS THE GROUND TRUTH. The operator who trains exclusively at low heart rate produces a library of techniques that do not exist in the environment the cocktail creates; the operator who deliberately trains at 145+ bpm through sprint-and-shoot, post-burpee combatives, and cognitive-overload drills carries techniques calibrated to the actual operating regime.

03.2.5Go-button, permission, operant conditioning

Three pre-encounter installations convert the decision cycle from concept into fire-able subsystem.

Pre-encounter installations
01GO-BUTTONPre-defined single trigger that shifts the operator from social to physical mode. Compresses OODA to Observe→Act.
02PERMISSIONPre-settled answer to "am I allowed to do what is required?" Closes the legal, moral, and psychological gate before the encounter.
03OPERANT CONDITIONINGNarrow consistent reality-matched stimulus + one simple motor pattern + reliable reward, drilled thousands of reps across weeks.

The go-button without permission produces a freeze at the moment of action; permission without operant conditioning produces permission to move a body that cannot move; conditioning without a go-button produces a reflex trained to fire at a stimulus that never arrives. The three install together or they fail together. PRE-SETTLED PERMISSION IS THE HINGE. The defender with awareness but unsettled permission freezes longer than the defender with no awareness at all; the operator who has pre-answered the permission question in advance, in cold-rational mode, with legal and moral posture already set, carries a nervous system that will fire when the go-button trips rather than stall against an internal debate the cocktail will not let it resolve.

03.2.6Install, function, failure, feed-forward

INSTALL. You run Cooper Yellow as passive posture, not conscious effort. You pre-define go-button criteria before the encounter — the single trigger that shifts you from social mode to physical response — so OODA compresses to Observe→Act with Orient and Decide pre-loaded. You install two or three gross-motor decision sticks through operant conditioning: narrow consistent reality-matched stimulus, one simple motor pattern, reliable reward, drilled thousands of reps across sessions and across weeks. You pre-settle the permission question before encounter, because the defender who has awareness without pre-settled permission freezes at the moment of action. You train all motor patterns at 145+ bpm so the cocktail does not erase them.

FUNCTION INDICATORS. Your freeze breaks inside a second through the drilled response. OODA runs at Observe→Act with sub-second latency. Decision sticks fire on class inputs without conscious classification. Fine-motor tasks depend on operant-conditioned sequences that run below conscious control. You produce directed action under cocktail, not paralysis.

FAILURE INDICATORS. Orient hangs on normalcy bias. No decision stick exists for the class of input encountered, so the mind searches the technique tree and burns the reaction window. Permission remains an open question in real time. Fine-motor protocols fail at 145+ bpm because they were never drilled there. The color code sits at White on contact.

FEED-FORWARD. Empty-hand combatives install next in 03.3 — the weight-in-motion methods, the Power Line, the semi-crouch, and the Golden Rule of Combat (Power × Targeting × Timing) that converts the decision cycle into actual force output at the fourth rung of the Miller-Kane continuum. The decision cycle is the conversion; the combatives are what the conversion produces.

SECTION 03.3

Empty-hand combatives — weight-in-motion, Power Line, effects taxonomy

CONTINUUM RUNG4 OF 6
GOLDEN RULEPOWER × TARGETING × TIMING (PRODUCT, NOT SUM)
WEIGHT-IN-MOTION METHODS4 — FALLING STEP · LEG SPRING · SHOULDER WHIRL · UPWARD SURGE
POWER LINESHOULDER → ELBOW → BACK-OF-HAND → LITTLE-KNUCKLE BASE
KE TRANSFER WITH FOLLOW-THROUGH40–50%
KE TRANSFER STOPPING ON SURFACE< 20%
EFFECTSMOVE · DAMAGE · SHOCK · (PAIN = UNRELIABLE)
IMOP GATE REQUIRED FOR FORCE
HIT HARD OR DO NOT HIT

Rung four on the Miller-Kane continuum is the first where strike produces damage rather than compliance, and the rung where Miller's Golden Rule of Combat — Power Generation × Targeting × Timing as a product rather than a sum — becomes load-bearing. Dempsey's Championship Fighting supplies the mechanical spine across the four methods of weight-in-motion, the Power Line, the semi-crouch, and the explosion-and-follow-through principle. Miller's Meditations on Violence supplies the effects taxonomy and the training-flaw catalogue that explains why most martial-arts programs fail under cocktail. Miller / Kane Scaling Force supplies the IMOP legal gate that every empty-hand engagement runs through before the first strike.

This section installs Dempsey's four methods of weight-in-motion as the mechanical basis of every unarmed strike, the Power Line as anatomical force-transmission axis, the semi-crouch as pre-loaded base stance, explosion-and-follow-through converting mass into kinetic energy, Miller's effects taxonomy (Move / Damage / Shock, Pain as failure), the Aggressive Defense compression of block-then-counter into strike-on-strike, Dempsey's Ten Wrongs as the training-flaw taxonomy, the Disparity of Force multiplier that scales the rung, and the install / function / failure / feed-forward handoff to the weapons subsystem. Sources: Dempsey Championship Fighting Ch 2–8 (methods of weight-in-motion, Power Line, semi-crouch, explosion); Miller Meditations on Violence Ch 7–8 (effects, hit hard or do not hit, training flaws); Miller / Kane Scaling Force (IMOP, Disparity of Force).

03.3.1The four methods of weight-in-motion

Dempsey catalogs every way body mass drives a fist.

Weight-in-motion methods
01FALLING STEPStraight jolt fires from a forward fall. Lead foot steps under relaxed falling mass; arm arrives late, synced to weight-arrival.
02LEG SPRINGHook and upper fire through rear-leg push and sudden hip-shoulder rotation.
03SHOULDER WHIRLBody rotates around the spinal axis; fist travels as the end of rotation. Hook, overhand, rotational cross.
04UPWARD SURGEUppercut and rising body blow fire through explosive leg extension from the semi-crouch.

All four deliver body mass rather than arm mass, and the gap between the two is the gap between a strike that moves a committed attacker and a strike that annoys him. A 150 lb fighter delivering 70 lb of weight-in-motion outstrikes a 220 lb fighter delivering 10 lb of arm. MASS TRAVELS, NOT ARM. The operator who has never drilled the Falling Step as a weight-drop rather than a forward-step punches with arm; under cocktail, with the fine-motor chain suppressed, that arm-punch produces neither Move nor Damage, and the encounter extends past the first second — which in empty-hand combat is where most encounters are won or lost.

03.3.2The Power Line and the semi-crouch

Mass transmits through a straight anatomical axis, and a pre-loaded base stance holds all four methods ready to fire.

The Power Line

Shoulder → elbow → back-of-hand → base of little-finger knuckle, as a single straight axis. Any kink at any joint bleeds force. The second knuckle aims; the little-knuckle base carries structure. Landing across the three-knuckle ridge distributes force through the strongest hand-bone geometry.

The semi-crouch preloads all four weight-in-motion methods simultaneously: feet shoulder-width, lead foot forward one foot-length, knees bent, hips loaded, torso forward of vertical, chin tucked, rear heel slightly raised. Dempsey's explosion-and-follow-through converts 40–50% of body kinetic energy into the strike when the fighter mentally extends four to six inches past the target surface; stopping on the surface converts under 20%. EXPLODE THROUGH, NOT TO. The surface is not the destination; the destination is four to six inches inside the skull. The fighter who trains to stop on contact trains his nervous system to halt the weight-in-motion at exactly the moment the effects-taxonomy depends on its continuing.

03.3.3Miller's effects taxonomy — Move, Damage, Shock, (Pain)

What a strike must produce to function against a committed attacker.

Strike effects
01MOVEShifts the attacker's body. Works on anyone, including drug-loaded subjects. Creates space, opens angles, resets tempo.
02DAMAGEDelivers structural injury. Reduces capability cumulatively across the encounter.
03SHOCKGross neurological interruption — concussion, vagal stimulus, spinal-column hit. Immediate incapacitation.
04PAINUnreliable. Works on none of the attackers who matter. A pain-only technique against a drunk, drugged, or adrenalized attacker converts one attacker into one angry attacker.

Dempsey's Aggressive Defense compresses OODA by collapsing block-then-counter into strike-on-strike: the defender's counter lands through the attacker's committed forward weight and collapses his structure on impact. HIT HARD OR DO NOT HIT. The rule is diagnostic for every technique in the library; if the technique cannot produce Move, Damage, or Shock against a 250 lb methamphetamine-loaded attacker in a hallway, it does not belong in the operator's decision-stick set, no matter how elegant the movement or prestigious the style.

03.3.4Dempsey's Ten Wrongs and the training-flaw taxonomy

Training produces flaws that cocktail reveals. Dempsey and Miller converge on the catalogue.

Common training flaws
01ARM-PUNCHPushing off rear leg; arm leads weight. Falling Step collapses to stepping jab.
02LINE KINKWrist bends at impact; elbow flares; shoulder disengages. Force bleeds at every joint.
03SURFACE STOPMental target = skin rather than four inches inside. KE transfer halves.
04FIRST-KNUCKLE STRIKEIndex-knuckle lands; bone breaks. Little-knuckle base carries load.
05TELEGRAPHWinding up, shoulder dip, footstep signal. Attacker reads intention before strike fires.
06RANGE BIASDrilling at arm's reach. Real assaults land closer than arm's reach.
07POINT SPARRINGTapping for score. Trains the nervous system to pull the very motion it must commit.
08COOPERATIVE UKEPartner falls on cue. Nervous system never meets resistance.
09STYLE PURITYRefusing techniques from outside the lineage. Reduces the decision-stick set below viability.
10FINE-MOTOR BIASJoint locks and fine grips drilled as primary. Fails at 145+ bpm.

Every flaw narrows the operator's cocktail-surviving set. TRAINING REALISM IS THE DIAGNOSTIC. The operator who drills a Falling-Step palm-heel against a moving pad at speed, with no step-off-line compliance, carries one decision stick; the operator who has drilled thirty techniques against a cooperative partner carries zero.

03.3.5Install, function, failure, feed-forward

INSTALL. You drill the semi-crouch until it is the default stance on any surprise stimulus. You drill the Falling Step until the lead foot moves under weight rather than ahead of it, drilled against a heavy bag or holder pad at speed. You build two or three gross-motor decision sticks — forearm shear, palm heel to jaw, forehead strike to nose — and drill them against class inputs rather than against specific telegraphed attacks. You accept fine-motor grappling as a training luxury, because joint locks fail at 145+ bpm. You run IMOP through your permission subsystem before every force decision, and you calibrate rung selection against Disparity of Force.

FUNCTION INDICATORS. Your first strike produces Move, Damage, or Shock inside the first two seconds of contact. Power Line stays straight at impact across all four weight-in-motion methods. Follow-through carries weight four to six inches past the surface. Decision sticks fire from the semi-crouch without Orient cost.

FAILURE INDICATORS. Strike produces only Pain. Power Line kinks at wrist, elbow, or shoulder under muscular tension. Rear leg drives push-off rather than falling-weight release, and the Falling Step becomes an arm-punch. Telegraph pre-announces the strike and burns the surprise advantage. Fine-motor joint-lock attempt fails at 145+ bpm and leaves the operator committed to a technique his nervous system cannot complete.

FEED-FORWARD. Pistol and rifle platforms install next in 03.4 — the Four Universal Safety Rules, the SEAL Seven fundamentals, the modified isosceles, the carbine stances, and the range-engagement calibration that takes the Golden Rule product (Power × Targeting × Timing) from rung 4 empty-hand into rungs 5 and 6 armed. The weight-in-motion principle generalizes: mass (bullet × velocity) through a straight line (barrel), released with precise timing (trigger press), onto a precisely chosen target. The mechanics carry; the platform changes.

SECTION 03.4

Weapons — pistol and rifle platforms

CONTINUUM RUNGS5 (LESS-LETHAL) · 6 (LETHAL)
FOUR UNIVERSAL SAFETY RULES · SEAL SEVEN FUNDAMENTALS
PISTOL STANCEMODIFIED ISOSCELES
PISTOL ENGAGEMENT3–7 m TYPICAL
RIFLE ENGAGEMENT0–300 m STANDARD · DM TERRITORY > 300 m
DRAW-TO-FIRST-ROUND1.5–2 s TRAINED
FOUR-COUNT DRAWGRIP · CLEAR · ROTATE/MEET · EXTEND-AND-ENGAGE
COMBAT-E3EDUCATION × EQUIPMENT × EXPERIENCE
IMOP GATEINTENT · MEANS · OPPORTUNITY · PRECLUSION
Legal posture

Firearms law varies by jurisdiction, by status of the operator, and by the legal posture of the engagement. Operational mechanics below run declaratively. The rung chosen on the continuum, the criteria that justify drawing, the Preclusion element of IMOP, and the aftermath protocol all route through local legal environment. You verify posture before you apply force.

Rungs five and six of the Miller-Kane continuum — less-lethal and lethal — are governed by a single non-negotiable safety scaffold and a seven-element fundamentals sequence that runs identically across pistol and rifle platforms. Sajnog's Navy SEAL Shooting and How to Shoot Like a SEAL anchor the doctrine through the Four Universal Safety Rules, the SEAL Seven, the modified isosceles, the carbine stance family, and the Combat-E3 framework that fixes the order of skill development. Miller / Kane Scaling Force supplies the IMOP gate that runs before every trigger press. The weapons subsystem inherits the Golden Rule from 03.3 — Power × Targeting × Timing — and re-instantiates it as Platform × Fundamentals × Decision.

This section installs the Four Universal Safety Rules as redundant preclusion layer, the SEAL Seven fundamentals as per-shot attention sequence, the modified isosceles pistol stance, the carbine stance family across standing / kneeling / prone, bone support and natural point of aim as skeletal-structure force-transmission, effective-range calibration across platform, the four-count draw stroke, Combat-E3 fixing Education → Experience → Equipment order, and the install / function / failure / feed-forward handoff into marksmanship under stress. Sources: Sajnog Navy SEAL Shooting Ch 2–6 (safety, SEAL Seven, stances, draw); Sajnog How to Shoot Like a SEAL (fundamentals translation to civilian shooter); Miller / Kane Scaling Force (IMOP, rung selection).

03.4.1The Four Universal Safety Rules — redundant by design

Four rules stand as layered preclusion, with any single rule alone preventing an unintentional discharge.

Universal Safety Rules
01TREAT EVERY WEAPON AS LOADEDregardless of what you just checked, what you were told, or how recently you cleared it.
02NEVER POINT THE MUZZLE AT ANYTHING YOU ARE UNWILLING TO DESTROYat any time, in any condition, under any circumstance.
03FINGER OFF THE TRIGGERstraight along the frame, until sights are on target and the decision to shoot is made.
04BE SURE OF THE TARGET AND WHAT LIES BEYOND ITidentification positive, background assessed, over-penetration considered.

Each rule alone prevents an unintentional discharge. Breaking any two simultaneously almost always produces tragedy, and every rule violation is a Preclusion issue under IMOP — the legal standard for deadly force holds an unused exit against the operator even when Intent, Means, and Opportunity are established. SAFETY IS PRECLUSION. The operator who violates a safety rule in training trains his nervous system to violate it under cocktail; the rule is non-negotiable not because of what might go wrong one time, but because reflex fires on what has been rehearsed — and rehearsed violations produce live-fire negligent discharges at the moment they are most consequential.

03.4.2The SEAL Seven — fundamentals as per-shot attention sequence

Every shot runs the same seven-step attention cycle.

SEAL Seven fundamentals
01SHOOTING PLATFORMstance, body orientation, skeletal structure. The base that carries recoil without muscular resistance.
02GRIPtwo-hand, maximum contact, minimum tension, thumb-forward on the modified isosceles.
03SIGHT REFINEMENTclarity on the front sight or red dot.
04SIGHT PICTUREsight + target + eye aligned.
05BREATHINGnatural respiratory pause for precision; unrestricted for combat shooting.
06TRIGGER CONTROLstraight rearward press without pre-load or jerk. Surprise break for precision, called break for combat.
07FOLLOW-THROUGHsights on target through and after the shot; trigger reset indexed without looking.

Each element multiplies with the others on the Golden Rule product; a zero on any element zeros the shot. FUNDAMENTALS ARE A PRODUCT, NOT A LIST. The shooter who runs six of the seven at high quality and one at zero produces a zero; the shooter who runs all seven at adequate quality outperforms the specialist who runs three at excellence and four at failure. The sequence is an attention cycle, not a memorized order — the hand does one, the eye does two more, and the trigger finger does the final three as a single unit of conditioned motion.

03.4.3The modified isosceles pistol stance and the carbine stance family

Stance carries recoil through skeletal structure so muscular fatigue does not degrade shot-to-shot accuracy.

Pistol stance — modified isosceles
FEETshoulder-width, both pointed at target.
KNEESbent, loaded.
HIPS AND SHOULDERSsquare to target.
LEANslight forward, nose past toes; forward lean manages recoil.
ARMSextended to equal length, not locked.
GRIPfiring hand high on backstrap; support hand overlapping with thumb forward along slide.
Carbine stance family
01STANDINGhips squared, support elbow under rifle, stock in shoulder pocket. Fast engagement, highest silhouette.
02KNEELINGsupport knee up, elbow on soft tissue above support knee (never bone-on-bone). Silhouette lowered roughly 18 in. Effective 50–200 m.
03PRONEbody 10–20° to bore-line, mag as monopod, bone support at elbows. Effective 100 m+, lowest silhouette.

Three rules hold across every stance: bone support carries the rifle, muscular relaxation prevents tremor, natural point of aim holds the rifle on target with zero muscular effort. BONE CARRIES WEIGHT, MUSCLE STEADIES. The shooter who muscles the rifle onto target burns through tremor threshold inside fifteen seconds and groups enlarge; the shooter who installs natural point of aim through close-eyes-breathe-relax-correct-by-moving-body-not-rifle carries a stance that holds accuracy across a full course of fire and across a full cocktail-duration engagement.

03.4.4Effective ranges and the four-count draw stroke

Range calibrates engagement expectation; the draw stroke indexes the first round to the first threat inside reliable timing.

Range calibration

PISTOL ENGAGEMENT · typically 3–7 m. Pistol is a close-range instrument; the shooter who drills only at 25 m carries precision that does not match the encounter. RIFLE STANDARD · 0–300 m. Most civilian rifle engagements sit inside 100 m. DESIGNATED MARKSMAN · > 300 m. Different rifle, different optic, different training set.

Four-count draw stroke
01GRIPfiring hand establishes high grip on holstered pistol; support hand moves to chest centerline.
02CLEARpistol rises vertically out of holster to chest level; muzzle still down.
03ROTATE / MEETmuzzle rotates forward to threat; support hand meets firing hand on pistol.
04EXTEND AND ENGAGEpistol extends to full length; sights rise into eye-line; trigger finger moves from frame to trigger only as sights meet target.

Trigger finger stays on frame through counts one through three; it crosses onto the trigger only at extend. Trained draw-to-first-round sits 1.5–2 s from concealment. FINGER ON FRAME UNTIL EXTEND. The four-count exists to sequence the draw inside safety-rule discipline; the shooter who indexes finger-on-trigger at count two carries a safety violation embedded in his fastest-available reflex, and under cocktail that reflex will fire before the sights have risen — into the floor, into the support hand, or into a bystander.

03.4.5Combat-E3 and the equipment-follows-skill rule

Sajnog's Combat-E3 fixes the order of skill development.

Combat capability = Education × Equipment × Experience. The product rule holds: a zero on any factor zeros the output. Equipment upgrades ahead of Education and Experience produce worse shooting, because the shooter inherits tool quirks without the foundation to diagnose them.03.4.5 · Combat-E3

Education runs the fundamentals library, the safety rules, the stance family, the SEAL Seven, the range calibration. Experience runs the drill volume under which fundamentals become automaticity — dry-fire reps, live-fire courses of fire, force-on-force iterations. Equipment runs the platform: pistol, rifle, optic, holster, sling, magazines, ammunition. The rule is order-sensitive: Education first, Experience second, Equipment upgraded only to remove a bottleneck Experience has already revealed. EQUIPMENT FOLLOWS SKILL, NOT THE OTHER WAY. The shooter who buys the optic to solve the sight-picture problem has not solved sight picture; he has installed a red dot on top of a fundamentals gap that now fires with tighter groups at low stress and falls apart under cocktail at the same rate as before.

03.4.6Install, function, failure, feed-forward

INSTALL. You drill the Four Universal Safety Rules until they run reflexively and route through every handling motion. You build the SEAL Seven as the attention sequence every shot runs — pistol, rifle, dry, live. You install natural point of aim through the close-eyes-breathe-relax cycle, correcting by moving the body rather than the rifle. You drill the four-count draw stroke to 1.5–2 s from concealment with finger-on-frame through count three. You follow Combat-E3 order — Education → Experience → Equipment — accepting that gear upgrades ahead of fundamentals produce worse shooting under stress.

FUNCTION INDICATORS. Draw-to-first-round sits under 2 s trained. NPA holds the weapon on target with zero muscular effort across a full course of fire. Every shot runs the SEAL Seven as automaticity. Safety-rule compliance holds under dry-fire, live-fire, and force-on-force conditions. IMOP gate runs before every trigger decision.

FAILURE INDICATORS. Any safety rule breaks during drill or live fire. The shooter muscles the rifle onto target and groups enlarge inside a single course of fire. Equipment substitutes for fundamentals — new optic, new holster, new caliber, with stance, grip, and trigger control unchanged. Draw stroke indexes finger-on-trigger before extend. The IMOP Preclusion question goes unanswered before the rung-6 decision fires.

FEED-FORWARD. Marksmanship under stress installs next in 03.5 — weakness-biased training, cognitive-overload drills, the flat-range-to-gunfight delta as the single best diagnostic for whether training builds reality or ritual, and the combat-accuracy vs. fundamental-accuracy regimes. The platform from 03.4 is the instrument; 03.5 is whether the instrument fires under the conditions the cocktail creates.

SECTION 03.5

Marksmanship under stress — weakness bias, cognitive overload, the flat-range-to-gunfight delta

WEAKNESS BIAS80% TIME ON WEAKEST FUNDAMENTAL
COGNITIVE-OVERLOAD LAYERS6
FLAT-RANGE-TO-GUNFIGHT DELTATHE SINGLE BEST DIAGNOSTIC
COMBAT-ACCURACY SPLITS0.2–0.5 s
FUNDAMENTAL-ACCURACY INTERVALS2–4 s
FINE-MOTOR COLLAPSE> 145 bpm
TRIGGER RESET~0.1 in PRECISION
DRY-FIRE PRIMARY · LIVE-FIRE CALIBRATION
COLD-BORE FIRST SHOT · LOGGED EVERY SESSION
STANDARD90TH-PERCENTILE BAD DAY

Flat-range performance and gunfight performance are distinct regimes, and the delta between them is the single best diagnostic for whether training builds reality or ritual. Sajnog's Navy SEAL Shooting installs weakness-biased training, cognitive-overload protocols, the dry-fire-primary / live-fire-calibration allocation, and the 90th-percentile bad day standard. Miller's Meditations on Violence supplies the training-flaw taxonomy that generalizes directly from empty-hand into shooting: the gunfight is closer, faster, more sudden, and with more force than the range prepares the shooter to meet. Every axis alone destroys a flat-range shooter at flat-range standard.

This section installs weakness-biased 80/20 allocation targeting the weakest of the SEAL Seven, cognitive-overload training across six layers of stress stacked on fundamentals, the flat-range-to-gunfight delta as primary diagnostic, fine-motor collapse above 145 bpm and its implications for weapon manipulation, the combat-accuracy / fundamental-accuracy regime distinction, dry-fire as primary trigger-control laboratory, the cold-bore first shot as single-best monthly diagnostic, the 90th-percentile bad day standard, the sights on threat, not on paper discipline, and the install / function / failure / feed-forward handoff into individual movement under fire. Sources: Sajnog Navy SEAL Shooting Ch 5–9 (weakness bias, overload, dry-fire, cold bore, bad-day standard); Sajnog How to Shoot Like a SEAL (civilian translation); Miller Meditations on Violence Ch 7 (four truths, training flaws).

03.5.1Weakness-biased training — the 80/20 allocation

The chain breaks at the weakest link under cocktail.

Identify the weakest fundamental of the SEAL Seven. Spend 80% of training time on it. Bringing a weakness from 30th to 60th percentile yields far more combat value than bringing a strength from 90th to 95th.03.5.1 · The weakness-bias rule

The amateur tendency runs opposite: practice what feels good — the strengths — and widen the gap between strongest and weakest without moving the weakest at all. The diagnostic runs through five baseline courses of fire on separate days, identifying the fundamental with least consistency across the set, and allocating the next training cycle accordingly. Re-baseline every quarter; weaknesses migrate as training advances. TRAIN THE WEAK LINK. The shooter who drills his strengths for years carries a fundamentals portfolio that looks excellent on a paper target and falls apart under cocktail at the moment of the one weakness he never trained; the cocktail-suppressing training prescription is adversarial to ego — the fundamentals that feel worst are the fundamentals the cycle budgets the most reps for.

03.5.2Cognitive overload — six layers stacked on fundamentals

Stress layers approximate combat cognitive load.

Cognitive-overload layers
01TIMER PAR-TIMEshot-to-shot discipline with buzzer cutoff. Forces trigger-control automaticity.
02DECISION TARGETScolor or number-coded targets requiring classification before engagement. Routes target ID through Orient.
03MOVEMENTlateral and advance-retreat through doorways. Breaks static-platform reliance.
04EXERTIONpost-sprint or post-pushup engagement at 140+ bpm. Installs fundamentals under fine-motor degradation.
05COMMUNICATIONSITREP while shooting. Splits cognition across speech and fire control.
06FORCE-ON-FORCEshoot/no-shoot, hostages, moving targets, return fire. Full cocktail load.

By the sixth layer, the shooter runs on pure operant-conditioned responses and any unconditioned fundamental collapses visibly. The collapse is the diagnostic — the layer at which a fundamental fails is the layer at which the operator now trains it until it does not. OVERLOAD FINDS THE GAP. The shooter who has never trained past layer one carries fundamentals verified at zero cocktail load; the shooter who routinely runs layers three through five carries fundamentals calibrated to the environment of actual use.

03.5.3The flat-range-to-gunfight delta and the Four Truths mapping

The delta between square-range groups and force-on-force groups measures how much training is ritual.

The delta

A shooter holding a 3 in group at 15 m on a square range frequently produces an 18 in group in force-on-force at the same distance. The delta quantifies ritual content. Smaller delta = more capability. Large delta = large ritual component.

Miller's Four Truths map directly from empty-hand into shooting. Closer: civilian engagements run 3–7 m pistol and 10–50 m rifle, not 25 m and 100 m square-range distances. Faster: the draw-to-first-round window leaves no time for the three-second sight-refinement cycle the flat range invites. More sudden: the first warning is often the first round, with the defender already 1–3 s behind. More force: the attacker is committed beyond his normal pain threshold by cocktail and / or chemistry. THE DELTA IS THE DIAGNOSTIC. The shooter who has never force-on-force tested is carrying unverified capacity; until the delta is measured, fundamental-accuracy performance and combat capability are unrelated, and confidence derived from square-range groups is the specific kind of confidence that evaporates the first time live cocktail dumps.

03.5.4Fine-motor collapse and weapon manipulation

Every fine-motor manipulation must be automated past the threshold where conscious control fails.

Fine-motor dependencies
01MAGAZINE RELEASE BUTTONprecision thumb motion.
02AR / M4 SELECTOR TRANSITIONprecision index finger rotation.
03SLIDE-LOCK RELOADthumb lever or support-hand slingshot, both fine-motor.
04TRIGGER RESET~0.1 in precision; the difference between a reset press and a push-through is below cocktail-degraded motor resolution.

Any drill that depends on fine motor must be automated to the point of running without conscious control, at which point the larger gross-motor pattern carries the fine motion through as sub-routine. Magazine changes under stress fail at seating rather than at dropping; shooters practice the drop endlessly and forget seat-and-strike, then the mag falls out of the well under recoil in force-on-force. AUTOMATE OR CUT. The rule for the drill library is binary: either the fine-motor sequence has been drilled past conscious-control dependency, or it does not belong in the operator's cocktail-surviving repertoire. The flinch-to-drop-mag reflex without the seat-and-strike reflex fails at exactly the moment it matters.

03.5.5Combat accuracy vs. fundamental accuracy

Two distinct regimes, not two points on a dial.

Accuracy regimes
01FUNDAMENTAL ACCURACYsurprise break · maximum precision · 2–4 s intervals · MOA-level groups. The regime of zeroing, long-range, precision shots.
02COMBAT ACCURACYcalled break · 0.2–0.5 s splits · A-zone hits at typical combat range. The regime of defensive engagement inside 7 m.

Training exclusively for fundamental accuracy produces shooters too slow for combat; training exclusively for combat accuracy produces shooters who cannot engage at medium range. Both regimes require drilling, at the distances and timings they actually run. TWO REGIMES, DRILL BOTH. The shooter who drills only one carries a capability curve with a cliff at the other end — the precision shooter who cannot hit a torso at 5 m in 0.3 s, or the close-range speed shooter who cannot hit a head at 25 m in 4 s.

03.5.6Install, function, failure, feed-forward

INSTALL. You run weekly dry-fire as primary trigger-control laboratory, 100+ reps per session, multiple sessions per week, with live fire as calibration and confirmation rather than learning. You fire a cold-bore first shot every range session, log it, and track monthly improvement as the single best indicator of gunfight shooting gain. You train to the 90th-percentile bad day — tired, distracted, cold, hungry — so the bad-day standard becomes the floor. You sight on the threat rather than on paper, because the threat is whatever part of the attacker produces the deadly action at this moment. You re-baseline weakness every quarter and allocate 80% of the next cycle to the weakest link.

FUNCTION INDICATORS. Your force-on-force performance approaches your flat-range performance. Cold-bore first shot improves measurably month over month. Fine-motor manipulations hold at 145+ bpm. Combat-accuracy splits sit under 0.5 s at A-zone. Fundamental-accuracy groups hold at MOA-level on demand.

FAILURE INDICATORS. Flat-range-to-gunfight delta stays large. Magazine changes fail at seating under stress. Fine-motor manipulation collapses under sprint-induced heart rate. The shooter drills strengths preferentially and widens the gap to the weakest fundamental. The cold-bore first shot trends flat or worse across the log.

FEED-FORWARD. Individual movement under fire installs next in 03.6 — cover vs. concealment, the RTR sequence (Return Fire / Take Cover / Return Effective Fire), the crawl family, the 3–5 s rush, and Move-Shoot-Communicate. The shooting subsystem from 03.4 and 03.5 now acquires a movement layer, because the shooter who cannot move under fire runs a single static engagement before the attacker's rounds arrive.

SECTION 03.6

Individual movement under fire — cover, crawls, rush, Move-Shoot-Communicate

COVER STOPS BULLETS · CONCEALMENT HIDES BODY
RTR SEQUENCERETURN FIRE · TAKE COVER · RETURN EFFECTIVE FIRE
CRAWL FAMILYHIGH CRAWL · LOW CRAWL · 3–5 S RUSH · COMBAT GLIDE
3–5 S RULEI'M UP, HE SEES ME, I'M DOWN
HUMAN ACQUIRE-AIM-FIRE~1.5 s
MOVE · SHOOT · COMMUNICATE (ALL THREE, ALWAYS)
COMMS CALLSMOVING / SET
COVER SHOOT3 ROUNDS PER LIKELY POSITION (R / C / L)

The operator moves under fire through a tempo regime that treats every second of exposure as lethal risk and every transition between cover positions as the most dangerous phase of the engagement. Dolio's Fieldcraft TW-02 and Scouting & Patrolling TW-04 anchor the individual movement techniques, the cover vs. concealment distinction, the crawl family, and Move-Shoot-Communicate. Hopkins's Small Unit Infantry Ambush Tactics supplies the British RTR (Return Fire / Take Cover / Return Effective Fire) sequence and the cover-shoot methodology for unknown threat positions. The shooter from 03.4 and 03.5 who cannot move under fire is a static target; this section converts the static marksman into a moving shooter whose rounds keep arriving while his position does not.

This section installs cover vs. concealment as operationally distinct categories, the British RTR sequence compressing reaction-to-contact, the crawl family across High Crawl, Low Crawl, and Combat Glide, the 3–5 s rush with the "I'm up, he sees me, I'm down" reset, Move-Shoot-Communicate as a non-negotiable simultaneous triad, the one-moves-one-watches buddy-pair rule, the obstacle-negotiation geometries for fences, walls, and linear danger areas, and the install / function / failure / feed-forward handoff into small-unit movement. Sources: Dolio Fieldcraft TW-02 (crawls, cover, RTR, MSC); Dolio Scouting & Patrolling TW-04 (linear danger areas, crossings); Hopkins Small Unit Infantry Ambush Tactics (cover shoot, suppression geometry).

03.6.1Cover vs. concealment — operationally distinct categories

The civilian confusion of these two categories produces a casualty rate out of proportion to the geometry.

Cover vs. concealment

COVER · stops bullets. Rated by caliber and round-count. Brick wall stops small arms indefinitely; car door stops pistol but not rifle; steel dumpster (filled) stops pistol and degrades rifle; engine block stops most rifle rounds; interior drywall stops nothing. CONCEALMENT · hides the body. A bush, a curtain, a shadow, a silhouette line. Stops observation; does not stop rounds.

Effective protection requires cover behind concealment, or concealment in front of cover: the attacker shoots where he sees, and what is behind the concealment stops the round. THE WRONG SIDE OF THE WALL IS A PAINTED TARGET. The defender who crouches behind an interior drywall wall in cinematic fashion has placed himself in what the attacker reads as a cover position and what is in fact a silhouette range target; the rule runs: rate every surface in the environment as cover or concealment before you move toward it, because choosing the wrong surface under cocktail cannot be undone once the rounds arrive.

03.6.2The RTR sequence — Return Fire, Take Cover, Return Effective Fire

The British RTR compresses the reaction-to-contact loop.

RTR sequence
01RETURN FIREpush a few rounds in the general direction of the threat, unaimed. Purpose: suppress the attacker's head long enough to move.
02TAKE COVERfind best true cover within 2–3 steps. Drop and crawl if the move is observed. Purpose: remove yourself from the attacker's sights.
03RETURN EFFECTIVE FIREaim. Identify actual threat. Deliver accurate rounds. Purpose: end the engagement.

If the threat position is unknown, a cover shoot places 3 rounds into each piece of likely cover — right, center, left — to flush or suppress. The cover shoot is not random fire; it is deliberate suppression of the highest-probability positions the attacker occupies. SUPPRESS BEFORE YOU MOVE. The shooter who runs "Take Cover" first and "Return Fire" never carries the sequence backwards; the attacker who is aiming at the moving defender without incoming rounds has a free shot, and the exposure window of the cover-dash becomes the attacker's best engagement window rather than the defender's escape window.

03.6.3The crawl family — scaling movement to threat level

Three crawls plus the rush cover the observed-movement to direct-fire spectrum.

Crawl family
01HIGH CRAWLprone on forearms and inside-knees, head up for forward observation. Partial concealment with medium observation. Used when rounds are distant or suppressed.
02LOW CRAWLflat, face sideways, rifle in arm crook, movement by hip-flex and feet-push. Used under direct fire or when movement is observed.
033–5 S RUSH"I'm up, he sees me, I'm down." Rises explosively from cover, runs 3–5 s mouthing the phrase, drops prone, rolls or crawls 2–3 body-lengths from drop point, re-engages from a position offset from where the attacker saw the drop.
04COMBAT GLIDElow, fast, weapon-ready walking posture for shorter exposures inside structures or between close cover.

The average human acquires, aims, and fires in roughly 1.5 s, and a second aimed shot typically follows in another 1–1.5 s; the 3–5 s rule keeps the mover below the 3 s threshold that would otherwise guarantee a hit, with the drop and roll resetting the attacker's acquired sight picture. NEVER REAPPEAR WHERE YOU DROPPED. The drop point is where the attacker's sights now sit; the 2–3 body-length offset converts the attacker's aimed second shot into a new acquisition, which buys the next 1.5 s window for the next rush.

03.6.4Move-Shoot-Communicate — the non-negotiable triad

All three run simultaneously on contact, or none of them run reliably.

Move-Shoot-Communicate
MOVEto cover, to a new covered firing position, to a flank. Movement is the default; static = target.
SHOOTsuppression first, then effective fire. Rounds keep the attacker's head down and his OODA in Observe.
COMMUNICATEcontact direction, relay movements, coordinate with buddy or team. MOVING / SET calls run every transition.

Under stress most trainees master two of three and drop the third, with Communicate the most commonly dropped. Silent advance converts the buddy pair into two unsupporting individuals and invites blue-on-blue. COMMS DROPS FIRST UNDER STRESS. The drill prescription runs directly from this failure mode — Move-Shoot-Communicate at 160+ bpm against a live role-player, with the fail condition being the loss of the Communicate channel rather than accuracy degradation, because the operator whose voice shuts off under cocktail now runs as a solo unit regardless of how many teammates he has.

03.6.5Obstacle negotiation — fences, walls, linear danger areas

Obstacle crossings are the engagement windows where the moving operator is most exposed.

Obstacle crossings
01FENCE CROSSINGfeet-first slide under the bottom strand with rifle across chest. Not a vault — vaulting silhouettes against skyline and exposes the full body during peak vulnerability.
02WALL CROSSINGbelly-roll minimizing silhouette time. The body crosses the wall laterally along its top rather than vertically over it.
03LINEAR DANGER AREA (road, trail, stream, ridge-line)coordinated crossing with one pair overwatching while the other crosses rapidly, one at a time. Never in parallel. Never without security.
04DOORWAYhigh-risk channel. Cross rapidly at angle, weapon up, ideally with a second shooter overwatching from behind. Never linger in the frame.

NO PARALLEL TRANSITIONS. The core rule across every obstacle type: one element moves while another watches. The operator who crosses a road without overwatch has installed himself as a sniper target; the buddy pair that crosses a fence simultaneously has converted its mutual-support structure into two simultaneous exposures and zero overwatch.

03.6.6Install, function, failure, feed-forward

INSTALL. You drill the crawl family on varied terrain — dirt, gravel, mud, broken ground — not on a flat mat, and you drill prone, kneeling, and transitional shooting. You rehearse the 3–5 s rush as reflex rather than decision, with the offset drop drilled until it is automatic. You run Move-Shoot-Communicate drills until the Communicate element survives at 160+ bpm. You commit to the rule that no buddy-pair transitions in parallel; one moves, one watches. You pre-rate environmental surfaces as cover or concealment through every transit, so the rating is already in hand when the cocktail dumps.

FUNCTION INDICATORS. Your exposure per cover-to-cover transition sits under 3 s. Your Communicate channel stays active at high heart rate. You never reappear where you dropped. RTR runs in order — suppress, move, engage. Cover is chosen by round-rating rather than by silhouette-obscuring appearance.

FAILURE INDICATORS. You freeze upright on first contact. You cross linear danger areas without overwatch. You confuse concealment for cover and drop behind interior drywall. The 3–5 s rush extends past 5 s and rises into the 1.5 s acquisition threshold of the second aimed shot. Communicate drops to zero under stress.

FEED-FORWARD. Small-unit movement installs next in 03.7 — fire-team formations, squad tempo regimes, buddy-pair discipline, patrol roles, react-to-contact, ACE reports, and patrol base doctrine. The individual movement subsystem from 03.6 scales: the crawls, the rush, the RTR, and Move-Shoot-Communicate now run inside a two-team / four-operator formation where the same rules apply at team-scale and the coordination rules layer on top.
