SECTION 03.7

Small-unit movement — formations, patrol base, react-to-contact

FIRE TEAM4 · SQUAD: 8 (TWO TEAMS)
FORMATIONSCOLUMN · LINE · WEDGE · SKIRMISHERS · ECHELON · Y · HALF-Y · V
TEMPO REGIMESTRAVELING · TRAVELING OVERWATCH · BOUNDING OVERWATCH
SPACINGTRAVELING 15–20 m · TRAV-OWATCH 30–50 m · BOUNDING BY COVER
BUDDY PAIR · NON-ROMANTIC · MUTUALLY-SUPPORTING
PATROL ROLESLEAD SCOUT · RTO · SECOND SCOUT · TEAM LEADER
CONTACT CALLFRONT / LEFT / RIGHT / REAR
CIVILIAN DEFAULTBREAK CONTACT
POST-CONTACT ACEAMMO · CASUALTIES · EQUIPMENT

The fire team of four and the squad of eight operate through formations, tempo regimes, and react-to-contact drills rehearsed to the point that contact produces coordinated response inside 3–5 s rather than chaotic individual reactions. Dolio's Scouting & Patrolling TW-04 and Fieldcraft TW-02 anchor the civilian-adapted doctrine across formations, buddy-pair structure, patrol roles, and break-contact protocol. Hopkins's Small Unit Infantry Ambush Tactics supplies corroborating small-unit discipline, patrol-base siting, and the rule that civilian patrols default to Break Contact rather than Squad Attack because they lack fire support, medevac, casualty absorption, and ammunition depth.

This section installs small-unit formations as fire-distribution and control geometry, the three squad tempo regimes indexed to threat level, the buddy pair as quantum unit, patrol roles assigning navigation / comms / decision responsibility, the CONTACT call and react-to-contact sequence, the Dolio civilian default toward Break Contact, the post-contact ACE report with 360° security, the patrol base siting and priority of work, the backtrack ambush fallback on post-break return, and the install / function / failure / feed-forward handoff into offensive ambush doctrine. Sources: Dolio Scouting & Patrolling TW-04 (formations, tempo, react-to-contact, patrol roles, patrol base); Dolio Fieldcraft TW-02 (buddy pair, route planning); Hopkins Small Unit Infantry Ambush Tactics (patrol base doctrine, backtrack ambush).

03.7.1Formations — distributing fire and control through space

Eight formations cover the envelope of patrol geometries.

Fire-team formations
01COLUMNsingle file. Fast in restricted terrain. Weak front and rear fire. Used in heavy vegetation, urban alleys, narrow trails.
02LINEabreast. Best front fire. Used in the assault phase of an ambush or engagement.
03WEDGEArmy diamond. Team leader at position 2. Best all-around fire and control. Default patrol formation in open terrain.
04SKIRMISHERSoffset line with lead pair forward. Best front fire when enemy is known.
05ECHELON (R or L)stepped back for flank protection. Fires front plus one flank.
06Ytracker behind, security forward. Used in tracking and pursuit.
07HALF-Yasymmetric Y for offset track or offset threat.
08Vteam leader at back row. All-around security in open terrain, weaker forward fire than Wedge.

USMC recruit training spends a week on formations alone. Civilian expectation of mastering them in an afternoon produces formation drift under stress, with the team collapsing into a column regardless of what the plan called for. FORMATION IS REHEARSAL, NOT PLAN. The rule for civilian small-unit operators: drill formation transitions under verbal cue until transitions run at < 3 s per change, and drop the formation from the library rather than carry it as a paper entry the team cannot actually execute — a list of eight formations the team cannot transition between under stress is worse than two formations it can.

03.7.2The three squad tempo regimes

Squad movement runs three tempo regimes indexed to threat level.

Tempo regimes
01TRAVELINGfire teams at 15–20 m spacing. Fastest. Contact not expected.
02TRAVELING OVERWATCHteams at 30–50 m, rear overwatching front's route. Medium tempo. Contact possible.
03BOUNDING OVERWATCHone team static in covered position; second bounds to covered position; alternate. Slowest tempo. Contact imminent or known.

The selection matrix indexes regime to threat level. Choosing one step too fast for the threat class produces ambush exposure: traveling through a known contact corridor is the canonical civilian error, and the casualty rate for that error is the reason the three regimes exist as a graduated hierarchy rather than as a menu. TEMPO INDEXES TO THREAT. The team leader's primary tempo discipline is the willingness to slow down when intel warrants, because the cost of slowing is minutes and the cost of not slowing in the wrong threat environment is the entire patrol.

03.7.3Buddy pair and patrol roles

The buddy pair is the quantum unit of small-unit operation; patrol roles distribute cognitive load across the team.

Buddy-pair rules
Two non-romantic members as mutually-supporting dyadone watches while the other movesone sleeps while the other stands watch · decisions communicated constantly · distance maintained for visual and auditory support.

Romantic partners degrade group safety through distraction and through risk-taking to protect each other. Trios produce unstable 2-on-1 grouping. Quartets work as pairs-of-pairs.

Patrol roles
01LEAD SCOUTbest navigator, quiet mover. Sets pace, routes, and reads terrain at point.
02RTO (radio / recorder)communications, paired with team leader decisions. Maintains the log.
03SECOND SCOUTnavigation backup, pace count, often medic.
04TEAM LEADERbacks up lead scout navigation, makes all patrol-level decisions.

NO DEMOCRACY IN THE FIELD. The team-leader role is non-negotiable once the patrol is moving; decisions under contact require a single voice calling, and the civilian temptation to vote every decision converts the coordination gain of a team into the coordination loss of a committee.

03.7.4React-to-contact and the civilian default toward Break Contact

The CONTACT call plus direction (FRONT, LEFT, RIGHT, REAR, or combinations) initiates the sequence.

React-to-contact sequence
01CONTACT [DIRECTION]called by the first element to identify the threat.
02Team in contact deploys into line facing contact, takes cover, runs RTR.
03Team leader decides SQUAD ATTACK or BREAK CONTACT.
04Execute decision via bounding overwatch (attack or withdrawal), each element calling MOVING / SET.
05Post-contact: ACE report, security 360°, reorient, continue or reroute.

Dolio's civilian default tilts toward Break Contact when enemy strength is unknown or greater, because civilians lack fire support, medevac, casualty absorption, and ammunition depth. Break Contact runs bounding overwatch rearward, each bound 30–75 m, until contact breaks. POST-BREAK RETURN IS INDIRECT. Civilian patrols do not return direct to base after break-contact; the team heads in general direction, arranges for a base element to set an ambush on the backtrack route, doubles back, and waits to see if pursuit develops — because the direct-return vector is the vector the pursuer expects, and the backtrack ambush is the protocol that converts pursuit into the pursuer's last decision.

03.7.5Patrol base — siting, occupation, priority of work

The patrol base is the overnight / long-halt position for the small-unit element.

Patrol base siting criteria
01OFF HIGH-SPEED AVENUESnot on a road, trail, or clear axis of approach.
02OFF LINEAR FEATURESnot on a ridgeline, stream, or fence-line that channels the attacker's search.
03CONCEALED APPROACHentry route invisible from likely observation points.
04DEFENSIBLE TERRAINnatural cover around perimeter; interior positions support each other.

The 4-5-6 configurations scale from fire team (triangle with security at each vertex) through squad (cigar, cloverleaf) to platoon. Priority of work runs security first, then weapons and equipment, then rest and eat rotation. Departure runs a new angle after sterilization — the team leaves on a vector different from entry, so the base is not a return target for any observer who might have tracked the approach. SECURITY FIRST, ALWAYS. The priority-of-work sequence is non-negotiable: a patrol base that eats before establishing security is a patrol base that gets overrun, because the attacker who finds the base finds it at the moment its occupants have the least weapons-in-hand and the most gear spread across the site.

03.7.6Install, function, failure, feed-forward

INSTALL. You drill formations until transitions run under verbal cue inside < 3 s. You drill the CONTACT call until response initiates inside 5 s. You pre-brief every patrol with formation, bounding distance, react-to-contact default (Break Contact for civilian baseline), rally points, and base-team backtrack ambush fallback. You assign patrol roles before step-off and rehearse buddy-pair discipline as the default sleep / watch / move unit.

FUNCTION INDICATORS. The team cycles through formation transitions, tempo-regime changes, and react-to-contact drills as reflex rather than decision. The CONTACT call produces coordinated response inside 5 s. Break-contact bounds run 30–75 m with MOVING / SET discipline. ACE runs post-contact under 360° security. The team returns to base indirect, with backtrack ambush set.

FAILURE INDICATORS. Civilians run three fire teams instead of two (coordination load exceeds command-and-control capacity above squad). In-contact decisions go to debate rather than to the team leader's single call. Post-break return is direct to base. The base is sited on a linear feature or along a high-speed avenue. Priority of work inverts — eat and rest precede security — and the base occupies unsecured for the most vulnerable window of the halt.

FEED-FORWARD. Offensive action — ambush geometries — installs next in 03.8. The small-unit movement subsystem from 03.7 is the delivery vehicle; 03.8 is what the team does when it has chosen to fight rather than to Break Contact, with the ambush taxonomy, the three ambush elements, formation geometries across Linear / L / V / Z / Y / X, the seven-step deliberate ambush, and the Claymore / enfilade / terrain-shaping doctrine that determines whether the ambush produces a single killed attacker or a killed column.

theFIELD.run / CONSTRUCT_APPLICATIONS / 03 APPLIED FORCE / 03.8 Offensive action — ambush geometries
SECTION 03.8

Offensive action — ambush geometries

TAXONOMY AXESHASTY / DELIBERATE · NEAR / FAR · POINT / AREA · FORMATION
FORMATIONSLINEAR · L · V · Z · Y · X
ELEMENTSSECURITY · SUPPORT · ASSAULT
SEVEN-STEP DELIBERATERECON · MOVEMENT · LEADER'S RECON · OCCUPATION · INITIATION · ENGAGEMENT · WITHDRAWAL
ENGAGEMENT WINDOW< 60 s
M18 CLAYMORE60° CONE · 50 m FORWARD · 16 m BACK-BLAST
NEAR AMBUSH< 50 m → ASSAULT THROUGH
CIVILIAN SCALESQUAD-HASTY ONLY
INITIATIONMOST LETHAL WEAPON FIRST

The ambush inverts OODA in one instant by placing the defender inside the attacker's decision loop with an initiation that registers only as effect, not cause, and every round after initiation arrives against a target whose Orient is still running on the route he was walking 2 s ago. Hopkins's Small Unit Infantry Ambush Tactics anchors the taxonomy, the three ambush elements, the formation geometries, the seven-step deliberate ambush, and the Claymore / enfilade / terrain-shaping doctrine that fixes round-for-round lethality. Dolio's Scouting & Patrolling TW-04 supplies the civilian-scale adaptation, reserving squad-scale hasty and harassing ambushes rather than platoon-deliberate operations, because command-and-control costs exceed civilian baselines above squad.

This section installs the four-axis ambush taxonomy (hasty / deliberate, near / far, point / area, formation), the three ambush elements Security / Support / Assault, ambush formation geometries across Linear / L / V / Z / Y / X with enfilade mechanics, the seven-step deliberate ambush, the engagement-priorities matrix as per-shooter decision stick, the M18 Claymore casualty / danger geometry, the terrain-shaping quartet (canalizing / blocking / turning / slowing), the mines-forcing-SOP principle, the 60-s engagement-window rule, the violence of action initiation discipline, and the install / function / failure / feed-forward handoff into defensive action. Sources: Hopkins Small Unit Infantry Ambush Tactics Ch 2–7 (taxonomy, elements, formations, seven-step, Claymore); Dolio Scouting & Patrolling TW-04 (civilian adaptation, squad-hasty rule).

03.8.1The four-axis ambush taxonomy

Every ambush occupies one position on each of four axes simultaneously.

Ambush taxonomy axes
01HASTY / DELIBERATEhasty improvises with speed priority. Deliberate runs planned recon, prepared positions, pre-laid obstacles, rehearsed priorities.
02NEAR / FARnear (< 50 m) routes into immediate assault-through because cover-fire cannot work at that range. Far (> 50 m) routes into RTR and bound-or-withdraw.
03POINT / AREApoint engages a single kill zone or route. Area strings coordinated point ambushes across a route network to attrit a larger moving force.
04FORMATIONLinear · L · V · Z · Y · X. Each geometry produces a different fire channel.

The taxonomy is not academic categorization — each axis routes different protocol. The near-ambush assault-through is incompatible with the far-ambush withdraw-after-engagement, and an operator who confuses the two burns his team's position for the wrong doctrine. TAXONOMY IS ROUTING, NOT LABELING. The team leader names the ambush on each axis before execution, because the four names together fix the engagement-priorities matrix, the initiation geometry, and the withdrawal plan — three sub-systems that cannot be resolved in real time.

03.8.2The three ambush elements — Security, Support, Assault

Three elements compose any ambush regardless of size.

Ambush elements
01SECURITYisolates the kill zone. Early-warning, flank protection, rear security. Typically 80–100 m out in schoolhouse convention; terrain-driven in outcomes-based practice.
02SUPPORTdelivers heavy sustained fires into the kill zone. Machine guns, rifle squads in depth, Claymores, indirect fire when available.
03ASSAULTcloses into the kill zone to finish, exploit intel and equipment, or execute hammer-and-anvil pin.

A four-person hasty ambush distributes all three roles across the same people — Security is one shooter with a view of the flank, Support is the first two shooters firing the initiator volley, Assault is the team leader calling the advance. A platoon-scale deliberate ambush separates the elements into distinct sub-units. The rule: no ambush fires without all three elements present. NO SECURITY, NO AMBUSH. The ambush that initiates without Security in place has installed itself as a fire-element that an unknown flanking enemy can route against from behind; the civilian error runs toward all-shooters-forward-none-on-flank, and the corrective is absolute — if the team cannot detach one shooter as Security, the ambush does not fire.

03.8.3Formation geometries and enfilade mechanics

Formation geometry determines how rounds concentrate into the kill zone.

Ambush formations
01LINEARfires across the column at its long axis. Simplest. Weakness: enemy drops into near-side ditch and escapes.
02Ladds a perpendicular short leg firing down the column's long axis. Converts the ditch into a fire channel. Round-for-round lethality 2–5× Linear. Preferred default.
03Vtwo lines meet at apex with converging fire onto enemy approaching into it. Friendly-fire risk if sectors are not disciplined.
04Zstaggers linear positions to defeat counter-battery fire.
05Ycovers a three-arm junction.
06Xcovers a central clearing through four converging lines.

The L is preferred because the short leg turns the enemy's natural cover response (drop to the near-side ditch) into the position that the short leg is already firing down. L CONVERTS THE DITCH INTO A CHANNEL. The geometric insight is worth 2–5× round-for-round casualty production: the same rounds, fired from the same distance, produce multiples of the casualties the linear ambush produces, because enfilade fire runs the long axis of the human body rather than the narrow axis.

03.8.4The seven-step deliberate ambush

The deliberate ambush runs seven sequenced steps.

Seven-step deliberate ambush
01RECONNAISSANCEterrain, route, enemy pattern, timing, likely composition.
02MOVEMENT TO OBJECTIVE RALLY POINTcovered assembly short of kill zone.
03LEADER'S RECONteam leader confirms kill zone, siting, obstacles, withdrawal route.
04OCCUPATIONelements emplace, Security out, Support zeroed, Assault briefed, obstacles set.
05INITIATIONmost lethal weapon fires first (Claymore, crew-served, designated rifleman). All others fire on that cue in one instant.
06ENGAGEMENTviolent, short, overwhelming. Hopkins's rule: ambushes over 60 s are failed or poorly set.
07WITHDRAWALpre-briefed sequence, route, rally point. No souvenir collection.

The initiation-on-most-lethal-weapon rule is load-bearing. The Claymore detonation, or the belt-fed opening burst, registers to the enemy as effect rather than cause — the column takes casualties before any shooter in the column has identified the direction of origin, and any return fire for the first 5–10 s fires in the wrong direction. INITIATE ON THE HEAVIEST WEAPON. The doctrine converts the first 10 s of the engagement into a one-way engagement, and the < 60 s window is sufficient to empty the kill zone if the initiation geometry holds.

03.8.5Claymore, terrain-shaping, and the mines-forcing-SOP principle

The M18 Claymore is the canonical ambush initiator; terrain-shaping obstacles set the kill zone; mines on approach force the enemy's clearance SOP into the ambush window.

M18 Claymore geometry

60° horizontal cone · 50 m forward casualty radius · 16 m back-blast and flank danger zone · command-detonation wire (not tripwire) for controlled initiation · emplaced behind hard cover or past 16 m, paired for redundancy.

Terrain-shaping obstacles
01CANALIZINGflank obstacles force enemy into corridor.
02BLOCKINGobstacle at kill-zone exit traps column.
03TURNINGmid-route obstacle exposes flank.
04SLOWINGcratered road or soft ground maximizes dwell time in the kill zone.

Mines on approach trigger the enemy's clearance SOP — stop, dismount, flank security, probe. The SOP itself creates the ambush window. THE MINE DOES NOT HAVE TO WOUND. The psychological / procedural effect of the mine is the ambush's actual function; a non-wounding tripwire that produces a stop-and-probe response gives the ambusher the stationary, dismounted, clustered target that the Claymore and the L-formation were designed around, and the round-for-round lethality produced is higher than if the mine had wounded one individual and moved the rest.

03.8.6Install, function, failure, feed-forward

INSTALL. You plan ambushes with KOCOA-driven kill-zone selection, cover-covered Security positioning, pre-briefed engagement-priorities matrix (each shooter holds a decision stick, not a tree), and rehearsed withdrawal. You emplace the initiator (Claymore, crew-served, designated rifleman) with redundancy. You reserve civilian groups to squad-scale hasty and harassing ambushes rather than platoon-deliberate operations because command-and-control costs exceed civilian baselines above squad. You name the ambush on all four taxonomy axes before occupation.

FUNCTION INDICATORS. Every weapon fires within 2 s of the initiator. Every round lands in the kill zone. Engagement completes under 60 s. Withdrawal runs on pre-briefed sequence. Security detects any flanking response before it arrives at the Support element. The L-formation short leg channels the enemy's cover response into the fire corridor.

FAILURE INDICATORS. The initiator fires late, and the cue becomes ambiguous. Security misses flankers who arrive inside the engagement window. Assault crosses the limit of advance into deeper ambush terrain the team has not reconned. Engagement extends past 60 s and the enemy consolidates response. The ambush is sited without an L short leg on a route where enemy cover response is predictable.

FEED-FORWARD. Defensive action — perimeter, engagement area, fighting position — installs next in 03.9. The offensive-ambush subsystem from 03.8 inverts: in 03.9 the team is the one occupying the ground the attacker is trying to cross, and the concentric rings, the engagement-area development, and the fighting-position standards are how the team takes the lessons of the ambush and runs them in reverse.

theFIELD.run / CONSTRUCT_APPLICATIONS / 03 APPLIED FORCE / 03.9 Defensive action — perimeter, engagement area, fighting position
SECTION 03.9

Defensive action — perimeter, engagement area, fighting position

CONCENTRIC RINGSOUTER 0.5–5 mi · INNER 100–500 m · CLOSE 0–100 m
KOCOAKEY · OBSERVATION · COVER · OBSTACLES · AVENUES
SALTSIZE · ACTIVITY · LOCATION · TIME
FIGHTING POSITIONARMPIT DEPTH 1.2–1.4 m · FRONTAL COVER 18–36 in · TWO-PERSON PREFERRED
SKIRMISHER'S TRENCH30 cm DEPTH · 30 cm PARAPET · 10–20 min WITH E-TOOL
OP2 PAX · 4 HR MAX · 30 MIN ROTATION · < 500 m FROM BASE
EA DEVELOPMENT7 STEPS
RULEHANDLE THREAT AS FAR OUT AS POSSIBLE

The defender wins by ending contact as far from the perimeter as possible, with every ring the attacker crosses lowering the defender's reserves and compressing the defender's decision window. Dolio's Defensive Operations TW-03 anchors the concentric-ring doctrine, KOCOA terrain analysis, SALT observer format, fighting-position standards, OP doctrine, and the rule that a hostile force handled 5 mi out costs the defender less across every axis than the same force handled on the perimeter. Hopkins's Small Unit Infantry Ambush Tactics supplies the engagement-area development methodology, the pre-registered fires doctrine, and the principle that obstacles without observation degrade to mere delay.

This section installs the three concentric rings (outer, inner, close) with role assignment, KOCOA as terrain analysis, SALT as observer report format, fighting-position standards and the skirmisher's trench as hasty alternative, the urban fighting position doctrine, the range card with TRPs and dead space, OP occupation doctrine, the seven-step engagement-area development, the personality list for baseline pattern drift, the tin-can alarm as WROL-superior to NVG OPs, and the install / function / failure / feed-forward handoff into evasion and escape. Sources: Dolio Defensive Operations TW-03 (concentric rings, fighting positions, OPs, personality list, tin-can alarms); Hopkins Small Unit Infantry Ambush Tactics (engagement-area development, pre-registered fires); Dolio Scouting & Patrolling TW-04 (KOCOA, SALT).

03.9.1The three concentric rings — routing threat handling to distance

The rings assign different instruments to different distances from the base.

Concentric-ring defense
01OUTER RING 0.5–5 mipatrols, OPs, standoff observation. Detect and deter. Instruments: route patrols, observation posts, long-range optics, listening posts.
02INNER RING 100–500 mobstacles, mine / IED equivalents, pre-registered engagement areas, perimeter OPs. Canalize and degrade. Instruments: wire, abatis, tin-can alarms, engagement-area fires.
03CLOSE RING 0–100 mfighting positions, perimeter walls, guard posts, safe rooms. Destroy at close range. Instruments: primary fighting positions, alternate positions, interior hard points.

Dolio's principle: handle a hostile force 5 mi out rather than on the perimeter. Every ring the attacker crosses without being engaged is a ring the defender has surrendered; every ring the defender forces the attacker to fight through degrades attacker reserves before close contact. DEAL WITH THREATS AS FAR OUT. The defender who runs all weight at the close ring has conceded the outer and inner rings as free approach terrain, and the attacker who arrives at the wire arrives with a fresh element, with intel from unopposed reconnaissance, and with a chosen time of initiation — three advantages that collapse the defender's close-ring geometry regardless of fighting-position quality.

03.9.2KOCOA terrain analysis and the SALT observer format

Terrain analysis precedes position construction.

KOCOA

KEY terrain · holds control advantages (high ground, junctions, bridges). OBSERVATION · fields of view, dead space, likely observation points. COVER AND CONCEALMENT · quality and availability across the defensive area. OBSTACLES · natural and man-made features shaping movement. AVENUES OF APPROACH · ranked by likelihood and risk.

SALT

SIZE of element observed · ACTIVITY they are performing · LOCATION (grid or bearing-distance) · TIME of observation.

SALT is the minimum observer report format, feeding the base from every OP. The SALT chain produces the baseline that the personality list runs pattern-drift analysis against. SALT IS THE MINIMUM. The observer who reports less than SALT has observed without value; the observer who reports more — appearance, vehicle type, direction of travel, associated patterns — produces the early-warning signal that the concentric-ring defense depends on.

03.9.3Fighting position standards and the skirmisher's trench

Fighting position construction follows a doctrine-anchored standard.

Primary fighting position
DEPTHarmpit (1.2–1.4 m) for aimed standing fire.
FRONTAL COVERpacked-dirt wall 18–36 in above ground. Upper end stops small arms through 7.62 NATO.
GRENADE SUMPat one end of the position, angled to contain and direct blast away from shooter.
OVERHEAD COVERlogs and dirt when time permits.
SPOILdispersed rather than piled (piled spoil signatures position from observation).
OCCUPANCYtwo-person preferred (one fires, one observes, rotation sustainable).
Hasty alternative — skirmisher's trench
DEPTHprone (30 cm)PARAPET · 30 cm · TIME · 10–20 min with e-tool · EFFECTIVE AGAINST · direct fire at prone shooter · NOT EFFECTIVE AGAINST · indirect, plunging fire, or standing observation.

The urban fighting position runs from upper floors (higher fire angle, harder to grenade, attacker must commit to stairwell chokepoint) and deep in the room (muzzle blast less detectable outside; attacker's daylight-adapted eye cannot see into darker interior), with pre-planned E&E route because structures burn, collapse, or get surrounded. COVER WITHOUT OBSERVATION IS A BUNKER OF CORPSES. The fighting position that cannot see its sector is not a defensive position; it is a coffin the defender dug for himself, and the rule that every position has observation of its assigned sector is non-negotiable — cover is the second priority, observation is the first.

03.9.4The range card, TRPs, and dead space

Every position records ranges, hold-overs, and identifiers for engagement points in its sector.

Range card contents
01PRIMARY AND SECONDARY SECTORSwith left and right azimuth limits.
02TRPs (target reference points)barn corner, fence junction, large rock, etc., with pre-measured ranges.
03DEAD SPACEnoted, with adjacent-position coverage cross-referenced.
04LEFT-RIGHT LIMITSdrawn and marked, physically indexed on the position.
05KEY WEAPONS DATAzero, hold-over by range band.

The shooter under stress does not estimate range; every likely target is pre-ranged by TRP. Dead space is noted so adjacent positions cover what this position cannot, and the interlocking-fires geometry across the perimeter depends on every card being accurate. PRE-RANGE EVERYTHING. The card exists because the cocktail suppresses range estimation reliably and catastrophically; the defender who looks up from his sights to estimate has installed a cognitive dependency that the cocktail will fail, and the pre-ranged TRP is the operator's answer to his own degraded brain.

03.9.5OP doctrine, EA development, and the tin-can alarm

Observation Posts feed the concentric-ring system; engagement-area development pre-registers fires; tin-can alarms outperform most electronic systems in the WROL civilian setting.

OP standards
PERSONNEL2 pax minimumSHIFT · 4 hr max · ROTATION · 30 min observer-recorder · SITING · approaches, not base itself (base signature = OP signature to counter-OPs) · DISTANCE · < 500 m from base.
Engagement-area development — seven steps
01Identify avenues of approach through KOCOA.
02Select the engagement area to canalize the enemy to an exposed position.
03Site fighting positions with overlapping fires and minimized dead space.
04Emplace obstacles to slow, turn, or block — each covered by a range-card TRP.
05Pre-register weapons.
06Rehearse triggers, signals, and withdrawal.
07Revise on new intel.

Obstacles without observation degrade to mere delay; obstacles covered in a range-card sector become kill triggers. Tin-can alarms (cord and tin-can trip wires) outperform NVG-equipped OPs in most civilian WROL settings through zero battery dependency, no shift requirement, and low rural false-alarm rate. THE OBSTACLE IS NOT THE KILL; THE FIRE ON THE OBSTACLE IS. The wire, the abatis, the cratered approach — none of these produce casualties on their own. They produce stationary or slowed targets that the range-card TRP then fires on; the obstacle-without-observation is a speed bump, and the speed bump alone does not defend a perimeter.

03.9.6Install, function, failure, feed-forward

INSTALL. You run the concentric-ring defense with outer-ring patrols rotating through OPs, inner-ring obstacles covered by pre-registered fires, and close-ring fighting positions rotated on cycle to prevent pre-targeting. You produce a personality list — running log of every individual, vehicle, and group observed in outer and inner rings — so baseline pattern drift registers before contact. You build every fighting position to standard, and every position has a range card with TRPs and dead space noted. You site OPs to approach routes rather than the base itself.

FUNCTION INDICATORS. Every obstacle is covered by fire. Every fighting position sees its sector. Every OP delivers SALT reports on pattern anomalies. The personality list registers baseline drift as SALT reports accumulate. Engagement areas are pre-rehearsed through trigger, signal, and withdrawal.

FAILURE INDICATORS. A fighting position has cover without observation (a bunker of corpses). Obstacles sit unobserved and degrade to delay. OPs are sited on the base rather than on approaches. Positions rotate on a schedule the attacker can observe and predict. The close ring carries all the weight because the outer and inner rings were never manned.

FEED-FORWARD. Evasion and escape installs next in 03.10 — Miller's hierarchy of response (Absence → Escape → Evasion → De-escalation → Force), the break-line-of-sight protocol, counter-tracking, the SERE checkpoint architecture, and the rule that winning is living. Where 03.9 ends contact as far from the perimeter as possible, 03.10 runs the other direction: when the defense fails, or when the operator is outside the perimeter and must not engage at all, evasion and escape preserve the operator at the cost of the position.

theFIELD.run / CONSTRUCT_APPLICATIONS / 03 APPLIED FORCE / Close — hand-off to 04 THE COMPOUND
CLOSE

Close — hand-off to 04 THE COMPOUND

SUB-MODULE 03 — INSTALLED. Eleven applied-force subsystems running in parallel, one 6×4 integration matrix binding them.
RSI BEAT CLOSED. Foundational Architecture (01 Primary Systems · 02 Traverse · 03 Applied Force).
RSI BEAT OPENING. Acceleration (04 The Compound).
THESIS. OODA tempo mismatch is the engine of force superiority; tempo emerges from pre-installed decision sticks and operant-conditioned motor patterns; every scale up subsumes the prior scale.
INTERLOCKS AHEAD. Four Acceleration-layer compositions — detection↔counter-detection, self-sufficient pharmacy, command under fire, operator physical specification.

You now hold eleven applied-force subsystems running in parallel and one integration matrix binding them into a single operational instrument. Miller's predator taxonomy and Hierarchy of Response route the encounter into its correct response class. Miller/Kane's Scaling Force calibrates the rung. Boyd's OODA converts perception into directed action faster than the adversary can recompose intent. Dempsey's four methods of weight-in-motion deliver unarmed force. Sajnog's SEAL Seven delivers pistol and rifle. Hopkins and Dolio install individual-movement-under-fire, small-unit movement, ambush geometry, defensive-area development, and the seven-step deliberate engagement. The Air Force SERE Handbook installs evasion and escape. The eleven subsystems do not sit in a shelf — they interlock through the 6×4 matrix into a unified applied-force architecture.

This close completes Sub-module 03 by consolidating the eleven installed subsystems into a single engineering claim, naming the Foundational Architecture beat closed, and handing off to the four Acceleration-layer interlocks that Sub-module 04 activates. It states the sub-module thesis — tempo mismatch as the engine of force superiority — in its final form. It names every scale subsuming the prior as the non-negotiable progression law. It hands off to four composition layers where the Foundational subsystems become feedback loops exceeding their arithmetic sum. Sources: Miller Meditations on Violence and Facing Violence; Miller/Kane Scaling Force; Dempsey Championship Fighting; Sajnog Navy SEAL Shooting and How to Shoot Like a SEAL; Hopkins Small Unit Infantry Ambush Tactics; Dolio Fieldcraft, Defensive Operations, and Scouting & Patrolling; USAF SERE Handbook.

The eleven-subsystem consolidation

Subsystem 1 — Predator classification. Routes the encounter. Resource, process, asocial, group-monkey-dance, status-seeking, educational-beatdown. The response class is selected before the decision cycle runs, not during it.

Subsystem 2 — Decision cycle. OODA drives tempo. Cooper Color Code drives readiness. Hick's Law limits the option set. The cocktail is survived through exposure.

Subsystem 3 — Empty-hand combatives. Dempsey's four methods of weight-in-motion — falling step, shoulder whirl, upward surge, springing-step-with-shoulder-whirl — deliver Move, Damage, or Shock through the Power Line.

Subsystem 4 — Pistol and rifle platforms. SEAL Seven installs grip, stance, sight alignment, sight picture, breath, trigger, follow-through. Modified Isosceles and carbine stances install the skeleton.

Subsystem 5 — Marksmanship under stress. Weakness-biased training and cognitive-overload rehearsal harden the platform against the chemical cocktail. 80 / 145 / 175 bpm are not numbers to memorize; they are thresholds to drill through.

Subsystem 6 — Individual movement under fire. Cover versus concealment. The crawl family. The 3-to-5-second rush. The operator moves as an individual before any unit movement fires.

Subsystem 7 — Small-unit movement. Fire-team and squad formations, three tempo regimes, buddy pair, react-to-contact, ACE, patrol base. The unit moves as one decision cycle.

Subsystem 8 — Ambush geometry. Four axes × three elements. L-formation enfilade. Seven-step deliberate ambush. M18 Claymore at 60° / 50 m / 16 m. OODA inverted inside 60 seconds.

Subsystem 9 — Defensive area development. KOCOA, SALT, fighting position standards, three concentric rings, engagement-area development. Contact ends as far outside the perimeter as the geometry permits.

Subsystem 10 — Evasion and escape. Break-line-of-sight protocol, SERE checkpoints, counter-tracking, Miller hierarchy collapsed into minutes of preparation converted into seconds of execution.

Subsystem 11 — Solo-to-unit integration. The 6×4 matrix. Force-multiplier progression 1.0 → 2.5-3.0 → 6-8 → 12-20. Tempo stacking. Unified power model (Dempsey + Sajnog + Miller). Miller pre-combat audit run on every encounter.

The thesis, stated in its final form

Force without decision cycle is violence. Force with decision cycle is application.

OODA tempo mismatch is the engine of force superiority. Tempo is not produced in the engagement — tempo is produced by the decision sticks and operant-conditioned motor patterns installed before the engagement. Every scale up subsumes the prior scale: the buddy pair is two trained individuals, the fire team is two buddy pairs, the squad is two fire teams, the ambush is a squad executing geometry, the defensive area is a squad executing terrain. You do not skip scales. You do not substitute equipment for mindset. You do not pattern-match asocial violence to social scripts. You do not run the chemical cocktail on pristine technique — you run pristine technique through the chemical cocktail. The sub-module closes on a single engineering claim: applied force is a trained system, not a trait.

The Foundational Architecture beat — closed

Sub-modules 01 Primary Systems, 02 Traverse, and 03 Applied Force close the Foundational Architecture beat of the RSI progression. Survival is installed. Traverse is installed. Applied force is installed. The three solo-to-unit subsystems are running in parallel, with their own tempo regimes, their own failure modes, and their own calibration schedules. The operator has a survivable baseline (01), the capacity to move through terrain under load (02), and the capacity to engage hostile force across the full rung continuum (03). The Foundational Architecture is no longer a plan — it is a running instrument. The Acceleration layer activates next.

The Acceleration layer — four interlocks ahead

Sub-module 04 The Compound activates the Acceleration layer, where the Foundational subsystems interlock into feedback loops that exceed the arithmetic sum of their parts.

Interlock 1 — Detection ↔ counter-detection. Tracking + navigation + evasion composes a closed-loop detection-counter-detection architecture. The operator tracks, and the operator's own sign is read through the tracker's eye to eliminate detection vectors. Navigation becomes invisible movement. Evasion becomes active concealment against a modeled pursuer.

Interlock 2 — Self-sufficient pharmacy. Medical + herbal + homestead composes a closed-loop care system. Trauma care stabilizes. Herbal medicine extends the shelf. Homestead pharmacology manufactures what the shelf lacks. The operator becomes a node of medical self-sufficiency rather than a consumer of commercial supply.

Interlock 3 — Command under fire. Force + leadership + strategy composes a closed-loop command architecture. The force subsystems of 03 scale past the squad through leadership protocols and strategic composition. The operator moves from trigger-puller to unit commander to campaign designer, with the same decision cycle compounding through each layer.

Interlock 4 — Operator physical specification. Fitness + combatives + mountaineering composes a closed-loop body-instrument architecture. Strength, endurance, and mobility produce the 95-percentile operator envelope. Combatives install force delivery through that envelope. Mountaineering installs environmental load through that envelope. The body is calibrated to specification.

Each of the four interlocks receives its feedback diagram, its failure modes, and its deployment calibration in Sub-module 04. The Foundational Architecture is installed — the Acceleration layer interlocks it.

Install, function, failure, feed-forward

INSTALLATION STATE. You hold eleven running applied-force subsystems and one 6×4 integration matrix binding them. Predator classification is routing. Decision cycle is directing. Empty-hand combatives deliver weight-in-motion. Pistol and rifle deliver SEAL-Seven-through-platform. Marksmanship survives the cocktail. Individual movement manages cover, crawls, and the 3-to-5-second rush. Small-unit movement runs formations and react-to-contact. Ambush geometry inverts OODA. Defensive-area development ends contact at the rings. Evasion converts preparation into seconds of execution. Integration runs across rung and scale. The matrix is live.

FUNCTION IN OPERATION. The applied-force architecture consumes input (threat presentation) and produces output (resolved encounter) across the full six-rung continuum, at the full solo-to-squad scale range, in the full asocial/social/predator/ambush encounter taxonomy. Tempo mismatch is manufactured against the adversary's decision cycle. Rung selection is manufactured against IMOP and Disparity of Force. Scale selection is manufactured against mission and terrain. The Foundational Architecture operates as a single instrument.

FAILURE INDICATORS. The operator treats the sub-module as a library of options rather than a running system. Subsystems are invoked individually without the integration matrix binding them. Force is delivered without decision cycle — violence rather than application. A scale is skipped — squad operations without fire-team drilling, ambush geometry without individual-movement mastery. The pre-combat audit lapses. Acceleration is attempted before Foundational is stable.

FEED-FORWARD. Sub-module 04 THE COMPOUND activates next. The four Acceleration-layer interlocks compose the Foundational subsystems into feedback loops. 01 + 02 + evasion composes detection-counter-detection. medical + herbal + homestead composes self-sufficient pharmacy. 03 force + leadership + strategy composes command under fire. fitness + combatives + mountaineering composes the operator physical specification. The Foundational Architecture stands installed — the Acceleration layer interlocks it.

You have installed the applied-force architecture. 01 keeps you alive. 02 moves you through terrain. 03 engages the adversary. 04 composes them.

You have read the ground, assessed self and team, walked the terrain. Now the adversary closes, and you deliver force. Sub-module 03 installs the capacity to apply force as a calibrated instrument across the full scale the operator commands, from the solo defender's posture through the fire team's bounding overwatch to the squad's L-shaped ambush. Force without a decision cycle is violence. Force with a decision cycle is application. The distinction governs every section that follows.

Sub-module 03 layers ten primary sources into a single force architecture. Miller's Meditations on Violence and Facing Violence supply the predator taxonomy, the five gates of defense, the chemical cocktail physiology, and the hierarchy of response that places absence, escape, and evasion above force itself. The Air Force SERE Handbook supplies evasion-under-contact protocols.

Tempo emerges from pre-installed decision sticks, operant-conditioned motor patterns, and rehearsed team protocols. Each scale up from solo to unit subsumes the prior, so a squad whose operators cannot fight solo degrades to less than a single competent solo. theFIELD.run / CONSTRUCT_APPLICATIONS / 04 THE COMPOUND / 04.1 The principle of compounding
SECTION 04.1

The principle of compounding

COMPOUND THRESHOLD≥ 3 DOMAINS RUNNING SIMULTANEOUSLY
REMOVAL DIAGNOSTICPULL ONE DOMAIN → OUTPUT COLLAPSES (COMPOUND) · OUTPUT DROPS TO ~2/3 (STACK)
PAIR VS INTERLOCK2 DOMAINS → TECHNIQUE · 3 DOMAINS → LOOP
FEEDBACK ARCHITECTURESDETECTION · PRODUCTION · INFORMATION · COMMAND · CONDITIONING
AUDIT CADENCEMONTHLY (4 QUESTIONS) · QUARTERLY (FULL LOOP UNDER STRESS)
MOTOR-PATTERN DECAY14–30 d DISUSE
COMPOUND-PATHWAY DECAYFASTER THAN CONSTITUENT
REBUILD COST2–5× ORIGINAL INSTALL
ARITHMETICSTACK = SUM · COMPOUND = PRODUCT

A compound is an emergent capability produced by the simultaneous operation of three or more domains against a shared problem, with output nonlinear in skill input. The stack is the additive version of the same skills. Boyd's OODA supplies the loop-tempo frame; Clausewitz supplies the friction-under-contact frame; Willink and Babin's Extreme Ownership supplies the Decentralized Command frame that lets a compound run across a team; the Training for the Uphill Athlete physiological model supplies the capacity substrate; Miller's Meditations on Violence supplies the chemical-cocktail stress conditions under which compounds must hold. Every interlock in 04 runs on this principle. Read it once, then read every section that follows as an instance.

This section installs the compound-vs-stack distinction as the architectural axis for the entire sub-module. You load the removal diagnostic that tests whether a capability is a compound or a stack, the pair-vs-interlock progression from two-domain technique to three-domain loop, the four feedback architectures (detection, production, information, command, conditioning) that every compound in 04 runs on, the load-bearing-domain rule that installation order determines whether the output is product or sum, the monthly four-question audit that reads compound state between rehearsals, the quarterly stressor rehearsal that runs the full loop under imposed cognitive load, the compound-pathway decay law that names why compound neural pathways atrophy faster than constituent ones, and the install / function / failure / feed-forward handoff into the five interlocks of 04.2 through 04.6. Sources: Boyd (OODA recursion); Clausewitz (friction, culminating point); Willink / Babin Extreme Ownership (Decentralized Command, Prioritize and Execute); House / Johnston Training for the Uphill Athlete (periodization, AeT / LT physiology); Miller Meditations on Violence Ch 3 (chemical cocktail); Combat Tracking Guide and Appear to Vanish (for the detection-loop exemplar); Area Intelligence Handbook (for the information-loop exemplar).

04.1.1The compound versus the stack — removal diagnostic

The architecture turns on a single test. Pull one domain out of the running capability. Watch the output.

The removal diagnostic

COMPOUND · Remove one of three domains under live conditions. Output collapses. The remaining two cannot produce the capability alone. STACK · Remove one of three skills from serial inventory. Output drops linearly to approximately two-thirds. The remaining two still produce their individual outputs.

An operator who can shoot, navigate, and treat a wound under serial conditions holds three skills in inventory. The same operator under time pressure delivering a fire-suppressed tourniquet to a casualty while navigating to a handrail under pursuit produces a combined capability the inventory alone cannot generate. The compound is the product. The stack is the sum. The compound's output is nonlinear in input because the three domains share an orientation frame, a tempo, and a feedback signal — remove any one and the remaining two lose the frame on which their outputs were calibrated. THE DIAGNOSTIC IS LIVE-ONLY. A capability that passes the removal diagnostic on paper and fails it under chemical-cocktail conditions is a stack dressed as a compound; the rehearsal under stress is where the classification is decided.

04.1.2Two-domain pair versus three-domain interlock

Compounds scale by count of simultaneously-running domains. Two-domain pairings produce techniques. Three-domain interlocks produce loops.

Domain-count architecture
011 DOMAINSKILL — a motor pattern, a protocol, an isolated capacity.
022 DOMAINSTECHNIQUE — two skills combined against a problem (e.g., shoot + move). One-shot execution.
033 DOMAINSINTERLOCK / LOOP — three domains composing a closed feedback cycle. The third domain supplies the environment that makes the technique recursive.
04N ≥ 4 DOMAINSCOMPOUND-OF-COMPOUNDS — multiple interlocks composing a higher-order system. Sub-module 06 COMMAND runs on this.

The third domain is the integration domain. Across the five interlocks of 04, the third domain is context-supplying: evasion for the tracking-navigation pair, homestead for the medical-herbal pair, strategy for the force-leadership pair, mountaineering for the fitness-combatives pair. Without the environment domain, the paired technique is a drill executed once and filed. With the environment domain, the technique feeds itself — the second iteration is informed by the first, the third by the second, and the compound's inner-loop tempo becomes the capability's signature. Boyd's OODA applies recursively here. A track-nav-evade compound running a 30-second inner adjustment loop outpaces a non-interlocked pursuer adjusting at 3-minute cadence by an order of magnitude. The faster inner loop wins because it gets inside the adversary's cycle, a result that scales from fighter-pilot cockpit to small-cell operator. THE INTERLOCK IS A LOOP, NOT A STACK. The count-of-domains test is necessary but not sufficient; the interlock passes only when the three domains compose a closed feedback cycle whose output is fed back as the next cycle's input.

04.1.3Four feedback architectures

Five compounds run across 04. They share four feedback architectures. Every compound in the sub-module instantiates one or more.

The feedback architectures of 04
01DETECTION LOOPSignal input → action → signal change → updated signal input. Each iteration refines both sides' picture. Interlock A (Track + Nav + Evade) is the canonical case.
02PRODUCTION LOOPRaw input → stored capacity → draw-down for output → feedback from consumption to production scheduling. Interlock B (Medical + Herbal + Homestead) is the canonical case.
03INFORMATION LOOPCollection → analysis → decision → action → new observables. OODA rendered at organizational scale. Interlock C (Comms + Intel + Strategy) is the canonical case.
04COMMAND LOOPDecision flows down, execution flows up, friction absorbs at the commander. Interlock D (Force + Leadership + Strategy) is the canonical case.
05CONDITIONING LOOPTraining stress → biological adaptation → higher training stress. The substrate under every other loop. Interlock E (Fitness + Combatives + Mountaineering) is the canonical case.

The architectures are not mutually exclusive. A mature operator runs detection feeding command feeding conditioning in parallel. The conditioning loop is biologically prior — it sits underneath every other loop because the body is the substrate on which the other loops execute. An operator whose conditioning loop has stalled carries a theoretical command loop that cannot cycle at contact tempo. The architectures compose in the order: conditioning (body) → detection (input) → information (orient) → command (decide / direct) → production (sustain). The five interlocks of 04 install each architecture in isolation; the sub-module's compound-of-compounds is the operator running all five simultaneously at ACTIVE state.

04.1.4Installation order — load-bearing domain first

Each compound has a load-bearing domain. The loop's structural memory lives there. The other two domains supply inputs and actuators.

Installation-order failure mode

If you install the supporting domains first, their outputs sit without a structure to feed. The operator accumulates skills whose integration target is absent. The wrong order produces a stack that looks like a compound in inventory and fails as a stack under stress.

The load-bearing domain per interlock: navigation in 04.A (the mental map holds adversary and self); the medical clinical framework in 04.B (SOAP / SAMPLE / differential are the orientation layer on which herbalism and homestead feed); area study in 04.C (the intelligence frame turns signal into oriented data); leadership in 04.D (force and strategy without leadership do not produce team behavior); fitness periodization in 04.E (the AeT engine underwrites combatives sustainment and alpine capacity). Install the load-bearing domain first. Install the other two onto it. The interlock layer — the drill, protocol, or rehearsal that runs all three simultaneously — installs last, only once each constituent holds its own threshold. ORDER IS A STRUCTURAL PROPERTY, NOT A PREFERENCE. Training log audits across multi-year operator development consistently show that compounds installed out-of-order require 2 to 5 times the rebuild cost of compounds installed in-order; the savings from doing it right the first time exceed any intensity advantage a faster-but-out-of-order program produces.

04.1.5The monthly four-question audit

The audit runs on calendar cadence. Monthly at minimum. The four questions orient toward the weakest-domain lead, because the compound's ceiling is set by its weakest constituent.

The four audit questions, per compound

01 · When did I last run this compound under realistic stress? 02 · Which constituent domain is the weakest link right now? 03 · What observable degradation signature would surface first if this compound were failing? 04 · What one-hour-per-week training investment would most strengthen the weakest link?

The sequence matters. Question 1 calibrates recency against the domain-specific decay clock. Question 2 forces the weakest-domain lead, inverting the natural attention bias toward the strongest constituent. Question 3 converts the audit into an observable test — the operator must name a signature, not a feeling. Question 4 converts the assessment into an investment, sized to a realistic weekly budget. The monthly audit takes 10 to 15 minutes per compound and is written, not thought. Written audits catch asymmetric-state concealment that mental audits miss. CADENCE BEATS INTENSITY. A compound audited monthly at 15 minutes retains calibration better than a compound audited yearly at four hours, because the drift window between audits determines how far state can decay before correction.

04.1.6Quarterly stressor rehearsal and the compound-pathway decay law

Audit alone is orientation layer. Rehearsal is physical layer. The quarterly rehearsal runs the full loop under imposed cognitive load.

Compound-specific neural pathways atrophy faster than constituent-specific pathways.

The decay law explains why compound maintenance is not derivable from constituent maintenance. An operator who keeps running, shooting, and navigating on separate tracks maintains three constituent pathways and lets the integration pathway — the pathway that fires all three in concert under stress — go silent. Motor-pattern decay begins at 14 days of disuse and reaches significant decay at 30 days. Compound-integration decay begins earlier and runs steeper, because the integration pathway fires only when all three constituents fire simultaneously under stress, which is rarer in normal training than any single-constituent firing. The quarterly rehearsal is the counter. It runs the full loop under imposed friction for a bounded session (typically 60 to 180 minutes), produces an after-action per 04.8 failure protocol, and resets the decay clock. THE REHEARSAL IS NON-NEGOTIABLE CALENDAR. Operators who schedule the quarterly rehearsal as "when time permits" consistently report compound-state reads one grade below operators who schedule it as fixed calendar; the difference is not motivation — it is the decay clock running silently in the gap between "when time permits" iterations.

04.1.7Install, function, failure, feed-forward

INSTALLATION PROTOCOL. Identify the load-bearing domain per interlock (see 04.2 through 04.6 for each). Install the load-bearing domain to threshold. Install the two supporting domains onto it to threshold. Install the interlock layer — the drill or protocol that runs all three simultaneously under stress — last. Schedule the monthly audit and the quarterly rehearsal before you finish the install; the maintenance infrastructure is part of the install, not an afterthought.

FUNCTION IN OPERATION. The compound consumes input from the environment, cycles it through the three domains in the loop's feedback architecture, and produces output nonlinear in input. The inner-loop tempo of the compound determines its OODA-superiority margin over any single-constituent adversary. The load-bearing domain holds the loop's structural memory; the two supporting domains supply inputs and actuators; the interlock layer is the active feedback mechanism that turns three sequential executions into one recursive loop. The compound reads ACTIVE when the operator narrates decisions across all three domains fluently, cites current calibration measurements on demand, and produces the compound-specific output under imposed stress.

FAILURE INDICATORS. Removal diagnostic fails — pulling one domain leaves the capability running, which means the remaining two were a stack, not a compound. Cross-domain narration collapses into single-domain logic under stress — the operator who was running three-variable route justification in training reverts to "it's shorter" under contact. Motor-pattern decay exceeds 30 days without rehearsal — constituent drift accumulates and the compound integration pathway atrophies silently. Monthly audit lapses past 45 days — drift window widens, weakest-domain lead gets lost, and the operator's self-assessment drifts ahead of reality.

FEED-FORWARD. Sub-module 04 installs five interlocks in sequence, each one an instance of the compound principle. Section 04.2 installs Interlock A, the detection / counter-detection loop across Track + Nav + Evade. Sections 04.3 through 04.6 install Interlocks B through E. Section 04.7 installs the compound-recognition layer, the quarterly audit protocol formalized. Section 04.8 installs the compound-failure doctrine, naming the three failure modes and the adversary-targeting patterns. The CLOSE hands off to Sub-module 05 SUSTAINMENT, where compound infrastructure maintains the compounds against multi-year horizons. Read every subsequent section as an instance of the architecture installed here.

← BACK04 HUBNEXT →04.2 INTERLOCK A — Track + Nav + Evade (detection / counter-detection loop)

theFIELD.run / CONSTRUCT_APPLICATIONS / 04 THE COMPOUND / 04.2 INTERLOCK A — Track + Nav + Evade (detection / counter-detection loop)
SECTION 04.2

INTERLOCK A — Track + Nav + Evade (detection / counter-detection loop)

ARCHITECTUREDETECTION LOOP
DOMAINSTRACK · NAV · EVADE
LOAD-BEARINGNAVIGATION (MENTAL MAP = STRUCTURAL MEMORY)
LOOP BEATSSIGNCUT → LOCALIZE → ROUTE → MOVE → SELF-SIGNCUT → UPDATE
ACTIVE-PURSUIT CADENCE5–15 min
PASSIVE-AVOIDANCE CADENCE30–60 min
CALIBRATIONROUTE-DECISION LATENCY < 90 s · SEVEN TARGET INDICATORS ≥ 5/7 · PACE-COUNT ERROR < 3% / 500 m · ADVERSARY LOCALIZATION ≤ 100 m BOX
KEY FRAMEWORKSSEVEN TARGET INDICATORS · APPEAR-TO-VANISH SIGNATURE STACK · HANDRAIL / BASELINE / CATCHING FEATURE · BREAK-LINE-OF-SIGHT

The compound is the capacity to read the ground while the ground is reading you. Tracking alone reads sign others have left; navigation alone moves you through terrain; evasion alone reduces your own signature. The compound is the live, recursive signcut-route-signature cycle, where a route decision is simultaneously a navigation problem, a tracking problem, and an evasion problem resolved from one integrated picture. Combat Tracking Guide supplies the Seven Target Indicators and the three-phase gait analysis; Appear to Vanish supplies the full-spectrum signature taxonomy across visible, thermal, acoustic, and intangible bands; Essential Wilderness Navigation supplies the handrail / baseline / catching-feature vocabulary on which terrain association rests; the USAF SERE Handbook supplies the Break-Line-of-Sight protocol from 03.10. The three sources do not run as a library — they run as a loop.

This section installs Interlock A as the detection / counter-detection loop. You load the six-beat loop architecture (signcut adversary → localize both → select route → move with signature discipline → self-signcut own output → update priors), the dual-cadence regime (5–15 min active pursuit / 30–60 min passive avoidance), the second-order signcut discipline where the operator reads sign against the planter's logic rather than with it, the navigation-as-load-bearing rule that terrain association is the structural memory on which both adversary position and own signature plot, the cutting-line-as-route drill that trains cross-domain route selection under instructor scoring, the three-variable route justification (sight-line degradation, substrate signature, catching-feature dump) that the ACTIVE compound produces under stress, and the install / function / failure / feed-forward handoff. Sources: Combat Tracking Guide (Seven Target Indicators, three-phase gait); Appear to Vanish (full-spectrum signature taxonomy); Essential Wilderness Navigation (terrain-reading vocabulary); USAF SERE Handbook (Break-Line-of-Sight); 00.3 (signature discipline); 02.6 (nav vocabulary); 03.6 and 03.10 (individual movement, evasion).

04.2.1The six-beat loop

The loop runs in a fixed sequence. Every beat feeds the next. Skipping a beat reverts the compound to a stack.

The signcut-route-signature cycle
01SIGNCUT ADVERSARY — read marks across ground, aerial, intangible, and signature bands. Seven Target Indicators running.
02LOCALIZE BOTH — plot adversary and self on the mental map. Adversary to a 100 m box minimum.
03SELECT ROUTE — use handrail, baseline, catching-feature logic. Minimize own-signature, maximize adversary-signature reading, maintain time budget.
04MOVE WITH SIGNATURE DISCIPLINE — individual movement technique, full signal stack from Appear-to-Vanish. No wasted motion, no wasted sign.
05SELF-SIGNCUT — ask what signature you just left and how the adversary reads it. Second-order reading.
06UPDATE PRIORS — both the adversary model and the self-signature model refine. Re-enter beat 01.

The amplification mechanism lives in the iteration. A novice reads sign once and moves. A compound operator reads sign, moves, self-signcuts, and refines on the next cycle. That second-order prediction produces decoys, varying-stride countermeasures, false bed-downs, and the recognition that an obvious direction may be a planted one. THE CYCLE RUNS CONTINUOUSLY, NOT SERIALLY. Under active pursuit the loop cycles at 5 to 15 minute cadence; in passive avoidance the cycle widens to 30 to 60 minutes. The operator who runs the loop serially — signcut, then route, then move, then stop — produces a stack, not a compound.

04.2.2Installation order — navigation first

Navigation is load-bearing because terrain association and the mental map are the structural memory on which both adversary position and own signature plot.

Installation-order failure

Install tracking first and Seven Target Indicators accumulate without a terrain frame to mean something operational. Install evasion first and signature discipline runs against an abstract observer. Navigation carries the frame both others layer onto.

Install first the navigation base from Sub-module 02: terrain association, handrail / baseline / catching-feature vocabulary, pace count, dead reckoning, compass work, contour interpretation. The operator must be able to produce the mental map under stress before sign reading or signature reduction can plot onto it. Install second the tracking base: Seven Target Indicators (disturbance, displacement, staining, weathering, littering, camouflage, regularity), three-phase gait analysis, the combat-tracking discipline that reads sign against the tracker's own hypothesis rather than for it. Install third the evasion base: the Break-Line-of-Sight protocol, the full Appear-to-Vanish signature stack across visible / thermal / acoustic / intangible bands, counter-tracking movement, stride variation, false bed-downs. The interlock layer is the cutting-line-as-route drill. The operator picks a route between two fixed points under an instructor's adversarial scoring; the instructor scores both own-signature and adversary-signature reading on the same traverse, and the drill does not reset until both scores cross threshold simultaneously. Any drill that scores only one domain trains a stack.

04.2.3The three-variable route justification — compound in observable form

The compound produces an observable output under stress: a route justification that spans all three domains in one sentence.

"We go through the re-entrant because it drops us below their line of sight, the substrate on the south side is rock so we leave less ground sign, and it dumps us onto the stream handrail at the catching feature."

Three variables, one sentence, under stress. Sight-line degradation (the evasion read). Substrate signature (the tracking read). Catching-feature dump (the navigation read). The operator who can produce this sentence under contact is running the compound; the operator who produces one variable and defaults to "it's shorter" is running a stack. The observable is the cross-domain narration itself, not the route's objective optimality — the route may be sub-optimal on any single axis, but optimal across the three simultaneously. CROSS-DOMAIN NARRATION IS THE ACTIVE-STATE TELL. The Quarterly rehearsal scores this narration explicitly, because it is the cheapest, fastest, hardest-to-fake read on compound state.

04.2.4Calibration thresholds

The compound reads ACTIVE when the full calibration table holds under stress.

Interlock A calibration

ROUTE-DECISION LATENCY under stress · < 90 s SEVEN TARGET INDICATORS reportable in current terrain · ≥ 5 of 7 PACE-COUNT ERROR · < 3% on 500 m mixed terrain ADVERSARY LOCALIZATION · ≤ 100 m box on the map THREE-VARIABLE NARRATION produced spontaneously · YES / NO LAST LIVE REHEARSAL · within 90 days

Drift in any single line flags DEGRADING. Drift across two or more flags DORMANT. Route-decision latency drift from 90 s toward 3 min is the first measurable signature of compound degradation, because latency reflects the integration-pathway cycle time directly. Cross-domain narration collapse is the second signature — the operator who was running three-variable justification reverts to "it's shorter." The third is catastrophic: the operator takes a route and cannot say why across any of the three domains.

04.2.5Adversary targeting of the integration layer

A sophisticated adversary targets the compound's integration rather than its constituents. The attack is cheaper and the damage is greater.

Three integration-layer attacks on Interlock A

01 · TRACK-TRAP PLANTING — adversary plants sign the operator's tracker is biased to read. The compound must read sign against the planter's logic, not with it. Second-order discipline is the counter. 02 · SENSOR ASYMMETRY — adversary holds CIR or LWIR imaging; the operator's signature-reduction protocols were calibrated against visible-spectrum observers. Full Appear-to-Vanish spectrum audit is the counter. 03 · BASELINE SHAPING — adversary modifies the terrain itself before the operator enters it. The baseline the operator built the mental map against is corrupted, producing false adversary-position estimates. Baseline cross-checking against independent sources is the counter.

Each attack is cheaper for the adversary than attritional attack on a constituent. A track-trap costs minutes to plant and degrades the operator's signcut output for hours. A thermal sensor one grade above the operator's calibration renders the evasion stack obsolete across the band. A baseline shaped in advance defeats the mental map before the loop starts. The counter to integration-layer attack is integration-layer defense — audit protocol, rehearsal cadence, second-order reading discipline — rather than harder training on any single constituent.

04.2.6Install, function, failure, feed-forward

INSTALLATION PROTOCOL. Install navigation from 02 to threshold (terrain association, handrail / baseline / catching feature, pace count, dead reckoning). Install tracking on top (Seven Target Indicators, three-phase gait, combat-tracking discipline). Install evasion on top (Break-Line-of-Sight, Appear-to-Vanish signature stack, counter-tracking). Drill the cutting-line-as-route layer under adversarial scoring until own-signature and adversary-signature scores cross threshold on the same traverse.

FUNCTION IN OPERATION. The loop cycles at 5 to 15 minute cadence under active pursuit, 30 to 60 minute cadence in passive avoidance. Each cycle refines both adversary model and self-signature model. The operator produces the three-variable narration spontaneously, route-decision latency holds under 90 s, and the adversary model resolves to a 100 m box at worst. The compound absorbs uncertainty faster than the adversary can generate it.

FAILURE INDICATORS. Route-decision latency drifts from 90 s toward 3 min. Cross-domain narration collapses to single-domain logic. The operator takes a route they cannot justify across all three domains. Motor-pattern decay in any constituent crosses 30 days without refresh. Monthly audit lapses past 45 days. Sensor asymmetry in the theater goes un-audited and the evasion stack remains calibrated against the wrong observer class.

FEED-FORWARD. Interlock A feeds into the cache-route planning of Sub-module 05 SUSTAINMENT, the comms emissions discipline of Sub-module 06 COMMAND, and the pursuit-and-detection condition classes of Sub-module 07 FIELD DEPLOYMENT. It composes with Interlock D (Command Under Fire) when the detection loop runs inside a team operation — the commander's orientation layer consumes Interlock A output as one of its highest-bandwidth inputs. Section 04.3 installs Interlock B, the self-sufficient pharmacy production loop.

SECTION 04.3

INTERLOCK B — Medical + Herbal + Homestead (self-sufficient pharmacy)

ARCHITECTUREPRODUCTION LOOP (NESTED DUAL-SCALE)
