Sub-module 04 is the beat where those installed systems stop functioning as a library and start functioning as a compound. The acceleration protocols live in the gaps between domains, in the feedback loops that no single domain produces alone, and in the emergent capabilities that appear only when three or more domains run simultaneously against a shared problem.

The RSI progression reaches its inflection point here. Baseline and foundational architecture move in additive beats; one skill installs on top of the last and the operator's capability grows arithmetically. The compound layer moves multiplicatively. A tracker with navigation produces more than tracking plus navigation; a medic with herbal pharmacology and homestead production becomes a pharmacy; a commander with force discipline and strategic frame holds coherence against Clausewitzian friction that would shatter any of the three constituents alone. The compound is the product, the stack is the sum, and the difference between them is what VOLUME_001 turns on.

theFIELD.run / CONSTRUCT_APPLICATIONS / 05 SUSTAINMENT / 05.1 Tiered kit architecture — EDC to BOB to INCH
SECTION 05.1

Tiered kit architecture — EDC to BOB to INCH

LADDER RUNGS6 (EDC · GHB · SURVIVAL KIT · BOB · EXTENDED · INCH)
BOB WINDOW72 h
FOUR PsPERIOD · PORTABILITY · PREPAREDNESS · PERSONALIZATION
SUPPLY CATEGORIES12
PACK SCALEP1 MINIMALIST · P2 STANDARD · P3 GEAR-DEPENDENT (INVERSE TO COMPETENCE)
HIP-BELT LOAD TRANSFERUP TO 90% TO PELVIS + FEMURS
CHASSIS THRESHOLDSFRAMELESS < 25 lb · EXTERNAL > 35 lb HOT CLIMATE · INTERNAL DEFAULT
FIVE-MILE CALIBRATION HIKE UNDER FULL LOAD

The kit ladder installs first because every downstream sustainment layer assumes its rungs are already in place. Stewart's Build the Perfect Bug Out Bag and Build the Perfect Survival Kit supply the six-rung ladder and the Four Ps test; Forgotten Skills of Self-Sufficiency supplies the Mormon-pioneer long-carry tradition that calibrates what the bag must support. The ladder reads as progressive capability windows stacked against progressive disruption durations. Every rung has an operational staging location, an audit cadence, and a load-out specification. Skipping a rung creates a time band where response capability drops to zero, and the skip is almost always at the middle rungs (GHB, survival kit) because the extremes are visible and the middle is inferred.

This section installs the six-rung ladder (EDC, GHB, survival kit, BOB, extended, INCH) each with its own staging location and audit cadence, the Four Ps test that filters bag from Bug Out Bag, the twelve supply categories that define completeness, the P1 / P2 / P3 pack-scale calibration that runs inverse to operator competence, the hip-belt load-transfer physics that keeps a loaded pack portable across distance, the chassis-selection thresholds (frameless / external / internal frame), the urban-camouflage principle that matches pack signature to surrounding population, and the five-mile calibration hike under full load that converts theoretical kit into verified kit. Sources: Stewart Build the Perfect Bug Out Bag (ladder, Four Ps, twelve categories, P1/P2/P3 scale); Stewart Build the Perfect Survival Kit (sub-BOB tier calibration); Forgotten Skills of Self-Sufficiency (long-carry rotation discipline, pioneer load calibration); 00.2 Kinesthetic baseline (pack fit against operator anthropometry); 02 Traverse (pack portability under movement load).

05.1.1The six-rung ladder

The ladder is either complete or it is not. The operator who carries EDC, stages a GHB, owns a BOB, and has not built a survival kit or extended bag occupies three of six rungs. The three empty rungs define a capability gap.

The six rungs
01EDC — on-person continuous carry. Pocket, belt, wallet. Audited daily. Covers disruption window measured in minutes to hours.
02GHB (Get-Home Bag) — staged in vehicle or workplace. Audited monthly. Covers the walk home from the furthest point of daily travel.
03SURVIVAL KIT — mini (Altoids-tin) to medium (shoulder-sling). Covers isolated-environment 24-hour window. Often a subset carried inside GHB or BOB.
04BOB (Bug Out Bag) — 72-hour pack, hallway-staged, sealed, packed. The canonical disaster-response bag.
05EXTENDED — 7-to-14-day pack for known-route relocation. Lives at BOL cache or secondary dwelling.
06INCH (I'm Never Coming Home) — one-way departure load-out. Cached at BOL or secondary dwelling.

Each rung carries its own disruption window and its own staging rule. The ladder is designed so that any reasonable disaster timeline has a bag sized to it, reachable in the time available. The operator does not reach for the BOB during a rush-hour earthquake; the operator reaches for EDC and the vehicle GHB. The BOB activates during evacuation orders, twelve-to-seventy-two-hour windows, when the dwelling is reachable. INCH activates when the dwelling is not reachable and return is not expected.

05.1.2The Four Ps test

Every BOB passes four tests or fails as a pretender to the designation.

The Four Ps

PERIOD · sized to the 72-hour window within which disaster zones typically stabilize or are declared unsalvageable. PORTABILITY · carryable on foot at sustained pace by its owner, with hip-belt transfer of up to 90% of pack load to pelvis and femurs. PREPAREDNESS · packed at a known location, reachable inside 5 minutes, with no assembly required. PERSONALIZATION · tailored across the 12 supply categories to the specific operator's geography, climate, medical profile, and likely disaster mix.

A bag that fails any one of the Four Ps is a bag, not a Bug Out Bag. Most BOB failures are Preparedness failures — the bag exists in theory, scattered across the house, never actually packed and sealed at the staging point. The audit question is binary: if the exit alarm sounds right now, does the packed bag leave the door on the operator's back without assembly. No is failure; yes is pass.

05.1.3The twelve supply categories

Personalization operates across twelve canonical categories. The categories define completeness; their specific contents define fit to operator and environment.

Twelve supply categories
01WATER — containers, filter, purification tablets.
02FOOD — 72-hour caloric supply, shelf-stable, minimal preparation.
03CLOTHING — season-appropriate layers, extra socks, rain shell.
04SHELTER — tarp, bivy, or tent; sleep system.
05FIRE — three redundant ignition methods (ferro, lighter, stormproof match).
06FIRST AID — IFAK plus personal-medication supply for the 72-hour window.
07HYGIENE — soap, toothbrush, feminine supplies, toilet provision.
08TOOLS — multitool, fixed-blade knife, folding saw, cordage.
09LIGHTING — headlamp plus spare batteries.
10COMMUNICATIONS — radio, signal mirror, whistle, whatever comms layer the operator's PACE plan specifies.
11PROTECTION — defensive tooling per legal jurisdiction and operator training.
12MISCELLANEOUS — documents, cash, keys, specific-terrain items.

A BOB missing a category is a GHB pretending to be a BOB. The twelve categories are the check sheet against which every rung gets audited.

05.1.4Pack scale calibration — P1 / P2 / P3

Pack scale calibrates inverse to operator competence. Knowledge is lightweight; equipment fills capability gaps.

P1 MINIMALIST — smallest pack. Knowledge substitutes for redundancy. One ferro rod, one cook pot, one blade, one shelter system, one medical kit. Operator runs at mastery across fire, shelter, water, navigation, medical, food acquisition. P2 STANDARD — mid-scale pack. Two-deep redundancy on critical functions. Most operators live here. P3 GEAR-DEPENDENT — largest pack. Every capability gap fills with equipment; three lighters, magnesium bar, propane stove, chemical heaters. Heavy pack, shallow skill.

The axis holds. A skilled operator carrying one ferro rod outcarries an untrained operator hauling three lighters, a magnesium bar, a propane stove, and a chemical heater pack. Competence reduces pack weight, increases range, and raises the operator's ceiling under extended timelines. The training log is the most effective pack-weight reduction program available.

05.1.5Chassis selection and urban camouflage

Pack chassis selection splits three ways by load and climate. Frameless packs hold loads under 25 lb only; above that the lack of structure transfers load to shoulders and fails the hip-belt physics. External-frame packs carry loads above 35 lb well in hot climates because the gap between pack and back ventilates. Internal-frame packs serve as the modern default for balance and off-trail stability, handling 25–60 lb loads with the best weight-to-stability ratio for mixed terrain. Choose chassis to the load the bag actually carries under audit, not to the load the bag is imagined to carry.

Urban camouflage applies to the pack itself. A tricked-out MOLLE ruck in coyote brown with patches reads as loot in a disaster zone and draws attention at every transit point. A civilian school-style internal-frame pack in neutral color reads as commuter and passes unnoticed. Signature discipline is a component of the pack choice. The pack that looks tactical in the parking lot looks like a target on the road.

05.1.6Installation, function, failure, feed-forward

INSTALL. Stage each rung at its operational location. EDC on person, audited daily. GHB in vehicle or workplace, audited monthly. BOB at hallway staging point, packed and sealed. Extended bag and INCH at BOL cache or secondary dwelling. Calibrate the BOB with a five-mile hike under full load on varied ground. Re-fit hip belt after any 15-lb change in body weight.

FUNCTION. The ladder delivers sized capability at every disruption window. EDC handles minutes-to-hours, GHB handles the walk home, survival kit handles isolated 24-hour windows, BOB handles 72-hour evacuations, extended handles week-to-two-week relocations, INCH handles one-way departures. At every window, the operator reaches for a bag sized to the window; no bag forces a category default.

FAILURE. The ladder fails when a rung is skipped, when any of the twelve categories falls empty, when the hip belt loses its buckle, when the owner has gained or lost 15 lb since last fit, or when the calibration hike has never been performed. The most common silent failure is a BOB built from a catalog rather than from the Four Ps and never audited under load.

FEED-FORWARD. The kit ladder preserves the buffer; 05.2 installs the rotation discipline that keeps the buffer's contents current. The ladder exists as staged capability; rotation is the calendar discipline that prevents the staged capability from expiring into waste.

theFIELD.run / CONSTRUCT_APPLICATIONS / 05 SUSTAINMENT / 05.10 Integrated sustainment doctrine
SECTION 05.10

Integrated sustainment doctrine

Three nested time horizons. Daily (hours), seasonal (months), rotational (years). All three sit on the calendar simultaneously. Neglect at any horizon propagates across the others.
Redundancy law. Two-deep paths for every critical function. Single-source = single failure mode.
Stock-flow-reserve accounting. Three columns — stock (what is on hand today), flow (consumption rate per week/month), reserve (stock minus one-cycle flow). Reserve threshold triggers procurement or production action.
Skills ladder. Ten trades-craft domainscarpentry, masonry, basic wiring (12V + 120V), plumbing, small-engine repair, blacksmithing/bladesmithing, butchery + preservation, silviculture, food preservation (canning/drying/smoking/salting/lacto-ferm), livestock husbandry.
Realistic competence target. One person competent in each domain + community redundancy for rare skills. No single household holds all skills at mastery.
Closure metric. Ratio of closed loops to open loops, trending upward year over year. Open loop = dependent on supply chain beyond trusted local network. Closed loop = produced on-site or by trusted close-community neighbor.

Sub-module 05 closes the operating chain on itself. Sub-modules 00 through 04 assume imported primitives — you carry water, you carry fire, you eat the calorie you brought, you wear the boot you bought. Sub-module 05 is the layer at which the homestead produces the water (catchment, well), the fuel (wood, biodiesel, gasifier, PV), the calorie (permaculture, silvopasture, preserved harvest), the tool (forge, heat-treat), and manages the forest that produces fuel and lumber and mast and wildlife. Without 05, the earlier sub-modules run on the countdown of the stockpile. With 05, they run for as long as the homestead ecosystem holds integrity.

This section installs the three nested time horizons, the redundancy law as two-deep paths for every critical function, the stock-flow-reserve accounting discipline that keeps production ahead of consumption, the ten-domain skills ladder and its realistic competence target, the interlock between 05 and the prior four sub-modules, and the closure metric that measures the homestead's sustainment trend across years. Sources integrated: all fifteen sources of sub-module 05, plus feedback-loop returns to 00, 01, 02, 03, and 04.

05.10.1The three nested time horizons

Daily (hours). Water drawn, stove fed, chickens fed, eggs collected, dishes washed, dishes rinsed, wood brought in, tools put back, livestock checked. Every day runs the same sequence with seasonal variation.
Seasonal (months). Plant, harvest, preserve, cull, cut firewood, drain lines, winterize, sugar the maples, start the chicks, turn the compost, plow the snow. Twelve-month rhythm repeats.
Rotational (years). Stand thinning, timber harvest, orchard pruning, battery replacement, gasifier rebuild, root-cellar roof re-tar, blade re-handle, roof replacement, well service, septic pump.

A homestead that runs only the daily horizon decays at the seasonal. A homestead that runs only seasonal decays at the rotational. Three horizons, one calendar. The calendar is the master control document — every production, maintenance, and replacement action lives on the calendar with its horizon, cycle, and owner.

05.10.2The redundancy law — two-deep on every critical function

Water. Well + rainwater catchment + surface (pond or stream with treatment).
Power. Solar + generator + wood heat. Three chains per 05.6.
Engine fuel. Biodiesel + stored diesel + wood gas (if gasifier installed).
Food. Garden + orchard + pasture livestock + woodlot mast + stored preserves. Deep redundancy.
Heat. Wood primary + propane secondary + electric baseboard (generator-fed) tertiary.
Tool-edge restoration. Sharpening stones (daily) + forge (re-profile) + stock steel (replacement).
Communications. Cellular + amateur radio + written mail + physical courier through trusted network.

Two-deep means single-source failure does not take down the function. Three-deep means single-source failure plus secondary degradation still leaves one path. The redundancy law does not mean every function needs every path installed — it means the function must not collapse when the primary path fails. Assess each function, install the second path before the first one breaks.

05.10.3Stock-flow-reserve accounting

DEF

Stock = inventory on hand today, measured in units appropriate to the item (pounds flour, gallons fuel, cords wood, cases canned goods). Flow = consumption rate per week or month, measured at steady-state use. Reserve = stock minus flow over the planned replenishment cycle.

Run-rate multiplied by time-to-replenish yields required reserve. Five gallons of lamp oil per month consumption × three months to order and receive = 15-gallon reserve floor. When stock drops to 15 gallons, a procurement action fires. Track stock-flow-reserve for every consumable: food staples, fuel, first-aid consumables, livestock feed, ammunition, fasteners and hardware, lubricants, chainsaw bar oil, two-stroke mix, soap, detergent, salt, sugar, vinegar, yeast. The accounting runs quarterly at minimum; monthly is safer. Spreadsheet, ledger book, or whiteboard — the medium is unimportant; the discipline of tracking is everything.

05.10.4The ten-domain skills ladder

No household contains all ten domains at mastery. The realistic target: one person competent in each, plus community redundancy for rare skills (welder, mechanic, midwife, large-animal vet, gunsmith). The autonomous household is not autonomous from the community — it is a functional node inside a trusted community that covers the full skills matrix collectively.

Carpentry for outbuildings and repair. Masonry for cellar walls and chimney repair. Basic wiring (12V DC and 120V AC) for inverters, batteries, solar controllers. Plumbing for pipe runs, valve replacement, winterization. Small-engine repair for chainsaw, generator, rototiller, tractor. Blacksmithing and bladesmithing per 05.7. Butchery and preservation for on-site protein handling. Silviculture per 05.8. Food preservation across canning, drying, smoking, salting, and lacto-fermentation. Livestock husbandry at minimum poultry, ruminant if pasture present. Train one household member per domain, cross-train a second, document in a household manual, rehearse annually.

05.10.5The interlock with sub-modules 00 through 04

DEF

Interlock runs as feedback, not hierarchy. Production in 05 replaces BOB consumables for 01 (water, fuel, food, cordage — all produced on-site rather than purchased for the go-bag). Forest-reading from Forest Forensics extends terrain-reading for 02 traverse and movement doctrine. Forged blade and tool and projectile from 05.7 supply 03 applied-force tooling. Closed-loop pharmacy links food forest (05.3) and medical herbalism (04) in 04 compound systems. And 05 hands command autonomy to 06: food and fuel security equals command autonomy. A leader who does not control the food supply does not control the decision.

The interlock is the reason sub-module 05 sits at the ACCELERATION-to-OPTIMIZATION hinge in the RSI progression. 00–03 install the operator's chassis. 04 builds the compound systems that amplify the chassis. 05 supplies the production layer that keeps the compounds running beyond the horizon of imported primitives. 06 directs the production toward strategic outcome. Every sub-module feeds the next and returns to the prior.

05.10.6The closure metric — the one diagnostic

Imagine the nearest town vanishing tomorrow. List every critical function that would stop. Every function that depends on the town is an open loop. Every function produced on-site or by a trusted close-community neighbor is a closed loop. The sustainment index is the ratio of closed loops to open loops, trending upward year over year. Closure is the test. The household's multi-decade work is moving loops from open to closed.

A closed-loop ratio of 0.2 (one in five functions produced locally) is a dependent household. A ratio of 0.6 is a resilient household. A ratio approaching 1.0 is a fully autonomous household, which is rare and requires community-scale production for rare skills and inputs. The trend matters more than the level. A household closing two loops per year is on an improving trajectory; a household opening one loop per year (converting wood heat to natural gas, canning to grocery-store purchase, garden to convenience) is on a degrading trajectory regardless of starting level.

05.10.7Install, function, failure, feed-forward

Install the integrated sustainment doctrine by mapping every function currently performed by the household, classifying each as closed or open loop, calibrating the closure ratio as the baseline metric, and setting a year-over-year close-rate target (e.g., close two loops per year for five years). Run quarterly stock-flow-reserve audits on all consumables. Maintain the ten-domain skills ladder through practice and cross-training. Run an annual whole-system drill — kill grid power for 72 hours, run the homestead on its two-deep paths, audit the failure points, close the gaps before winter.

The system functions when the closure ratio trends upward, reserve levels hold above threshold across all consumables, every critical function has a tested second path, and skills are current enough to execute under stress rather than nostalgic hobby practice. The three time horizons stay in sync on the calendar. The interlock with 00–04 operates as feedback, with every sub-module returning inputs to every other.

It fails when a household runs only the daily horizon and seasonal decay compounds silently across years until a rotational failure (roof, well, battery bank) cascades simultaneously. It fails when single-source critical functions collapse under foreseeable shock (sole well fails in drought, sole power line fails in ice storm). It fails when reserves drop below threshold because stock-flow-reserve was not tracked. It fails when the skills ladder is aspirational rather than practiced. It fails when the closure ratio drifts open because convenience wins against production discipline.

Sustainment hands forward to 06 command. The homestead that produces kilowatt-hours, calories, gallons, and finished edges is the homestead that can afford to command from strategic posture rather than react from scarcity. uProduce the resource first. Command the deployment of the resource second.u The ACCELERATION-to-OPTIMIZATION hinge closes; the COMMAND layer opens.

theFIELD.run / CONSTRUCT_APPLICATIONS / 05 SUSTAINMENT / 05.2 Supply rotation, stockpile depth, FIFO doctrine
SECTION 05.2

Supply rotation, stockpile depth, FIFO doctrine

FAILURE MODESEXPIRE-IN-PLACE · RUN-OUT-BEFORE-RESUPPLY
ROTATION DISCIPLINEFIFO
REVIEW CADENCEBIANNUAL NOVEMBER + MAY (FIXED DATES, NOT EXPIRY-DRIVEN)
STOCKPILE DEPTHS72 h BOB · 30 d PANTRY · 1 yr SUSTAINMENT
RULE OF THREES DRIVERWATER 3 d · FIRE 3 h COLD · SHELTER 3 h EXPOSURE
CACHE DISTRIBUTIONPRIMARY HOME · SECONDARY BOL · TERTIARY VEHICLE + WORK · QUATERNARY TRUSTED OFF-SITE
WATER STORESREPLACE ANNUALLY SEALED OR NOT
INVENTORY RULESTORE WHAT YOU EAT, EAT WHAT YOU STORE

The stockpile is the buffer between consumption and production, and it fails in two directions. Contents expire before use, or contents run out before resupply. Stewart's Build the Perfect Bug Out Bag supplies the biannual-review protocol that solves expire-in-place; the Mormon-pioneer long-storage tradition captured in Forgotten Skills of Self-Sufficiency supplies the depth stratification and container discipline that solves run-out-before-resupply. Combined, the two produce one coherent rotation system that preserves the buffer's value across the multi-year timelines the homestead operates under. Rotation is the lowest-glamour discipline in 05 and the one whose failure does the most damage, because an expired stockpile is indistinguishable from no stockpile at the moment of activation.

This section installs the FIFO rotation discipline that captures full stockpile value without waste, the biannual fixed-date review that decouples audit from expiry labels, the three-horizon depth stratification (72-hour BOB, 30-day pantry, 1-year sustainment), the Rule of Threes redundancy math that scales backup count to hazard time horizon, the four-cache multi-location distribution that prevents single-point stockpile failure, the container and label discipline that converts pile into inventory, and the store-what-you-eat rule that prevents the stockpile from becoming a shrine. Sources: Stewart Bug Out Bag (biannual review, eat-the-BOB rotation period); Forgotten Skills of Self-Sufficiency (Mormon long-storage tradition, one-year depth doctrine, pioneer container discipline); Rule of Threes baseline (Stewart, canonical survival doctrine); 01 Primary Systems (water/fire/shelter survival priorities that drive redundancy horizon).

05.2.1FIFO — First In, First Out

FIFO is the rotation discipline that captures the full value of the stockpile without waste.

FIFO rotation

Every dated item — BOB food, pantry goods, medicine, fuel, batteries — gets consumed in the order it was stored. Newest additions load to the back of the shelf. Oldest items come out the front. Items that expire in place are capability loss. Items that rotate through the kitchen before expiry are cost recovery.

The discipline is simple; its enforcement is the difficulty. Shelf layout either enforces FIFO automatically (dispensing racks that load from the back, gravity-fed can organizers) or the discipline depends on labeled pack dates and conscious shelf management. Automatic enforcement beats conscious enforcement at every scale above a single household member's daily attention. Invest in shelving that makes the wrong choice hard.

05.2.2The biannual fixed-date review

The biannual BOB review runs in November and May regardless of expiration dates printed on packaging. Fixed dates beat expiry-driven dates because fixed dates land on the calendar and never slip, while expiry-driven review requires continuous surveillance of a sprawling inventory and fails silently when surveillance lapses.

Biannual review protocol
01PULL — empty the BOB onto a staging surface. Every item inspected.
02EAT — food pulled from the pack gets eaten across the following 30 days (the intentional eat-the-BOB period). No stockpile food wasted; household meals absorb the rotation.
03SWAP — winter clothing swaps for summer or vice versa per the calendar half.
04ROTATE — medication replaced, batteries replaced, fuel checked and topped.
05REPACK — fresh replacements load the pack in the canonical twelve-category layout. Seal.

The November and May pair places one review at the boundary between summer and fall, one at the boundary between winter and spring, and both at points where household routines typically allow a two-to-four-hour window. One calendar event, zero additional cognitive load across the rest of the year.

05.2.3Three-horizon depth stratification

Stockpile depth stratifies into three nested horizons, each calibrated to a different class of disruption.

Stockpile depth horizons
0172-HOUR BOB DEPTH — mobile in a pack. Handles the first three days of any natural-disaster aftermath. Covers the window in which most disaster zones either stabilize or are declared unsalvageable.
0230-DAY PANTRY DEPTH — static in the home. Handles a short supply-chain outage that has not yet become civilizational. Covers the window in which regional logistics typically restore even under significant disruption.
031-YEAR SUSTAINMENT STOCKPILE — static in root cellar or outbuilding. Handles agricultural, currency, or grid-scale collapse. Composed of bulk grain, legumes, salt, rendered fat, medicine, fuel, and seed. Covers the window across which production systems (05.3 onward) can stand up and begin yielding.

Each depth protects against a different event class. The three horizons nest; the 72-hour sits inside the 30-day sits inside the 1-year. A household missing any horizon carries a capability gap at that event class. The 1-year horizon's contents should overlap the production-system outputs in 05.3 through 05.7 so that sustainment stockpile can rotate into production cadence as the ecosystem comes online.

05.2.4The Rule of Threes and redundancy math

Redundancy count scales to hazard time horizon via the canonical Rule of Threes.

Three minutes without air · Three hours without shelter in extreme exposure · Three days without water · Three weeks without food. Redundancy count calibrates to the time horizon of the hazard: water opens a three-day failure window, so three water containers. Fire opens a three-hour failure window in extreme cold, so three ignition methods. Shelter opens a three-hour failure window in extreme exposure, so three-deep shelter capability (shell, insulation, external structure).

The Rule of Threes generalizes to every redundancy decision in sustainment. The shorter the failure window, the higher the redundancy count, because the time to rebuild capability after a failure must fit inside the failure's lethality window. This principle continues into 05.6's three-chain energy architecture and 05.5's three-chain water infrastructure.

05.2.5Four-cache multi-location distribution

Single-location stockpile fails to single events. A house fire, flood, burglary, or seizure takes the whole inventory. Multi-location distribution prevents single-point failure of the complete stockpile.

Cache distribution
01PRIMARY — home root cellar or pantry. Majority of depth. Daily access.
02SECONDARY — Bug Out Location cache. Duplicates the 30-day pantry and portions of the 1-year sustainment stockpile. Inaccessible from the home.
03TERTIARY — vehicle kit and workplace get-home bag. Duplicates the 72-hour BOB depth in mobile form.
04QUATERNARY (OPTIONAL) — trusted-party off-site cache. Insurance against total geographic displacement.

Any one cache fails without total failure. The four-cache architecture treats stockpile the same way 05.6 treats power and 05.5 treats water: two-deep minimum, three-deep preferred, on every critical function. Cache geography is decided by failure-mode orthogonality, not by convenience; a secondary cache two blocks from the primary shares too many failure modes to count as redundant.

05.2.6Container and label discipline

Container and label discipline converts an undifferentiated pile into a running inventory.

Container standard

Every stored item sits in a container that is moisture-, light-, rodent-, and oxygen-impermeable to the threat profile of its contents. Container labeled with contents and pack date in permanent marker. Every container indexed on a master list that tracks location and expiry. Master list version-controlled; current version accessible at the primary cache and at one off-site location.

Without the master list, the operator's inventory lives in memory, and memory fails under stress precisely when inventory access matters most. The master list is the documentation infrastructure that makes the stockpile operable by anyone in the household, not just the member who built it. This is Extreme Ownership's Decentralized Command applied to the stockpile: the inventory is a shared asset whose operability does not depend on any single person.

05.2.7Store what you eat, eat what you store

The store-what-you-eat rule is the anti-shrine principle. A stockpile containing foods the household does not actually eat is a capital pile that converts to waste at expiry, because the household will not eat them voluntarily and therefore the stockpile never rotates.

A shrine of wheat berries no one knows how to bake is a failed stockpile. The canonical pioneer example holds: Mormon households built long-storage inventories of foods they ate weekly, baked bread from stored grain routinely, and rotated through the 1-year depth via normal household consumption. The discipline runs two rules: store only foods the household eats, and eat from the stockpile routinely. The dual rule guarantees rotation and guarantees that the stockpile contains foods the household has the skill to prepare under stress.

05.2.8Installation, function, failure, feed-forward

INSTALL. Set the November and May calendar events as recurring appointments. Install shelving that enforces FIFO automatically where possible. Build the master inventory list and version-control it to the primary cache plus one off-site location. Designate primary, secondary, tertiary, and quaternary caches by geographic orthogonality. Inventory quarterly for moisture, rodent, and insect intrusion at the root cellar, grain stores, and fuel caches. Replace water stores annually, sealed or not.

FUNCTION. The rotation system preserves stockpile value across the multi-year timelines the homestead operates under. No item expires unconsumed. Any cache loss leaves the others intact. Stockpile contents rotate through the kitchen on a cadence that confirms both the food supply and the household skills to prepare it.

FAILURE. The rotation fails when a review date goes unmet, when a container goes unlabeled, when the master inventory list is out of date, when the stockpile contains foods the household does not actually eat, or when cache distribution reduces to a single location. A failed rotation converts capital into waste silently; the failure is visible only at activation, when the expired stockpile meets the operator who expected it to function.

FEED-FORWARD. Rotation discipline preserves the buffer. 05.3 installs the food-production layer that refills the buffer from within the homestead envelope, converting the stockpile from countdown to recurrence.

theFIELD.run / CONSTRUCT_APPLICATIONS / 05 SUSTAINMENT / 05.3 Food production — permaculture, regenerative ag, forest farming
SECTION 05.3

Food production — permaculture, regenerative ag, forest farming

CORE PRINCIPLEWORK WITH SUCCESSION, NOT AGAINST IT
SUCCESSION STAGESANNUAL WEEDS → PERENNIAL HERBS → SHRUBS → PIONEER TREES → CLIMAX FOREST
KEYSTONE BIOMEOAK SAVANNA (TEMPERATE)
FOOD-FOREST LAYERS6 VERTICAL STRATA
MAPLE SYRUP40:1 SAP:SYRUP · FINISH 219°F · 7/16" TRAD / 5/16" MODERN TAP
GINSENG70% SHADE · 8–10 yr MATURATION · MAPLE/BASSWOOD/POPLAR INDICATORS
SILVOPASTURE~100 TREES/ACRE
MASTING CYCLES2–7 yr
VAN HELMONT5-LB WILLOW → 169 LB IN 5 yr WITH 2 oz SOIL LOSS
JUGLONE RADIUS50 FT BLACK WALNUT
DEER DENSITY CEILING> 20 PER SQ MI BLOCKS HARDWOOD REGEN
SUCCESS VECTORS13 (HENDERSON)

Food production converts a stockpile that counts down into a harvest that recurs. Shepard's Restoration Agriculture supplies the succession-mimicking design principle and the six-layer food-forest architecture; Henderson's Farms with a Future supplies the thirteen success vectors that determine whether a production enterprise survives economically; Backyard Woodland supplies the site-level integration of woodlot, pasture, and cultivated ground; Dougherty's American Hemp Farmer supplies the diversified-crop and value-added-processing discipline. The central move is to design a perennial polyculture that sits near climax equilibrium and harvests from it, rather than arresting succession at stage one via annual soil disturbance the way industrial monocrop does.

This section installs the succession-mimicking design principle, the six-layer food-forest architecture (emergent, canopy, understory, shrub, herbaceous, vine) that harvests six slices of the light column where monocrop harvests one, the oak-savanna Rosetta Stone for temperate-zone design, the specific-production-stream parameter set (maple, ginseng, silvopasture, masting cycles), the Van Helmont mechanism that explains why biomass is fixed carbon plus water and not soil mineral, the allelopathic and browse-pressure constraints (juglone radius, deer-density ceiling), the dry-year / wet-year pioneer split that hedges weather variance, and the Henderson thirteen success vectors that govern economic viability. Sources: Shepard Restoration Agriculture (succession, food-forest strata, oak savanna, Van Helmont); Henderson Farms with a Future (thirteen success vectors, whole-farm planning); Backyard Woodland (silvopasture, masting, deer-density rules); Dougherty American Hemp Farmer (diversified crop, value-added processing); Forgotten Skills of Self-Sufficiency (Mormon-pioneer dry/wet-year split).

05.3.1Succession-mimicking design

Every bare patch of earth moves through an obligatory succession from annual weeds to perennial herbs to shrubs to pioneer trees to climax forest. Design against succession and the land fights the operator every year; design with succession and the land does the work.

The succession-mimic principle

Industrial monocrop agriculture arrests succession at stage 1 by disturbing soil annually, importing all fertility, and spending energy resisting the natural trajectory. Restoration agriculture designs a perennial polyculture that sits near the climax equilibrium for the latitude and harvests from it. Caloric output per acre of a mature perennial polyculture exceeds monocrop corn on the same soil because six vertical forest strata harvest six slices of the light column rather than one, and because the system runs on trapped solar gain rather than on imported nitrogen and fuel.

The design move is to identify the climax biome of the operator's latitude and mimic its architecture with edible and utilitarian species. In the temperate zone this is the oak savanna; in warmer latitudes, the tropical multistrata forest; in arid zones, a chaparral-mimicking or desert-oasis polyculture. Each biome has its Rosetta Stone.

05.3.2The oak-savanna Rosetta Stone and the six-layer food forest

The oak savanna is Shepard's Rosetta Stone biome for the temperate zone. Scattered oaks above, grasses between, shrub layer at shoulder height, forest-floor herbs at ground level, vines climbing where light permits. Per unit area it is the richest mammal-supporting biome on earth, and every layer is food or fodder.

Six-layer food-forest stack
01EMERGENT — mature oak at the top, 80-to-150-year rotation, canopy dominant.
02CANOPY — chestnut, walnut, pecan, hickory. Mast staple crops.
03UNDERSTORY — paw-paw, persimmon, serviceberry. Shade-tolerant fruit.
04SHRUB — hazelnut, currant, gooseberry, elderberry. Nuts and berries at shoulder height.
05HERBACEOUS — ginseng, ramps, strawberry, medicinal herbs at the floor.
06VINE — hardy kiwi, grape, hops climbing canopy and understory.

Total yield compounds because niches do not overlap. Canopy mast does not compete with herbaceous ginseng for the same light; they harvest different slices of the column. The six-layer stack is the single highest-leverage architectural decision in 05.3 because it multiplies annual yield per acre without increasing land area, imported inputs, or labor beyond the establishment years.

05.3.3Specific production-stream parameters

Specific streams carry specific parameters. These parameters are the operational detail without which the principle remains theoretical.

Production-stream parameters
01MAPLE SYRUP — 40:1 sap-to-syrup ratiotapped in late winter when daytime thaw and nighttime freeze drive sap flow · 7/16" traditional tap bits or 5/16" reduced-stress modern bits · finished at 219°F (boiling point of water plus 7°F at standard pressure) to indicate syrup density.
02AMERICAN GINSENG — shade-simulated under 70% hardwood canopykeyed to sugar maple, basswood, tulip poplar indicator species · matures in 8–10 yr · long-horizon cash crop, not short-cycle vegetable.
03SILVOPASTURE — integrates ~100 trees per acre into grazed pasturetree shade reduces livestock heat stress · livestock manure fertilizes trees · mast fall supplements grazed forage.
04MASTING CYCLES — 2–7 yr in oak, hickory, chestnut, beechevolutionary strategy overwhelms seed predators in heavy years and starves them in light · store mast-year surplus, diversify across species so one off-year is another's on-year.

Each stream has its own establishment cost, its own maturation window, and its own yield pattern. The establishment window for mast-bearing canopy (10–20 years) is the longest clock on the homestead, which is why canopy plants first and short-cycle herbaceous plants last.

05.3.4Van Helmont's willow and the carbon-fixation mechanism

The mechanism under the yield is carbon fixation, not soil mining. Van Helmont's experiment anchors the claim.

A 5-lb willow planted in 200 lb of soil weighed 169 lb five years later while the soil had lost 2 oz. Tree mass is built from air and water, with soil supplying only trace minerals. Carbon fixation drives biomass. The operational implication: soil fertility is necessary but not sufficient, and the highest-leverage production investment is the canopy that fixes the most carbon per acre. The perennial polyculture wins on carbon-fixation throughput, not on fertility extraction.

The principle reshapes allocation. Soil amendment carries diminishing returns past a minimum threshold; canopy selection and succession-stage design carry compounding returns across decades. A well-chosen canopy compounds yield for eighty years; a well-amended annual bed compounds yield for one growing season.

05.3.5Allelopathic and browse-pressure constraints

Two specific constraints govern polyculture design in the temperate zone.

Design constraints

01 · JUGLONE RADIUS — walnut family (black walnut, butternut, hickory, pecan) secretes juglone from roots and canopy leaf-fall. Poisons sensitive crops (tomato, apple, blueberry, pine) out to 50 ft from a mature black walnut. Design segregates the allelopathic radius; juglone-tolerant species plant inside, sensitive species plant outside. 02 · DEER DENSITY CEILING — deer density above 20 per sq mi stops hardwood regeneration entirely via browse pressure on seedlings. Corrective culling must include does, because bucks-only harvest leaves reproductive capacity intact and fails the forest.

Both constraints are failure-mode avoidance rather than yield optimization. Violate them and the polyculture collapses at the seedling stage or at the juglone-sensitive crop. Respect them and the design proceeds.

05.3.6Dry-year / wet-year pioneer split

Weather variance kills single-crop systems. The Mormon-pioneer response is to diversify across water regimes every year.

Dry-year / wet-year split

Plant drought-tolerant crops (squash, amaranth, sorghum) every year. Plant moisture-loving crops (leafy greens, potatoes) every year. The season's weather decides which crop produces the bulk of that year's calories. The household eats from the winner and stores what the loser produced. Across 10 years the split averages to full caloric coverage against any weather pattern the region delivers.

The principle holds under any climate variance: hedge by planting against the full variance range, not against the mean expectation. This is the agricultural analog to the two-deep redundancy law in 05.2 and the three-chain architecture in 05.6.

05.3.7Henderson's thirteen success vectors

A production system that produces calories can still fail economically. Henderson's Farms with a Future names thirteen success vectors that together determine whether the enterprise survives.

The vectors: beginner footing (do not enter overextended), market niche (occupy a defensible product position), land access (own or secure multi-year lease), financing (match term to asset lifespan), whole-farm plan (every enterprise serves the plan), equipment (right-sized to scale), soil and water management (long-horizon capital), harvest processing (on-site where possible), marketing (direct-to-consumer captures value), records (measure what matters), accounting (monthly, not annual), human resources (labor is the critical constraint), and value-added products (raw commodity is a commodity; processed product is an asset).

Operator audit: every food-production initiative runs against the thirteen vectors before capital commits. An initiative strong on four vectors and weak on nine will fail regardless of caloric yield.

05.3.8Installation, function, failure, feed-forward

INSTALL. Read the climax biome of your latitude. Plant mast-bearing canopy first because the 10-to-20-year maturation is the longest clock on the homestead. Install the six-layer food-forest stack with niche-non-overlapping species at each level. Segregate juglone-sensitive species outside the 50-foot radius of any black walnut. Stand up a dry-year / wet-year crop split against weather variance. Run every production enterprise against Henderson's thirteen success vectors.

FUNCTION. The production system delivers annual harvest that replaces annual consumption, stores the mast-year and wet-year surplus against off-years, and compounds yield year over year as canopy matures and soil ecology builds. The oak-savanna-mimicking polyculture carries caloric output per acre above monocrop on the same ground and does so on trapped solar gain rather than on imported nitrogen and fuel.

FAILURE. The system fails when monoculture planting collapses to a single weather pattern, when deer overbrowse prevents regeneration, when a single crop's off-year becomes a terminal year, when juglone radius is ignored and sensitive crops die in place, or when the enterprise is weak on multiple Henderson success vectors and the economics fail before the polyculture matures.

FEED-FORWARD. 05.3 produces the calorie. 05.4 installs the passive-thermal storage envelope — root cellar and pit greenhouse — that bridges harvest to hungry gap without fossil heat or refrigeration.

SECTION 05.4

Food storage — root cellar, greenhouse, cold rooms

SUBSURFACE BASELINE~50°F YEAR-ROUND
CELLAR ENVELOPE32–40°F · 85–95% RH · GENTLY VENTILATED · ABOVE FREEZING ALWAYS
MICRO-ZONESCOLD-WET · COLD-DRY · COOL-DRY
GREENHOUSE GLAZING LOSS18× ALL-GLASS / 10× DOUBLE-GLAZED VS 4" INSULATED WALL
ROOF PITCHLATITUDE +20° (40–70° BAND EFFECTIVE)
MOVABLE INSULATION50% NIGHT LOSS REDUCTION · 90% WITH 0.5" DEAD-AIR GAP
THERMAL MASS55-GAL DRUM = 457 LB WATER · 457 BTU/°F SWING
VENT PIPE4" SOLID PLASTIC, GALVANIZED HOOD, SCREEN
DRAIN TILEPERFORATED AT FOOTING, GRAVEL BED, SLOPE AWAY

Production without storage is a feast followed by a famine. Storey bulletins A-76 (Build Your Own Underground Root Cellar) and A-37 (Building a Solar-Heated Pit Greenhouse) supply the passive-thermal infrastructure that bridges harvest to hungry gap. Both exploit the same thermodynamic fact: subsurface ground tracks at roughly 50°F year-round, buffered by soil thermal mass against the surface swings that kill stored food. The root cellar holds the cold-wet end of the storage spectrum; the pit greenhouse holds the cool-light end and doubles as off-season root storage. Brace Research Institute's solar-roof-pitch findings calibrate the greenhouse glazing geometry; the 4-inch insulated-wall comparison numbers from A-37 govern the wall-versus-glass tradeoff.

This section installs the subsurface 50°F thermodynamic baseline that makes passive thermal storage viable, the four-condition cellar envelope (cool, above freezing, humid, gently ventilated), the three micro-zone stratification (cold-wet, cold-dry, cool-dry) that segregates produce by storage chemistry, the pit-greenhouse glazing geometry with latitude-plus-twenty roof pitch and movable night insulation, the thermal-mass calibration via 55-gallon water drums, the pit-to-house symbiotic heat cycle that links greenhouse and dwelling into one thermal loop, and the pioneer dry-store methods (dehydration, salt-pack, lard-pack, root burial, smoking) that extend storage without electricity. Sources: Storey A-76 (Underground Root Cellar); Storey A-37 (Solar-Heated Pit Greenhouse); Brace Research Institute (roof-pitch optimization findings); Forgotten Skills of Self-Sufficiency (pioneer dry-store methods); 05.3 (the produce stream that storage receives).

05.4.1The subsurface 50°F baseline

Both cellar and greenhouse run on the same thermodynamic fact. Below the frost line, soil thermal mass buffers the surface swings.

Subsurface thermal baseline

Ground temperature below the frost line tracks at the regional annual mean — for most of the temperate US, approximately 50°F year-round. Soil thermal mass dampens diurnal swings to near zero and seasonal swings to under 10°F at typical cellar depths. The result: subsurface space is cooler than summer surface, warmer than winter surface, and effectively free heating and cooling.

Every storage decision in 05.4 exploits this baseline. The cellar wraps the subsurface in an envelope that holds 32–40°F by venting against the warmer baseline; the pit greenhouse uses the baseline as a heat reservoir against winter freeze. Without the subsurface anchor, the structures fail.

05.4.2The four-condition cellar envelope

The root cellar maintains four conditions simultaneously. Failure at any one collapses the storage.

Four cellar conditions
01COOL — 32–40°Fbelow the metabolism-acceleration threshold of most tubers and fruits.
02ABOVE FREEZING ALWAYS — cell-wall rupture at 32°F terminates the crop. The cellar runs cold but never freezes.
03HUMID — 85–95% RHbecause desiccation shrivels the harvest. Dirt floor supplies the humidity reservoir.
04GENTLY VENTILATED — stagnant air concentrates ethylene, CO₂, and mold. 4" solid plastic sewer pipe through roof with galvanized hood and plastic screen.

Construction follows the conditions. Dirt floor and concrete block walls under an earth-bermed roof supply passive thermal mass. The dirt floor doubles as the humidity reservoir. A two-door air-lock entry (outer door, buffer stairwell, inner door, cellar proper) eliminates direct atmospheric exchange during access; one-door entry breaches the envelope on every visit. The two classic failure modes are water intrusion and venting failure. Drainage installs perforated drain tile at footing, sloped away under two cubic yards of coarse gravel. Venting runs the 4" pipe with hood and screen.

05.4.3The three micro-zone stratification

Inside the cellar envelope, produce stratifies into three micro-zones by storage chemistry.

Cellar micro-zones
01COLD-WET (32–40°F90–95% RH) — carrots, beets, turnips, parsnips, cabbage, celery. Packed in damp sand or sawdust.
02COLD-DRY (32–40°F60–70% RH) — onions, garlic, shallots. Hung or stored in slatted crates.
03COOL-DRY (50–60°F60–70% RH) — winter squash, pumpkin, sweet potato. Typically outside the main cellar in a warmer pantry shelf.

Apples segregate entirely because they emit ethylene that accelerates ripening in nearby produce. STORE COLD WHAT YOU GROW COLD; STORE DRY WHAT YOU GROW DRY. Mismatching produce to micro-zone collapses the storage in weeks; matching extends storage to months.

05.4.4Pit-greenhouse glazing geometry

The solar-heated pit greenhouse extends the growing season into winter without fossil heat. The geometry is unforgiving.

Pit-greenhouse construction parameters

Walls sit underground in contact with the 50°F subsurface, insulated with 2" of foam from frost line to ground level. Only the south-facing roof is glazed. All-glass traditional greenhouse loses 18× more heat than a 4" fiberglass-insulated wall; even double-glazing loses 10× more. Roof pitch runs at latitude +20°, perpendicular to mid-winter noon sun for maximum gain when light is scarcest. Brace Research Institute: any slope from 40° to 70° effective, higher angles favor mid-winter, lower angles favor spring/fall. Movable roof insulation (rigid foam-core shutters or fiberglass-batt flexible blankets) clipped in place at dusk and removed at dawn cuts night heat loss by ~50%, and by ~90% when a 0.5" dead-air space sits between shutter and glazing.

The geometry calibrates to the operator's specific latitude. A pit greenhouse built to latitude-plus-twenty at 45°N has a 65° roof pitch; at 35°N, 55°. The Brace Research findings give a 30° range of acceptable error, but optimization at the operator's exact latitude maximizes mid-winter gain when it matters most.

05.4.5Thermal-mass calibration

Daytime solar gain stores in water mass; nighttime release extracts it.

55-gallon water drum = 457 lb water = 457 BTU per °F of thermal swing. A bank of dozens of drums against the north wall yields kilowatt-hours of buffer that release through the night, holding the greenhouse above 40°F when outside drops below freezing. Off-season, the pit greenhouse doubles as root storage, with carrots and beets held in sand boxes on the floor where the subsurface 50°F baseline preserves them through summer.

The drum bank is the simplest, lowest-cost thermal mass available. Other media (rock, concrete, phase-change materials) work but cost more per BTU stored. Drums are the canonical solution because they are cheap, replaceable, and high-density.

05.4.6Pit-to-house symbiotic heat cycle

The pit greenhouse and the dwelling can run a symbiotic thermal loop that reduces both heating loads simultaneously.

Pit-to-house heat cycling

DAY · greenhouse solar surplus vents into the dwelling through a duct in the shared wall. The greenhouse runs slightly cooler, the dwelling runs warmer, the operator burns less wood. NIGHT · dwelling heat ducts back to the greenhouse through the same path or a separate return. The dwelling cools slightly, the greenhouse holds above freeze. NET · house heating load reduces, greenhouse freeze risk eliminates.

The cycling loop is the highest-leverage upgrade to a pit-greenhouse-plus-dwelling pair. It converts two separate thermal systems into one coupled loop and the coupled loop runs at higher net efficiency than either alone. THE LOOP REQUIRES SHARED-WALL CONSTRUCTION OR AT MINIMUM A SHORT INSULATED DUCT RUN. Site placement decides whether the loop is even available; the cellar-greenhouse-dwelling triangle is sited together for this reason.

05.4.7Pioneer dry-store methods

Storage extends past the cellar's reach via the pioneer dry-store methods, all of which run without electricity.

Dry-store techniques
01DEHYDRATION — solar racks or wood-fired drying. Fruits, vegetables, meats. Multi-year shelf life.
02SALT-PACK — meat, fish. Salt draws water out, prevents bacterial growth.
03LARD-PACK — meat sealed in rendered fat. Anaerobic preservation.
04ROOT BURIAL — root vegetables stored directly in straw-insulated outdoor pits. Crude form of cellar storage.
05COLD AND HOT SMOKING — meat, fish. Phenols and dehydration combine for long preservation.

Each method handles a different produce class and a different storage horizon. The household that runs the cellar plus three or four of the pioneer methods covers nearly all preservation needs without refrigeration. The Mormon long-storage canon in Forgotten Skills documents the full pioneer methodology.

05.4.8Installation, function, failure, feed-forward

INSTALL. Site cellar and greenhouse together for one excavator visit. Place pit greenhouse on the south side of the dwelling for the symbiotic heat-cycling loop. Drainage first, then walls, then roof, then ventilation. Movable insulation built and fitted before first winter.

FUNCTION. The cellar holds stored produce intact from October through April; the pit greenhouse grows through January at temperate latitudes; the symbiotic heat cycle reduces dwelling heating load and eliminates greenhouse freeze risk; the pioneer dry-store methods extend storage further into multi-year horizons without electricity.

FAILURE. The cellar fails on water intrusion, venting failure, mismatched produce-to-zone, or temperature drift outside the 32–40°F band. The greenhouse fails on roof-pitch error, undersized thermal mass, missing night insulation, or shading from poorly placed structures. Both fail when calibration logging is skipped through the first year and adjustments are not made.

FEED-FORWARD. Produce stored requires water to grow. 05.5 installs the water infrastructure that runs the homestead's hydraulic balance.

SECTION 05.5

Water infrastructure at homestead scale

COUPLED PROBLEMSCOLLECTION · TREATMENT · STORAGE
YIELD ARITHMETIC1" RAIN × 1,000 SQ FT = 600 GAL
SAMPLE HOMESTEAD1,500 SQ FT ROOF × 30" ANNUAL = ~27,000 GAL/YR
CATCHMENT CHAINROOF → GUTTERS → DOWNSPOUT → FIRST-FLUSH DIVERTER → LEAF SCREEN → CISTERN → IN-LINE FILTER → POU
HEAT DISINFECTION185°F × 10 MIN (CONSERVATIVE CYST KILL) · 212°F × 1 MIN SEA-LEVEL (× 3 MIN ABOVE 5,000 FT)
RIPARIAN BUFFERS100 FT PERENNIAL · 50 FT INTERMITTENT
WATER MASS1 GAL = 8.3 LB · 2-PERSON HOUSEHOLD = 33 LB/DAY
REDUNDANCY3-DEEP (WELL · RAINWATER · SURFACE)

Water at homestead scale is three coupled problems: collection, treatment, storage. Harvesting H2O supplies the catchment-chain architecture and the volumetric arithmetic; Living Off The Grid supplies the off-grid well and distribution doctrine; Backyard Woodland supplies the Six Woodland Rules that govern on-land water (riparian buffers, BMP for logging operations, erosion control); Storey A-76 supplies the cellar-drainage architecture that generalizes to every below-grade structure. The volumetric arithmetic is unforgiving and the arithmetic is also the operator's freedom: 1 inch of rain on 1,000 square feet of collection area yields 600 gallons, which means a 1,500-square-foot roof under 30 inches of annual rainfall yields roughly 27,000 gallons per year — far above a two-person household's drinking-water need. Collection surface caps the yield, not rainfall frequency.

This section installs the volumetric arithmetic of rainwater catchment, the canonical seven-stage catchment chain from roof to point of use, the two-threshold heat-disinfection standard that makes any collected water potable, the Six Woodland Rules that preserve water quality on the land the homestead sits on, the best-management practices for operations that disturb soil and water (waterbars, stream crossings, riparian buffers, skid-trail closure), the cellar-drainage architecture as a specific application of soil-water-management principles, the off-grid well and distribution system that makes the homestead its own water utility, and the three-deep water redundancy (well, rainwater, surface) that prevents single-source failure. Sources: Harvesting H2O (catchment chain, volumetric arithmetic, first-flush diverter); Living Off The Grid (well doctrine, off-grid distribution, winterization); Backyard Woodland (Six Woodland Rules, riparian buffers, BMP for logging); Storey A-76 (cellar drainage as general principle); 01 Primary Systems (the 3-day water survival horizon that sets redundancy).

05.5.1The volumetric arithmetic

Rainwater yield is a linear function of collection area and annual rainfall.

Catchment volumetric arithmetic

1 inch of rainfall × 1,000 sq ft of collection area = 600 gallons. Extended: a 1,500-sq-ft roof under 30 inches of annual rainfall yields ~27,000 gallons per year. Collection surface caps the yield, not rainfall frequency. In most temperate climates, total annual rainfall far exceeds household drinking-water need; the constraint is storage and seasonal distribution, not annual total.

The arithmetic reshapes intuition. An operator worried about "enough rainfall" is almost always over-worried about annual volume and under-worried about seasonal distribution. The design challenge is storing wet-season surplus against dry-season deficit, not capturing a thin annual yield.

05.5.2The seven-stage catchment chain

The canonical chain runs from precipitation to potable output.

Rainwater catchment chain
01ROOF — collection surface. Metal preferred for water quality; asphalt shingle contributes particulates.
02GUTTERS — route precipitation to downspouts. Must be debris-cleaned.
03DOWNSPOUT — conducts water to first-flush diverter.
04FIRST-FLUSH DIVERTER — discards the initial gallons of each rain event (roof dust, bird waste, pollen, leaf debris). Sized to roof area.
05LEAF SCREEN — blocks bulk organic matter before cistern.
06CISTERN — bulk storage. Above-ground for lower cost and access; below-ground for colder darker storage that retards algae.
07IN-LINE FILTER — sediment plus carbon plus UV or ceramic at point of use for potable output.

Skipping any stage degrades the system. A catchment without first-flush diverter loads the cistern with the worst of the rain event; a cistern without in-line filter delivers raw surface water to the tap. EACH STAGE HANDLES A SPECIFIC CONTAMINANT CLASS THAT THE OTHERS DO NOT ADDRESS.

05.5.3The two-threshold heat-disinfection standard

Heat-based disinfection is the canonical off-grid potable-water treatment.

185°F for 10 minutes — catches heat-resistant cysts conservatively. Used where fuel is scarce and simmer is easier to maintain than rolling boil. 212°F rolling boil for 1 minute — sea-level standard for bacteria, viruses, and protozoan cysts. Extended to 3 minutes above 5,000 ft elevation where boiling point drops. Boiling is 100% effective against pathogens because heat denatures microbial protein. The only question is achieving and holding the temperature long enough. Chemical treatment (chlorine, iodine) is slower, less reliable against protozoan cysts, and requires proper dosing.

The two thresholds cover every pathogen class the operator encounters in temperate-zone surface water. Heavy metal contamination and industrial chemicals require filtration beyond heat treatment; but for microbial contamination, a fire and a pot suffice.

05.5.4The Six Woodland Rules and water discipline

Backyard Woodland's Six Woodland Rules govern the land the homestead sits on. Two are explicit water rules.

Six Woodland Rules (water-relevant subset)
RULEPROTECT SOIL — because erosion is water-quality loss downstream and root-zone destruction upstream.
RULEPROTECT WATER — through 100-ft buffer strips along perennial streams and 50-ft strips along intermittent streams, with no harvest in riparian zones and hardened stream crossings rather than direct drive-throughs.

The buffer distances are not arbitrary. Riparian vegetation roots stabilize stream banks, filter surface runoff before it reaches the channel, and shade the water column against temperature spikes that stress aquatic life. Violating the buffer on one harvest may not produce visible damage; violating it repeatedly across decades collapses the stream's ecological integrity and with it the water-quality basis for any downstream draw.

05.5.5Best Management Practices for operations

Logging and grading operations either honor water discipline or damage it.

Logging and grading BMPs

WATERBARS — angled ditches across logging roads that shed runoff sideways before it channels into erosive flow. Installed at intervals calibrated to slope. STREAM CROSSINGS — bridges, culverts, or hardened fords. No direct drive-through of flowing water. RIPARIAN BUFFERS — no-cut zones. Equipment excluded. SKID-TRAIL CLOSURE — waterbar and seed every trail at job's end. Unclosed trails channel water and erode.

These practices extend beyond logging to any homestead operation that moves equipment over soil: road construction, garden expansion, pond creation, driveway maintenance. The discipline is the same. EVERY DISTURBED SURFACE EITHER DRAINS CORRECTLY OR EROSDES. Install the drainage as the operation completes, not after the first rain.

05.5.6Cellar-drainage architecture as general principle

The Storey A-76 cellar-drainage specification generalizes to every below-grade structure on the homestead.

The specification: 40 feet of perforated drain tile at the footing, sloped away under two cubic yards of coarse gravel, intercepts groundwater before it ponds against the cellar wall. The principle: perimeter drainage plus gravel bed plus slope-away routing extracts hydraulic pressure from the wall before it can migrate through. Applied to root cellar, greenhouse, basement, foundation, retaining wall — the architecture is identical. Skip it and water finds its way through concrete or block within years; install it and the structure stays dry across decades.

05.5.7Off-grid well and three-deep redundancy

The homesteader becomes the water utility. Three-deep redundancy is the standing architecture.

Three-deep water redundancy
01WELL WITH SUBMERSIBLE PUMP — primary draw. Grid-optional through solar or generator-backed pressure system. Pressure tank plus bulk cistern delivers buffer and flow.
02RAINWATER CATCHMENT — secondary. The seven-stage chain, gravity-fed or pump-assisted.
03SURFACE WATER OR SPRING — tertiary backup. Pond or stream or spring box. Heat-disinfected before potable use.

Winterization buries lines below frost line and runs heat tape on any exposed segment. Emergency draw taps gravity-fed rainwater or surface-water backup when the pump fails. Water is heavier than the operator intuits: 1 gallon is 8.3 lb, and a two-person household at 2 gal/day each moves 33 lb of water daily without plumbing. Infrastructure (pipe, cistern, hand pump) is the labor-saving heart of a sustainment homestead, and the labor it saves is the operator's back.

05.5.8Installation, function, failure, feed-forward

INSTALL. Read the site for drainage and slope before any construction. Site the cistern uphill from the dwelling where possible, because gravity flow eliminates pump load. Install the seven-stage catchment chain on the primary collection surface. Drill and equip the well as the primary draw. Identify and develop a surface-water or spring backup. Install riparian buffers and BMP for every land-disturbing operation.

FUNCTION. The system meets daily household demand across the driest month of the year. Emergency draw activates within 5 minutes of primary failure. Rainwater catchment captures enough wet-season surplus to carry through dry-season deficit. Heat-disinfection thresholds hold for any potable output from non-primary sources.

FAILURE. The system fails when the cistern runs dry before the next rain (undersized storage), when drainage ponds against the dwelling foundation (drainage architecture violated), when winterization gaps produce a frozen pipe at -10°F (insulation or heat-tape failure), when the first-flush diverter goes unmaintained (cistern contaminated), or when riparian buffers are violated and upstream water quality degrades.

FEED-FORWARD. Everything downhill drinks your runoff. Water management is a community obligation, not a private one. 05.6 installs the three-chain power architecture that runs the pumps, the lighting, the tools, and the heating that the homestead depends on.

SECTION 05.6

Power — wood gas, biodiesel, solar, generator

CHAIN COUNT3 (THERMAL · LIQUID/GAS FUEL · ELECTRICAL)
WOOD GAS COMPOSITION~20% CO · 15–20% H₂ · 2–5% CH₄ · BALANCE N₂ + CO₂ + H₂O
TAR CRACK TEMP1,600–2,200°F (IMBERT REDUCTION ZONE)
BIODIESEL REACTION~60°C · CATALYST 3.5 g KOH/L OR 5.0 g NaOH/L VIRGIN OIL · TITRATION ADJUSTMENT
FFA PRETREATMENT THRESHOLD> 3–5% FFA
PV SIZING3–5 kWh/DAY LOAD → 1.5–2 kW ARRAY (4 PSH) · 10–20 kWh BATTERY (2–4 DAYS AUTONOMY)
FUELWOOD CALORIFICHICKORY/LOCUST/WHITE OAK 26–28 MBTU/CORD · MAPLE/RED OAK/BEECH/ASH 22–24 · PINE/SPRUCE/ASPEN 14–18
SEASONING< 20% MOISTURE MINIMUM · 50% GREEN UNUSABLE

An off-grid homestead runs three parallel energy chains. Single-chain failure kills the homestead; three chains buffer against any one chain's failure mode. Gasifiers (Mother Earth News reprint of the FEMA wartime manual and related sources) supplies the wood-gas doctrine; Biodiesel Basics and Beyond supplies the transesterification chemistry and the titration-based catalyst calibration; Living Off The Grid supplies the solar PV plus battery bank plus inverter plus generator architecture that runs electrical loads. Each chain handles a different energy form and a different failure mode. Wood thermal runs on solid fuel and releases energy as heat; the liquid/gas fuel chain runs engines and drives mechanical work; the electrical chain powers pumps, lights, electronics, and tools. Three chains, three independent failure modes, one resilient system.

This section installs the three-chain energy architecture, the wood-gasification doctrine (Imbert downdraft and FEMA stratified) with its tar-crack chemistry and producer-gas composition, the biodiesel transesterification chemistry with titration-based catalyst calibration and post-reaction quality control, the solar PV sizing math that translates daily kWh load into array plus battery plus generator specification, the fuelwood calorific ordering that determines species selection for the thermal chain, the seasoning threshold that separates usable fuelwood from unusable, the sequential installation order (thermal first, electrical second, gasifier third) that matches skill growth, and the two-chain-failure resilience standard that defines system success. Sources: Gasifiers (FEMA wartime manual, Imbert downdraft, stratified downdraft, producer gas composition, CO hazard); Biodiesel Basics and Beyond (transesterification, titration, FFA pretreatment, wash protocol, 27/3 quality check); Living Off The Grid (PV sizing, battery architecture, generator backup, winterization); Backyard Woodland (fuelwood calorific species ordering, seasoning discipline).

05.6.1The three-chain architecture

Energy arrives in three forms on the homestead. The architecture handles each form with its own chain.

Three-chain energy architecture
01SOLID-FUEL THERMAL — wood in a stove. Space heat, cooking, hot water through coils. Simplest and most reliable. Runs without batteries or electronics.
02LIQUID / GAS FUEL FOR ENGINES — wood gas from a gasifier, biodiesel from vegetable oil and methanol, propane purchased when available. Drives chainsaws, tractors, generators, vehicles.
03ELECTRICAL — solar photovoltaic plus battery bank plus inverter as primarygenerator as backup · micro-hydro or small wind when site permits. Powers pumps, lighting, electronics, refrigeration, tools.

Each chain handles a different energy form and each is physically independent. A solar-grid failure does not stop the wood stove; a chainsaw failure does not stop the PV array. INDEPENDENCE IS THE POINT. The homestead that runs one chain is fragile; the homestead that runs three chains is resilient to any single-chain failure mode.

05.6.2Wood gasification — Imbert and FEMA stratified

Wood gasification converts solid wood fuel into combustible gas suitable for internal combustion engines.

Gasifier designs

IMBERT DOWNDRAFT — gas flows downward through the reduction zone where tars crack at 1,600–2,200°F into combustible gases. Produces tar-lean output suitable for engines. Tradeoff: tight geometry requires uniform dry sized blocks. FEMA STRATIFIED DOWNDRAFT — simpler, fuel-tolerant of mixed sizes. Produces tar-heavier gas, better for direct thermal use than engine work without post-cleanup.

Producer gas composition from a well-run gasifier runs approximately 20% carbon monoxide, 15–20% hydrogen, 2–5% methane, and balance nitrogen with secondary CO₂ and H₂O. CO is the combustion workhorse; H₂ adds flame speed; CH₄ adds energy density; N₂ deadweight dilutes the mix, which is why wood gas has roughly half the energy density of natural gas per unit volume.

05.6.3The CO hazard — design implications

The lethal hazard of wood gas is direct. CO is invisible, odorless, and 20% of the output.

Wood-gas plumbing standards

Plumbing runs hard-piped, flange-sealed, and leak-tested. Engine rooms sit outside the dwelling, or are sealed-and-ventilated with CO monitoring at multiple points. Operator wears a personal CO monitor during startup, shutdown, and any maintenance on running plumbing. Startup and shutdown procedures vent producer gas through a flare until engine is confirmed drawing; no inhabited space draws producer gas during these transitions.

Non-negotiable. Every wood-gas installation carries this discipline or it carries the risk of silent fatality. The FEMA manual, written under wartime necessity, embeds this discipline in every procedure.

05.6.4Biodiesel — transesterification chemistry

Biodiesel production runs transesterification on plant oil.

Transesterification reaction

Triglyceride + methanol + catalyst (KOH or NaOH) → biodiesel (methyl ester) + glycerin. The three fatty-acid chains on the triglyceride swap onto methanol, producing three molecules of fatty-acid methyl ester plus one glycerin byproduct. FAME viscosity matches petroleum diesel and burns in any diesel engine without modification. Reaction runs at approximately 60°C.

Catalyst quantity calibrates by titration. A 0.1% KOH solution titrated against feedstock oil with phenolphthalein indicator produces a millimeter-per-liter figure for the extra catalyst needed to neutralize free fatty acids. Base catalyst for virgin oil runs roughly 3.5 g KOH per liter or 5.0 g NaOH per liter, plus the titration adjustment. Feedstock with FFA content above 3–5% requires acid esterification pretreatment, because soap formation dominates otherwise and the batch fails.

05.6.5Biodiesel — post-reaction quality control

Post-reaction, biodiesel gets washed with water to remove residual methanol, soap, and glycerin. Finished-product verification runs three canonical tests.

Biodiesel quality checks
01SOAP TEST — phenolphthalein in wash water stays clear when soap is gone. Pink indicates residual soap and further washing.
02METHANOL REMOVAL CHECK — finished fuel should not flash at low temperature; residual methanol signals incomplete wash.
0327/3 HOT-PAN CHECK — low-tech quality verification; residual water or contamination produces visible foam or bubble pattern in the hot pan.

Producing biodiesel without running the quality tests gambles every diesel engine the fuel enters. The tests are cheap; the failure cost is an injector pump or a cracked engine block.

05.6.6Solar PV sizing math

PV sizing targets daily kilowatt-hour consumption plus battery-bank autonomy across cloudy weather.

Canonical small-household sizing

DAILY LOAD · 3–5 kWh/day (typical small off-grid household with efficient appliances). PV ARRAY · 1.5–2 kW (assuming 4 peak-sun hours). Oversize array reduces cloud-deficit risk. BATTERY BANK · 10–20 kWh (2–4 days autonomy). Oversize the battery bank before oversizing the array because storage buffers cloud risk. MPPT CHARGE CONTROLLER + PURE-SINE INVERTER · required for efficient conversion and for loads sensitive to waveform quality (motors, electronics). GENERATOR BACKUP · mandatory, not optional.

The generator is mandatory because multi-day cloud events deplete batteries below safe draw, and deep discharge damages the bank irreversibly. Generator restores charge during cloud cycles, covers well-pump surge loads, and handles power-tool use during construction and winter short-day deficits.

05.6.7Fuelwood calorific ordering and seasoning

The thermal chain runs on wood. Species selection and seasoning discipline determine output.

Fuelwood calorific values (seasoned cord, MBTU)
01SHAGBARK HICKORYBLACK LOCUST · WHITE OAK — 26–28 MBTU/cord. Highest-density hardwoods.
02SUGAR MAPLERED OAK · BEECH · ASH — 22–24 MBTU/cord. Mid-density hardwoods.
03PINESPRUCE · ASPEN · BASSWOOD — 14–18 MBTU/cord. Softwoods, higher creosote deposition in flue.

Seasoning threshold: green wood at 50% moisture cannot gasify efficiently and produces creosote; seasoned wood below 20% moisture is the minimum standard. Split-and-stack timing is one to two years ahead of use for most hardwoods, longer for dense species like oak. The operator who cuts in spring and burns the same fall burns creosote, not wood.

05.6.8Sequential installation order

The three chains install sequentially against available capital and mechanical skill.

THERMAL FIRST — simplest and most reliable. Cast-iron stove with a seasoned cord stack runs without batteries or electronics. SOLAR PV SECOND — against typical daily load. Oversize the battery bank before oversizing the array because storage buffers cloud risk. GASIFIER THIRD — once mechanical skill matures. Tar-cleanup discipline separates a working gasifier from a clogged museum piece.

Calibrate by logging daily kWh draw across seasons and watching battery state-of-charge trends. Any one chain will fail; the three-chain architecture is the response to that certainty.

05.6.9Installation, function, failure, feed-forward

INSTALL. Stand up wood thermal in the first construction cycle. Install PV array, battery bank, inverter, MPPT, and generator backup in the second. Build gasifier in the third, only after diesel experience gives the operator the mechanical base to run tar cleanup properly.

FUNCTION. The system functions when simultaneous failure of two chains leaves the third covering critical load. Wood thermal covers space heat and cooking without any other chain. PV with generator backup covers pumps, lights, and refrigeration. Gasifier or biodiesel covers engine fuel for mechanical work.

FAILURE. The system fails when CO leaks into an occupied space (wood-gas plumbing violation), when the battery bank sulfates from chronic under-charge (PV under-sized or cloud-deficit unmitigated), when no fuel stockpile remains against a week-long cloud event (reserve discipline violated), or when green wood gets burned and the flue creosotes into fire risk.

FEED-FORWARD. Engines break and blades dull. 05.7 installs the forge and heat-treat doctrine that restores edge tools indefinitely.
