theFIELD.run / CONSTRUCT_APPLICATIONS / 06 COMMAND / 06.4 Intelligence — cycle, disciplines, area study
SECTION 06.4

Intelligence — cycle, disciplines, area study

Intelligence cycle. Five phases — Planning & Direction → Collection → Processing & Analysis → Production → Dissemination → back to Planning.
Four disciplines. OSINT (open source), HUMINT (human), SIGINT (signals), IMINT (imagery). Each has distinct strengths, failure modes, counter-intel vulnerabilities.
Five product requirements. Timely, Relevant, Accurate, Specific, Predictive. Miss any one and the product may be useless.
Spatial bounding. AO (Area of Operations, authorized action space), AI (Area of Interest, 1–3× AO radius scaled to threat speed), NAI (Named Area of Interest, specific geography cued to collection).
Four threat types. Conventional, irregular, catastrophic, disruptive. Serious area study addresses all four.
Admiralty Code. Reliability A–F, credibility 1–6. Source quality evaluation two-dimensional.
Cooper's color codes. White (unprepared/unaware — never in public), Yellow (relaxed aware baseline), Orange (alert to specific threat), Red (acting), Black (panic — failure mode).
Daily Intelligence Check-Up. 5–10 minutes every morning — local weather (≤ 72-hr forecast), local social media, local news, emergency alert feeds.

Intelligence feeds the Orient step of OODA. Without intelligence, orientation operates on priors alone. The Area Intelligence Handbook and FM 34-36 supply the cycle and the disciplines. The Green Beret Area Study Workbook and Base Line Training supply the living-document methodology. Intelligence is not a report; it is a process. The product is the process of staying current.

This section installs the five-phase intelligence cycle, the four collection disciplines with strengths and vulnerabilities, the five product requirements, the AO/AI/NAI spatial bounding, the four-threat-type adversary stratification, the Area Study as central artifact with its structure and update cadence, Cooper's color codes for personal readiness calibration, Anderson's Daily Intelligence Check-Up, and the Admiralty Code for source evaluation. Sources: Area Intelligence Handbook; FM 34-36; Green Beret Area Study Workbook; Base Line Training; Cooper via Base Line Training.

06.4.1The five-phase intelligence cycle

Planning & Direction. Specify what you need to know, for whom, by when. Priority Intelligence Requirements (PIRs) express the question set.
Collection. Gather raw information through the appropriate disciplines. Match discipline to question.
Processing & Analysis. Convert raw material into evaluated intelligence. Correlate across sources. Apply the Admiralty Code.
Production. Package the intelligence for the consumer — decision-maker, operator, analyst downstream.
Dissemination. Deliver the product. Consumer feedback generates the next planning cycle.

The cycle is continuous. Feedback from Dissemination refines Planning. No phase runs once; every phase runs continuously with shifting emphasis.

06.4.2The four collection disciplines

OSINT (Open Source). News, social media, public records, commercial satellite, academic literature, corporate filings. Cheapest. Often the most valuable. Vulnerable to deliberate disinformation.
HUMINT (Human). Interviews, observation, sources, informants. Expensive and rare. Subject to deception, source motivation drift, compromise.
SIGINT (Signals). Interception of communications and electronic emissions. Requires technical capability. Vulnerable to spoofing, encryption, emissions discipline from target.
IMINT (Imagery). Satellite, aerial, ground photography, mapping. Requires platform access. Vulnerable to concealment, weather, revisit-time gaps.

Each discipline has characteristic strengths, failure modes, and counter-intelligence vulnerabilities. The mature operator runs multiple disciplines in parallel; single-discipline intelligence is brittle.

06.4.3The five product requirements

DEF

Timely. In hand before the decision deadline. Late intelligence is historical curiosity. Relevant. Answers the decision-maker's question. Not adjacent. Not interesting. Relevant. Accurate. Corresponds to reality. Corroborated where possible. Specific. Actionable at the tactical level. Vague intelligence is useless intelligence. Predictive. Forecasts what is likely to happen, not only what has happened.

A product satisfying four of five may be useless if it misses the fifth. Accurate-Timely-Relevant-Specific without Predictive leaves the decision-maker reacting instead of anticipating.

06.4.4Spatial bounding — AO, AI, NAI

DEF

Area of Operations (AO). The geographic space where the unit is authorized to act. Defined in coordinates. Area of Interest (AI). Surrounds the AO at 1–3× its radius, scaled to threat speed. Captures events that could affect the AO without being inside it. Threat arriving by foot → small AI; threat arriving by vehicle → medium; threat arriving by air or cyber → large. Named Area of Interest (NAI). Specific geography where a predicted event will manifest or confirm. Cued to collection. The NAI is the place you look to answer a PIR.

The boundary set structures the entire collection effort. Without AO/AI/NAI, collection drifts — you watch everywhere and see nothing.

06.4.5The four threat types

Conventional. State armies, armor, air, naval, strategic-level forces.
Irregular. Insurgents, guerrillas, militias, armed criminal groups.
Catastrophic. WMD, mass-casualty attack, grid-scale infrastructure attack (see 06.9).
Disruptive. Novel technologies that break the current paradigm — AI, drones, cyber, biotech.

A serious area study addresses all four. Stratifying the adversary picture prevents the common error of optimizing against one type while another dominates the actual threat environment.

06.4.6The Area Study — central artifact

The Area Study is a standing, continuously updated document capturing geography, demographics, economy, politics and governance (formal and informal), infrastructure, security, and local key personalities for a specified AO. The product is the process of staying current, never a one-shot report. An area study you stop updating is a lying document within weeks.

Section structure: terrain and climate; population and demographics; political and governance structures (formal government, informal power centers, religious, tribal, criminal); economy and infrastructure; security forces and law-enforcement; key personalities with relationship maps; historical context; current events summary. Version the document. Date every update. Track confidence levels on claims. Expire claims that have not been refreshed within their relevance window.

06.4.7Cooper's color codes and the Daily Check-Up

DEF

White. Unprepared and unaware. Never be in White in public. The failure state from which all other failures compound. Yellow. Relaxed and aware. The baseline for the operator in uncontrolled environments. Not paranoid — attentive. Orange. Alert to a probable specific threat. Indicators have triggered; you have raised posture. Red. Acting. The engagement, pursuit, or evasion is under way. Black. Panic. The failure mode to prevent. Operators who spend their daily life in White skip straight to Black when a threat materializes. Yellow-baselined operators de-escalate through Orange to Red without Black.

Anderson's Daily Intelligence Check-Up supplies the cadence that keeps Yellow fresh. Five to ten minutes every morning. Sample local weather (never more than a 72-hour forecast; longer forecasts are noise). Local social media for ground-level event reports. Local news for official-frame events. Emergency alert feeds (NOAA weather, state emergency management, AMBER/Silver Alerts). Compound the daily samples into a weekly pattern recognition pass.

06.4.8The Admiralty Code — source evaluation

Reliability is graded A through F: A = completely reliable, B = usually reliable, C = fairly reliable, D = not usually reliable, E = unreliable, F = unknown. Credibility is graded 1 through 6: 1 = confirmed by other sources, 2 = probably true, 3 = possibly true, 4 = doubtful, 5 = improbable, 6 = unknown. Every intelligence claim tags with a two-character grade (e.g., B-2). Single-source intelligence rarely rates above C-3 until corroborated. Multiple independent sources reporting the same fact push the grade upward.

06.4.9Install, function, failure, feed-forward

Install the subsystem through structured sequence. Define AO boundaries in coordinates. Map the AI at 1–3× radius scaled to threat speed. Pull the OSINT baseline across all four threat types. Conduct terrain, population, infrastructure, and threat sub-studies. Identify PIRs. Set NAIs to cue collection. Publish version 1.0 with a daily or weekly update cadence. Evaluate every claim on the Admiralty Code. Enforce compartmentation — not everyone needs to know everything.

The subsystem functions when you can answer, for any operational question, which layer of the area study holds the answer and which NAI is cued to confirm. The Daily Check-Up feeds the Area Study continuously. Sources stay diverse across OSINT, HUMINT, SIGINT, IMINT. PIRs stay current against changing operational questions.

It fails when the Area Study ossifies and becomes a historical document rather than a current one, when a single source dominates collection (source capture → single-source failure), when intelligence and operations run on separate loops (intelligence produces reports no one reads; operations act without intelligence support), or when the operator stays in White daily and skips to Black when a threat emerges.

Intelligence hands forward to 06.5 (PSYOP — where the intelligence on audience shapes the messages that move the moral level). uOrient on evidence, not on preference.u

theFIELD.run / CONSTRUCT_APPLICATIONS / 06 COMMAND / 06.5 PSYOP and influence — the moral-strategic domain
SECTION 06.5

PSYOP and influence — the moral-strategic domain

Doctrinal frame. Guerrilla PSYOP — every combatant is simultaneously a propagandist; every act is a propaganda act.
Armed Propaganda Team (APT). 6–10 members, ≥ 14 days training, deployed in rotations to 6 selected towns, ≤ 3 days per visit.
Target-audience matrix. 2 × 2 — Primary/Secondary × Interior/Exterior. Four quadrants, four distinct messages.
Three-person cell. Member A knows B and C; B knows A and D in another cell; C knows A and E in another cell; D and E unknown to each other and to A. Compromise of one exposes ≤ 2.
Mass meeting four-role template. Inside commando, shock troops, placard carriers, messengers. Engineered event.
Speech structure handles. Anaphora, antithesis, prolepsis, litotes, preterition.
Truth-first rule. Guerrilla propaganda must be truthful because it must be believed. A single caught lie costs months of credibility.
Inform vs Influence (FM 3-13). Inform = transmit truth. Influence = change behavior. Same message may do either or both. Legal and ethical rules differ.

Intelligence tells you what is; PSYOP shapes what is believed. The CIA Manual for Psychological Operations in Guerrilla Warfare and FM 3-13 supply the doctrine. The 4GW Handbook supplies the moral-level frame that makes influence the decisive domain. In 4GW, the strategic-moral cell is the dominant terrain. PSYOP is how you fight on that terrain.

This section installs the propagandist-combatant identity, armed propaganda and the APT delivery vehicle, the target-audience matrix that structures message design, the three-person clandestine cell architecture, the front-organization principle, mass-meeting engineering with the four-role template, speech-structure mechanical handles, the truth-first rule, and the Inform/Influence doctrinal distinction. Sources: CIA Manual for Psychological Operations in Guerrilla Warfare; FM 3-13 Inform and Influence Activities; 4GW Handbook.

06.5.1Every combatant is a propagandist — the inverse holds identically

Every act is a propaganda act. Help given to a farmer, the correction of a subordinate, the treatment of a prisoner, the respect shown to a woman — all transmit your message to anyone who witnesses or hears reported. The inverse holds identically. Every atrocity, every theft, every arrogance is adversary propaganda delivered by your own hand. There are no neutral acts in 4GW.

The implication for command is direct. Discipline of the cadre is not only a tactical-military matter; it is a strategic-moral matter. A unit that behaves with restraint and respect builds the moral reservoir on which 4GW victory rests. A unit that behaves badly burns the reservoir and loses regardless of tactical performance.

06.5.2Armed propaganda and the Armed Propaganda Team

DEF

Armed propaganda. Propaganda that travels with and is protected by armed force, aiming to demonstrate through visible presence that an alternative power exists, can protect, can organize, can deliver services, and can endure. Armed Propaganda Team (APT). Unit of 6–10 members, trained ≥ 14 days, deployed in rotations to 6 selected towns, ≤ 3 days per visit.

APT tasks: introduce the cause, identify local sympathizers, conduct target-audience analysis on the ground, organize front groups, depart before triggering regime response. The APT does not hold ground; it builds connection and disperses before counter-pressure can concentrate.

06.5.3The target-audience matrix

Primary-Interior. Those inside the contested area whose behavior you need to change directly. Reach by face-to-face, local radio, leaflet, neighborhood meeting.
Secondary-Interior. Those inside the area who influence the primary — religious leaders, elders, teachers, local journalists. Reach by personal relationship, indirect briefing, hosted event.
Primary-Exterior. Those outside the area whose behavior you need to change — international donors, diaspora communities, decision-makers in the metropole. Reach by written communique, foreign press, social media targeted by geography.
Secondary-Exterior. Those outside who influence the primary-exterior — international press, NGOs, academic experts. Reach by background briefing, leaked document, expert interview.

Each quadrant demands a distinct message, channel, and tone. Message-per-audience beats message-for-all every time. The same factual core may need different framing for each quadrant; the truth is preserved while emphasis shifts.

06.5.4The three-person clandestine cell

DEF

Cell architecture. Member A knows B and C. B knows A and D in another cell. C knows A and E in another cell. D and E do not know each other or A. Compromise of any one member exposes at most two others. Cells federate upward in the same three-branching structure.

The architecture is mathematically minimal for clandestine work. Two-person cells lack redundancy; four-person cells expand exposure on compromise. Three is the discipline. Apply equally to digital cells, mutual-aid networks, and any organization that must continue function under hostile observation.

06.5.5Front organizations

Unions, student groups, mothers' committees, sports clubs, agricultural cooperatives, cultural associations — these serve as the overt face of clandestine political work. The front is legitimate on its surface; it pursues real interests of its membership; it does not advertise the political program. Compromise of the front does not compromise the underlying organization because the front is what it appears to be plus an additional layer of purpose. Front-name discipline keeps the name neutral, aspirational, locally resonant — Committee for Water Rights, Mothers Against the Curfew, Cooperative Farmers' League — never ideological.

06.5.6Mass meeting engineering — four roles

Inside commando. Sits in front rows. Applauds on cue. Leads chants. Shouts down opposition speakers. Sets emotional tempo.
Shock troops. Supply physical security and plausible counter-demonstrators if hecklers organize. Visible enough to deter, not visible enough to provoke.
Placard carriers. Hold pre-made signs expressing pre-approved slogans. Visual narrative for press photography.
Messengers. Run between inside commando, outside commando, and political leadership. Real-time coordination.

A mass meeting is an engineered event. The side that fails to engineer it loses its narrative regardless of how strongly its position would have polled. The opposition that thinks attendance equals support has missed the engineering layer entirely.

06.5.7Speech-structure handles

DEF

Anaphora. Repetition at the start of successive clauses. We will fight, we will rebuild, we will not yield. Antithesis. Paired opposition. They built walls; we built bridges. Prolepsis. Anticipating the objection and answering it before it is raised. Litotes. Understatement by negation. No small thing. Preterition. Pretending to omit what you emphasize. I will not speak of the children.

Mechanical handles. Apply them consciously in prepared speech, in interview, in written communique. The trained speaker stacks two or three handles per minute; the untrained speaker leaves the audience without rhythmic anchors and the message dissipates.

06.5.8The truth-first rule and Inform/Influence

Guerrilla propaganda must be truthful because it must be believed, and it must be believed because the insurgent has no monopoly on broadcast. A single caught lie costs months of credibility. State propaganda can sustain falsehood through monopoly control of the channel; insurgent propaganda cannot. The truth-first rule is not ethics; it is operational survival.

FM 3-13 locks the doctrinal distinction. Inform activities transmit truth. They report facts, explain operations, build situational awareness. Influence activities change behavior. They persuade, motivate, deter, dissuade. The same message may do either or both. Legal and ethical rules differ — Inform operations carry lower restrictions on US-person reach; Influence operations carry higher restrictions and require explicit authority. Operate inside both rule sets explicitly; do not blur.

06.5.9Install, function, failure, feed-forward

Install the subsystem through the target-audience matrix. Write a distinct message for primary-interior, secondary-interior, primary-exterior, secondary-exterior. Match each message to channel. Build stories before slogans — stories survive retelling and amplification; slogans do not. Audit every cadre's behavior for consistency with the moral message, because witnesses retell what they observe. Train APT-equivalent units in your community; deploy in rotation; build connection through visible service.

The subsystem functions when your tactical acts reinforce your strategic narrative, when every cadre carries one or two simple stories that compound through retelling, when the four target audiences each receive a message tuned to their channel and concern, and when the truth-first rule holds across every communication.

It fails when the message and the behavior diverge — because the behavior is the message and the audience trusts behavior over claim. It fails when single-message-for-all dilutes resonance across the four quadrants. It fails when the truth-first rule is broken once, because the credibility cost compounds against future messages. It fails when the front-organization principle is abandoned and overt political work signals adversary intelligence.

PSYOP hands forward to 06.6 (the communications architecture that delivers the messages this section designed). uThe behavior is the message; the message is the behavior.u

theFIELD.run / CONSTRUCT_APPLICATIONS / 06 COMMAND / 06.6 Communications — PACE, radio, OPSEC
SECTION 06.6

Communications — PACE, radio, OPSEC

PACE plan. Primary, Alternate, Contingency, Emergency — four pre-designated channels ranked by preference. Extends beyond comms to routes, caches, water sources, meeting points.
Three radio bands. HF (3–30 MHz, ionospheric skywave, large antennas, inter-regional). VHF (30–300 MHz, line-of-sight + knife-edge diffraction, marine/aviation/public-safety workhorse). UHF (300 MHz–3 GHz, building penetration, short range).
Baofeng UV-5R coverage. VHF 136–174 MHz, UHF 400–470 MHz.
Repeater range multiplier. 5W UV-5R direct = ~ 2 km line-of-sight. Through repeater = ~ 80 km.
CTCSS / DCS. Subaudible tones that open receiver squelch only for matching signals. UV-5R menu 13 = T-CTCS (transmit), menu 11 = R-CTCS (receive).
US license bands. FRS (UHF, no license, low power, fixed antenna). GMRS (UHF, family license, higher power). MURS (VHF, no license, limited channels). Amateur HAM (HF/VHF/UHF, individual license, highest power and freedom).
Direction-finding. Triangulates transmitter position within minutes of sustained transmission. Keep transmissions short, irregular, mobile.
Procedure words. Roger (received), Wilco (will comply), Break (pause within), Out (end, no reply), Over (end, reply expected).
9-line CASEVAC. Pickup location, freq + call sign, patients by precedence, special equipment, patients by type, site security, marking method, nationality, NBC contamination.

Comms transmit the Decide step of OODA to the rest of the team. Without comms, decentralized command degrades to independent action. Base Line Training, Frequencies of Survival, Prepper Communications, and the amateur-radio texts supply the doctrine. FM 34-36 supplies the EW and OPSEC spine. The team that cannot communicate cannot coordinate, and the team that cannot coordinate is a collection of individuals.

This section installs the PACE plan as the universal communications architecture, the three-band radio spectrum with antenna-scaling rules, the licensed and unlicensed US bands, repeater architecture and CTCSS/DCS tones, the irreducible OPSEC reality of unencrypted voice and direction-finding vulnerability, procedure-word brevity discipline, the 9-line CASEVAC format, and the Task Unit Bruiser rooftop case as PACE-in-practice. Sources: Base Line Training; Frequencies of Survival; Prepper Communications; ARRL Operating Manual; FM 34-36; Willink/Babin Extreme Ownership.

06.6.1The PACE plan — four-channel ranked architecture

DEF

Primary. First-choice channel. Used for routine traffic. Alternate. Pre-agreed second channel. Activated when Primary fails. No discussion required. Contingency. Pre-agreed third channel. Activated when Alternate fails. Emergency. Last-resort channel. Often a physical rendezvous at a time and place rather than a radio frequency.

PACE extends beyond comms to routes (primary route, alternate, contingency, emergency exfil), food caches, water sources, meeting points. If you have not used your comms plan, you do not have a comms plan. Quarterly drill of the full PACE — including the emergency physical rendezvous — is the discipline.

06.6.2The three radio bands and antenna scaling

HF (3–30 MHz). Ionospheric skywave — long distance, depends on time-of-day, season, solar cycle. Antennas are large (tens of meters for half-wave dipoles). Inter-regional emergency-net band of choice.
VHF (30–300 MHz). Line-of-sight + some over-horizon knife-edge diffraction. Less absorbed by foliage and weather. Workhorse of marine, aviation, public safety. UV-5R covers 136–174 MHz.
UHF (300 MHz–3 GHz). Shorter wavelength, better building penetration, shorter propagation range. UV-5R covers 400–470 MHz.

Antenna length scales with wavelength. Longer waves demand long antennas; shorter waves fit a handheld whip. The Nagoya-style aftermarket whip on a UV-5R nearly doubles effective range over the stock antenna because the stock is a compromise too short for the band. Antenna upgrade is the single highest-ROI radio modification.

06.6.3US license bands — legal operation

FRS (Family Radio Service). UHF. No license. Low power (≤ 2 W). Fixed antenna. Channels 1–22.
GMRS (General Mobile Radio Service). UHF. Family license ($35, 10 years, covers immediate family). Higher power (up to 50 W base). External antenna allowed. Repeater channels.
MURS (Multi-Use Radio Service). VHF. No license. 5 channels, ≤ 2 W.
Amateur (HAM). HF/VHF/UHF. Individual license (Technician/General/Extra). Highest power (up to 1,500 W). Highest freedom — repeater building, emissions modes, frequency selection. The serious operator's band.

Operate inside the legal frame. Unauthorized operation invites enforcement action and burns the operational asset; the radio confiscated by the FCC does not transmit during the emergency.

06.6.4Repeaters multiply range

DEF

Repeater. Receives on one frequency, transmits on another, with high antenna elevation and high power. A 5-W UV-5R that reaches ~ 2 km line-of-sight to another UV-5R reaches ~ 80 km through a repeater because the repeater elevates the effective transmit point.

Repeaters are identified by output frequency, input offset (typically ± 5 MHz on UHF, ± 600 kHz on VHF), and CTCSS or DCS subaudible tone. Programming a repeater into the UV-5R requires entering the output frequency, the offset direction and magnitude, and the access tone. Pre-program every regional repeater into the UV-5R's 128 channel slots before deployment; do not attempt frequency entry under stress.

06.6.5CTCSS and DCS — sub-audible tone access

DEF

CTCSS (Continuous Tone-Coded Squelch System). Continuous sub-audible tone transmitted on top of voice carrier. Receiver squelch opens only for matching-tone signals. DCS (Digital-Coded Squelch). Digital code variant of CTCSS. Same function, different signaling.

On the UV-5R, menu item 13 sets transmit tone (T-CTCS); menu item 11 sets receive tone (R-CTCS). Two networks can share the same frequency without hearing each other, each operating on a distinct tone. Repeaters require the access tone to relay your transmission. Get the tone wrong, your transmission goes nowhere.

06.6.6The OPSEC reality — DF and interception

Unencrypted voice on an unlicensed or licensed band is interceptable by any competent SIGINT actor. Frequency-agility, brevity codes, and pre-arranged schedules mitigate; they do not eliminate. Direction-finding can triangulate a transmitter's physical position within minutes of sustained transmission. Treat every transmission as if the adversary heard it and located you while doing so.

You keep transmissions short. You keep transmissions irregular in timing. You move between transmissions where possible. You use the minimum power that achieves the link — high power burns through the air to the adversary's antennas as fast as it does to the friendly ones.

06.6.7Procedure words and net discipline

Procedure words shorten airtime and remove ambiguity. Roger = received. Wilco = will comply. Break = pause within transmission. Out = end of transmission, no reply expected. Over = end of transmission, reply expected. Never combine Over and Out; they contradict each other. Brevity codes add a second compression layer (e.g., Lima Charlie = loud and clear; Bravo Zulu = well done). Net discipline installs the structural frame — a Net Control Station (NCS), a schedule of check-ins, a PACE of frequencies, authentication per transmission.

06.6.8The 9-line CASEVAC format

Line 1. Pickup location (grid coordinate).
Line 2. Radio frequency and call sign of requester.
Line 3. Number of patients by precedence (Urgent, Priority, Routine).
Line 4. Special equipment required (hoist, jungle penetrator, ventilator).
Line 5. Number of patients by type (litter, ambulatory).
Line 6. Security at pickup site (no enemy / possible enemy / enemy in area / enemy in area, armed escort required).
Line 7. Method of marking pickup site (panels, smoke, IR strobe).
Line 8. Patient nationality and status (US military, US civilian, non-US military, non-US civilian, EPW).
Line 9. NBC contamination (Nuclear / Biological / Chemical, type if known).

Memorize the sequence. Practice in monthly drills. Pass the format under simulated stress. The Task Unit Bruiser hostage-rescue case illustrates PACE in live use — concrete walls absorbed radio inside the building; Babin sprinted to the rooftop, extended his antenna, made direct contact with the patrol, passed 9-line by building reference, and tanks rolled. The alternate channel was physical elevation.

06.6.9Install, function, failure, feed-forward

Install the subsystem through pre-operational discipline. Pre-program the UV-5R's 128 channel slots with a full regional plan — primary net, alternate net, NOAA weather, local repeaters, itinerant business frequencies, GMRS channels, MURS channels — named for fast access. Carry a Nagoya-style whip as spare. Rotate two batteries per radio; charge fully, store partially, avoid temperature extremes. Run the PACE quarterly with the full team, including the emergency physical rendezvous. Drill 9-line CASEVAC monthly.

The subsystem functions when every team member can execute the full PACE under stress, when 9-line passes cleanly under simulated overload, when net discipline holds without drift into open-mic chatter, and when transmission patterns avoid DF triangulation through brevity, irregularity, and movement.

It fails when the first problem is a dead battery (no rotation discipline), when a single unencrypted habit reveals position through DF (sustained transmission from fixed location), when net discipline collapses into open-mic chatter and bleeds OPSEC, when programming was not done before deployment and the operator is keying frequencies under fire, or when the team has never drilled the emergency physical rendezvous and discovers that nobody remembers the location.

Comms hand forward to 06.7 (leadership under fire — where the messages this section transmitted convert into team action). uIf you have not used your comms plan, you do not have a comms plan.u

theFIELD.run / CONSTRUCT_APPLICATIONS / 06 COMMAND / 06.7 Leadership under fire — the Willink laws
SECTION 06.7

Leadership under fire — the Willink laws

Extreme Ownership. The leader owns every failure. First word after failure begins with I, never with they.
Four Laws of Combat. Cover and Move; Simple; Prioritize and Execute; Decentralized Command.
Span-of-control cap. 6–10 direct reports cognitive maximum. 4–5 preferable for combat elements.
Believe. If the team does not believe the mission, they cannot execute it. Leader must understand and transmit the why.
Lead up the chain. Subordinate's duty to push situational awareness upward. Superior's "dumb questions" usually trace to subordinate's information-push failure.
Decisiveness amid uncertainty. No options are good options → choose the least-bad and commit. Indecision is worse than any available bad choice.
Dichotomy of Leadership. Every leadership trait pushed too far becomes its opposite vice. Continuous rebalancing.
Discipline = Freedom. Disciplined leader has the freedom to respond creatively because standard behaviors are automatic.

Leadership converts the Act step of OODA into team output. Willink's Four Laws of Combat, anchored by Extreme Ownership and balanced by The Dichotomy of Leadership, supply the doctrine proven across the Ramadi deployment. Modern Ninja Warfare supplies the complementary stealth-command frame. The team that operates without a leader is anarchy; the team led by ego is fragile; the team led by the Four Laws under Extreme Ownership executes coherently under conditions that paralyze less-disciplined units.

This section installs Extreme Ownership as the leader's first diagnostic move, the Four Laws of Combat as the operational doctrine, Believe as the motivational layer, Lead-Up-the-Chain as the subordinate leader's duty, Decisiveness amid Uncertainty as the common-case protocol, the Dichotomy of Leadership as continuous rebalancing, the Discipline-equals-Freedom paradox, and three Ramadi cases (Delta Charlie's humility, the MiTT lieutenant's patrol, the Building 94 fratricide-averted) as illustrations under load. Sources: Willink/Babin Extreme Ownership, The Dichotomy of Leadership, Leadership Strategy and Tactics; Modern Ninja Warfare.

06.7.1Extreme Ownership — the first diagnostic move

The leader owns every failure in the team's performance. No excuses, no blaming subordinates, no blaming the environment. Every failure traces to a leadership omission — a plan not made, a brief not given, a standard not enforced, a question not asked. The practical test: when something fails, does the first word out of the leader's mouth begin with I or with they.

Ego is the single most common obstacle. The leader's ego attributes failure to the team; Extreme Ownership attributes failure to the leader. Check the ego. Own the failure. Diagnose the leadership omission that allowed the failure. Correct it before the next operation. Subordinates trust leaders who own; they distrust leaders who blame.

06.7.2The Four Laws of Combat

Cover and Move. The most fundamental tactic — the only tactic Willink credits as irreducible. Teamwork as force multiplier. Two elements in coordination multiply effectiveness exponentially rather than doubling it.
Simple. Plans, orders, communications comprehensible by the lowest common denominator on the team. The brief is not a performance for the senior officer; it is a transfer of understanding to the junior operator. Simple plans degrade gracefully; complex plans fail catastrophically.
Prioritize and Execute. Name the highest-priority problem aloud. Commit the team's resources to it. Solve it. Name the next. Repeat. Target fixation on yesterday's priority is a failure mode equal to paralysis.
Decentralized Command. Cap cognitive span-of-control at 6–10 (4–5 for combat elements). Break larger teams into fire teams with designated leaders. Push decision authority down. Retain big-picture coordination at the top. The senior leader intervenes only where the fire-team leader's decision space is exceeded.

The Four Laws are not a menu. All four operate continuously. A team that runs three of four still loses on the missing one.

06.7.3Believe — the motivational layer

If the team does not believe in the mission, they cannot execute it. The leader must understand and transmit the why. When the why is not clear, the leader asks up the chain until it is, and only then briefs down. A subordinate who briefs a mission they do not believe in transmits disbelief along with the words; the team senses it; execution suffers. Believe is the precondition for execution under hardship.

06.7.4Lead Up the Chain — subordinate's duty to superior

The subordinate leader's duty to the superior is to push situational awareness upward. If the superior asks dumb questions, the likely cause is the subordinate's failure to push enough information. The superior is operating on the information they were given; expand the information set, and the questions improve. Build the relationship in peacetime so wartime asks are trusted. The superior who has not been informed cannot be expected to make informed decisions; the failure is the subordinate's omission.

06.7.5Decisiveness amid Uncertainty

DEF

The common case. No options are good options. The leader must choose the least-bad and commit. Indecision is almost always worse than any of the available bad choices, because indecision allows the situation to deteriorate while options remain unselected.

The 70-percent rule applies. With 70 percent of the information you would ideally have, decide and act. Waiting for 90 or 100 percent guarantees the decision arrives after the window closes. Decisiveness is not recklessness; it is the disciplined acceptance that perfect information is unavailable and that committed action on imperfect information beats hesitant inaction on the same information.

06.7.6The Dichotomy of Leadership — continuous rebalancing

Aggressive but not reckless.
Calm but not robotic.
Confident but not cocky.
Disciplined but not rigid.
Detail-oriented but not micromanaging.
Resolute but not stubborn.
Humble but not passive.

Every trait pushed too far becomes its opposite vice. The leader continuously rebalances. The detachment discipline of 06.2 is the cognitive move that allows rebalancing — without stepping back, the leader cannot see which pole they are drifting toward.

06.7.7Discipline equals Freedom

The disciplined leader has the freedom to respond creatively because the standard behaviors are automatic. Cognitive bandwidth that would have gone to managing routine actions is freed for the novel decisions that combat constantly demands. Discipline is not the opposite of freedom; discipline is the substrate on which freedom operates.

06.7.8Three Ramadi cases under load

Delta Charlie's humility. Willink's second-platoon commander, already a senior chief before commissioning, took out the trash in the platoon hut. That two-minute act signaled that he was of the platoon, not above it. Subordinates followed him willingly because he did not demand it. Rank is position, not person.

The MiTT lieutenant's patrol. The lieutenant planned a 2 km presence patrol across three battlespace owners. Willink pushed him to keep the first patrol short and inside a single battlespace. Twelve minutes after stepping off, the patrol was in a firefight. It was saved only because the plan had been kept Simple and supporting SEAL overwatch had direct radio. The complex plan would have failed catastrophically; the simple plan degraded gracefully.

Building 94 fratricide-averted. A Bradley crew reported enemy snipers at building 79. Willink forced verification by counting buildings from the intersection. The recount returned building 94 — his own men. Decentralized Command pushed the engagement decision down; the senior leader's strategic coordination caught the error invisible to the fire team. The verification protocol prevented a friendly-fire kill.

06.7.9Install, function, failure, feed-forward

Install the subsystem through drilled protocol. Run the post-operational debrief after every mission — what went right, what went wrong, what will we change — no blame, only learning. Brief to the lowest common denominator on the team. Stand back and let subordinates plan the details; the leader at altitude catches errors invisible to those in the weeds. Drill the Four Laws in training so they execute under fire. Practice the Dichotomy through deliberate self-observation.

The subsystem functions when the team acts coherently without the leader in the room (Decentralized Command works), when the leader's first word after failure begins with I (Extreme Ownership operates), when subordinates believe the mission (Believe transmits), when difficult decisions resolve into committed action rather than hand-wringing (Decisiveness holds), and when the Dichotomy stays in balance through continuous rebalancing.

It fails when ego substitutes for diagnosis, when briefs perform for the senior rather than transfer to the junior, when the leader is too far back to feel the fight or too far forward to coordinate it, when complex plans collapse under stress, when target fixation traps the team on yesterday's priority, or when the leader does not believe the mission and the team senses the disbelief.

Leadership hands forward to 06.8 (the team architecture that scales the Four Laws from fire team through task unit). uThe first word after failure is I.u

theFIELD.run / CONSTRUCT_APPLICATIONS / 06 COMMAND / 06.8 Team architecture and command structure
SECTION 06.8

Team architecture and command structure

Fire team 4–5 shooters · Squad 2–3 teams · Platoon 2 squads + HQ ≈ 16 · Task unit 2 platoons + command ≈ 35 · Span of control 6–10 max, 4–5 preferred · Command pair Commander's Intent + SOPs · Decision bounds left-and-right limits · Cell federation 3-cell branch, 3-branch region · Education Scharnhorst Militaerische Gesellschaft · Cycle plan → brief → execute → debrief

*Leadership produces coherent action; architecture scales the action. Extreme Ownership and Leadership Strategy and Tactics* supply the fire-team-through-task-unit stack. FM 31-21 supplies the clandestine cell architecture. The 4GW Handbook** supplies the Scharnhorst professional-education model that produced the Prussian general staff and with them Third Generation doctrine.

This section installs the conventional tier stack, the Commander's Intent / SOPs command pair, the left-and-right decision-authority rule, the battlefield-position dichotomy, the No Bad Teams, Only Bad Leaders diagnostic, the clandestine three-cell federation, the Scharnhorst continuous-education layer, and the operational cycle of plans, briefs, debriefs. Sources: Willink & Babin (Extreme Ownership, Leadership Strategy and Tactics, Dichotomy of Leadership), FM 31-21 Guerrilla Warfare, 4GW Handbook.

06.8.1The conventional tier stack

Four to five shooters per fire team. Two to three fire teams per squad. Two squads plus a headquarters element per platoon, approximately sixteen personnel. Two platoons plus command element per task unit, approximately thirty-five. Each tier has a designated leader in charge of the next-lower tier; each tier's leader reports to one leader above. The architecture exists because span-of-control and communications capacity are the actual constraints, not doctrinal elegance. Six to ten direct reports is the cognitive maximum; four to five is preferable for combat elements.

FIRE TEAM — 4–5 shooters, one team leader, single tactical task
SQUAD — 2–3 fire teams under a squad leader, coordinates fire and movement
PLATOON — 2 squads + HQ ≈ 16, platoon commander plus senior enlisted
TASK UNIT — 2 platoons + command ≈ 35, multi-element operation

Task Unit Bruiser's MOUT training at Fort Knox demonstrated the failure mode directly. Senior leaders initially tried to control every individual. The training collapsed under load. They were forced to break into four-to-five-person elements with designated fire-team leaders, and only then did the training become functional. Span of control is a law of cognition, not a preference.

06.8.2Commander's Intent paired with SOPs

Intent is the why — the purpose and end-state in one or two sentences. SOPs are the how — the standard operating procedures for common tactical tasks: how we clear a building, how we break contact, how we call a CASEVAC. Intent changes per mission. SOPs stay stable across missions and become the common reflex language of the unit. A fire-team leader who holds both acts without further direction; he knows the end-state, he knows the default procedures, he fills the gap between them with judgment.

DEF

COMMANDER'S INTENT — one- or two-sentence statement of purpose and end-state, sufficient for a subordinate two levels down to act coherently when communications fail and the plan breaks.

The pair is the complete command transfer. Intent without SOPs leaves subordinates improvising the basics under stress. SOPs without Intent leaves subordinates executing procedures against an obsolete objective. Both installed together permit Decentralized Command — the leadership doctrine of 04 — to actually operate.

06.8.3Left-and-right limits

Left-and-right limits bound the subordinate's decision authority across three zones: what he may decide alone, what he must check before deciding, what he may never decide. Ambiguity produces over-reach (subordinate acts where he should have escalated) and under-reach (subordinate waits where he should have acted). The leader writes the limits in advance for the predictable categories — weapons employment, engagement of non-combatants, cross-boundary movement, resource expenditure, coordination with unknown units — and makes the limits explicit.

Left-and-right limits and Commander's Intent are reciprocal. Intent expands the space of permissible action toward the objective; limits fence the space against catastrophic error. Together they create what the leader actually wants: subordinates who move aggressively within a bounded envelope and escalate only for what falls outside it.

06.8.4The battlefield position dichotomy

Aloof versus micromanaging is the senior leader's dichotomy. The right position is neither — it is adaptive, moving to where most needed.

The aloof leader is so far back that he has no feel for what his troops face. He appears to control but actually does not. The micromanaging leader is so far forward that he is sucked into every room-clearance and loses the altitude required for coordination. Willink's dichotomy framework specifies the calibration: the senior leader's position is a variable that must be managed consciously across the engagement. Forward when the decisive point demands presence. Back when the coordination problem demands altitude. The adaptive position is the skill.

06.8.5No Bad Teams, Only Bad Leaders

The diagnostic crystallizes the relationship between leader quality and team output. The same personnel under different leadership perform at radically different levels. Willink's BUD/S boat-crew rotation demonstrated the mechanism directly. The boat crew placed last across multiple evolutions was swapped at the leader position with the first-place crew's leader. The last-place crew became first. The first-place crew dropped but did not collapse — the personnel retained the performance standards their prior leader had installed.

WARN

When a sub-team is failing, first change its leader and observe. Do not re-organize the personnel, do not add training, do not rebrief the mission. Swap the leader. The diagnostic result arrives within one evolution.

06.8.6Guerrilla architecture — three-cell federation

FM 31-21 specifies the clandestine architecture that scales the three-person cell (installed in 06.5) without compromising operational security. Three cells form a branch under a branch leader who knows all three cell leaders but no cell non-leaders. Three branches form a regional element under a regional leader who knows the three branch leaders but no cell leaders. The structure federates upward in the same three-branching pattern.

Infiltration at any point exposes the immediate branch and no further. The architecture is slow — information travels through the hierarchy on a longer loop than a conventional chain of command — but it is survivable, which is the trade-off the guerrilla accepts. The SAR26 operator uses the same architecture for civilian coordination under sustained grid-down conditions when an unknown adversarial element may penetrate.

06.8.7The Scharnhorst continuous-education layer

Gerhard von Scharnhorst's Militaerische Gesellschaft was a voluntary officer study society that met weekly in late-eighteenth-century Prussia. Junior officers briefed each other on military history, terrain, tactical problems, and professional readings. Failures were analyzed without rank-blame. Innovation was rewarded. The society produced the institutional culture from which the Prussian general staff emerged, and through the general staff the command doctrine that became Third Generation Warfare.

The SAR26 operator runs the same institution at household or small-team scale. A weekly tactical-decision exercise — one realistic scenario, each member plans and briefs, the group debriefs without personal attack — builds the reflex library that no single mission can install. Continuous education compounds. Single missions do not.

06.8.8The operational cycle — plan, brief, execute, debrief

Mission analysis understands higher intent, states your own intent, identifies personnel, assets, resources, time. Decentralized planning empowers subordinates to develop the plan at their level. Course-of-action selection biases toward the simplest option that meets Intent. Contingency planning pre-identifies the likely failure modes and pre-maps responses so the team already knows what to do when failure occurs. Risk mitigation reduces downside. The brief transfers the plan to the lowest common denominator in language every participant understands. Execution runs the plan. The post-op debrief closes the loop: what worked, what failed, what changes into the SOP, what changes into the next plan.

The cycle is the unit's learning architecture. Units that plan and execute without debriefing accumulate the same errors. Units that debrief without planning produce war stories without mechanism. Units that run the full cycle compound.

06.8.9Install, function, failure mode, feed-forward

You install the subsystem through three operating rules. Rank is position, not person — Willink's Delta Charlie took out the trash to reinforce that the position commands, the man serves. Run a weekly tactical-decision exercise even on a team of three. Apply the no-bad-teams test — when a sub-team is failing, first change its leader and observe.

The subsystem functions when every tier can execute without the tier above in direct contact, when trust has been built in peacetime, and when u the Intent propagates two levels down intact u.

It fails when span-of-control is exceeded, when Intent is not transmitted, or when left-and-right limits are ambiguous. The telltale is a subordinate who is simultaneously over-reaching and under-reaching — acting where he should have escalated on one decision, waiting where he should have acted on another.

Team architecture feeds forward into 06.9. Architecture is the medium through which commands move; the strategic-infrastructure envelope is the space within which the whole architecture must operate. A command stack that is elegant but depends on grid-era communications collapses the moment the envelope contracts.

theFIELD.run / CONSTRUCT_APPLICATIONS / 06 COMMAND / 06.9 Strategic infrastructure targeting — blackout warfare
SECTION 06.9

Strategic infrastructure targeting — blackout warfare

Four vectors cyber · physical sabotage · NNEMP · HEMP · HEMP components E1 fast gamma pulse · E2 lightning-analog · E3 slow magnetohydrodynamic · Metcalf 2013 17 transformers, 19 minutes, weeks offline · Grid dependency 99% of CONUS military-base electricity sourced from civilian grid · EMP Commission estimate up to 90% population loss from 1-year nationwide blackout · Household envelope 72 hours · 30 days · 1 year · Capability vectors water · food · power · medical · Faraday sealed metal container, tested before reliance

*Command operates inside a strategic envelope. Peter Vincent Pry's Blackout Warfare* maps the envelope for the contemporary operator: a revolution in military affairs in which state and non-state adversaries combine cyber attack, physical sabotage of electric-grid substations, non-nuclear EMP, and high-altitude nuclear EMP into calculated sequences that blackout national grids as a first-strike weapon. The 4GW Handbook's** moral-strategic frame supplies the reason this matters — catastrophic infrastructure attack is the 4GW version of decapitation strike: anonymous, near-instant, requiring no force-on-force engagement.

This section installs the four-vector attack architecture, the cascading-failure amplification mechanism, the weather-synergy multiplier, the strategic consequence stack running from household to military base, and the household-scale grid-independence envelope protocol across 72 hours, 30 days, and one year. Sources: Pry (Blackout Warfare, The Power and the Light), 4GW Handbook, EMP Commission findings.

06.9.1The four-vector attack architecture

A competent planner combines vectors. Each vector attacks a different grid subsystem; combined application produces cross-catalyzed failure that any single vector could not produce alone.

CYBER — hacking, worms, logic bombs, SCADA penetration targeting the operational-technology networks controlling utilities; the SolarWinds pattern applied to electric sector
PHYSICAL SABOTAGE — small trained teams attacking a surprisingly small number of key substations and high-voltage transformers
NON-NUCLEAR EMP (NNEMP) — stealthy cruise missile, cheap drone, or man-portable form factor, localized but repeatable
HIGH-ALTITUDE NUCLEAR EMP (HEMP) — E1 fast gamma-induced pulse damaging semiconductors, E2 lightning-analog, E3 slow magnetohydrodynamic damage to long-line transformers

The vectors stack along an escalation ladder. Cyber is deniable and constant. Physical sabotage is localized and attributable. NNEMP is localized and difficult to attribute. HEMP is catastrophic and unambiguously state-level. A contemporary adversary plans the ladder before the first rung is climbed.

06.9.2Metcalf — the small-team proof of concept

Metcalf, California, April 2013. A small sniper team attacked Pacific Gas and Electric's Metcalf substation. Over nineteen minutes, seventeen transformers were damaged by rifle fire. The substation went offline for weeks. No attackers were apprehended. The attack was investigated by the FBI and found to have required reconnaissance, precise targeting of transformer cooling oil tanks, and pre-positioned egress.

Seventeen transformers. Nineteen minutes. Weeks offline. Small-team action against one unguarded high-voltage facility produces outsized grid impact — a demonstrated proof of concept, not a hypothetical.

The Metcalf lesson is architectural. High-voltage substation transformers are custom-manufactured, often imported, with replacement lead times measured in months to years. Small numbers are spare-held. Coordinated sabotage of a surprisingly small number of key substations — the exact number has been the subject of ongoing classified analysis — produces regional blackout lasting long enough to collapse secondary systems.

06.9.3Cascading failure — the amplification mechanism

An electric grid operating near full capacity sits on the edge of collapse normally. One substation failure overloads neighbors, which trip, which overload theirs, in a cascade propagating faster than human operators can respond. Small-scale sabotage yields regional-scale blackout. The mechanism is the same whether the initiating event is a squirrel, a cyber intrusion, a rifle round, or an EMP pulse.

DEF

CASCADING FAILURE — the propagation of grid collapse across interconnected substations in which each failed node forces load onto adjacent nodes, exceeding their rating and triggering their protective trip, accelerating faster than operator intervention can arrest.

Texas February 2021 demonstrated the mechanism without adversary action. A severe cold-weather event stressed ERCOT, cascading generator failures produced rolling blackouts, secondary water system failures compounded, and roughly two hundred deaths followed. The event required no attacker; ordinary weather running against an optimized-for-efficiency grid produced the cascade. An adversary targeting the same grid at the same moment would have multiplied the outcome.

06.9.4Weather synergy

Severe weather stresses the grid at the verge of operating capacity, lowers cybersecurity safeguards as utilities trade security for nimbleness during emergency response, strips neighboring states of mutual-aid resources, and masks deliberate damage as natural failure. A competent military planner attacks under weather. Hurricane season, ice storms, extreme heat waves — each compresses the envelope inside which the grid can absorb a deliberate shock.

Mumbai October 2020 illustrated the adversary-action version. Himalayan border tensions had escalated between India and China. During this window, an apparent cyber-intrusion produced a Mumbai blackout. Attribution was never formally confirmed, but the pattern — cyber intrusion timed to strategic tension, localized to a command city — matches the Blackout Warfare doctrine exactly.

06.9.5The strategic consequence stack

The consequences compound across scales. Ninety-nine percent of continental United States military base electricity comes from the civilian grid. A nationwide blackout paralyzes both civilian and military recovery simultaneously. The EMP Commission estimates up to ninety percent United States population loss from a one-year nationwide blackout. Even short-duration weather-induced blackouts of one to two days produce looting, curfew enforcement, refugee flow.

Protracted blackout compounds geometrically. Running water stops when electric pumps fail. Food storage fails when refrigeration dies. Fuel pumps die with grid power. Hospitals go dark when generator fuel exhausts. Social order fragments along pre-existing fracture lines. Psychological asymmetry amplifies further. Americans accept roughly fifty thousand auto deaths per year with equanimity; three thousand terrorist deaths produced two decades of continuous military engagement. A blackout attributable to foreign action is an order of magnitude more destabilizing than a weather-induced blackout of equal physical impact.

06.9.6The household grid-independence envelope

You run the audit across three time horizons. At seventy-two hours, enumerate what fails — refrigeration, heating or cooling, water pressure if on municipal pump, medical devices, cellular towers once battery backup exhausts. At thirty days, enumerate what additionally fails — municipal water treatment, fuel station pumps, supply-chain-dependent food, prescription medications not pre-positioned. At one year, the question becomes structural: does the household run independently or does it evacuate, and what is the plan for each case.

WARN

The grid is not permanent infrastructure. It is optimized-for-efficiency brittle architecture. A household that treats grid availability as a constant rather than a variable inherits the grid's failure modes without the grid's redundancy budget.

06.9.7Faraday protection for critical electronics

A metal ammo can lined with non-conductive material, properly sealed so the metal skin closes a continuous Faraday cage, protects contents against the E1 pulse of HEMP and against NNEMP. The critical items are a backup radio (handheld VHF/UHF per 06.6), a backup GPS or paper map and compass set, a backup AM radio for emergency alerts, and spare batteries. The cage is tested before reliance — a cell phone placed inside and called from outside should not ring. Untested Faraday protection is theatrical.

06.9.8Integration with 01, 02, 05

The 01 baseline (everyday carry, seventy-two-hour kit, thirty-day sustainment) hardens against the shortest envelope. The 02 baseline (medical, casualty care, evacuation) hardens against grid-loss health consequences. The 05 baseline (food production, water capture and disinfection, off-grid power, tool production) hardens against protracted envelopes measured in months to years. The 06.9 audit confirms that the baselines hold under the specific load case of deliberate grid attack, not only under the generic load case of natural disaster.

The audit is run once, reviewed annually, and re-run after any major household change — move, new family member, infrastructure upgrade or degradation, major acquisition or divestiture of capability.

06.9.9Install, function, failure mode, feed-forward

You install the subsystem through four operating protocols. Run the grid-independence audit across the three time horizons. Deploy Faraday protection for critical electronics and test it. Pre-position fuel, water, food, and medical per the 01 and 05 baselines explicitly hardened against blackout duration. Build a physical security plan for extended grid-down conditions per the 07 deployment matrix.

The subsystem functions when you read weather forecasts as potential attack indicators, when your household can run the four capability vectors — water, food, power, medical — through a thirty-day envelope without resupply, and when Faraday-protected comms are staged and tested.

It fails when the grid is treated as permanent infrastructure rather than optimized-for-efficiency brittle architecture, when the audit is run once and never reviewed, or when Faraday protection is assumed rather than tested.

Infrastructure targeting feeds forward into 06.10. The envelope defines the strategic space; integration binds the nine command subsystems into the closed loop that operates inside that space.

CLOSE

Close — from command to field deployment

You now hold a nine-section command stack running as a closed loop. Strategy foundations anchor the ends-ways-means test. OODA and detachment run the cognitive engine. The 4GW grid locates the contemporary terrain. The intelligence cycle feeds the Orient. PSYOP shapes the moral domain where wars are decided. Comms transmit the Decide through PACE across HF, VHF, and UHF. The Four Laws of Combat convert decision into team action. Team architecture scales action from fire team through task unit. Infrastructure targeting bounds the strategic envelope against cascading grid failure. Integration binds all nine into one command capacity that aggregates the individual capabilities from 00 through 05 into a collective capability coordinated across time and space.

06 completes the optimization layer of the RSI progression. 05 sustained the household across long-horizon infrastructure; 06 commands the household across contested time. Together they constitute the Optimization and Stabilization beat of the spine — how the operator and the team persist after the initial subsystems are installed and the acceleration compounding of 04 has started producing output. Below 06 there are individuals with skills. At 06 there is a unit with a mission. At 06 legitimacy is made or lost, because every command act is a moral-strategic statement.

Field Deployment installs next. Sub-module 07 takes the full 00-through-06 stack and indexes it into a condition-to-subsystem activation matrix. Observable field conditions — perceptual, environmental, adversarial, resource, physiological, temporal, command — index declarative if/then chains that call specific subsystems in calibrated sequence. The command stack you now hold becomes the set of protocols 07 activates when the condition class demands decision, information, communication, or team coordination. You out-cycle the adversary by running 06 continuously; you out-deploy the adversary by running 07 on top of 06 under live condition load. The optimization layer hands off to the deployment layer. The volume moves from building the system to running it.

theFIELD.run / CONSTRUCT_APPLICATIONS / 07 FIELD DEPLOYMENT / 07.1 The condition taxonomy — how the matrix classifies
SECTION 07.1

The condition taxonomy — how the matrix classifies

First-order classes 7 · Compound class 1 · Classes Perceptual · Environmental · Adversarial · Resource · Physiological · Temporal · Command · Severity bands BASELINE · WARNING · CRITICAL · Termination rule set resolution · degradation · scope exceeded · priority override · Primary sub-module draw each class indexes into specific 00-06 subsystems

**S**even first-order condition classes feed the matrix. Each class is a domain of observable reality with a primary sub-module draw. Classification is the first operator move — you name the class that is loudest, then the severity, then the chain.

This section installs the seven-class taxonomy, the three-band severity scale, the four termination rules that close every chain, and the classification-first discipline that converts ambient stimulus into declarative subsystem activation. Sources: the 00 Baseline stack, 06.4 intelligence cycle, 06.8 span-of-control architecture, and the 04 compound structures.

07.1.1The seven first-order classes

PERCEPTUAL — sign, sound, signature, indicatordraws from 00 in full, 02.8 tracking, 03.1 threat indexing
ENVIRONMENTAL — terrain, weather, light, seasondraws from 01.2 shelter, 02 navigation/mountaineering, 05.8 forest
ADVERSARIAL — threat signature, distance, intent, numbersdraws from 03 in full, 00.4, 06.3
RESOURCE — supply state, infrastructure integrity, comms posturedraws from 01, 05, 06.6 PACE, 06.9
PHYSIOLOGICAL — operator/team state, casualty presencedraws from 00.7, 01.6–01.8, 02.10, 04.E
TEMPORAL — duration horizon, engagement cadence, extraction windowdraws from 00.8, 02.5 Naismith, 05.10 three horizons
COMMAND — span of control, information environment, authority chaindraws from 06.7, 06.8, 00.7

The eighth class is compound — two or more first-order classes active at once — and routes to 07.9.

07.1.2Classification as the first operator move

A torn cobweb across a game trail is perceptual. A wind chill that takes exposed skin to frostbite threshold inside ten minutes is environmental. A stranger closing distance while asking a diversion question is adversarial. A cache disturbed since last access is resource. A teammate's resting heart rate ten beats above baseline is physiological. A sixty-minute engagement window that will not allow a seven-minute casualty extraction is temporal. A leader casualty on a dispersed team with no pre-briefed successor is command. Two or more present at the same decision point is compound.

Naming the class out loud — in a two- or three-person team — is the operational discipline. Naming replaces vague alarm with activated chain. A teammate who says "environmental WARNING" is commanding a specific subsystem response in three syllables.

07.1.3The three-band severity scale

DEF

BASELINE — condition present at background rate, chain runs at routine cadence without overriding other subsystems. WARNING — condition elevated, chain runs at compressed cadence, budget begins shifting from other subsystems. CRITICAL — condition at threat-to-mission or threat-to-life level, chain runs at maximum intensity and shortest cadence, commands budget from other subsystems.

A wind temperature below zero Celsius with operator in motion reads environmental WARNING. The same temperature with operator static over twenty minutes and shivering reads environmental CRITICAL. A surveillance hit on a single observer across two contexts reads adversarial BASELINE; three hits in twenty-four hours reads adversarial WARNING; active closure of the observer toward the operator reads adversarial CRITICAL. Severity bands drive calibration. The operator reads the band off the ground, not off the abstract threat.

07.1.4Termination rules — the four exits

Every chain closes on one of four exits. Resolution — the condition returns to baseline and the chain completes cleanly. Degradation — the named failure signature appears and the chain escalates, re-routes, or aborts. Scope exceeded — the condition moves outside the operator's capacity and the chain hands off to external aid or E&E. Priority override — a higher-class condition activates and commands budget away from the current chain.

WARN

No chain runs open-ended. Every activation carries its own exit. An open chain is a subsystem consuming budget without returning to the picture — the canonical failure signature of an undisciplined operator.

07.1.5Install, function, failure mode, feed-forward

You install the taxonomy through three habits. Name the class out loud before activating any chain. Name the severity band before calibrating the chain. Name the termination rule at the moment of activation, so the exit is pre-specified.

The subsystem functions when classification runs in under three seconds under normal load, when severity tracks ground truth rather than felt alarm, and when the termination rule fires cleanly on every chain.

It fails when the operator runs a chain without naming the class (vague response), when severity inflates under emotional load (every WARNING reads CRITICAL), or when termination rules are omitted (chains run until the operator is exhausted).

Taxonomy feeds forward into 07.2 through 07.8 — one section per first-order class, each populated with the chains the class activates.

SECTION 07.10

VOLUME_002 extension notes — where the next sources slot

Named gaps 4 primary · 9 extension classes · CBRN extends 07.2 / 07.3 / 07.6 · LOGISTICS extends 07.5 / 07.7 · COMSEC extends 07.5 / 07.8 · TEAM MEDICAL extends 07.6 / 07.8 · Integration rule VOLUME_002 composes above VOLUME_001, does not rewrite it · Binding VOLUME_002 sub-modules add to 01 / 05 / 06 by new section number (01.10 / 05.11 / 05.12 / 06.11)

**VOLUME_001 closes as a coherent matrix against the 157-source corpus. Four domain gaps sit explicitly named and unresolved. This section tags the condition classes and matrix entry points where VOLUME_002 extensions compose without disturbing VOLUME_001** integrity.

This section installs the four primary VOLUME_002 extension classes (CBRN, LOGISTICS, COMSEC, TEAM MEDICAL), the nine secondary extension sub-classes, the matrix-entry-point pre-routing that lets VOLUME_002 compose above rather than rewrite, and the binding rule for new sub-module numbers. Source: the 157-source corpus indexed against the integrated matrix.

07.10.1CBRN indicators — new condition class

CBRN INDICATORS as a VOLUME_002 condition class extends 07.2 Perceptual, 07.3 Environmental, and 07.6 Physiological. Perceptual entry points absorb chemical and biological plume signatures, radiation-meter readings (dosimetry), unusual animal mortality baseline shifts, and olfactory triggers beyond the 00.2 scope. Environmental entry points absorb hot-zone and warm-zone and cold-zone designation, wind-direction calculus for downwind avoidance, and decontamination corridor staging. Physiological entry points absorb toxidrome identification (cholinergic, opioid, anticholinergic, sympathomimetic, sedative-hypnotic), radiation-dose management, and mask-fit and air-filtration protocols.

Every existing chain in 07.9 that names a generic environmental hazard has an unresolved reference point for CBRN. VOLUME_002 sources (HAZMAT operator-level reference, civilian dosimetry and shelter-in-place doctrine, field-level mask and filter discipline) complete the reference.

07.10.2Logistics state — new condition class

LOGISTICS STATE as a VOLUME_002 condition class extends 07.5 Resource and 07.7 Temporal. Resource entry points absorb formal stock-flow-reserve accounting beyond the implicit FIFO of 05.2, audit cycles, and depletion-rate forecasting. Temporal entry points absorb multi-year horizon supply planning, seasonal re-balancing, and supply-chain degradation curves. Compound stacks in 07.9 gain cascading-depletion, contaminated-cache, lost-inventory-discovery, and intra-team allocation-conflict scenarios.

07.10.3COMSEC state — new condition class

COMSEC STATE as a VOLUME_002 condition class extends 07.5 Resource and 07.8 Command. Resource entry points absorb encryption-key state, device inventory, and secure-store state. Command entry points absorb information-environment classifications beyond permissive and denied (adversary-controlled digital infrastructure, surveillance-state baseline) and cryptographic reinforcement of cell compartmentation. Compound stacks gain key-compromise, DF-triangulation, platform-takedown, and metadata-correlation scenarios.

07.10.4Team medical architecture — new condition class

TEAM MEDICAL ARCHITECTURE as a VOLUME_002 condition class extends 07.6 Physiological and 07.8 Command. Physiological entry points absorb multi-casualty management with team-level medical command (medic, recorder, gatherer, runner), documentation discipline across casualties, and handoff protocols. Command entry points absorb medical-specific command structure within 06.8 architecture, pre-designated medic rotation, and training-cycle discipline for non-specialists. Compound stacks gain mass-casualty-plus-constrained-evacuation-plus-fatigued-responders-plus-hostile-environment scenarios.

07.10.5Secondary extension queue

Vehicle + maritime signcutting extends 07.2
Urban CCTV + facial-recognition + digital surveillance extends 07.2 / 07.8 / COMSEC
Night-vision + IR laser discipline extends 07.2 / 07.4
Legal + ROE + civilian Use-of-Force matrix extends 07.4 / 07.8
Pediatric + obstetric pharmacy extends 07.6
Technical SIGINT + ECM + EW detection extends 07.5 / COMSEC
Advanced rifle + reloading + precision long-range extends 07.4 beyond 300 m
Digital influence operations extends 07.8 / 07.5
Strategic leadership historical case material extends 07.8 at higher altitude

07.10.6Binding rule

Per operator sign-off, VOLUME_002 slots as extension, not rewrite. CBRN and logistics extend SUSTAINMENT (05) through new 05.11 and 05.12 sections and condition classes added to 07.3, 07.5, and 07.6. COMSEC extends COMMAND (06) through a new 06.11 section and condition classes added to 07.5 and 07.8. Team medicine extends PRIMARY SYSTEMS (01) through a new 01.10 section and condition classes added to 07.6 and 07.8.

When VOLUME_002 executes, each new sub-module extraction produces the new subsystem names the matrix calls by reference and the calibration thresholds that differentiate those subsystems from the placeholder references flagged here. VOLUME_001's matrix does not change. VOLUME_002's matrix entries compose above it.

07.10.7Install, function, failure mode, feed-forward

You install the extension discipline through the pre-routing map (every VOLUME_002 class knows its entry point before extraction begins), the composition-not-rewrite rule, and the binding-by-section-number that preserves VOLUME_001 integrity.

It functions when VOLUME_002 sources drop into named gaps without forcing restructure, when matrix entries compose rather than overwrite, and when the integrated system reads as one document across volumes.

It fails when VOLUME_002 is treated as rewrite, when new classes are bolted on without pre-routing, or when binding numbering collides with existing 07 references.

Extension feeds forward into the sub-module close — the matrix hands off to the operator as a running system.
